Philadelphia Overview

Philadelphia (city and county)
TypeConsolidated city-county; Pennsylvania's only "city of the first class"
Led byMayor Cherelle Parker (took office January 2024); Council President Kenyatta Johnson
EstablishedConsolidated 1854; current Home Rule Charter in effect since 1952
PopulationAbout 1.6 million (2020 Census: 1,603,797)
WorkforceNearly 29,000 city employees (September 2025, as reported)
BudgetFY2027 operating budget about $7.1 billion, adopted by Council in June 2026
Governing lawPhiladelphia Home Rule Charter; Pennsylvania law
Websitephila.gov

Philadelphia is both a city and a county, with one geographic footprint and, since 1854, one government. It is the largest city in Pennsylvania and the only one classified as a "city of the first class" under state law. Its government is organized by a locally written home rule charter, but it operates inside a state that retains broad authority over what the city may tax, regulate and spend. Understanding Philadelphia politics largely means keeping track of which of several overlapping bodies is responsible for a given problem.

1 City and county in one

Before 1854 the City of Philadelphia was a small municipality inside a much larger Philadelphia County that contained dozens of separate boroughs, townships and districts. The Act of Consolidation of that year merged them, so the city's boundaries became the county's boundaries (see City-County Consolidation). Today Pennsylvania's constitution provides that in Philadelphia the functions that elsewhere belong to a county government are performed by the city. A few offices that elsewhere would be county offices survive here as independently elected "row offices" (see Philadelphia Row Offices).

2 The main institutions

The government created by the Home Rule Charter has a strong-mayor design. The mayor is the chief executive, serves a four-year term and may serve two consecutive terms. The mayor appoints a cabinet (see Mayor's Cabinet and Offices) and a Managing Director who supervises most service departments. The City Council has 17 members: ten elected from districts and seven elected at large, with the charter reserving two of the at-large seats for candidates outside the majority party. Council writes ordinances, approves the budget and sets taxes within the authority the state grants.[1] For a department-by-department guide, see How Philadelphia Government Is Organized.

3 Bodies outside City Hall's chain of command

Several important institutions are not run by the mayor. The independently elected City Controller, District Attorney, Sheriff, City Commissioners and Register of Wills answer to voters. The courts of the First Judicial District are part of Pennsylvania's unified state judiciary. Authorities such as SEPTA, the Philadelphia Housing Authority and the Philadelphia Parking Authority were created under state law and have their own boards. The School District of Philadelphia is governed by a Board of Education appointed by the mayor, and the state has also constrained local finances through PICA.

4 Money

The fiscal year runs July 1 to June 30. In June 2026 Council approved a fiscal year 2027 operating budget of about $7.1 billion; it rejected several of the mayor's proposed new taxes (rideshare, hotel and short-term rental, and retail delivery), which did not reach the nine votes needed, and added a use-and-occupancy tax on cell towers.[2] The wage tax remained 3.74 percent for residents and 3.43 percent for non-residents. Philadelphia's taxing power rests on state enabling legislation (see Philadelphia Taxes and Philadelphia City Budget Process).

5 Where to take a problem

For routine service requests, residents can use Philly311. For land use, zoning and neighborhood questions, the first call is often the district Council member's office (see Councilmanic Prerogative). For voting, the City Commissioners; for court and eviction matters, the courts; for transit, SEPTA. Questions about whether a government decision was lawful or ethical may reach the Board of Ethics or the Inspector General. This wiki is general civic education, not legal advice.

See also: How Philadelphia Government Is Organized, Philadelphia Political History, Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia, Glossary.

Philadelphia Home Rule Charter

Philadelphia Home Rule Charter
TypeMunicipal constitution of the City of Philadelphia
ApprovedBy voters, April 17, 1951; in force from January 1952
Governing lawPennsylvania Constitution (home rule); First Class City Home Rule Act (1949)
ReplacedThe 1885 Bullitt Bill framework of city government
Amended byVoter-approved ballot questions, many since 1951
Websitephila.gov (Charter text); Philadelphia Code

The Philadelphia Home Rule Charter is the city's governing document, adopted by voters in 1951 as part of a mid-century "good government" reform movement aimed at ending patronage and machine control. It sets the structure of the executive branch and City Council, creates the independent offices and commissions, and sets rules for the budget, civil service and ethics. The 1951 Charter is still in force, though amended many times.[1]

1 Background

For much of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, Philadelphia was governed under state-written legislation and dominated by a Republican organization. Reformers, including future mayors Joseph Clark and Richardson Dilworth, who won citywide office in 1949 as Democrats, campaigned against that arrangement. Pennsylvania voters approved a constitutional home rule amendment in 1922, and the legislature passed the First Class City Home Rule Act in 1949, allowing Philadelphia to draft its own charter. A charter commission produced the document, and voters approved it on April 17, 1951. It took effect with the new administration in January 1952.[2] The reform tradition also produced the Civil Service Commission and professionalized departments. For earlier context see Philadelphia Political History.

2 What the Charter establishes

The Charter creates a strong-mayor system. The mayor serves four-year terms and is limited to two consecutive terms; the mayor appoints most department heads. The Charter creates the position of Managing Director, the Finance Director and the City Solicitor (head of the Law Department); the Chief Administrative Officer sits alongside these in the mayor's team. It sets Council at 17 members, ten district and seven at large, and a rule that no voter may vote for more than five at-large candidates, so that a majority party can win at most five of the seven at-large seats and minority parties can win the other two. It names the elected row offices, requires an annual operating and capital budget (see Philadelphia City Budget Process), and provides for the Board of Ethics; the Inspector General is a related oversight office. It also contains the "resign-to-run" rule, which requires city officials to resign before running for another office.[3]

3 Amending the Charter

Charter changes require voter approval. Council typically places amendments on the ballot by ordinance. Dozens of amendments have added departments and duties over the decades, creating a document that Pew has described as long and prescriptive.[4] The resign-to-run rule has been the subject of repeated ballot-question debates, including in 2007 and 2014, according to WHYY coverage. In spring 2026, a Council committee removed a new resign-to-run proposal from the May ballot, according to press reports. See Ballot Questions and Charter Changes.

4 Limits on home rule

Home rule in Pennsylvania is not a grant of unlimited local power. The city may act on municipal matters unless the Constitution or an act of the General Assembly says otherwise. The state has repeatedly been held to preempt local laws on subjects such as firearms, and Philadelphia may impose only taxes the legislature has authorized. See Home Rule Limits and State Preemption and Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia.

5 Criticism and reform debates

Supporters credit the Charter with ending patronage-era corruption and providing stability. Critics, including some civic groups, argue that it has accumulated outdated detail, that Council's informal land-use customs sit awkwardly with it (see Councilmanic Prerogative), and that its structure divides accountability among the mayor, Council and independent offices. Proposals to convene a new charter review commission have been raised periodically.

See also: City-County Consolidation, How Philadelphia Government Is Organized, Philadelphia Overview.

  2. Billy Penn, "How Philly works: a look at the city's governance," December 1, 2025; City Cast Philly, charter explainer.
  3. Philadelphia Home Rule Charter, as codified in the Philadelphia Code (phila.gov).

City-County Consolidation

City-County Consolidation
TypeState statute merging a city with its surrounding county
EnactedFebruary 2, 1854 (Pennsylvania General Assembly)
EffectCity boundaries expanded to match Philadelphia County
Later changeCounty offices folded into city government under the 1951 Home Rule Charter and related constitutional amendments
Surviving legacyElected "row offices"; Philadelphia is one of the few places where city and county are identical

City-County Consolidation refers to the 1854 act of the Pennsylvania legislature that merged the old City of Philadelphia, then a small area between the Delaware and Schuylkill rivers, with every other municipality in Philadelphia County. The result was a single city whose boundaries equal those of the county. It remains the defining fact of local government structure: there is no separate county government, and the city performs county functions.[1]

1 Before 1854

In the early nineteenth century the chartered city was only a few square miles. Around it in Philadelphia County sat independent districts, boroughs and townships, including Northern Liberties, Spring Garden, Southwark, Moyamensing, Kensington, and West Philadelphia, each with its own officials, police and services. Industrialization and population growth made the patchwork difficult to govern. Fire companies and gangs crossed jurisdictional lines, disorder was a recurrent problem (including the May 1844 anti-Catholic riots in Kensington), and reformers argued that a unified government would deliver better policing, water and infrastructure. These pressures drove the push for merger.[2]

2 The Act of Consolidation

The General Assembly passed the consolidation act, signed by Governor William Bigler on February 2, 1854. It extended the city's boundaries to the county line, abolished the separate municipal governments, and gave the enlarged city a single mayor and council structure with authority over services across the whole territory. The act absorbed the remaining townships, boroughs and districts of the county into the city. It was a state law rather than a local choice, a reminder that Pennsylvania's cities derive their powers from the commonwealth.

3 From two governments to one

For nearly a century after 1854 the city and county remained legally distinct entities, even though they covered the same territory. Each had its own officers: city government handled municipal services while the county had its own elected officials such as the sheriff, register of wills, and city commissioners. Reform advocates considered the duplication inefficient and a source of patronage. In 1951 Pennsylvania voters amended the state constitution to allow cities and counties to fully merge, and Philadelphia's Home Rule Charter, which took effect in January 1952, merged nearly all city and county institutions into one government, although some county row offices persisted as independently elected offices.

4 What survives today

Several former county offices remain as independently elected row offices: the City Controller, the District Attorney, the Sheriff, the City Commissioners and the Register of Wills and Clerk of Orphans' Court. The county courts of Philadelphia are state courts within the First Judicial District. Philadelphia's county-level functions, such as property assessment, elections and the courts' administration, are therefore split among city departments, row offices, and the state judiciary, a division that confuses many residents.

5 Why it matters

Consolidation means that city taxes fund services that elsewhere in Pennsylvania are split between municipalities and a county, and that a single set of voters elects both city and county officials. It also means that Philadelphia's mayor is the closest equivalent to both a mayor and a county executive. Comparisons with other consolidations, such as those in Denver, Nashville and Louisville, are common in academic literature.

See also: Philadelphia Overview, How Philadelphia Government Is Organized, Philadelphia Political History, Council Districts and Wards.

  2. Philadelphia Encyclopedia (philadelphiaencyclopedia.org), entries on Consolidation of 1854 and Kensington riots.
  3. Pew Charitable Trusts, "Philadelphia's Guiding Document at 75" (March 2026).

How Philadelphia Government Is Organized

Philadelphia government at a glance
FormStrong mayor, 17-member Council
Chief executiveMayor Cherelle Parker (since January 2024)
LegislatureCity Council: 10 district and 7 at-large members
Independent elected officesCity Controller, District Attorney, Sheriff, City Commissioners, Register of Wills
WorkforceRoughly 29,000 employees (as reported)
Fiscal yearJuly 1 to June 30

Philadelphia's government is best understood as several systems operating side by side: the mayor's departments, the legislature, independently elected officials, the state-run court system, state-created authorities, and layers of state and federal law. This article is a map for the rest of the wiki.

1 The executive branch

The mayor heads the executive branch and appoints most department heads. Day-to-day operations of many line departments are overseen by the Managing Director, a position that changed hands in July 2026 when Adam Thiel's departure and the naming of Carlton Williams as his successor were announced.[1] Central support functions include the Finance Department, the Law Department, the Office of Human Resources, Procurement, and the Chief Administrative Officer. The full list is in Mayor's Cabinet and Offices. Service departments include public safety (Police, Fire, Prisons), health and human services (Public Health, Human Services), and land and infrastructure (Licenses and Inspections, Streets, Water, Parks and Recreation).

2 The legislative branch

City Council passes ordinances, approves the operating and capital budgets, and conducts oversight hearings. Its leadership and procedures are described in Council Committees and the Legislative Process. Council can override a mayoral veto by a two-thirds vote. In practice, district members also exercise informal control over land-use decisions in their districts (see Councilmanic Prerogative).

The annual budget shows how the pieces fit together. The fiscal year runs from July 1 to June 30. In March the mayor presents a proposed budget to Council in a budget address; for fiscal year 2027, Mayor Cherelle Parker proposed a $6.97 billion budget on March 12, 2026. Council holds hearings with each department and elected office and then votes, and for FY2027 Council approved the operating and capital budgets on June 11, 2026.[4] The School District has its own separate budget, adopted by the Board of Education (see Philadelphia Board of Education). More detail is in Philadelphia City Budget Process.

Philadelphia is both a city and a county. Since the 1854 consolidation, one government has performed both roles, and the 1951 Home Rule Charter, effective in January 1952, folded most county functions into city government while leaving several county offices as independently elected row offices (see City-County Consolidation). Residents therefore deal with four layers at once: the city, the commonwealth, the federal government and independent bodies such as the School District and state-created authorities.

3 Elected row offices

Five offices are elected separately and are not under the mayor's control: the Controller (auditor), the District Attorney (prosecutor), the Sheriff, the City Commissioners (who administer elections), and the Register of Wills. See Philadelphia Row Offices. The personnel system is policed by the Civil Service Commission.

4 Boards, commissions and authorities

Dozens of boards advise or regulate. Land-use examples include the City Planning Commission, the Zoning Board of Adjustment, and the Historical Commission. Ethics and oversight are handled by the Board of Ethics and the Inspector General. Independent public authorities created under state law, with their own boards and budgets, include SEPTA, the Philadelphia Housing Authority, the Redevelopment Authority, and the Parking Authority. The mayor typically appoints some or all board members, but the bodies are legally distinct from city departments.

5 Courts, state and federal layers

Philadelphia's trial courts, the Court of Common Pleas and Municipal Court, form the First Judicial District and are part of Pennsylvania's state judiciary; judges are elected (see Court of Common Pleas and Municipal Court). The commonwealth shapes city powers through preemption, taxing authority and oversight bodies like PICA (see Home Rule Limits and State Preemption and Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia). Federal grants, courts and law enforcement are covered in Federal Government and Philadelphia.

See also: Philadelphia Overview, Philadelphia Home Rule Charter, City-County Consolidation, Index.

Mayor of Philadelphia

Mayor of Philadelphia
TypeElected chief executive of the City and County of Philadelphia
Led byCherelle L. Parker (Democrat), took office January 2024
TermFour years; limited to two consecutive terms
Governing lawPhiladelphia Home Rule Charter
OfficeCity Hall, Room 215
Websitephila.gov/departments/mayor

The Mayor of Philadelphia is the chief executive officer of a city of about 1.6 million people and of the county government that the city absorbed in 1854. Cherelle Parker, a former state representative and Council member, took office on January 1, 2024 as the 100th mayor and the first woman elected to the post. The mayor presides over a workforce of roughly 29,000 employees, as reported, and proposes the annual budget, but shares power with an independent City Council and several elected officials.[1]

1 Election and term limits

The mayor is elected in odd-numbered years before the presidential cycle, in November, after a party primary in May. Because Philadelphia has long had a Democratic voter-registration majority, the Democratic primary is usually decisive (see Elections in Philadelphia). The Charter limits mayors to two consecutive four-year terms; a former mayor can run again after sitting out a term. The mayor is the only city official subject to a term limit. A "resign-to-run" rule requires Council members and other city officials to resign before running for mayor.[2] See Mayors of Philadelphia Timeline.

2 Powers

The Charter vests executive power in the mayor. Key powers include:

  • Appointment: the mayor appoints the Managing Director, the Finance Director, the City Solicitor and most department heads, plus members of many boards (see Mayor's Cabinet and Offices). Civil service positions are filled through the merit system (see Civil Service Commission).
  • Budget: the mayor submits the operating and capital budgets and a five-year plan to Council in March (see Philadelphia City Budget Process). For FY2027, Parker proposed a $6.97 billion budget in March 2026, and Council approved the FY2027 operating and capital budgets on June 11, 2026.[3]
  • Veto and signature: the mayor signs or vetoes ordinances; Council can override a veto with a two-thirds vote (12 of 17).
  • Executive orders and collective bargaining: the administration negotiates with city unions (see Public Sector Bargaining in Pennsylvania) and issues executive orders directing departments.
  • Emergency authority: the mayor can declare a disaster emergency, coordinated through the Office of Emergency Management.

3 Relationship with Council

The mayor cannot spend money Council has not appropriated and cannot raise taxes alone. Council sets tax rates by ordinance, often within authority granted by the state. Tensions arise over land use, where district Council members hold informal control (see Councilmanic Prerogative), and over taxes: in spring 2026 Council members clashed publicly with the mayor and the School District over school closures and a proposed $1-per-ride tax on ride-hailing services, according to the Inquirer and Billy Penn.

4 Limits on the office

The mayor does not control the independently elected row offices, the courts, or state-created authorities such as SEPTA. Pennsylvania law limits what the city may tax or regulate (see Home Rule Limits and State Preemption), and the PICA oversight board reviews five-year plans. The mayor appoints members of the Board of Education but does not directly run the school district.

5 The Parker administration

Parker's agenda has emphasized public safety, housing, and neighborhood cleanliness under the label "One Philly." Her FY2027 budget was titled "One Philly, One Future." Managing Director Adam Thiel's departure and the naming of Carlton Williams as his successor were announced on July 28, 2026, according to local reports. Her administration has also dealt with federal funding and immigration pressures (see Federal Government and Philadelphia).

See also: Philadelphia Home Rule Charter, Philadelphia Political History, How Philadelphia Government Is Organized.

Managing Director's Office

Managing Director's Office
TypeCity executive office (Home Rule Charter)
Led byManaging Director, appointed by the mayor. Adam Thiel (January 2024 to mid-2026); Carlton Williams named successor on July 28, 2026
Reports toMayor of Philadelphia
Websitephila.gov/departments/managing-directors-office

The Managing Director's Office (MDO) is the part of the executive branch that runs the city's operating departments on the mayor's behalf. The Home Rule Charter created the Managing Director as the mayor's principal administrator, so that the elected mayor can focus on policy and politics while a professional manager oversees day-to-day delivery. The office coordinates agencies that deliver most of the services residents encounter.[1]

1 Role and legal basis

Under the Charter the Managing Director supervises the departments and agencies in the managing director's portfolio, coordinates their budgets and performance with the Finance Director and the mayor, and acts as the chief operating executive for the city. The Managing Director is appointed by the mayor and serves at the mayor's pleasure. The position is distinct from the Chief Administrative Officer, who leads internal administrative functions such as technology, fleet and human resources, and from the Finance Director, who oversees the budget and revenue (see Finance Department).

2 Departments supervised

As reported by the Inquirer in 2026, the portfolio includes health agencies, homeless services, the Streets Department, parks and libraries, prisons and the fire department. In practice that covers units such as the Fire Department, Department of Prisons, Streets Department, Parks and Recreation, Free Library, Public Health, Human Services, Homeless Services, Emergency Management and the Office of Violence Prevention. Exact reporting lines change with reorganizations; the official organization chart on phila.gov is the authority. The Police Commissioner, the City Solicitor and some other officers report more directly to the mayor, and the Police Department is covered separately.

3 Leadership

Adam Thiel, previously Fire Commissioner and head of the Office of Emergency Management, became Managing Director when Mayor Cherelle Parker took office in January 2024. On July 28, 2026 the mayor announced that Thiel was leaving for a job in the private sector after about two and a half years and that Carlton Williams would succeed him; the Inquirer described Williams as having risen from leading the Department of Licenses and Inspections to the managing director's post.[2] The change was part of a broader cabinet shuffle reported by WHYY. Residents should check phila.gov for the current leadership page.

The July 2026 change came as part of a wider shuffle of senior appointees, and the Inquirer reported in August 2026 that Mayor Parker had seen higher turnover among her top appointees than her recent predecessors had. Turnover at the managing director level matters to residents because the office sets priorities across many service departments at once. Because the Managing Director serves at the mayor's pleasure, accountability runs through the mayor, the budget process and public oversight such as Council hearings and the City Controller's audits.

4 Working with residents

Most residents interact with the office indirectly, through Philly311 and individual departments. The MDO also coordinates cross-agency efforts, such as responses to encampments, neighborhood cleanups and major events, and manages city boards and commissions that sit under its portfolio. Complaints about a service are usually best directed to the relevant department or, for follow-up, to the district Council member's office.

See also: Mayor's Cabinet and Offices, Mayor of Philadelphia, How Philadelphia Government Is Organized.

Mayor's Cabinet and Offices

Mayor's Cabinet and Offices
TypeExecutive-branch leadership team
Led byMayor Cherelle Parker
Appointed byThe mayor (department heads generally serve at the mayor's pleasure)
Governing lawHome Rule Charter; Philadelphia Code; executive orders
Websitephila.gov/departments (current roster)

The Mayor's Cabinet and Offices are the senior officials who carry out the mayor's policies. Unlike many state governments, Philadelphia has no single statute listing every cabinet post; the Charter names a few core officers, and the rest of the structure comes from the Philadelphia Code and from executive orders that mayors adopt and revise. Rosters change often, so readers should check phila.gov for current names.[1]

1 Charter-created posts

The Home Rule Charter establishes the Managing Director, the Finance Director (see Finance Department), the City Solicitor (see Law Department), and the City Representative role, among others, and sets up departments for services such as police, fire, public health, streets and licenses. The mayor appoints each of these officials. The Chief Administrative Officer oversees administrative support units. A Chief of Staff and policy advisers work directly in the mayor's office.

2 Operating departments

Departments are grouped by function. Public safety includes the Police Department and Fire Department. Health and human services include Public Health, Human Services and Behavioral Health and Intellectual disAbility Services. Infrastructure and land use include Streets, Water, Licenses and Inspections, and Planning and Development. Support functions include Procurement, Human Resources, Innovation and Technology, and Revenue. Many departments are overseen by the Managing Director; the Police Commissioner and some other heads report closer to the mayor.

3 Mayoral offices

Alongside departments, mayors create offices by executive order to advance priorities, usually housed within the Managing Director's or mayor's portfolio. Examples relevant to this wiki include the Office of Immigrant Affairs, Office of LGBT Affairs, Office for People with Disabilities, Office of Sustainability, Office of Violence Prevention and Office of Worker Protections. Executive orders can be amended or revoked by the next mayor, so these offices are less permanent than Charter departments, though some have since been written into the Code by Council. Council has also created some offices by ordinance, which a mayor cannot unilaterally eliminate.

4 Boards and the civil service

Mayors appoint members to many boards and commissions, such as the Board of Education, the Civil Service Commission (through a nominating panel), the Historical Commission and the Zoning Board of Adjustment. Most non-cabinet city employees are covered by the merit system or collective bargaining agreements, which limits direct political control over their jobs.

Two features of the structure are worth keeping in mind. First, the cabinet is not the whole executive branch: the elected row offices, the Civil Service Commission and state-created authorities such as SEPTA sit outside the mayor's chain of command even when the mayor appoints some of their board members. Second, because the mayor can reorganize by executive order, the same function may sit under different offices in different administrations, so a resident looking for help is often better served by calling Philly311 or checking the current department directory at phila.gov than by relying on an older organization chart. For the Managing Director's portfolio, see Managing Director's Office.

5 Changes and turnover

New mayors typically reshape the cabinet at the start of a term and again as appointees leave. On July 28, 2026, the administration announced that Managing Director Adam Thiel was leaving and that Carlton Williams would succeed him, part of a wider cabinet shuffle that WHYY reported also included a new city solicitor. The Inquirer reported in August 2026 that Mayor Parker has seen higher turnover among her top appointees than her recent predecessors.[2] Because departments can be merged or renamed (for example, the Office of Transportation, Infrastructure and Sustainability), the roster on phila.gov should be treated as authoritative.

See also: Mayor of Philadelphia, How Philadelphia Government Is Organized, Open Data and Transparency Tools.

Philadelphia City Council

Philadelphia City Council
TypeMunicipal legislature (City of Philadelphia)
Members17: 10 district, 7 at-large; four-year terms, no term limits
Led byPresident Kenyatta Johnson (since January 2024); Majority Leader Katherine Gilmore Richardson
Composition (2026)14 Democrats, 2 Working Families Party, 1 Republican (as reported)
MeetsCity Hall, Room 400; regular "stated meetings" most Thursdays while in session
Governing lawHome Rule Charter; Philadelphia Code
Websitephlcouncil.com

Philadelphia City Council is the legislative branch of the city and county government. It passes ordinances, adopts the annual operating and capital budgets, sets tax rates within the limits of state law, and oversees departments through hearings. Its 17 members are elected on a partisan basis in the municipal election cycle, in the same years as the mayor.[1]

1 Membership and elections

Ten members represent geographic districts (see Council Districts and Wards); seven are elected citywide. Under the Charter no voter may vote for more than five at-large candidates, so a single party can win at most five of the seven at-large seats and the other two go to minority-party candidates. The Working Families Party holds both of those seats as of 2026, and one Republican serves, according to Billy Penn.[2] Members serve four-year terms with no term limits, but under the "resign-to-run" rule must resign to run for another city or state office (see Ballot Questions and Charter Changes). Elections are run by the City Commissioners.

2 Leadership

Members elect a President at the start of each term. Kenyatta Johnson, who represents the 2nd District, has held the post since January 2024. The President appoints committee chairs, assigns bills and acts as the main legislative liaison to the mayor. Other leaders include Majority Leader Katherine Gilmore Richardson and Minority Leader Kendra Brooks of the Working Families Party. The Chief Clerk's office manages records and the legislative calendar. See Council Committees and the Legislative Process.

3 Powers

Council's main powers are lawmaking, the purse, and oversight. It can pass ordinances on any subject within the city's home rule authority, approve the budget (it approved the FY2027 operating and capital budgets on June 11, 2026), and override a mayoral veto with 12 votes. New taxes need a majority of the full Council, which is nine votes.[3] It reviews zoning and land transactions (see Philadelphia Zoning Code). It also holds hearings and can request testimony from city agencies.

4 Limits

Council cannot exceed the authority of the Charter and state law (see Home Rule Limits and State Preemption). It does not control the independently elected row offices and has no authority over state-created bodies such as SEPTA. Informal customs, especially councilmanic prerogative, shape how district members exercise power over land use. Ethics rules apply to members (see Board of Ethics), and members have been prosecuted in the past (see Political Corruption Cases in Philadelphia).

5 Reaching Council

Each member has a district or citywide office with constituent services staff, and Council posts meeting schedules, bill texts and hearing notices at phlcouncil.com. Residents may testify at committee hearings and stated meetings, typically by signing up in advance. Council meetings are open under the state's Sunshine Act (see Sunshine Act and Open Meetings).

See also: Philadelphia Home Rule Charter, Philadelphia City Budget Process, Democratic City Committee.

References

  2. Billy Penn, "How Philly works: a look at the city's governance," December 1, 2025; Wikipedia summary of Council composition and leadership (accessed 2026).
  3. Philadelphia City Council, "City Council approved the Fiscal Year 2027 operating and capital budgets on Thursday, June 11" (2026).

Council Committees and the Legislative Process

Council legislative process
TypeProcedure of the Philadelphia City Council
Led byCouncil President (Kenyatta Johnson); committee chairs
Votes to passMajority of members present with a quorum; 9 of 17 for new taxes
Veto overrideTwo-thirds (12 of 17)
Governing rulesHome Rule Charter; Council Rules; Sunshine Act
Websitephlcouncil.com (legislation search: phila.legistar.com)

The Philadelphia legislative process is the path that proposals take through City Council before they become binding ordinances. It is built around weekly meetings, standing committees that hold public hearings, and a requirement that bills be read and voted on in public.[1]

1 Types of legislation

Council acts through bills that become ordinances, which amend the Philadelphia Code and have the force of law; resolutions, which express opinions or authorize hearings and are not binding law; and charter amendments proposed for voters (see Ballot Questions and Charter Changes). Bills are numbered with a six-digit identifier that begins with the two-digit year of introduction.

2 Committees

The Council President appoints the chairs and members of standing committees at the start of each term. These cover subjects such as appropriations, finance, law and government, public safety, housing, transportation and utilities, rules, education, and licenses and inspections. Committee chairs control hearing schedules, so they strongly affect which bills move. Hearing notices appear on the Council calendar. The annual budget is examined in departmental hearings each spring (see Philadelphia City Budget Process), and bills that change zoning are heard in the committee that handles land use (see Philadelphia Zoning Code). Committee names and jurisdictions can change each term.

3 From introduction to passage

  1. Introduction: any member may introduce a bill at a stated meeting, often at the request of the mayor, an agency, or an advocacy group. The mayor's administration usually works through a sponsoring member.
  2. Referral: the President refers the bill to a committee.
  3. Hearing and amendment: the committee may hold a public hearing, take testimony from departments and the public, amend the bill, and vote it out. Many bills are held in committee indefinitely.
  4. First and final passage: a bill reported from committee is read and voted on at stated meetings; final passage requires a vote of the full Council.
  5. Mayoral action: the bill goes to the mayor.

Council generally meets on Thursdays during its session and takes a recess in summer, with returning sessions beginning in September. Bills affecting the Charter, taxes or land have additional requirements, including legal advertisement for zoning and the nine-vote minimum for taxes.[2]

4 Mayoral action

The mayor may sign a bill, let it become law without signature, or veto it within the time the Charter allows. Council can override a veto with a two-thirds vote, or 12 of 17 members. Vetoes are rare; Billy Penn reported in December 2025 that Mayor Parker had not yet issued one.

5 Participating

Hearings and meetings are open to the public under the Sunshine Act, and agendas are posted in advance. Residents can sign up to testify, submit written comments, and track bills through Council's legislative search tool. Members' district offices help constituents ask for hearings. Records are available under the Right-to-Know Law and the city's open data tools.

See also: Councilmanic Prerogative, Philadelphia Home Rule Charter, Safe and Healthy Homes Act.

References

  1. Philadelphia Home Rule Charter, legislative provisions; Philadelphia City Council (phlcouncil.com and Legistar).
  2. Philadelphia City Council, FY2027 budget approval release (June 2026), on the nine-vote requirement for new taxes.
  3. Billy Penn, "How Philly works: a look at the city's governance," December 1, 2025.

Councilmanic Prerogative

Councilmanic prerogative
TypeInformal legislative custom (not in the Charter or Code)
Applies toThe 10 district members of City Council
CoversZoning changes, sales of city-owned land, and many related land-use decisions in a member's district
Legal statusCourtesy among members; not binding law
Studied byPew Charitable Trusts (2015 report), news media, civic groups

Councilmanic prerogative is the Philadelphia custom under which the other members of City Council, and city agencies, defer to the district member on land-use decisions inside that member's district. The practice is not written into the Charter, but it is widely treated as an unofficial veto power.[1]

1 How it works

Ordinances require a Council vote, and Council members traditionally vote for or against a land-use bill according to the wishes of the district member. When a district member opposes a bill, colleagues generally vote no; when a district member sponsors one, they vote yes. Press and Pew accounts have found that Council has rarely overridden a district member in recent years.[2] Beyond the formal vote, executive agencies, including the Philadelphia Redevelopment Authority and the Land Bank, often seek the district member's approval before moving forward on a property.

2 Where it applies

Reported areas include rezoning bills and zoning-code amendments that change a lot's permitted uses (see Philadelphia Zoning Code), sales or transfers of publicly owned land (see Philadelphia Redevelopment Authority and Philadelphia Land Bank), designation of historic districts, and street changes such as bike lanes or parking rules. Members also influence which developers are chosen for city land and sometimes shape community benefit agreements. District members work with Registered Community Organizations, whose views they often weigh, but the final choice is theirs.

3 Arguments for

Supporters, often including Council members, say prerogative keeps decisions accountable to the officials closest to neighbors, who must face those voters at the next election. They argue it prevents citywide interests or well-funded developers from overriding residents' concerns, and that a district member knows block-level conditions better than a citywide body.

4 Arguments against

Critics say the custom concentrates decisions in one person, slows or blocks housing and development, and creates opportunities for favoritism, which is a particular concern because land decisions can be worth large sums of money. They argue that decisions should follow published criteria and the planning process rather than individual preference. Some opponents say it has contributed to unequal housing growth across districts. Prerogative itself is a legal custom, not a crime; for cases involving public officials, see Political Corruption Cases in Philadelphia.

5 Reform efforts

Reform ideas include formal criteria for land disposition, requiring written reasons for decisions, creating an independent land-disposition process, and giving the City Planning Commission a stronger role. Candidates for Council and mayor have debated whether to restrict the custom; WHYY has reported that it is unlikely to disappear soon, and the Inquirer reported in March 2025 on how prerogative intersects with the Parker administration's housing goals and the Land Bank. Any statutory change would be passed by the same Council whose members hold the prerogative. Residents who want to influence a land decision typically contact the district office, the local RCO, and the Department of Planning and Development.

See also: Council Districts and Wards, Council Committees and the Legislative Process, Tax Abatement and Development Incentives.

References

  1. Pew Charitable Trusts, "Philadelphia's Councilmanic Prerogative: How It Works and Why It Matters" (July 2015).
  2. WHYY News, "Why Philadelphia's councilmanic prerogative isn't going away"; Billy Penn, "Philly councilmanic prerogative, explained" (February 2024).
  3. Philadelphia Inquirer, "Parker, councilmanic prerogative, Land Bank, City Council, housing" (March 25, 2025).

Home Rule Limits and State Preemption

Home rule limits and state preemption
TypeLegal doctrine and state statutes limiting local power
Source of limitsPennsylvania Constitution; First Class City Home Rule Act; acts of the General Assembly
Key exampleFirearms preemption (18 Pa.C.S. 6120), upheld November 20, 2024
Taxing powerOnly taxes authorized by the General Assembly
Challenges decided byPennsylvania Commonwealth Court and Supreme Court

Home rule limits and state preemption describe the ways Pennsylvania law narrows what Philadelphia can do under its Home Rule Charter. The city may govern itself on local matters, but the General Assembly can override local ordinances by statute, and the courts enforce that hierarchy.[1]

1 The basic rule

Pennsylvania's Constitution lets home rule municipalities exercise any power not denied by the Constitution, their charter or the General Assembly. Philadelphia is governed by a special statute, the First Class City Home Rule Act of 1949, which lists powers the city cannot exercise without state authorization. In effect, a local ordinance is valid unless a state law forbids it or occupies the field. Courts distinguish between "express" preemption, where a statute says so, and "implied" or field preemption, where state law is so comprehensive that no room remains for local rules. Disputes are litigated in the Commonwealth Court, with appeals to the Pennsylvania Supreme Court.

2 Taxes

The city's tax power is the most important limit. Philadelphia may levy only taxes the legislature has authorized. Its wage and business taxes, for example, rest on enabling acts such as the 1932 Sterling Act, and the beverage tax Council adopted in 2016 was challenged as exceeding that authority; the state Supreme Court upheld it in 2018.[2] In March 2026 Mayor Cherelle Parker proposed a $1-per-ride tax on ride-hailing services to help fund the School District, according to CBS News. Whether the city can create a tax often depends on whether state law already covers the subject. See Philadelphia Taxes.

3 Firearms

State law bars municipalities from regulating the ownership, possession, transfer or transportation of firearms. Philadelphia has repeatedly tried to adopt stricter local gun laws and has been repeatedly stopped by the courts. On November 20, 2024, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled 6-0 in a suit brought by the city, relatives of gun violence victims and CeaseFirePA that the preemption laws stand, with Justice Kevin Brobson writing that there was nothing for the court to do absent a constitutional violation. The court said the remedy is for the legislature.[3]

4 Other fields

State law also sets or limits local action on landlord-tenant rules, minimum wage and paid leave in some respects, labor relations (see Public Sector Bargaining in Pennsylvania), school governance and funding (see School District of Philadelphia), alcohol and gaming, and authorities such as SEPTA and the Parking Authority. The legislature has also imposed financial oversight on the city through PICA. Where Philadelphia has acted, as with local worker-protection and housing laws, the extent of its authority can be contested in court.

5 Working within the limits

When it cannot legislate directly, the city lobbies Harrisburg through the mayor's intergovernmental office, uses executive orders, funds local programs, or sues. Council sometimes passes resolutions urging the state to act. The politics of preemption is partly partisan: Philadelphia is heavily Democratic, while the legislature has included Republican majorities in one or both chambers. See Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia.

See also: Law Department, Philadelphia Home Rule Charter, Federal Government and Philadelphia.

References

  1. Pennsylvania Constitution, Article IX; First Class City Home Rule Act (1949); Pennsylvania General Assembly (legis.state.pa.us).
  2. Pennsylvania Supreme Court decision upholding Philadelphia's beverage tax (2018), as reported by Philadelphia Inquirer and WHYY.
  3. WHYY News, "Philadelphia loses lawsuit that sought greater power for the city to regulate firearms" (November 2024); Pennsylvania Capital-Star, "Pennsylvania Supreme Court upholds state laws blocking local gun control."

Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia

State government and Philadelphia
TypeIntergovernmental relationship (commonwealth to municipality)
Key actorsGovernor Josh Shapiro; General Assembly; Pennsylvania Supreme Court; state agencies
FY2026-27 state budget$50.85 billion, signed July 12, 2026
Philadelphia school aidMore than $157 million in additional funds in the 2026-27 budget (as reported by the mayor's office)
Legal basisPennsylvania Constitution; statutes

The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania is the source of Philadelphia's legal powers and a major funder of its schools, transit, health and human services, and courts. The relationship is shaped by the fact that Philadelphia is a municipality created under state law, with a home rule charter that the state constitution and statutes bound (see Home Rule Limits and State Preemption).[1]

1 The General Assembly

Pennsylvania's House and Senate pass the laws that define Philadelphia's authority: tax enabling acts, preemption statutes, election law, landlord-tenant law, labor law and the creation of authorities. Philadelphia's members make up a significant bloc of the Democratic caucuses (see Philadelphia Congressional and State Delegation), but control of one or both chambers has often rested with Republicans representing other parts of the state. The legislature has at times used its power to override or constrain city policy, for example by preempting gun regulation, and in 2022 the state House impeached District Attorney Larry Krasner; the Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled in September 2024 that the articles of impeachment were null and void because the process could not carry over to a new legislative session.[2]

2 The governor and agencies

The governor, Josh Shapiro as of 2026, proposes the state budget and signs or vetoes bills. State agencies such as the Department of Education, Department of Human Services, Department of Health, Department of Environmental Protection and PennDOT regulate city programs and fund them. The Public Utility Commission regulates the Philadelphia Gas Works rates. State-run bodies such as the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission or the Department of State (which oversees election administration alongside the City Commissioners) also affect residents daily.

3 Money flows

Pennsylvania signed a $50.85 billion 2026-27 budget on July 12, 2026. Mayor Cherelle Parker's office said it delivered more than $157 million in additional funding for the School District of Philadelphia, and the budget moved some sales-tax revenue toward transit, though a permanent long-term funding fix for SEPTA was reported as unfinished.[3] The state also funds child welfare, Medicaid-related health services, courts, and capital projects. Philadelphia's own revenue depends on state authorization (see Philadelphia Taxes). Budget impasses in Harrisburg can delay money to schools and nonprofits.

4 Courts

Philadelphia's trial courts, the Court of Common Pleas and Municipal Court, are part of the Unified Judicial System of Pennsylvania, funded largely through the state and the city and supervised by the state Supreme Court (see First Judicial District). Appeals go to the Superior Court or Commonwealth Court and then to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court has also ruled on major disputes between the city and the legislature.

5 Oversight and friction

The legislature created PICA in 1991 to oversee city finances during a fiscal crisis, a function it retains while city bonds are outstanding. It appoints board majorities or sets structures for authorities, and it set the 2018 end of the School Reform Commission, after which the mayor began appointing the Board of Education. Tensions arise on guns, education funding, transit, and policing and prosecution. The city lobbies in Harrisburg and also relies on state partners in the delegation.

See also: Federal Government and Philadelphia, Philadelphia Home Rule Charter, Philadelphia District Attorney's Office.

  3. City of Philadelphia, "Statement of Mayor Cherelle L. Parker on passage of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania's 2026-2027 budget" (July 15, 2026); MyChesCo, "Pennsylvania enacts $50.85B budget, avoids tax hike."

Federal Government and Philadelphia

Federal government and Philadelphia
TypeIntergovernmental relationship (federal to municipality)
Federal courtsU.S. District Court, Eastern District of Pennsylvania; Third Circuit
Law enforcementU.S. Attorney's Office; FBI; ICE; others
Funding channelsGrants (e.g., housing, transportation, public health), Medicaid, education
Key disputeImmigration "sanctuary" policies and conditions on federal grants

The federal government affects Philadelphia through money, courts, law enforcement and regulation. Federal law is supreme over state and local law, and federal funding supports large parts of the city budget, but the city retains independent authority to decide how to use its own officers and resources. The relationship has been particularly contested over immigration enforcement.[1]

1 Funding

Federal dollars reach Philadelphia through block grants such as Community Development Block Grants, housing vouchers and public housing support, transit capital funds, Medicaid and public-health grants, education aid including Title I, and disaster relief. Much of this flows through state agencies or directly to city departments and authorities such as the Philadelphia Housing Authority, SEPTA and the School District. Because of that dependence, city budget planners treat federal policy shifts as a risk: for fiscal 2026, Mayor Cherelle Parker proposed a $95 million reserve in anticipation of possible federal funding cuts.[2] See Philadelphia City Budget Process.

2 Federal courts and prosecutors

Philadelphia sits in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, whose federal trial court hears civil rights, immigration-related, bankruptcy and criminal cases, with appeals to the Third Circuit in Philadelphia. The U.S. Attorney's Office prosecutes federal crimes and has brought public corruption cases against city and union officials (see Political Corruption Cases in Philadelphia). Federal courts also review local policing and jail conditions, as in long-running consent decrees and class actions affecting the Department of Prisons. Local prosecution is separate: the District Attorney handles state-law crimes.

3 Immigration and "sanctuary" policy

Philadelphia's policies limit city cooperation with federal civil immigration enforcement, and the city describes itself as a welcoming city (see Office of Immigrant Affairs). During President Trump's first term, the Justice Department sought to condition certain grants on cooperation; a federal judge sided with Philadelphia in 2018. In August 2025 the Justice Department published a list of 35 jurisdictions it described as sanctuary jurisdictions, according to CBS News. In June 2026 the Trump administration sued Philadelphia over its "ICE Out" law, according to the South Philly Review. On July 2, 2026, a federal judge ruled that Philadelphia could not enforce its ban on masking against federal immigration agents, as reported by WHYY and the Inquirer, and in August 2026 the Inquirer reported that the Justice Department was targeting another "ICE Out" ordinance.[3] As of October 2026 the litigation and related funding conditions were still developing; readers should consult current coverage. The legal arguments typically invoke the Tenth Amendment, which limits federal commandeering of local resources, against the federal government's authority over immigration.

4 Housing, transit and other agencies

Federal agencies such as HUD, the Department of Transportation, the Environmental Protection Agency and the Department of Education impose requirements on city programs as a condition of money. Federal civil rights law, the Fair Housing Act, and the Americans with Disabilities Act also apply to local government. Federal elections are administered locally by the City Commissioners under state and federal law. Members of Congress representing Philadelphia help the city advocate in Washington (see Philadelphia Congressional and State Delegation). Federal rules sit above, and sometimes override, both state and local law (see Home Rule Limits and State Preemption).

See also: Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia, Philadelphia Overview, Law Department.

Philadelphia Row Offices

Philadelphia row offices
TypeIndependently elected city-county offices
OfficesCity Controller; District Attorney; Sheriff; City Commissioners (3); Register of Wills and Clerk of Orphans' Court
TermFour years
OriginPre-1854 and pre-1951 county government
Accountable toVoters, not the mayor

Row offices are the elected offices in Philadelphia that exist outside the mayor's chain of command. The term comes from the practice of listing county offices in a row on the ballot or in county buildings. In Philadelphia, which consolidated city and county in 1854 (see City-County Consolidation), the remaining row offices are the City Controller, the District Attorney, the Sheriff, the City Commissioners and the Register of Wills.[1]

1 What makes an office a row office

Each row office has an independent electoral mandate. The officeholder is chosen by citywide vote in the municipal cycle, is not appointed or removable by the mayor, and hires and manages their own staff, though the budget is appropriated by City Council as part of the city budget. Some offices have duties assigned by state law (the Sheriff's court functions, the District Attorney's prosecutions), while others derive from the Home Rule Charter.

2 The five offices

  • City Controller: the city's independent auditor and a pre-audit check on payments. Christy Brady, elected in 2023 and re-elected in 2025.
  • District Attorney: prosecutes crimes in Philadelphia. Larry Krasner, elected in 2017 and re-elected in 2021 and 2025.
  • Sheriff: serves court papers, runs sheriff sales, transports prisoners and provides court security. Rochelle Bilal, elected in 2019 and re-elected in 2023.
  • City Commissioners: a three-member board that runs elections and voter registration. Omar Sabir (chair), Lisa Deeley, and Seth Bluestein as of 2026.
  • Register of Wills and Clerk of Orphans' Court: probates wills and issues marriage licenses. John Sabatina Jr., elected in 2023.

Other former county functions, such as recording deeds, are now handled by city departments (see Department of Records).

3 Elections and budgets

Row offices are on the ballot in off-year municipal elections, with the Controller and District Attorney elected in 2025 and the Sheriff, City Commissioners and Register of Wills in 2023 and 2027. Their budgets are part of the city's operating budget, appropriated by Council.[2] See Elections in Philadelphia and Philadelphia City Budget Process.

4 Accountability

Because row officers answer only to voters, oversight comes through elections, Council budget hearings, courts, the Board of Ethics and the Inspector General, and in some cases state and federal investigators. The Controller audits other row offices as well as city departments. In August 2026 a judge imposed six months of outside supervision over the Sheriff's Office's property auctions, and in October 2026 the Inquirer reported that the office had told the judge it found about $20 million in city money (see Philadelphia Sheriff's Office).

5 Reform debates

Civic groups have long debated whether some row offices should be elected at all. Arguments for appointment include professional management and clearer accountability to the mayor; arguments against include loss of independence, particularly for auditing and prosecution. Changing the structure of offices named in the Charter would require voter-approved amendments (see Ballot Questions and Charter Changes), while changes to duties set by state law would require the General Assembly.

See also: How Philadelphia Government Is Organized, Civil Service Commission, Philadelphia Overview.

City Controller

City Controller
TypeIndependently elected city-county row office (Home Rule Charter)
Led byChristy Brady (Democrat); acting Controller from November 2022; elected November 2023; re-elected November 2025
TermFour years
Address1230 Municipal Services Building, 1401 John F. Kennedy Blvd., Philadelphia, PA 19102
Phone / email(215) 686-6680; controller@phila.gov
Websitecontroller.phila.gov

The City Controller is Philadelphia's independent fiscal watchdog. Elected citywide, the Controller audits city departments, agencies and the School District, and reviews payments before they are made. Christy Brady, a longtime employee of the office, was appointed acting Controller by Mayor Jim Kenney on November 7, 2022, after Rebecca Rhynhart resigned. Brady resigned in February 2023 to run for the post under the Charter's resign-to-run rule, won the November 2023 election, and was re-elected in November 2025, defeating Republican Ari Patrinos, according to the Inquirer.[1]

1 Duties

Under the Home Rule Charter the Controller conducts financial, performance and compliance audits of city departments, offices and agencies, and prepares reports for the public and City Council. The office is one of the row offices, meaning it is not part of the mayor's administration. Its independence is intended to let it criticize the same administration whose contracts and payments it checks. Its work touches the Finance Department, which issues the payments the Controller reviews.

2 Pre-audit and payments

A Controller's best-known function is the pre-audit of city payments. Before the city's Finance Department pays contractors and vendors, the Controller's Pre-Audit Division checks that spending is lawful, properly authorized and supported. In its fiscal 2027 testimony to Council, the office reported identifying projects where taxpayer funds were spent on work that did not meet required standards. The pre-audit step gives the Controller leverage over procurement and contract compliance.

3 Audits and reports

The office publishes performance reviews of departments, annual departmental audits, and special reports on particular programs or issues. It has also agreed to conduct a performance audit of the School District of Philadelphia, which Council had requested in 2026.[2] Audits are published at controller.phila.gov. Audit findings are recommendations; the Controller cannot order a department to change, though reports can lead to press scrutiny, Council hearings and changes in practice. Departments may respond in writing and those responses are generally published.

4 Boards and independence

The Controller sits on city boards that oversee money, including the Board of Pensions and Retirement, the Gas Commission and the Sinking Fund Commission. The Controller's budget is set by Council as part of the city budget, which some observers note can be a pressure point for independence. The office is separate from the Inspector General, which investigates misconduct and waste in the executive branch, and the Board of Ethics, which enforces ethics and campaign finance rules. Controllers have run for higher office, and the Charter's resign-to-run rule applies; it was tested in January 2023 when Brady, then acting Controller, sued the city over the rule and a judge rejected her bid to avoid it, according to the Inquirer. She resigned in February 2023 and Mayor Kenney named Charles Edacheril as interim Controller.

5 Reporting fraud

Residents and city employees can report suspected waste, fraud or abuse through the office's fraud-reporting page at controller.phila.gov, by phone or email. Reports can be made confidentially. More serious criminal matters may be referred to the District Attorney or to federal prosecutors (see U.S. Attorney's Office).

See also: Philadelphia City Budget Process, Open Data and Transparency Tools, PICA.

Philadelphia District Attorney's Office

Philadelphia District Attorney's Office
TypeElected county prosecutor (row office under state law)
Led byLarry Krasner (Democrat), in office since January 2018; re-elected 2021 and 2025
TermFour years
2025 resultKrasner about 76 percent, Republican Pat Dugan about 24 percent (WHYY)
JurisdictionProsecution of state-law crimes in Philadelphia County
Websitephillyda.org

The Philadelphia District Attorney's Office is the agency that prosecutes crimes under Pennsylvania law in Philadelphia. The District Attorney is elected countywide and is independent of the mayor. Larry Krasner, a former criminal defense and civil rights attorney, first won the office in 2017, was re-elected in 2021, and was re-elected again in November 2025.[1]

1 Role and structure

The District Attorney decides whether to charge crimes, what to charge, whether to offer plea agreements, and whether to seek sentences, and represents the Commonwealth in the Court of Common Pleas and Municipal Court. Assistant district attorneys work in trial, charging, homicide, special investigations, appeals and other units. Police departments, chiefly the Philadelphia Police Department, investigate and bring cases to the office. The office is a row office funded through the city budget but not controlled by the mayor. Defendants unable to afford counsel are generally represented by the Defender Association.

2 Policies and units

Krasner ran as a "progressive prosecutor," pledging to reduce incarceration, stop prosecuting some low-level offenses, and examine police misconduct. The office created a Conviction Integrity Unit in 2018 which, according to press reports, has been credited with more than 35 exonerations. Reports in 2025 said two top officials in the unit had resigned amid legal scrutiny, and in September 2026 the Inquirer's editorial board commented on an investigation concerning wrongful-conviction work. Those matters are contested and ongoing; readers should consult current coverage. The office also maintains lists of officers with credibility issues, commonly called the "Brady list" after the Supreme Court decision requiring disclosure of exculpatory evidence.[2]

3 Impeachment and political conflict

In November 2022 the Republican-led Pennsylvania House voted to impeach Krasner, citing alleged failures to enforce the law and crime in Philadelphia. The Commonwealth Court ruled in December 2022 that the articles did not allege misbehavior in office, and on September 27, 2024 the Pennsylvania Supreme Court held the articles were null and void because the process could not continue into a new legislative session, with one dissent. The office issued a statement welcoming the ruling.[3] The dispute illustrates the state-city tension described in Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia.

4 Debate and criticism

Supporters say the office has focused resources on serious crime, corrected wrongful convictions and challenged abusive practices. Critics, including the police union (see Fraternal Order of Police Lodge 5), some elected officials and opponents, argue that its charging and plea policies have undermined public safety and morale. Both sides cite data on homicide, clearance and conviction rates, which are themselves debated. Federal and state judges have also commented in particular cases. Opinions on all of this differ; the wiki does not take a position.

5 Residents and the office

Crime victims and witnesses can contact the office's victim services unit. Residents can report concerns about police misconduct to the Citizens Police Oversight Commission and may request records under the Right-to-Know Law, subject to exemptions for criminal investigations. Pennsylvania's Attorney General and the U.S. Attorney's Office have overlapping jurisdiction in some cases.

See also: Police Accountability Systems, First Judicial District, Elections in Philadelphia.

  3. Pennsylvania Capital-Star and WHYY, reports on the Pennsylvania Supreme Court's September 2024 impeachment ruling; Philadelphia DA's Office statement.

Philadelphia Sheriff's Office

Philadelphia Sheriff's Office
TypeElected county row office; law enforcement and court-support agency
Led bySheriff Rochelle Bilal (Democrat)
TermFour years
BudgetSet by City Council as part of the annual city budget
StaffSee the annual city budget documents
Websitephillysheriff.com

The Philadelphia Sheriff's Office is the elected agency that provides security for the courts, transports prisoners, serves court orders and warrants, and conducts sheriff sales of real property. As in the rest of Pennsylvania the sheriff is a county officer; in Philadelphia, where county government merged into the city, the Sheriff is one of the independently elected row offices. Rochelle Bilal, a retired Philadelphia police officer, defeated the incumbent in the 2019 Democratic primary, took office on January 6, 2020 as the first woman to serve as Philadelphia Sheriff, and was re-elected in 2023.[1]

1 Responsibilities

Deputy sheriffs provide security in courtrooms and court buildings of the First Judicial District, transport people in custody between the city's jails and court, serve process such as summonses, eviction orders and protection orders, and execute certain warrants. They are separate from the Philadelphia Police Department. In landlord-tenant matters, a court order for possession is carried out by the Sheriff, which is why the office appears in discussions of the eviction process (see Eviction Diversion and Landlord-Tenant Court).

2 Sheriff sales

The office auctions real estate ordered sold by a court, most often because of unpaid mortgages or delinquent taxes and water bills. Proceeds are supposed to be distributed to the parties and taxing authorities entitled to them, including the city's Revenue Department and Water Department, and a deed is issued to the buyer. A 2003 consent order requires deeds to be issued within 40 days of settlement. The Inquirer first reported delays in deed processing in July 2024.[2]

3 Budget and staffing

The Sheriff's budget is set by City Council as part of the city budget, and the office presents testimony at Council's annual budget hearings. Staffing, pay and technology have been recurring topics in that testimony. Staffing figures and the amount requested each year are posted in the budget documents at phila.gov.

4 2026 audit and court supervision

On August 26, 2026, the Inquirer reported that a Philadelphia judge had imposed six months of outside supervision over the Sheriff's Office's property auctions. On October 1, 2026, the Inquirer reported that the office had told the judge it found about $20 million in city money, and that it had backed away from a court-supervision agreement. These accounts come from press reports of court proceedings, which may continue; the office's positions are stated in its court filings and public statements.

5 Residents and the office

Homeowners facing a sheriff sale, buyers, and tenants affected by eviction orders deal with the office, while counseling and legal help are available through housing programs (see Division of Housing and Community Development). Complaints can go to the Sheriff's office, the courts, the City Controller (which can audit the office) or the Inspector General. Sheriff's records are subject to the Right-to-Know Law.

See also: Philadelphia Row Offices, Court of Common Pleas and Municipal Court, Philadelphia City Budget Process.

City Commissioners

City Commissioners
TypeElected three-member board; Philadelphia County Board of Elections
Led byOmar Sabir (Chair); Lisa M. Deeley (Vice Chair); Seth Bluestein (as of 2026)
TermFour years, same cycle as mayor and Council
EstablishedPhiladelphia Home Rule Charter; Pennsylvania Election Code
Websitevote.phila.gov

The City Commissioners are a three-member elected board that serves as Philadelphia's county board of elections. They register voters, certify candidates' paperwork, run polling places, count ballots and certify results for every election held in the city. They are one of the five row offices and are separate from the mayor and City Council.[1]

1 Structure and election

The office dates to the 1854 city-county consolidation, and commissioners are county officials who report to neither the mayor nor City Council. Three commissioners are elected citywide, and each voter chooses two candidates, so that no party can hold more than two of the three seats and the minority party holds the third. Omar Sabir (elected 2019) and Lisa Deeley (elected 2015) are Democrats, and Seth Bluestein (who joined the board in 2022) is a Republican. Sabir became chair in January 2024, succeeding Deeley, who had chaired the board previously, and Deeley serves as vice chair.[2] Commissioners are paid city salaries and run a professional staff. The board holds public meetings, for which transcripts are posted at vote.phila.gov.

2 What the office does

Key functions include voter registration (see Voter Registration and Mail Voting), receiving nomination petitions and ballot questions, assigning polling places and training poll workers, administering mail-in and absentee ballots, operating voting machines (the city adopted a new system in 2019), canvassing and counting ballots, and certifying results. They also publish election results and a Citizens Handbook. The board decides petition challenges and adopts policies for processes such as pre-canvassing. Candidates should read Running for Office in Philadelphia, and voters Elections in Philadelphia.

Because the board is a county board of elections, it is also the body that sets many of the practical details residents experience: where polling places are located, how many divisions each ward has, which sites accept mail ballots, and how voters are notified about problems with their ballot. The commissioners hold hearings on petition challenges and publish the election calendar for each cycle. Their budget is set by City Council as part of the city budget, and the City Controller audits their finances (see City Controller).

3 Recent elections

The office publishes mail-ballot status updates on election days and posts unofficial and certified results at vote-results.phila.gov. Citywide turnout in that primary was about 22.3 percent, down from 23.6 percent four years earlier, according to an Inquirer commentary. Results for November 2025, including races for District Attorney and Controller, were posted at vote-results.phila.gov.

4 Oversight and state role

Elections follow the Pennsylvania Election Code, so many rules, including mail-ballot deadlines and the dating of ballot envelopes, are set by the General Assembly and the courts rather than the commissioners (see Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia). The Pennsylvania Department of State certifies voting systems and issues guidance, and federal law applies to federal elections. Candidates for the board are subject to campaign finance rules (see Campaign Finance in Philadelphia). The City Controller audits the office's finances. Ward-level party officials also play a role at the polls (see Ward Leaders and Committeepersons).

5 Contacting the office

Voters can check registration, find polling places, request a mail ballot and report problems at vote.phila.gov. Residents can also attend the board's public meetings. Voter questions about the election system are covered in the Glossary.

See also: Council Districts and Wards, Political Parties in Philadelphia, Ballot Questions and Charter Changes.

Register of Wills and Clerk of Orphans' Court

Register of Wills and Clerk of Orphans' Court
TypeElected county row office under Pennsylvania law
Led byRegister John Sabatina Jr. (Democrat), elected 2023; predecessor Tracey L. Gordon served 2020-2023
TermFour years
PredecessorTracey L. Gordon (2020-2023), who succeeded Ronald Donatucci (served about 40 years)
Related courtOrphans' Court Division, Court of Common Pleas
Websitephila.gov/departments/register-of-wills

The Register of Wills and Clerk of Orphans' Court is the Philadelphia officeholder who handles the paperwork of death and inheritance. As Register of Wills the officer probates wills, meaning formally confirms that a will is valid, and issues letters of administration when a Philadelphia resident dies without a will. As Clerk of the Orphans' Court the officer keeps the records of the court that supervises estates, trusts and guardianships. The office also issues marriage licenses in the city. It is one of the five independently elected row offices.[1]

1 What the office does

Pennsylvania law gives each county a register of wills with authority over probate of estates. In Philadelphia the office accepts wills and petitions for appointing an executor or administrator, collects probate fees and Pennsylvania inheritance tax filings, issues certified copies, and maintains the public estate records. Registers are not judges and do not resolve disputes; contested matters go to the court. The officeholder is elected countywide and is separate from the mayor, though funded through the city budget.

2 Probate in practice

When someone dies leaving a will, the named executor generally presents the will and a death certificate to the Register for probate and receives letters testamentary. When there is no will, a relative seeks letters of administration, and Pennsylvania's intestacy law determines the heirs. Fees are based on the size of the estate. The office also operates programs on title problems for homes that remain in a deceased owner's name, which can block access to repair programs, tax relief and sales; see the city's Probate Deferment Initiative and Title Clearance Unit on phila.gov.[2] Housing-related help is further described in Division of Housing and Community Development.

3 Orphans' Court

The Orphans' Court Division of the Court of Common Pleas hears disputes over estates, trusts, adoptions, guardianships of incapacitated people and some nonprofit matters, despite its name. The Register, acting as Clerk, processes filings, dockets cases and maintains records for the court. The judges are part of the state-run First Judicial District, so the Clerk's office is a bridge between the elected row office and the state court system.

4 History and leadership

Ronald Donatucci held the office for about 40 years before Tracey Gordon, a Democrat who ran as an outsider challenger, defeated him in the 2019 Democratic primary and became the first Black woman to win the office, as reported by Philadelphia magazine and the Philadelphia Tribune.[3] Gordon took office in January 2020. In the May 2023 Democratic primary she lost to John Sabatina Jr. by about 3,500 votes, according to the Inquirer; Sabatina succeeded her at the start of the next term. During and after her tenure the city paid settlements to former employees who alleged retaliation, according to Inquirer reporting in 2024 and 2025; those were civil employment claims. Elections for the post occur in the municipal cycle (see Elections in Philadelphia), and officeholders are subject to the Board of Ethics and to audit by the City Controller. Candidates who run against party-endorsed nominees often rely on local organizing (see Democratic City Committee).

5 Help for families and heirs' property

Families dealing with a death can contact the office for filing instructions and forms, and legal aid organizations can help low-income residents with probate and title problems. This wiki gives general information only and not legal advice; the court, an attorney or a legal aid group should be consulted on specific estates.

See also: City-County Consolidation, Department of Records, Philadelphia Taxes.
