Civil Service Commission

Civil Service Commission
TypeIndependent city board (Home Rule Charter), quasi-judicial
MembersFive commissioners; current members are listed on the Commission's page at phila.gov
Appointed byMayor, from names recommended by a Nominating Panel
AddressMunicipal Services Building, 1401 JFK Blvd., 16th Floor, Philadelphia, PA 19102
Contact(215) 686-2320; phl.csc@phila.gov
Websitephila.gov/departments/civil-service-commission

The Civil Service Commission is the body that protects the merit principle in Philadelphia city employment. Created by the Home Rule Charter of 1951 as part of the reform movement that sought to end patronage hiring, it hears appeals from city workers, reviews the rules that govern hiring and promotion, and rules on exceptions. It advises the mayor and the Director of Human Resources on personnel administration.[1]

1 Purpose and history

Before the 1951 Charter, city jobs were commonly handed out through party organizations. The Charter established a merit system under which most positions are filled by examination and cannot be removed arbitrarily, and it put the personnel director under the supervision of the Commission. The Commission's role is therefore as an independent check on the executive branch's personnel decisions (see Philadelphia Political History).

2 Functions

According to the city, the Commission has three principal roles. First, it serves as an appellate tribunal for employee appeals, conducting fact-finding public hearings. Second, it rules on proposed changes to the Civil Service Regulations and the Classification and Pay Plans, which set job titles, qualifications and salary structures. Third, it rules on requests for exemptions from civil service and for waivers of the city residency requirement.[2] The daily administration of the system, including testing, certification of eligible lists and classification, is handled by the Office of Human Resources.

3 Appeals process

A city employee who believes wrongful action has been taken against them at work, such as a discipline, demotion or dismissal, may file an appeal with the Commission, which acts as a quasi-judicial body. It issues formal written decisions with factual and legal conclusions. Hearings are generally public. Employees covered by a union contract may instead use the contract's grievance and arbitration procedures; which route applies depends on the position, the contract and the type of action (see AFSCME District Council 33 and Public Sector Bargaining in Pennsylvania). Commission decisions can be challenged in court. Deadlines for filing are strict, so employees should check the Commission's regulations or consult their union or an attorney.

4 Relationship to unions and HR

The Commission is separate from both the administration and the unions. Its commissioners are appointed by the mayor, but from names recommended by a Civil Service Commission Nominating Panel, which is meant to insulate selection from direct political choice. The HR director, whom the Charter describes as reporting to the Commission, enforces its regulations, while pay and benefits for most workers are negotiated through collective bargaining. Police and fire have their own disciplinary processes (see The FOP Contract and Police Discipline).

5 Controversies and debates

Debates about civil service in Philadelphia tend to concern the speed of hiring, the residency requirement and the number of exempt positions. Mayors and some business groups argue that the process is slow and rigid, while labor and good-government advocates say it protects against patronage and arbitrary discipline. Residency waivers have been a recurring issue, and they are among the matters the Commission decides. These debates are policy disagreements and not findings of wrongdoing.

See also: Mayor's Cabinet and Offices, Philadelphia Row Offices, Organized Labor in Philadelphia.

References

  1. City of Philadelphia, Civil Service Commission (phila.gov/departments/civil-service-commission); Philadelphia Home Rule Charter.
  2. City of Philadelphia, Office of Human Resources, "Civil Service Commission" (phila.gov/personnel/civilservice.html).
  3. Office of the Chief Integrity Officer, "Significant boards and commissions" (phila.gov).

Philadelphia Political History

Philadelphia Political History
TypeHistorical overview
Period1854 consolidation to the present
Key turning pointsConsolidation (1854); Republican machine era; Home Rule Charter and Democratic takeover (1951-1952); fiscal crisis and PICA (1991); progressive insurgency (2010s-2020s)
Dominant party since 1952Democratic (mayoralty held continuously)
Related bodiesMayor, City Council, party city committees, ward system

Philadelphia political history is the story of how a consolidated city-county of about 1.6 million people has been governed since 1854, and who has controlled its offices. For roughly seven decades before 1952 the city was run by a Republican organization; since the 1951 Home Rule Charter, Democrats have held the mayoralty and nearly every other citywide office. In recent years the contest has shifted from party versus party to a struggle inside the Democratic coalition among the traditional ward organization, labor, business, and a newer progressive movement. This article is a general orientation, not a complete chronicle.[1]

1 Consolidation and the Republican machine

Before 1854 Philadelphia city was a small municipality surrounded by independent districts and townships. The Act of Consolidation merged these into a single city whose boundaries match Philadelphia County; see City-County Consolidation. In the decades after the Civil War, Republican leaders built a patronage-based organization that controlled city jobs, contracts and nominations, with state-level figures such as Matthew Quay and Boies Penrose influential alongside local bosses. Republicans held the mayor's office from the 1880s until 1952, and historians commonly describe the system as a "machine" because loyalty in the wards was rewarded with municipal employment.[1]

The same era produced early reform movements, including the Committee of Seventy, founded in 1904 as a civic watchdog, which still operates as a nonpartisan good-government group (see Good Government Groups).

2 The 1951 reform and Democratic ascendancy

After scandals in the late 1940s, reformers such as Joseph S. Clark Jr. and Richardson Dilworth won the city controllership and district attorney's office in 1949 and then pushed through a new Home Rule Charter, approved by voters in 1951. The charter strengthened the mayor, created a merit-based civil service, and set up the cabinet-style departments that exist today. Clark was elected mayor in 1951 and took office in January 1952, beginning an unbroken run of Democratic mayors. Dilworth succeeded him in 1956. When Dilworth resigned in 1962 to run for governor, Council President James H. J. Tate became mayor and was later elected, serving until 1972.[1][2]

3 Race, policing and the Rizzo-Goode era

Frank Rizzo, a former police commissioner, won the mayoralty in 1971 and served two terms to 1980; his tenure is remembered for both strong support among many white voters and sharp conflict with Black residents and civil-rights groups over policing. William J. Green III followed (1980-1984). W. Wilson Goode became the city's first Black mayor in 1984; his administration included the May 1985 confrontation with the group MOVE, which ended with a police helicopter bombing, the deaths of eleven people, and the destruction of a West Philadelphia neighborhood. Later official inquiries and public apologies addressed that event. The period also saw growing Black political power, including council members and ward leaders elected from Black neighborhoods.[2]

4 Fiscal crisis and rebuilding

By 1990 Philadelphia faced severe deficits. Mayor Ed Rendell (1992-2000) negotiated labor concessions and worked with the state-created PICA, an oversight authority formed in 1991, to restore balance. John F. Street (2000-2008) and Michael Nutter (2008-2016) presided over redevelopment, tax reform and the Great Recession. See the Mayors of Philadelphia Timeline for dates.

5 Progressive insurgency and the present

Jim Kenney was mayor from 2016 to 2024; Cherelle Parker, a former Council majority leader, won a crowded Democratic primary in May 2023 and took office in January 2024. Beginning in the late 2010s, organizations such as Reclaim Philadelphia and the Working Families Party built a left-leaning bloc that won district attorney races (Larry Krasner, first elected in 2017) and at-large Council seats, and has contested ward leadership. As of mid-2026, Bob Brady, who has led the Democratic City Committee since 1986, was re-elected chair in June 2026 with no challenger, even as progressives won several ward leader posts.[3] See Progressive and Grassroots Politics and Democratic City Committee.

See also: Philadelphia Overview, Political Parties in Philadelphia, Political Corruption Cases in Philadelphia, Mayor of Philadelphia.

References

  1. Encyclopedia of Greater Philadelphia (philadelphiaencyclopedia.org), entries on political history, Republican organization and the 1951 charter.
  2. City of Philadelphia, Home Rule Charter (1951, as amended), and Philadelphia City Archives mayoral records (phila.gov/records).
  3. Philadelphia Inquirer, "Democratic City Committee chair Bob Brady reelected," June 15, 2026.

Mayors of Philadelphia Timeline

Mayors of Philadelphia Timeline
TypeChronology
Covers1952 to the present (charter-era mayors)
Current mayorCherelle Parker (Democrat), since January 2024
TermFour years; limited to two consecutive terms
Election cycleOdd years not divisible by four (2023, 2027)
Governing lawPhiladelphia Home Rule Charter

The mayors of Philadelphia since 1952 have all been Democrats. The office was reshaped by the Home Rule Charter of 1951, which created a strong-mayor system with a four-year term and a limit of two consecutive terms. This article lists the charter-era mayors and the defining issues of each administration. For the powers of the office, see Mayor of Philadelphia.[1]

1 Before the charter

Until 1952 the mayor's office was held by Republicans; the last Republican mayor, Bernard Samuel, served from 1941 until January 1952. That era is summarized in Philadelphia Political History.

2 Mayors 1952-1992

  • Joseph S. Clark Jr. (1952-1956): first mayor under the new charter; reform and civil-service emphasis.
  • Richardson Dilworth (1956-1962): resigned to run unsuccessfully for governor.
  • James H. J. Tate (1962-1972): succeeded as Council president, then won election in his own right; a leader of the Democratic organization.
  • Frank L. Rizzo (1972-1980): former police commissioner; polarizing tenure on policing and race.
  • William J. Green III (1980-1984): confronted fiscal strain.
  • W. Wilson Goode (1984-1992): first Black mayor; the 1985 MOVE confrontation and the late-1980s fiscal crisis marked his tenure.

Dates and order are drawn from official city records and standard reference works.[1][2]

3 Mayors 1992-2024

  • Edward G. Rendell (1992-2000): closed a large deficit with labor concessions and oversight from PICA.
  • John F. Street (2000-2008): former Council president; the Neighborhood Transformation Initiative and a federal investigation of City Hall contracting that ended with convictions of associates, not the mayor (see Political Corruption Cases).
  • Michael A. Nutter (2008-2016): Great Recession budgets, zoning-code rewrite, and strengthened ethics rules (see Board of Ethics).
  • James F. Kenney (2016-2024): enacted the beverage tax for pre-kindergarten, led the city through the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2020 unrest.

4 The Parker administration

Cherelle L. Parker, a Democrat and former Council majority leader, won the May 2023 Democratic primary in a crowded field and the November 7, 2023 general election, defeating Republican David Oh with about 75 percent of the vote to about 24 percent, according to the official results summarized by Wikipedia. She took office on January 1, 2024 as the city's 100th mayor and its first woman mayor. Her stated priorities have included public safety, housing and neighborhood economic development. As of October 2026 she is serving her first term; the next mayoral election is in 2027.[3]

Because Philadelphia mayors cannot serve more than two consecutive terms, each open-seat election attracts a large field and a multi-million-dollar fundraising race; see Campaign Finance in Philadelphia and Elections in Philadelphia.

Ten Democrats served between Clark and Kenney, and the office has not changed parties since 1952. Because of the two-consecutive-term limit, an open seat attracts a crowded Democratic primary, as in 2023, while incumbents running for a second term have generally prevailed; the Inquirer observed in June 2026 that no Philadelphia mayor has lost a re-election bid in modern history.[4] The Charter's resign-to-run rule means that sitting city officials who want to run for mayor must resign first, which shaped the 2023 field (see Running for Office in Philadelphia). The next mayoral election is in November 2027, with the primary in May 2027.

Two practical points help in reading the list. First, the dates above refer to terms that begin in the first week of January after a November election, so a mayor elected in November 2023 took office in January 2024. Second, a mayor who leaves early is succeeded by an acting mayor chosen under the Charter's succession rules; the 1962 transition from Dilworth to Tate, who was Council president at the time, was an example. The mayor's relationship with City Council and the independently elected row offices has shaped every administration; see How Philadelphia Government Is Organized.

See also: Mayor of Philadelphia, Mayor's Cabinet and Offices, Philadelphia Political History.

References

  2. Encyclopedia of Greater Philadelphia (philadelphiaencyclopedia.org), mayoral biographies.
  3. City of Philadelphia, Office of the Mayor (phila.gov/departments/mayor); Philadelphia Inquirer 2023 election coverage.
  4. Wikipedia, "List of mayors of Philadelphia" and "2023 Philadelphia mayoral election"; Philadelphia Inquirer, "No Philly mayor has lost reelection in modern history. So does Mayor Parker have anything to worry about?" (June 15, 2026).

Political Parties in Philadelphia

Political Parties in Philadelphia
TypeOverview
Major partiesDemocratic (large majority of registered voters); Republican
Other active partiesWorking Families Party, Green, Libertarian, others
Primary typeClosed (party-registered voters only for partisan races)
Registered votersAbout 1.08 million (2026 primary)
Governing lawPennsylvania Election Code; Philadelphia Home Rule Charter

Political parties in Philadelphia operate within a system in which the Democratic Party holds a large registration advantage, the Republican Party competes mainly in parts of the Northeast and River Wards, and minor parties play a limited but increasingly visible role. Because the Democratic primary effectively decides most local general elections, the real contest for most offices occurs inside the Democratic Party. Pennsylvania uses closed primaries, so only voters registered with a party may vote in that party's primary for partisan offices.[1]

1 Registration and the primary

As of the May 2026 primary the city had about 1.08 million registered voters, according to the City Commissioners' election results.[2] Democrats make up a large majority of registrants. Voters registered as Independent or with a minor party cannot vote in the Democratic or Republican primaries for candidates, although they may vote on ballot questions. Candidates for city office run in a May primary held in odd-numbered years; general elections follow in November. See Elections in Philadelphia.

2 The major parties

The Democratic City Committee, led since 1986 by Bob Brady, is the largest local party organization. The Republican City Committee is far smaller but retains ward organizations, particularly in the Northeast. Both parties are formally organized by the 66 wards and committeepeople described in Ward Leaders and Committeepersons. Parties endorse candidates, circulate petitions, staff polling places and distribute "street sheets" or sample ballots, but under state law the party cannot place a candidate on the ballot without voters' nominating petitions or primary victory.

3 Minor parties and minority representation

The Home Rule Charter reserves two of Council's seven at-large seats for minority-party candidates by limiting how many at-large candidates a single party can elect. Republicans traditionally held these seats; in 2019 Kendra Brooks of the Working Families Party became the first third-party candidate to win one, and the party has since held two seats. See Philadelphia City Council and Progressive and Grassroots Politics. Ranked-choice voting is not used in city elections.

4 Party structure

Each party's local committee is a private organization governed by its own rules and the state Election Code. Its members are elected every four years at the primary. Party chairs are elected by ward leaders. State parties (Pennsylvania Democratic Party, Republican Party of Pennsylvania) sit above the city committees; as of 2026, state Sen. Sharif Street chairs the state Democratic Party.[3] Philadelphia's large Democratic delegation gives the city committee influence over state-level nominations. Campaign money flowing through parties and committees is discussed in Campaign Finance in Philadelphia.

See also: Philadelphia Political History, City Commissioners, Running for Office in Philadelphia.

Democratic City Committee

Democratic City Committee
TypeLocal political party organization (private, not a government body)
ChairRobert A. (Bob) Brady, chair since 1986; re-elected June 2026
MembersWard leaders and ward committeepeople (3,406 ward committee seats reported in 2026)
TermFour years
HeadquartersPhiladelphia
Websitephldems.org
Governing lawPennsylvania Election Code; party bylaws

The Democratic City Committee (also called the Philadelphia Democratic Party or the Democratic Executive Committee) is the local organization of the Democratic Party in Philadelphia. Because Democrats hold a large majority of the city's registered voters, the committee is often described as the most influential party organization in the city. It is a private political association, not a city agency, but its ward structure is recognized by the Pennsylvania Election Code.[1]

1 Structure and leadership

The committee is built from the bottom up. Registered Democrats in each of the city's roughly 1,700 voting divisions elect two committeepeople every four years; the committeepeople in each of the 66 wards then elect a ward leader; and the ward leaders elect the citywide chair. Details are in Ward Leaders and Committeepersons. The party's website lists a chair, vice chairs, treasurer and staff, including an executive director.[2] Bob Brady, a former U.S. representative, has been chair since 1986.

2 Functions

The committee endorses candidates before primaries (its endorsement is influential but not binding), raises money, maintains voter-contact networks, and coordinates Election Day staffing. Ward leaders often help select candidates for judicial vacancies and special elections, and in some circumstances party committees choose replacement nominees under state law. The committee works alongside labor unions and elected officials; see Labor and Politics in Philadelphia. Party finances are subject to campaign finance reporting; see Campaign Finance in Philadelphia.

3 The 2026 elections

The May 19, 2026 primary included elections for ward committee seats. The Philadelphia Citizen reported that at least 1,018 of the 3,406 ward committee seats would be filled by newcomers, about 30 percent, and highlighted organized challenges by the progressive group Reclaim Philadelphia in several wards.[3] In June 2026 ward leaders re-elected Brady to another four-year term; the Inquirer reported that no challenger stepped forward, while left-leaning candidates had won at least five ward leader posts the week before.[4] After the primary, District Attorney Larry Krasner publicly called on Brady to resign, a call Brady did not heed according to the same reporting.

4 Criticism and reform efforts

Critics, including progressive groups and some good-government advocates, argue that low turnout in committee elections and long-serving ward leaders make the organization difficult to change; supporters respond that the committee provides neighborhood-level organizing and voter turnout that other groups lack. Several reform efforts focus on filling vacant committee seats with younger and more diverse members and on competing for ward leadership. See Progressive and Grassroots Politics.

5 Getting involved

Any registered Democrat can run for committee person in their division by filing a petition in the primary year, or can win a seat by write-in votes; the City Commissioners publish write-in results after each primary. Vacancies are filled by the ward committee. To find your ward and division, use How to Find Your Elected Officials.

See also: Republican City Committee, Political Parties in Philadelphia, Council Districts and Wards.

Republican City Committee

Republican City Committee
TypeLocal political party organization (private, not a government body)
Recent chairsMike Meehan (to 2019); Martina White (2019-2022); Vince Fenerty (elected 2022)
StructureWard leaders and committeepeople in Philadelphia's 66 wards
Strongest areasParts of the Northeast and the River Wards
Governing lawPennsylvania Election Code; party rules

The Republican City Committee (formally the Republican Party of Philadelphia) is the local organization of the Republican Party in Philadelphia. It governed city politics for generations as the dominant machine, but since the 1950s it has been a minority party; Democrats vastly outnumber Republicans among registered voters. It remains the organization through which Republicans choose endorsements, circulate petitions and compete for the minority seats Council reserves for non-majority-party candidates.[1]

1 From machine to minority

Republicans controlled the mayor's office and patronage until Democrat Joseph Clark won the 1951 mayoral election and took office in January 1952, ending the Republican era at City Hall; see Philadelphia Political History. Over the following decades, Democratic voter-registration growth and the migration of voters from the city shrank the party's base. Its strength today lies in a handful of Northeast and riverfront neighborhoods, where it still wins some state legislative seats and, as of the 2023 results, a Council district seat.

2 Leadership

Mike Meehan stepped down as chair after the November 2019 election, and State Rep. Martina White was elected chair that month, becoming the first woman to lead the committee. White did not seek a full term in 2022; ward leaders elected Vince Fenerty, a former Philadelphia Parking Authority executive director, in June 2022.[2][3] Ward leaders elect the chair after the party's committee elections, which occur every four years (most recently with the May 2026 primary), so readers should check the party's website or news reports for the current leadership.

3 Structure and activity

Like the Democratic organization, the Republican City Committee is built from division-level committeepeople, ward leaders and a citywide executive. Many divisions have vacant seats, which can be filled by the ward committee. The party recruits judges of elections and inspectors, runs voter outreach, and endorses candidates for Council, row offices and the state legislature. See Ward Leaders and Committeepersons. Republicans hold seats on the City Commissioners board by virtue of the minority-party representation rule.

4 Electoral position

Seven of Council's 17 seats are at-large, and no voter may vote for more than five at-large candidates, so a single party cannot win more than five of them and minority-party members can be elected. Republicans historically filled those seats, but Working Families Party candidates have won the two minority seats in recent elections.[4] In the 2025 general election, Republican candidates trailed Democratic incumbents in citywide races: Christy Brady defeated Republican Ari Patrinos for Controller, and Larry Krasner won a third term as District Attorney over Republican Patrick Dugan, according to the Inquirer.[5] For how this fits into the system, see Political Parties in Philadelphia and Philadelphia City Council.

See also: Democratic City Committee, Elections in Philadelphia, Philadelphia Parking Authority.

Ward Leaders and Committeepersons

Ward Leaders and Committeepersons
TypeElected party offices (unpaid)
Units66 wards; roughly 1,700 voting divisions
SeatsTwo committeepeople per division (3,406 Democratic ward committee seats cited in 2026)
TermFour years; elected in the primary of midterm years (2022, 2026)
Selection of ward leaderElected by the ward's committee members after the primary
Governing lawPennsylvania Election Code; party rules

Ward leaders and committeepersons form the base of each party's organization in Philadelphia. A committeeperson is an elected representative of one voting division within a ward; the committeepeople of a ward together form its committee and elect its ward leader. Despite their low profile, these offices matter because the ward leaders choose the citywide party chair and heavily influence endorsements and Election Day operations.[1]

1 Wards and divisions

Philadelphia is divided into 66 numbered wards, each subdivided into divisions (precincts), which are the places where residents vote. Ward boundaries are an election geography distinct from the ten Council districts; see Council Districts and Wards.

2 Committeepersons

Each party elects a "committeeperson" and a second member, usually one man and one woman, in every division at the primary election held every four years. The Philadelphia Citizen counted 3,406 ward committee seats in the Democratic system in 2026, which equals two seats in each of roughly 1,703 divisions, and reported that at least 1,018 newly elected members would join, about 30 percent of seats.[2] Many seats go unfilled or are won by write-in votes; the City Commissioners publish unofficial write-in results after each primary.[3] Committeepeople canvass voters, distribute party literature, recruit poll workers and vote in the ward's internal elections.

3 Ward leaders

After the primary, the newly elected committee members of each ward meet to elect a ward leader, normally in June. Ward leaders then form the citywide party committee, which elects the chair; see Democratic City Committee and Republican City Committee. Some ward leaders are also elected officials, including members of City Council or the state legislature, which has led reformers to criticize overlap between party and public office. Ward leaders typically recommend candidates for local judgeships and may distribute sample ballots.

4 Election Day roles

Separate from party committee seats, each division elects a Judge of Elections and a Majority and Minority Inspector of Elections in municipal-year elections. The City Commissioners oversee and train these poll workers. Party committeepeople often recruit candidates for these jobs, and vacancies can be filled by court appointment. The distinction matters: committeepeople are party officers; election board members run the polls.

5 How to run

To run for committeeperson, a registered voter living in the division files a short nominating petition with the City Commissioners during the petition window for the primary, or may win by write-in vote. The office is unpaid. Reform organizations such as Reclaim Philadelphia recruit slates, and the 2026 cycle saw a wave of contested races; see Progressive and Grassroots Politics. For general candidate rules, see Running for Office in Philadelphia.

See also: Political Parties in Philadelphia, Elections in Philadelphia, How to Find Your Elected Officials.

Council Districts and Wards

Council Districts and Wards
TypeElectoral geography
Council districts10 (each elects one district member), plus 7 at-large seats
Wards66 (party and election units)
DivisionsRoughly 1,700 voting precincts
RedistrictingCouncil districts redrawn by ordinance after each decennial census (most recently after the 2020 Census)
Administered byCouncil (districts); City Commissioners (wards and divisions in practice)

Council districts and wards are two different ways of dividing Philadelphia, and residents often confuse them. Council districts determine which member of City Council represents a neighborhood; wards and their divisions determine where residents vote and how political parties are organized. A single Council district generally contains parts of several wards, and one ward can be split between districts.[1]

1 Council districts

The Home Rule Charter provides for a 17-member Council: ten members elected from districts and seven elected at large citywide. District members serve four-year terms with no term limits. Informally, the member for a district also holds strong influence over land-use decisions there, a custom known as Councilmanic Prerogative. The ten numbered districts together cover the whole city, from South and Southwest Philadelphia to the Northeast. A resident can look up the district member at the City's website or via How to Find Your Elected Officials.

2 Wards and divisions

The city has 66 numbered wards. Each ward is split into divisions, the polling-place units in which votes are cast and counted, with numbers running from about 1 to more than 50 in the largest wards. Divisions typically contain a few hundred to a thousand voters. Under the Pennsylvania Election Code, the county board of elections, which in Philadelphia is the City Commissioners, administers the polling places and the division maps. Party organization follows wards: each ward elects a leader and committeepeople; see Ward Leaders and Committeepersons.

3 Redistricting

Under the Charter, Council redraws the district lines after each decennial census to equalize population. The process takes place by ordinance, and in recent cycles it has involved public hearings, a Council redistricting committee and objections from community groups concerned about splitting neighborhoods. Federal Voting Rights Act requirements also constrain the lines. Ward boundaries change less often than district lines; sometimes a ward is split between two districts, creating confusion about who represents a given block.[2]

The numbers help show the scale of the two systems. Philadelphia has 66 wards, and the two committee seats in each division add up to 3,406 Democratic ward committee seats, which implies roughly 1,703 divisions citywide (see Ward Leaders and Committeepersons). By contrast, only ten district seats exist on City Council, plus seven at-large seats elected by the whole city. Under the Charter, no voter may vote for more than five at-large candidates, so a single party cannot win more than five of the seven at-large seats. District boundaries therefore matter most for the ten district races, while the at-large races are decided citywide regardless of ward or district.

Because the lines are drawn by ordinance only once a decade, a neighborhood can remain in the same Council district for many years even as its population changes. Residents who want to know who represents them, where to vote, and which ward leader to contact should look up their address on the City Commissioners' voter lookup rather than infer one answer from another.

4 Why the difference matters

  • Services and zoning: you contact your district councilmember, not your ward leader, about a land-use or service problem.
  • Voting: your ward and division determine your polling place; your district determines which Council race is on your ballot.
  • Party politics: your ward leader chairs a party committee and influences endorsements but holds no government power.
  • Boundaries: because wards and districts do not align, ward-based vote totals do not map directly onto Council results.

Residents can find their ward, division, polling place and district on the City Commissioners' voter lookup at vote.phila.gov.

See also: Elections in Philadelphia, Registered Community Organizations, Philadelphia Home Rule Charter.

Elections in Philadelphia

Elections in Philadelphia
TypeOverview of the electoral system
Administered byCity Commissioners (county board of elections)
City election yearsOdd-numbered years (mayor and Council in 2023, 2027; row offices and judges in 2025)
PrimaryThird Tuesday of May (closed partisan primary)
GeneralFirst Tuesday after the first Monday in November
Registered votersAbout 1.07 million (Nov. 2025); about 1.08 million (May 2026)
Governing lawPennsylvania Election Code; Philadelphia Home Rule Charter

Elections in Philadelphia are run by the county board of elections, which in Philadelphia is the three-member City Commissioners board, under rules set largely by the Pennsylvania Election Code and the Home Rule Charter. Philadelphia is both a city and a county, so voters choose city, county, state and federal officers; see City-County Consolidation.[1]

1 The election calendar

Pennsylvania holds primaries in May and general elections in November. In odd-numbered years Philadelphia elects city and county officials: the mayor and all 17 Council members (every four years, most recently 2023), the City Controller, the District Attorney, the Sheriff, the City Commissioners and the Register of Wills (see Philadelphia Row Offices), and local judges. Even-numbered years bring federal and state races. Special elections fill vacancies in Council or the legislature.

2 What is on the ballot

Voters also decide judicial retention questions and, often, ballot questions amending the Charter; see Ballot Questions and Charter Changes. Council at-large contests let voters choose up to five of seven seats, ensuring minority-party members win; see Philadelphia City Council. Party committee seats appear only on primary ballots; see Ward Leaders and Committeepersons.

3 How votes are cast and counted

Voters may vote in person at their division's polling place on Election Day, by mail ballot, or at in-person early mail-ballot options offered by the county. Philadelphia uses ballot-marking devices with a paper record, and mail ballots are counted at a central location; see Voter Registration and Mail Voting. Each polling place is staffed by an elected Judge of Elections, majority and minority inspectors, and appointed clerks. Results are reported at vote-results.phila.gov and are unofficial until certification.

4 Recent elections

  • 2023: Cherelle Parker won the Democratic primary for mayor and the general election; Council saw gains for the Working Families Party. The Democratic primary was the most expensive in city history. See Campaign Finance in Philadelphia.
  • 2025 primary (May 20): turnout was about 16.5 percent; Larry Krasner won renomination for District Attorney. Voters approved three Charter amendments on homeless services, prisons and affordable housing.[2]
  • 2025 general (November 4): about 382,600 ballots were cast of roughly 1.07 million registered voters, a turnout of 35.73 percent. Krasner won a third term with about 76 percent, Controller Christy Brady won with about 86 percent, and all three state Supreme Court justices on the ballot were retained.[3]
  • 2026 primary (May 19): turnout was 22.32 percent (241,186 ballots). Chris Rabb won the Democratic nomination for the 3rd Congressional District seat of retiring U.S. Rep. Dwight Evans, and two Charter questions were on the ballot.[4]

5 Oversight and disputes

The Commissioners' decisions can be challenged in the Court of Common Pleas, and election-law disputes often reach the state Supreme Court. The District Attorney's Office and the Pennsylvania Attorney General can prosecute election crimes. Election-fraud prosecutions have occurred, for example the 2022 sentencing of a former congressman for bribing election officials; see Political Corruption Cases in Philadelphia.

See also: Political Parties in Philadelphia, Running for Office in Philadelphia, Council Districts and Wards.

Voter Registration and Mail Voting

Voter Registration and Mail Voting
TypeCitizen guide
Administered byCity Commissioners; Pennsylvania Department of State
Registration deadline15 days before an election (Oct. 19, 2026 for the Nov. 3 general election)
Mail ballot application deadlineSeven days before the election (Oct. 27, 2026)
Return deadlineReceived by 8:00 p.m. on Election Day
Websitevote.phila.gov; vote.pa.gov
Governing lawPennsylvania Election Code (including Act 77 of 2019)

This article explains how voter registration and mail voting work for Philadelphia residents. It is general civic information, not legal advice; deadlines and rules can change, so confirm with the City Commissioners before relying on it. Details are as of October 2026.[1]

1 Registering and updating your registration

To register, a person must be a U.S. citizen, a Pennsylvania resident for at least 30 days before the election, and at least 18 by Election Day; 17-year-olds may register if they will be 18 by the election. Registration is available online at the state's voter services site, by mail, in person at the Commissioners' office, and automatically through some PennDOT transactions. The deadline is 15 days before the election; for the May 2026 primary it was May 4, and for the November 3, 2026 general it is October 19.[2] Party registration matters because primaries are closed; see Political Parties in Philadelphia.

2 Voting by mail

Since Act 77 of 2019, any Pennsylvania voter may vote by mail without giving a reason. A voter applies to the county board, receives a ballot and two envelopes, marks the ballot, seals it in the inner secrecy envelope, places that in the outer return envelope, signs and dates the declaration, and returns it. Applications are due seven days before the election; for November 3, 2026, that is October 27. Completed ballots must be received by the county by 8:00 p.m. on Election Day; postmarks do not count in Pennsylvania. Voters may return ballots by mail, in person at the Commissioners' office, or at drop boxes and satellite offices that the Commissioners designate; check locations and hours at vote.phila.gov. Ballots without an inner secrecy envelope, so-called naked ballots, are not counted under state court rulings.

3 Identification

Voters casting a ballot at a precinct for the first time must show an acceptable ID. For mail ballots, the applicant must supply a driver's license number or the last four digits of a Social Security number on the application, and the same identifier must be matched on the return envelope. Anyone whose eligibility is questioned may vote by provisional ballot.

4 Disputed rules

The requirement to handwrite a date on the outer envelope has been litigated for years. In August 2025 the Third Circuit ruled that discarding mail ballots over an incorrect or missing envelope date is unconstitutional, according to Law.com. The Republican National Committee then asked the U.S. Supreme Court to take up the Pennsylvania dispute (The Hill, February 2026), and on June 29, 2026, Reuters and other outlets reported that the Court had signaled interest, asking the Trump administration for its views.[3] As of early October 2026 no final Supreme Court decision on the date requirement had been reported; check the Department of State and the Commissioners for the rule that applies to the November election, and make sure to sign and date the outer envelope as the instructions direct. Other issues in dispute include pre-canvassing (counting before Election Day), drop boxes and correcting defective ballots, called ballot curing, which counties handle differently. See Elections in Philadelphia.

5 If something goes wrong

Voters who do not receive a mail ballot can request a replacement or vote provisionally at their polling place after surrendering the original. Problems at the polls can be reported to the Commissioners and the Pennsylvania Department of State. For a general help directory, see How to Get Help From the City.

See also: Council Districts and Wards, How to Find Your Elected Officials, Ballot Questions and Charter Changes.

Running for Office in Philadelphia

Running for Office in Philadelphia
TypeCitizen guide
Filing officeCity Commissioners (nominating petitions for city offices)
Key rulesResidency, nominating petitions, resign-to-run, campaign finance limits and reporting
Governing lawPennsylvania Election Code; Philadelphia Home Rule Charter; Philadelphia Code Chapter 17-1400
OfficesMayor, Council (district and at-large), row offices, judges, party committee seats

Running for office in Philadelphia involves a mix of state election law, the city Charter and campaign finance rules enforced by the Board of Ethics. This article is a general orientation, not legal advice; prospective candidates should read the City Commissioners' candidate guide and consult the Board of Ethics before raising money.[1]

1 Choosing an office

City offices fill on a four-year cycle in odd-numbered years: mayor and 17 Council seats (2027 next), row offices such as City Controller and District Attorney (2025, next 2029), and judgeships; see Philadelphia Row Offices. State and federal offices run in even-numbered years. The lowest-barrier entry point is party committeeperson; see Ward Leaders and Committeepersons.

2 Qualifications and petitions

The Charter sets residency requirements for mayoral and Council candidates (and district Council candidates must live in their district); the exact lengths are in the Charter and should be confirmed with the Commissioners before circulating petitions. To appear on a primary ballot, a candidate files nominating petitions with a required number of valid signatures from registered voters of the candidate's party; the required number varies by office and is set by the Pennsylvania Election Code, so candidates should get the exact figure for their office and cycle from the City Commissioners. Petition circulation begins in February and petitions are due in early March of the election year, according to the City Commissioners' calendar for recent cycles. Petitions are routinely challenged in court on technical grounds such as invalid signatures, so candidates usually collect well beyond the minimum.[2] Candidates also file a statement of financial interests with the Board of Ethics.

3 The resign-to-run rule

Under Article X of the Home Rule Charter, city officers and employees must resign before running for another public office, with limited exceptions. The rule has led several officials to resign their posts to seek other offices, notably in advance of the 2023 mayor's race. Candidates running for their current office do not need to resign. Reformers and some officials have debated the rule; see Ballot Questions and Charter Changes.

4 Forming a campaign

A candidate must register a campaign committee, open a bank account, and file periodic finance reports. Contribution limits apply per source; see Campaign Finance in Philadelphia. Public employees' political activity is restricted by the Charter, the civil service rules and ethics law; see Conflicts of Interest and Pay-to-Play.

5 Party endorsement and the primary

In a city where Democrats dominate, the Democratic primary is usually decisive. The party committee and ward leaders endorse before the primary, and labor unions and groups like Reclaim Philadelphia or the Working Families Party also endorse; see Democratic City Committee and Progressive and Grassroots Politics. Minor-party and independent candidates qualify through nomination papers rather than a primary. After the primary, the general election in November follows; see Elections in Philadelphia.

See also: Philadelphia City Council, Political Parties in Philadelphia, Mayor of Philadelphia.

  2. Pennsylvania Election Code (25 P.S. 2867 et seq., nomination petitions); Pennsylvania Department of State, "Candidate Guide" (vote.pa.gov).
  3. City of Philadelphia, Home Rule Charter, Article X (Prohibited Activities).

Campaign Finance in Philadelphia

Campaign Finance in Philadelphia
TypeLegal and regulatory overview
Enforced byBoard of Ethics
Governing lawPhiladelphia Code Chapter 17-1400; Board of Ethics Regulation No. 1
Individual limit$3,700 per year to a candidate committee (effective January 1, 2024); adjusted for inflation every four years
Committee limit$14,800 per year (political committees, business organizations and other non-individuals)
Doubling triggerCandidate contributes personal funds above the threshold in the law (limits then double for that race)
Independent expendituresNot limited; subject to reporting

Campaign finance in Philadelphia is governed by city law that caps contributions to candidates for city office, requires periodic disclosure, and lets the Board of Ethics enforce the rules through fines and, in the most serious cases, court action. Pennsylvania state law, by contrast, has no contribution limits for state candidates, so Philadelphia's limits are among the strictest in the state. Contribution limits are adjusted every four years for inflation; the figures below reflect the adjustment certified for January 1, 2024, the most recent quadrennial adjustment, and the Board's Regulation No. 1 should be checked for any later change.[1]

1 Contribution limits

Under the city law, an individual may give up to $3,700 per calendar year to a candidate's political committee, a litigation fund committee or a transition and inauguration committee; political committees, business organizations and other non-individuals may give up to $14,800, according to the Board of Ethics' February 2024 advisory. If a candidate gives personal funds above the threshold set in the law, the limits double for all candidates for that office, to $7,400 and $29,600 respectively under the 2024 figures. The Board of Ethics issues advisories when the doubling is triggered, as it did for the 2023 mayor's race (January 2023) and the 2023 Council at-large race (May 2023).[2] Candidates may spend unlimited personal funds, a consequence of U.S. Supreme Court precedent.

2 Reporting and disclosure

Candidate committees file periodic reports listing contributions and expenditures; reports become public through the city's election offices and the Board of Ethics. Candidates and officials also file annual statements of financial interests. For state and federal offices, reports are filed with the Pennsylvania Department of State and Federal Election Commission. See Running for Office in Philadelphia.

3 Independent expenditures

Outside groups, including super PACs, can raise and spend unlimited sums to support or oppose candidates as long as they do not coordinate with the candidate. Coordination, if proven, converts such spending into contributions subject to the limits. The Inquirer reported on September 16, 2026 that political parties can now spend unlimited amounts in coordination with their candidates. See Political Action Committees and Big Money.

4 The 2023 mayoral race

The 2023 Democratic mayoral primary was the most expensive in city history. The Inquirer reported that Democratic candidates and the independent groups supporting them raised more than $34.6 million and spent about $37.7 million, with super PACs accounting for nearly $5 million; Allan Domb gave more than $11 million of his own money and Jeff Brown $4 million.[3] Cherelle Parker won the primary.

5 Enforcement and debate

The Board of Ethics settles most violations by negotiated agreement and fine. In April 2023 the Board sued a super PAC supporting mayoral candidate Jeff Brown, alleging coordination to circumvent the limits. In September 2023 a judge ruled against the Board, according to the Inquirer, and in May 2024 the Board updated its campaign finance regulation.[4] The defendants denied wrongdoing. Supporters of strict limits say they reduce the influence of large donors; critics argue limits push money into outside groups and favor wealthy self-funders. See also Conflicts of Interest and Pay-to-Play.

See also: Elections in Philadelphia, Good Government Groups, Labor and Politics in Philadelphia.

Board of Ethics

Board of Ethics
TypeIndependent city board (created by the Home Rule Charter)
Executive DirectorJ. Shane Creamer Jr., in the post since 2007
Established2006 Charter amendment; operating since 2007
AddressOne Parkway Building, 18th Floor, 1515 Arch Street, Philadelphia
Governing lawHome Rule Charter; Philadelphia Code Chapters 20-600 (public integrity) and 17-1400 (campaign finance)
Websitephila.gov/departments/board-of-ethics

The Board of Ethics is the independent city body that administers and enforces Philadelphia's ethics, campaign finance, lobbying and financial-disclosure rules for city officials, employees and candidates. It is a city-charter body, separate from the state-level Pennsylvania State Ethics Commission and from the law-enforcement role of the District Attorney and federal prosecutors. It was created after voters approved a Charter amendment in 2006, in a period of public concern about public integrity.[1]

1 Structure

The Board has five members, appointed by the mayor and approved by City Council, who serve five-year terms, according to the city's website. A professional staff is led by an executive director. J. Shane Creamer Jr. has led the staff since 2007, according to the Board's website.[2] Staff handle investigations, legal advice, campaign finance review, training and enforcement. The Board's budget is part of the city budget set by Council; see Philadelphia City Budget Process.

2 Responsibilities

  • Public integrity: rules on gifts, conflicts of interest, nepotism, post-employment limits and use of public resources for political activity.
  • Campaign finance: contribution limits, reporting and disclosure; see Campaign Finance in Philadelphia.
  • Lobbying: registration and reporting by people paid to influence city decisions.
  • Financial disclosure: annual statements of financial interests for officials, which are public.
  • Advice and training: the Board issues advisory opinions, regulations and trainings for city staff and candidates.

3 Complaints and enforcement

Anyone may file a complaint, anonymously or by name. Staff review it, and if they find a likely violation they may negotiate a settlement agreement approved by the Board, which typically includes a fine. The Board can also go to court to enforce rules. Settlements and advisory opinions are posted on the Board's website. The Board does not prosecute crimes; criminal matters go to the District Attorney, the U.S. Attorney's Office or other authorities. Employee misconduct within mayor-controlled agencies is also investigated by the Office of the Inspector General. For a how-to, see How to Report Corruption or Misconduct.

4 Notable disputes

In April 2023 the Board sued a super PAC supporting mayoral candidate Jeff Brown, alleging the group coordinated with his campaign to exceed limits. A judge ruled against the Board in September 2023, according to the Inquirer, and in May 2024 the Board updated its campaign finance regulation. The respondents denied violating the law.[3] In an earlier episode in 2009 the Board fined its own executive director a small sum for a minor violation, as reported by the Inquirer. Elected officials and the Board have also disagreed publicly over the boundaries between the Board's authority and that of the Inspector General.

5 Other watchdogs

The Board is one of several oversight bodies: the City Controller audits finances, the Inspector General investigates fraud and misconduct, and private groups monitor government; see Good Government Groups. For state-level rules, the Pennsylvania Public Official and Employee Ethics Act applies to city officials in some respects, such as financial-interest statements.

See also: Conflicts of Interest and Pay-to-Play, Philadelphia Home Rule Charter, Political Corruption Cases in Philadelphia.

Office of the Inspector General

Office of the Inspector General
TypeCity oversight office (executive branch)
Led byInspector General Alexander F. DeSantis, appointed 2020 (as reported by the office)
EstablishedReported as 1985 (Mayor W. Wilson Goode); reinforced by later executive orders
Address601 Walnut Street, Suite 300 East, Philadelphia, PA 19106
Contact(215) 686-1770; oig@phila.gov
Websitephila.gov/ig
JurisdictionDepartments, agencies, boards and commissions under the Mayor; city contractors and funding recipients

The Office of the Inspector General (OIG) is the city's internal investigative office responsible for rooting out fraud, waste, abuse and misconduct in city government. It is part of the executive branch, not an independent elected office, and is separate from the Board of Ethics, which enforces ethics and campaign-finance law, and from the City Controller, who audits finances.[1]

1 History

The OIG was reportedly created in 1985 under Mayor W. Wilson Goode. Mayor Michael Nutter later issued an executive order to strengthen its authority, as CBS Philadelphia reported.[2] Alexander F. DeSantis, who joined the office in 2012 and served as deputy and first deputy, was appointed Inspector General by Mayor James Kenney in 2020, as reported in May 2020. The office's website continues to list him in that role as of October 2026.

2 Powers and jurisdiction

The OIG has authority under the Home Rule Charter and executive orders to investigate and audit departments, agencies, commissions and boards under the Mayor's jurisdiction, and individuals or companies doing business with the city or receiving city funds. It can subpoena records and interview witnesses in administrative matters, and it refers evidence of crimes to prosecutors such as the District Attorney and the U.S. Attorney's Office. It does not generally have jurisdiction over City Council, the courts or independent row offices; see Philadelphia Row Offices. Authorities such as the Philadelphia Parking Authority and the Philadelphia Housing Authority have their own inspectors general or oversight.

3 How investigations work

The OIG receives complaints from the public and city employees, from hotlines and from referrals. Staff investigators, attorneys and auditors review contracts, payroll, procurement and timekeeping. Outcomes can include recommendations for discipline, policy changes, recovery of money, contractor debarment or referral for prosecution. The office publishes annual reports summarizing cases, recoveries and recommendations. Matters involving procurement overlap with the Procurement Department; see Understanding City Contracts and Bids.

4 Reporting wrongdoing

Anyone, including employees and members of the public, can report suspected fraud, waste or misconduct by phone at (215) 686-1770, by email at oig@phila.gov, or through the online form on the OIG's website. Reports may be made anonymously, though providing contact information helps investigators. City policy prohibits retaliation against employees who report in good faith. See How to Report Corruption or Misconduct.

5 Limits and debate

Because the Inspector General is appointed by the Mayor and the office was created by executive order, observers have debated whether it can investigate the mayor's own administration with enough independence, and whether it should have its own Charter protection. Supporters note that its credibility has rested on professional staff and public reporting. Jurisdictional overlap with the Board of Ethics prompted public disagreement in the Nutter era, as reported by the Inquirer.[3]

See also: Conflicts of Interest and Pay-to-Play, Good Government Groups, Mayor's Cabinet and Offices.

Conflicts of Interest and Pay-to-Play

Conflicts of Interest and Pay-to-Play
TypeLegal concepts and compliance framework
Enforced byBoard of Ethics; Inspector General; prosecutors
Governing lawHome Rule Charter Art. X; Philadelphia Code ethics and campaign finance chapters; Pennsylvania Ethics Act; federal bribery statutes
Related rulesGift limits, contribution limits, procurement and disclosure requirements

A conflict of interest arises when a public official or employee has a private financial or personal stake in a matter in which they act officially. Pay-to-play refers to the practice, or appearance, of exchanging government contracts or favors for campaign contributions or gifts. Both are regulated in Philadelphia by a layered system of city, state and federal law. This article describes the framework in general terms; it is not legal advice, and officials and contractors should consult the Board of Ethics.[1]

1 Conflict-of-interest rules

Article X of the Home Rule Charter and the Philadelphia Code bar city officers and employees from having certain financial interests in city contracts, from using their office for private gain, and from taking official action on matters in which they or relatives have a financial interest. Nepotism rules limit hiring and supervising relatives, and post-employment rules restrict former officials from lobbying or representing clients before the city for a period. Public officials file annual statements of financial interests that are open to the public.

2 Pay-to-play and contracting

Philadelphia combats pay-to-play partly through contribution limits that apply to all donors, including contractors; see Campaign Finance in Philadelphia. Competitive bidding rules, publicly posted contracts and bid evaluation procedures administered by the Procurement Department are designed to make awards transparent; see Understanding City Contracts and Bids. Concern over political influence in contracting led to changes in city law and policy after investigations in the early 2000s, but contracts that are exempt from competitive bidding, such as certain professional services, remain a recurring subject of reform debates. The specific rules on contractor donations have been amended over time, so consult the Board's current guidance.

3 Gifts and outside income

City employees and officials are subject to gift restrictions: they may not accept gifts from people with business before the city beyond limited exceptions, and they must disclose gifts and outside income as the Code requires. The state Public Official and Employee Ethics Act separately restricts gifts and conflicts and requires financial-interest statements. The Civil Service Commission and department rules also limit political activity of city workers.

4 Who investigates

The Board of Ethics handles civil enforcement of city ethics rules through settlements and fines. The Office of the Inspector General investigates fraud and misconduct in mayoral agencies and contracting. The City Controller audits contracts and spending. Criminal violations are handled by the District Attorney, the Pennsylvania Attorney General and the U.S. Attorney's Office. See How to Report Corruption or Misconduct.

5 Criminal law

Federal law criminalizes bribery and honest-services fraud, though court decisions have narrowed what counts as an official act. Several Philadelphia prosecutions turned on whether payments were bribes in exchange for official action or lawful campaign contributions and jobs; see Political Corruption Cases in Philadelphia. A charge or an investigation is not proof of guilt, and outcomes in the cases summarized there ranged from convictions to acquittals.[2]

See also: Developers and the Real Estate Lobby, Right-to-Know Law and Public Records, Labor and Politics in Philadelphia.

  2. Pennsylvania Public Official and Employee Ethics Act (65 Pa.C.S. 1101 et seq.); U.S. Supreme Court, McDonnell v. United States (2016).
  3. Philadelphia Office of the Inspector General, annual reports (phila.gov/ig).

Political Corruption Cases in Philadelphia

Political Corruption Cases in Philadelphia
TypeCase summary (public record only)
Cases coveredFumo (2009); Fattah (2016); Dougherty and Henon (2021 onward); Johnson (2022); Myers (2022)
ProsecutorsU.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania
CourtsU.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania; Third Circuit
NoteAn accusation or indictment is not proof of guilt; outcomes ranged from convictions to acquittal

This article summarizes several widely reported political corruption cases in Philadelphia, limited to what is on the public record: charges, verdicts, sentences and appeals. It is not a complete list. Federal prosecutors from the U.S. Attorney's Office have brought most of these cases; the city's own watchdogs are described in Board of Ethics and Office of the Inspector General.[1]

1 Vincent Fumo

Vincent Fumo, a longtime Democratic state senator from South Philadelphia, was convicted in federal court on March 16, 2009, on 137 counts including conspiracy, fraud and obstruction of justice, relating to the use of state resources and funds from a nonprofit for personal and political purposes. On July 14, 2009, he was sentenced to 55 months in federal prison; in November 2011 the sentence was lengthened by six months after judicial review. He was released in 2013, according to published accounts.[2]

2 Chaka Fattah

U.S. Rep. Chaka Fattah was convicted on June 21, 2016, of racketeering conspiracy, bribery, bank fraud and other counts, and resigned from Congress. On December 12, 2016, he was sentenced to 10 years in prison. In 2018 an appeals court vacated some of the bribery convictions in light of the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in McDonnell v. United States, and in July 2019 he was resentenced to 10 years. In 2020 he was released from federal prison; the Inquirer reported in July 2020 that federal officials would not say why he came home early.[3]

3 John Dougherty and Bobby Henon

John Dougherty, business manager of IBEW Local 98, and City Councilmember Bobby Henon were charged in a federal case alleging that Henon took official actions in exchange for a union salary; both denied the allegations at trial. On November 15, 2021, a jury convicted Henon on 10 of 18 counts and convicted Dougherty on conspiracy and wire-fraud counts. Henon was reportedly sentenced to about 3.5 years in prison and reported to federal prison in April 2023. In December 2023, Dougherty was separately convicted on embezzlement counts together with other union officials. In July 2024 he was sentenced to six years in prison (72 months), and he surrendered on October 1, 2024. On September 3, 2026, news outlets including CBS News and NBC News reported, citing Dougherty's lawyer, that President Trump had commuted his sentence; he was reported released from prison on September 4, 2026.[4][5] The case prompted debate about the relationship between unions and elected officials; see Labor and Politics in Philadelphia.

4 Kenyatta Johnson

In 2019 federal prosecutors charged then-Councilmember Kenyatta Johnson and his wife, Dawn Chavous, along with two executives of the nonprofit Universal Companies, alleging a scheme in which payments were exchanged for official help with real estate; the defendants denied the charges. A first trial ended in a mistrial on April 20, 2022, when the jury deadlocked. At a retrial, a jury acquitted Johnson and Chavous on November 2, 2022.[6] Johnson was elected Council President in January 2024; see Philadelphia City Council.

5 Ozzie Myers and election fraud

Former U.S. Rep. Michael "Ozzie" Myers, who had been convicted in the 1980 Abscam bribery case, pleaded guilty in 2022 to conspiracy to deprive voters of civil rights and related charges, admitting that he paid election officials to add votes for candidates in South Philadelphia ward divisions in several elections between 2014 and 2018. He was sentenced on September 27, 2022, to 30 months in prison, according to news reports and the U.S. Department of Justice.[7] A former Judge of Elections was also prosecuted. See Elections in Philadelphia.

6 Reform responses

Corruption investigations, including inquiries during the early 2000s into city contracting, contributed to the strengthening of city ethics rules, the creation of the Board of Ethics, contribution limits and expanded powers for the Inspector General. See Conflicts of Interest and Pay-to-Play, Campaign Finance in Philadelphia and Good Government Groups. To report suspected misconduct, see How to Report Corruption or Misconduct.

See also: Philadelphia Political History, Right-to-Know Law and Public Records, Local News Media in Philadelphia.

Progressive and Grassroots Politics

Progressive and Grassroots Politics
TypePolitical movement overview
Key groupsReclaim Philadelphia, Working Families Party, Philadelphia DSA, Sunrise and tenant, labor and community organizations
StrategiesWard committee races, endorsements, field organizing, minority-seat Council campaigns
Recent winsAt-large Council seats (2019 onward); Chris Rabb's 2026 Democratic nomination in the 3rd Congressional District
Opposed by / in tension withParts of the Democratic ward organization, some business and building-trades interests

Progressive and grassroots politics in Philadelphia refers to the network of membership organizations, campaigns and community groups that push the city's politics to the left of its traditional Democratic establishment. Since the mid-2010s this movement has moved from protest and issue campaigns to winning elections, including at-large Council seats, the District Attorney's office and, in 2026, a congressional nomination.[1]

1 Organizations

Reclaim Philadelphia formed after the 2016 presidential primary as a membership organization that endorses and supports candidates and issue campaigns. The Working Families Party is a minor party that runs and endorses candidates, often cross-endorsing Democrats. Philadelphia DSA is the local chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America. Labor groups, tenant unions, immigrant-rights organizations and neighborhood groups also play a role; see Tenant and Housing Advocacy Groups and Civic and Neighborhood Associations.

2 Electoral milestones

  • 2017: Larry Krasner, a former civil-rights defense lawyer backed by progressive groups, won the Democratic primary and general election for District Attorney; he won renomination and re-election in 2021 and a third term in November 2025 with about 76 percent of the vote.[2] See Philadelphia District Attorney's Office.
  • 2019: Kendra Brooks of the Working Families Party became the first third-party candidate elected to Council at large, using the minority-representation rule described in Philadelphia City Council.
  • 2023: Brooks and Nicolas O'Rourke, both Working Families Party, won the two minority seats; progressive Rue Landau and others won Democratic seats. Helen Gym, a former at-large councilmember, ran for mayor and lost the Democratic primary to Cherelle Parker.
  • 2026: Chris Rabb, a state representative who describes himself as a democratic socialist, won the Democratic primary for the 3rd Congressional District with about 44 percent of the vote, ahead of state Sen. Sharif Street and Dr. Ala Stanford, for the seat of retiring Rep. Dwight Evans.[3]

3 Contesting the party machinery

Progressive groups have recruited candidates for ward committee seats and ward leader posts in order to influence endorsements, as discussed in Ward Leaders and Committeepersons and Democratic City Committee. In the 2026 cycle the Philadelphia Citizen reported that about 30 percent of Democratic ward committee seats would have new occupants. The Inquirer reported that left-leaning candidates won at least five ward leader posts in June 2026, short of what would threaten the sitting leadership, and that incumbent chair Bob Brady was re-elected unopposed.[4] District Attorney Krasner publicly called for Brady to resign after the primary.

4 Tensions and criticism

Critics argue that some progressive proposals increase costs or pose risks for business, policing or housing supply; building-trades unions and the real estate industry have at times opposed progressive candidates (see Developers and the Real Estate Lobby and Labor and Politics in Philadelphia). Supporters respond that the movement broadens participation and responds to poverty and housing costs. The groups also differ among themselves on strategy, including whether to work through the Democratic Party or third parties.

5 How to get involved

Residents can join a membership organization, run for a committee seat or volunteer in campaigns; see Running for Office in Philadelphia and How to Organize a Block or Neighborhood Group.

See also: Philadelphia Political History, Political Parties in Philadelphia, Political Action Committees and Big Money.

Political Action Committees and Big Money

Political Action Committees and Big Money
TypeOverview of political spending
RegulatorsBoard of Ethics (city); Pennsylvania Department of State; Federal Election Commission
Legal basisPhiladelphia Code Chapter 17-1400; Pennsylvania Election Code; U.S. Supreme Court decisions on independent expenditures
Key limitNo limit on independent expenditures; coordination with a candidate is prohibited
RelatedCampaign finance, labor PACs, self-funding

Political action committees (PACs) are organizations that raise and spend money to influence elections. In Philadelphia, as elsewhere, they range from union-sponsored committees and business groups to super PACs that spend unlimited sums on independent expenditures. This article describes how money flows through these channels and what rules apply, without assessing the motives of any donor.[1]

1 Types of committees

  • Candidate committees: subject to Philadelphia's contribution limits; see Campaign Finance in Philadelphia.
  • Party and ward committees: see Democratic City Committee.
  • Labor PACs: union committees fund candidates and field programs; see Labor and Politics in Philadelphia and Philadelphia Building and Construction Trades Council.
  • Business and industry PACs: including real estate and development interests; see Developers and the Real Estate Lobby and Chamber of Commerce for Greater Philadelphia.
  • Super PACs and independent-expenditure groups: may raise unlimited funds but may not coordinate with campaigns.
  • Issue and advocacy groups: nonprofits and 501(c)(4) organizations whose donors may be less visible.

2 Rules on independent spending

Following U.S. Supreme Court decisions on independent expenditures, governments cannot cap how much outside groups spend independently of candidates. City law instead requires disclosure and prohibits coordination: spending that is coordinated with a candidate is treated as a contribution subject to the limits. The line between coordination and permissible parallel activity has been contested, as discussed below. State-level and federal-level committees file with the Pennsylvania Department of State or the Federal Election Commission respectively.

3 Examples from recent races

The 2023 Democratic mayoral primary was the most expensive in city history. Democratic candidates and the independent groups backing them raised more than $34.6 million; super PACs accounted for nearly $5 million of that, and four candidates, including eventual winner Cherelle Parker, had a super PAC supporting them. Allan Domb gave more than $11 million of his own money and Jeff Brown $4 million.[2] In April 2023 the Board of Ethics sued a super PAC backing Brown, alleging coordination to exceed contribution limits; a judge dismissed the suit in September 2023, finding the claim contradicted part of the Board's own regulation, and the Board dropped the case and said it would revise its rules. The PAC denied the allegations.[3]

4 Transparency and debate

Advocates for stricter rules say large donors and independent groups can overshadow ordinary voters and encourage pay-to-play appearances; see Conflicts of Interest and Pay-to-Play. Opponents say limits on contributions to candidates push money toward less accountable outside groups and that spending is protected speech. Good-government organizations such as the Committee of Seventy publish analyses of spending; see Good Government Groups. Local reporters track filings; see Local News Media in Philadelphia. Progressive groups also operate PACs; see Progressive and Grassroots Politics.

See also: Board of Ethics, Elections in Philadelphia, Running for Office in Philadelphia.

Philadelphia Congressional and State Delegation

Philadelphia Congressional and State Delegation
TypeLegislative delegation overview
U.S. Senators (statewide)Dave McCormick (R); John Fetterman (D)
U.S. House seats covering PhiladelphiaPA-2 (Brendan Boyle), PA-3 (Dwight Evans, retiring), parts of PA-5 (Mary Gay Scanlon)
State SenateDistricts 1 (Nikil Saval), 2 (Christine Tartaglione), 3 (Sharif Street), 4 (Art Haywood), 7 (Vincent Hughes) include Philadelphia territory
State HouseRoughly two dozen Philadelphia-based members of the 203-seat chamber
Sourceshouse.gov; legis.state.pa.us

The Philadelphia congressional and state delegation consists of the federal and state legislators whose districts include parts of the city. Because Philadelphia is a city and a county (see City-County Consolidation), residents are represented at four levels: City Council, the state legislature, Congress, and statewide offices. This article lists the delegation as of October 2026, based on official state and federal rosters, and districts are subject to change; confirm names at the sources listed below.[1]

1 U.S. Congress

Pennsylvania's two U.S. Senators, Dave McCormick (Republican) and John Fetterman (Democrat), represent the whole state. In the U.S. House, Philadelphia is covered by the 2nd District (Rep. Brendan Boyle, Democrat, covering parts of the Northeast), the 3rd District (Rep. Dwight Evans, Democrat, covering much of Center City, West and North Philadelphia) and a portion of the 5th (Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon, Democrat, South and Southwest Philadelphia and Delaware County). Evans is retiring; State Rep. Chris Rabb won the Democratic primary on May 19, 2026, according to the Inquirer and other outlets, in a four-candidate race that included state Sen. Sharif Street; the district is heavily Democratic.[2] See Federal Government and Philadelphia.

2 Pennsylvania Senate

Five state senators represent districts that include Philadelphia territory: Nikil Saval (District 1), Christine Tartaglione (District 2), Sharif Street (District 3), Art Haywood (District 4) and Vincent Hughes (District 7), all Democrats, according to the Senate's member list.[3] Several chair committees. Street chairs the Pennsylvania Democratic Party and was a candidate in the 2026 PA-3 primary, which Rabb won. Pennsylvania's Senate is controlled by Republicans, so Philadelphia senators are in the minority party in that chamber.

3 Pennsylvania House

Roughly two dozen of the House's 203 members represent Philadelphia districts, nearly all Democrats; a small number of Northeast Philadelphia seats have been held by Republicans. Joanna McClinton has served as the House Democratic majority leader. The House is narrowly divided, so the Philadelphia delegation's votes are often decisive on issues such as school funding, transit and the city's tax authority; see Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia and Home Rule Limits and State Preemption. Many members are also active in party and ward leadership; see Ward Leaders and Committeepersons.

4 Why the delegation matters

Harrisburg decides issues that heavily affect Philadelphia: the state's share of School District of Philadelphia funding, SEPTA funding (see SEPTA), the city's authority to tax or regulate, and the rules for elections. The federal delegation influences housing, transit and public-health funding that flows to the city; see Philadelphia Housing Authority.

5 Contacting your representatives

You can find the legislators for your address using the lookup tools at the Pennsylvania General Assembly (legis.state.pa.us), house.gov and senate.gov. Each member has a district office in Philadelphia that helps constituents with state or federal agency problems. See also How to Find Your Elected Officials.

See also: Philadelphia City Council, Elections in Philadelphia, Progressive and Grassroots Politics.
