Ballot Questions and Charter Changes

Ballot Questions and Charter Changes
TypeDirect-democracy mechanism (legislative referral)
Who places them on the ballotCity Council by ordinance, in most cases
Who can voteAll registered voters, regardless of party, even in a primary
Governing lawHome Rule Charter; Pennsylvania Home Rule Charter and Optional Plans Law; Pennsylvania Election Code
Recent measuresMay 2025: three ballot questions; May 2026: two Charter questions, both approved

A ballot question is a measure placed before voters for a yes-or-no decision, and a Charter change is an amendment to the Home Rule Charter, Philadelphia's local constitution. Because the Charter can only be amended with voter approval, questions are the main way structural changes to city government are made, such as creating new offices, boards or powers. Philadelphia does not have a general citizen initiative process for ordinances; changes usually begin in Council.[1]

1 How a question reaches the ballot

A Charter amendment normally begins as a bill introduced in City Council authorizing the question. After public hearings and passage by Council, usually signed by the Mayor, the question's exact text is submitted to the City Commissioners and the court of common pleas as required by the state's home rule law and appears on the next primary or general election ballot, subject to statutory deadlines. The Charter can also be changed by a Charter commission process or through state law, but those routes are rarely used; see Philadelphia Home Rule Charter. Council can also place advisory or non-binding questions on the ballot in some cases. For the bill process, see How a Bill Becomes Law in Philadelphia.

2 Recent measures

  • May 2025 primary: voters decided three ballot questions on May 20, 2025; the Inquirer and WHYY published explainers on each, and the official results are posted at vote-results.phila.gov.[2]
  • May 2026 primary: voters were asked whether to create the Philadelphia Retirement Savings Board to oversee a program for private-sector workers without employer retirement plans, and whether to make the Office of the Youth Ombudsperson permanent and give it additional powers; the office was created by executive order in 2022. The Inquirer reported on May 19, 2026 that voters approved both measures.[3] Official results are posted at vote-results.phila.gov.

3 Voting on questions

Ballot questions are open to every registered voter, including voters not enrolled in a party, even when they appear on a closed primary ballot. The wording on the ballot is a short summary; the Commissioners and many news organizations publish the full text and explanations. See Elections in Philadelphia and Voter Registration and Mail Voting.

4 Debates over the process

Reformers have argued that placing questions on low-turnout primary ballots means a small share of voters decide Charter changes: turnout in the May 2026 primary was about 22.3 percent, according to an Inquirer commentary.[4] Others note that Council control of the process prevents hastily drafted amendments. Past debates have involved proposals on the resign-to-run rule, Council term limits and the structure of the school governance system; see Philadelphia Board of Education and Good Government Groups.

See also: Running for Office in Philadelphia, Home Rule Limits and State Preemption, City Commissioners.

AppealTo the Pennsylvania Office of Open Records within 15 business days of a denial
Appeals officeCommonwealth Keystone Building, 400 North Street, Harrisburg; 717-346-9903; openrecords@pa.gov
Applies toCommonwealth, local and judicial agencies, including Philadelphia city agencies

The Right-to-Know Law (RTKL) is Pennsylvania's public-records statute. Under a 2008 revision, records held by a government agency are presumed to be public unless a specific exemption applies, reversing the burden from the requester to the agency. The law covers city departments, boards and authorities in Philadelphia as local agencies. For step-by-step instructions, see How to Request Public Records. This article is general information, not legal advice.[1]

1 What is a public record

A public record is a record of an agency that documents a transaction or activity, is created, received or retained under law or in connection with agency business, and is not exempt under the RTKL, other state or federal law, or a court order. Records can include emails, contracts, reports, spreadsheets and meeting minutes. Agencies are not required to create new records or to answer questions, only to provide existing records.

2 Making a request

A request must be in writing and must identify or describe the records with enough specificity for the agency to locate them. A requester does not have to explain why the records are wanted. Each agency designates an open-records officer. The agency must respond within five business days, either granting the request, denying it, or sending a notice that it needs more time; the extension, up to 30 additional days, is allowed for reasons the law lists, such as voluminous records or legal review. A request not answered in time is treated as denied. Agencies may charge fees for duplication and certain other costs. Philadelphia's departments accept requests through the city's online request system, and the Law Department advises agencies on responses; see also Department of Records.

3 Exemptions

The RTKL lists categories that are not public, including certain personal identification information, records relating to a noncriminal investigation, internal predecisional deliberations, attorney-client privileged material, some public-safety records and certain procurement material before an award. Agencies bear the burden of proving an exemption applies by a preponderance of the evidence. Court records are governed by separate rules. Records of criminal investigations are largely exempt, which matters for police and prosecutor files; see Philadelphia Police Department.

4 Appeals

A requester whose request is denied, or deemed denied, may appeal to the Pennsylvania Office of Open Records within 15 business days. For local agencies such as Philadelphia's, the Office of Open Records appoints an appeals officer who issues a final determination, generally within 30 days; either side may then seek review in the Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas. The Office also provides training and a hotline for requesters and agencies.[2]

5 Related transparency tools

Many Philadelphia records are proactively published on the city's open data portal; see Open Data and Transparency Tools. Meetings are governed by the separate Sunshine Act. Journalists and watchdog groups use the RTKL to examine contracts, spending and disciplinary records; see Local News Media in Philadelphia and Good Government Groups.

See also: How to Request Public Records, City Controller, Conflicts of Interest and Pay-to-Play.

References

  2. Pennsylvania Office of Open Records (openrecords.pa.gov), requester and agency guidance; PA agency Right-to-Know policy pages.

Sunshine Act and Open Meetings

Sunshine Act and Open Meetings
TypeState open-meetings statute
Governing lawPennsylvania Sunshine Act, 65 Pa.C.S. 701 et seq.
Applies toBoards, commissions and authorities of state and local agencies, including City Council and many Philadelphia boards
EnforcementCourt of Common Pleas; fines and invalidation of improper actions possible
Companion lawRight-to-Know Law (records)

The Sunshine Act requires that official actions and deliberations of covered government bodies take place at meetings open to the public. In Pennsylvania the law applies to agencies with authority to take official action or make recommendations on matters of agency business, such as City Council, school boards and many city boards and commissions. This article is general information, not legal advice.[1]

1 Core requirements

A covered body must hold its meetings where the public can attend, give advance public notice of regular meetings (generally at least three days) and of special meetings (generally 24 hours), post notices at its principal office and, where it maintains a website, online, and keep written minutes recording who attended, what votes were taken and how members voted. Official action, such as voting to approve a contract, must occur in public. A quorum of members cannot deliberate agency business in private except in the narrow circumstances the law allows, which is why gathering a majority at an informal meeting can raise legal questions. Minutes are public records under the Right-to-Know Law.

2 Executive sessions

The Act allows closed-door "executive sessions" only for specified purposes, including personnel matters, collective bargaining strategy, certain real estate transactions, attorney-client consultation about litigation, and confidential information protected by law. The body must announce the reason for the session before or after it, and official action on the matters discussed must still be taken in public. See Public Sector Bargaining in Pennsylvania for why labor negotiations often involve closed discussions.

3 Public comment

Since a 2021 amendment, Pennsylvania law requires covered bodies to provide a reasonable opportunity for residents to comment on matters of concern, official action or deliberation before a vote on the matter, though bodies may set reasonable rules such as time limits and sign-up procedures. Some bodies hold comment at the start of meetings. See How to Testify at City Council for the rules specific to Council.

4 Philadelphia in practice

Council meets in public in City Hall and posts agendas and video; its committees hold public hearings; see Council Committees and the Legislative Process. Boards that decide residents' cases, such as the Zoning Board of Adjustment and the Philadelphia Historical Commission, publish agendas and hold public hearings. The Board of Education and authorities such as the Philadelphia Housing Authority and SEPTA also fall under the Act. Some bodies are exempt or only partly covered, for example the Mayor's office and individual officials acting alone; meetings of a single official are not "agency" meetings.

5 Enforcement

A person who believes an agency violated the Act can file suit in the Court of Common Pleas, generally within 30 days of the violation (or 30 days after discovering it, if it was concealed, up to a limit). A court can invalidate action taken in violation, order compliance, and impose a fine and attorney fees in some cases. The Act has criminal penalties for intentional violations. The Pennsylvania Office of Open Records does not hear Sunshine Act complaints; it handles Right-to-Know appeals. Residents can also raise concerns with their council member; see How to File a Complaint.

See also: Open Data and Transparency Tools, Registered Community Organizations, Good Government Groups.

Organized Labor in Philadelphia

Organized Labor in Philadelphia
TypeCivil-society sector (private and public-sector unions)
Central bodyPhiladelphia Council AFL-CIO (over 100 local unions, per City & State, 2026)
Largest city-government unionsDC 33, DC 47, FOP Lodge 5, IAFF Local 22
Governing lawNational Labor Relations Act (private sector); Pennsylvania Act 111 and Act 195 (public sector)
Recent flashpoint2025 DC 33 strike (July 2025)

Organized labor in Philadelphia consists of the unions that represent workers in city government, the school district, transit, construction, health care, hospitality, building services and other sectors, together with the councils that coordinate them. Philadelphia is a heavily unionized city by American standards, and because it is both a city and a county, its municipal government is one of the region's largest union employers. The relationship between unions and elected officials shapes budgets, hiring, public safety policy and development.[1]

1 Historical background

Philadelphia has a long labor history. The 1806 Philadelphia cordwainers (shoemakers) conspiracy trial is a landmark in early American labor law, and the city saw a 1910 general strike and major transit and industrial disputes in the twentieth century. As manufacturing declined, union strength shifted toward the public sector, the building trades, health care and education. Municipal workers gained bargaining rights under state law in the 1960s and 1970s, and city employee strikes, such as the DC 33 strike of 1986, have periodically shaped city politics. The most recent was the July 2025 strike, covered in 2025 DC 33 Strike.

2 Public-sector unions

The city's civilian workforce is mainly represented by two AFSCME councils: District Council 33, which represents roughly 9,000 blue-collar and related workers, and District Council 47, which represents white-collar, professional and supervisory employees. Uniformed workers bargain separately: FOP Lodge 5 for police and IAFF Local 22 for firefighters and paramedics. Under Pennsylvania law, police and firefighters cannot strike and instead use binding interest arbitration, while most other public employees may strike under defined conditions; see Public Sector Bargaining in Pennsylvania. The Philadelphia Federation of Teachers represents roughly 14,000 school district employees.

3 Building trades and construction

Construction unions are organized through the Philadelphia Building and Construction Trades Council, which represents more than 50 affiliated unions according to 2026 reporting, and individual locals such as IBEW Local 98. Their influence over public works, development and zoning debates is described in Prevailing Wage and Project Labor Agreements.

4 Transit, education, health care and service workers

Transit workers at SEPTA are largely represented by TWU Local 234; see also SEPTA. Teamsters locals cover trucking, warehousing, school bus and other work. Hospital, nursing home, building-service and hotel workers are covered in Service and Health Care Unions. Large private employers, including the universities and hospital systems described in Eds and Meds Anchor Institutions, have seen growing organizing activity in recent years.

5 Coordinating bodies and advocacy

The Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO coordinates political and community campaigns among its affiliates. Outside traditional unions, worker centers and advocacy groups organize workers who lack a union contract; see Worker Centers and Labor Advocacy. City enforcement of local labor standards is handled by the Office of Worker Protections.

6 How unions interact with the city

City unions bargain with the mayor's administration, whose labor negotiators work with the Office of Human Resources and the Law Department, within a budget overseen by the Finance Department and reviewed by PICA. Council approves the funding. Unions also endorse and campaign in elections; see Labor and Politics in Philadelphia. Contract outcomes are widely reported and compared across unions, as in the 2025-2026 coverage of police, firefighter and civilian settlements.

See also: Philadelphia AFL-CIO Council, Mayor of Philadelphia, Civil Service Commission.

Public Sector Bargaining in Pennsylvania

Public Sector Bargaining in Pennsylvania
TypeState labor statutes
Police and fire lawAct 111 of 1968 (Policemen and Firemen Collective Bargaining Act)
General public employee lawAct 195 of 1970 (Public Employe Relations Act)
Enforcing agencyPennsylvania Labor Relations Board (PLRB)
Impasse methodAct 111: binding interest arbitration; Act 195: mediation, fact-finding, limited right to strike
Websitepa.gov (Labor Relations Board)

Public sector bargaining in Pennsylvania is governed by two statutes passed by the General Assembly. Because Pennsylvania is a state that sets labor rules for its local governments, Philadelphia's home rule charter does not give the city independent power to rewrite bargaining rights for its employees; see Home Rule Limits and State Preemption. The two laws explain why police and firefighters settle contracts through arbitrators, while civilian unions such as DC 33 may walk off the job.[1]

1 Act 111: police and firefighters

Act 111, enacted in 1968, gives police officers and firefighters the right to bargain collectively through their chosen representatives. In exchange, they give up the right to strike. When bargaining reaches an impasse, either side may demand interest arbitration before a panel, typically made up of one arbitrator chosen by the union, one chosen by the employer and a neutral chair. The award is binding on both parties. Judicial review of Act 111 awards is traditionally narrow, which means courts will overturn an award only on limited grounds such as exceeding the arbitrators' jurisdiction or violating the Constitution.[1]

In Philadelphia, Act 111 governs FOP Lodge 5 and IAFF Local 22. The August 2025 FOP award and the July 2026 firefighter award were both issued by Act 111 panels, and in the firefighter case the union's own arbitrator filed a dissent.[2]

2 Act 195: other public employees

Act 195, the Public Employe Relations Act of 1970, covers most other public employees, including municipal civilians, teachers and transit authority workers. It recognizes the right to organize and bargain, defines mandatory subjects such as wages, hours and working conditions, and sets a graduated impasse process of mediation and fact-finding. The PLRB administers elections, certifies bargaining units and adjudicates unfair-practice charges under both acts.

Act 195 sorts employees into categories. Some, such as prison guards, court employees and certain others, may never strike and are instead sent to binding arbitration. Others, described as "essential" employees, may strike only after the process is exhausted and only if the strike would not threaten public health, safety or welfare. This is why a 2025 report noted that within DC 47 only one local, Local 2187, was legally able to strike.[3]

3 Strikes and injunctions

Where Act 195 permits a strike, the employer may ask the Court of Common Pleas for an injunction if it argues that the strike creates a clear and present danger to public health, safety or welfare. During the July 2025 DC 33 strike, the city suspended residential trash collection and closed pools while continuing emergency services. Teachers in Pennsylvania school districts, including the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers, are also covered by Act 195; the school-year calendar limits when a strike may last.

4 The Philadelphia context

Philadelphia's labor contracts are bargained by the mayor's administration and must fit within the city budget and the five-year plan reviewed by PICA. The 2025 FOP award was described by the city as costing $343 million over the five-year plan. Council appropriates the funds but does not sit at the bargaining table. Elected row officers and the courts have separate employee relationships; see Philadelphia Row Offices and First Judicial District.

5 Criticism and debate

Supporters say Act 111 provides labor peace in essential services and a neutral forum. Critics, including government-reform groups and some city officials, argue that arbitration panels can limit disciplinary reforms and impose costs without the same public process as legislation; the discipline issue is discussed in The FOP Contract and Police Discipline. Union representatives respond that arbitration protects due process and that awards are tied to statutory criteria, including the employer's ability to pay.

See also: Organized Labor in Philadelphia, Civil Service Commission, Office of Human Resources.

AFSCME District Council 33

AFSCME District Council 33
TypePublic-sector union (AFSCME council)
PresidentGreg Boulware (per afscme33.org, October 2026)
MembersApproximately 9,000 city employees (as reported by news outlets in 2025)
RepresentsSanitation, water, streets, recreation, libraries (non-professional), crossing guards and other city workers
Governing lawPennsylvania Act 195 of 1970
Current contractThree years, July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2028 (per the 2025 term sheet)
Parent bodyAmerican Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME)

AFSCME District Council 33 (DC 33) is the union representing roughly 9,000 blue-collar and related employees of the City of Philadelphia. It is one of the two AFSCME councils in city government, alongside District Council 47, which represents white-collar workers. DC 33 members include trash collectors, water department workers, street crews, recreation staff and school crossing guards, among many job titles.[1]

1 Structure and leadership

DC 33 is a council made up of affiliated AFSCME locals, each covering particular departments or job groups; the union's website lists a president and a secretary-treasurer for each local, and Greg Boulware as council president. The same website lists the council's headquarters at 3001 Walnut Street in West Philadelphia. Boulware is also listed as DC 33's representative on the executive board of the Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO.[2]

2 Bargaining and the legal framework

DC 33 bargains with the mayor's administration under Pennsylvania's Public Employe Relations Act (Act 195), which, unlike the law covering police and firefighters, allows many civilian public employees to strike after mediation and fact-finding; see Public Sector Bargaining in Pennsylvania. Contract costs must fit the city's five-year plan reviewed by PICA, and DC 33 wages are a significant part of the city budget. Employees in the union are also covered by the civil service rules described in Civil Service Commission.

3 The 2025 strike and contract

DC 33 went on strike at the start of July 2025, after talks with the Parker administration did not produce a deal. On July 9, 2025, Mayor Cherelle Parker and Boulware announced that the strike was over and that the union had accepted a deal. The union's website lists a "2025 3-Year Agreement" and posts the term sheet dated July 9, 2025, which applies to employees represented by DC 33, including former Traffic Court employees and school crossing guards. According to that term sheet, the agreement runs for three years, from July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2028. It provides a 3 percent increase in each step of each pay range when strikers return to work, and further 3 percent increases effective July 1 of 2026 and 2027; a one-time $1,500 bonus for permanent full-time employees on the payroll at ratification; a fifth pay step (and a third step for school crossing guards) effective July 1, 2026; a differential for certain Medical Examiner's Office forensic classes; and city payments covering a shortfall in the DC 33 Health and Welfare Fund. Earlier in the bargaining the union had asked for 8 percent annual raises, and the city had countered with a smaller total increase, according to news coverage. Details of the dispute are in 2025 DC 33 Strike.[3]

4 Politics and relations with the city

DC 33 is an influential political actor: it endorses candidates, mobilizes members and has historically been a strong presence in mayoral and Council races. See Labor and Politics in Philadelphia. The union is affiliated with the Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO. Strikes by city workers, as in 1986 and 2025, tend to dominate local news because of the visible effect on trash pickup, pools and libraries; see Philadelphia Water Department and Streets Department for departments whose workers it represents.

5 Contacting the union

DC 33 lists its headquarters at 3001 Walnut Street, Philadelphia, PA 19104. Members with grievances typically begin with their shop steward and local. Residents who need city services during a work stoppage should consult Philly311.

See also: Organized Labor in Philadelphia, Office of Human Resources, Philadelphia City Council.

AFSCME District Council 47

AFSCME District Council 47
TypePublic-sector union (AFSCME council)
PresidentApril Gigetts (per dc47.org, October 2026)
MembersWorkers and retirees in nonprofit, higher-education, cultural and government sectors
RepresentsCity, Parking Authority, Housing Authority and court employees (Locals 2186 and 2187), plus workers at the Defender Association, Penn, Temple, the Zoo, museums and nonprofits
Current contractThree-year city agreement, tentative agreement reported July 15, 2025
Websitedc47.org

AFSCME District Council 47 (DC 47) is a union council of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees. Its website describes it as representing workers and retirees in the nonprofit, higher-education, cultural/arts and government sectors of the Philadelphia area. Its best-known city-government locals cover professional, technical and administrative employees (Local 2187) and first-level supervisors (Local 2186) of the City, the Philadelphia Parking Authority and the Philadelphia Housing Authority. The city's blue-collar workforce is represented by the larger DC 33.[1]

1 Structure and leadership

DC 47 is made up of locals, each covering a particular employer or job group. The union's website lists, among others, Local 2186 (first-level supervisors of the City, the Parking Authority, the Housing Authority and the First Judicial District), Local 2187 (professional, technical and administrative assistants of the City, the Parking Authority and the Housing Authority), Local 810 (First Judicial District employees), Local 3190 (employees of the Defender Association of Philadelphia) and locals at the University of Pennsylvania, Temple University, the Philadelphia Zoo, several museums and nonprofit organizations. April Gigetts is listed as the council's president; the Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO also lists her as DC 47's representative on its executive board.[2] News outlets have reported differing membership figures, so none is used here.

2 Bargaining and strike rights

Like other civilian city employees, DC 47's city locals bargain under Pennsylvania's Public Employe Relations Act (Act 195); see Public Sector Bargaining in Pennsylvania. Under that law most public employees may strike only after mediation and fact-finding have been exhausted, while some categories, including prison guards and employees necessary to the functioning of the courts, may not strike at all. Because DC 47 includes court employees and private-sector workers at universities and nonprofits as well as city workers, its members do not all operate under the same legal rules, so a strike authorization by one group does not necessarily describe the others. In July 2025, as the DC 33 strike was ending, DC 47 members voted on whether to authorize a strike of their own, according to news coverage.

3 The 2025 contract

WHYY and other outlets reported that DC 47 and the city reached a tentative three-year agreement on July 15, 2025, averting a walkout. The city was bargaining with several unions at about the same time, including DC 33, FOP Lodge 5 and IAFF Local 22. Wage and benefit terms are set out in the agreement itself and in the union's member materials; readers should consult those documents for the percentages.[3]

4 Role in city politics

DC 47 publishes election endorsements and a voter guide for each cycle; its site lists 2026 General Election endorsements and a 2026 voter guide. It is a member of the Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO. Its members work in city offices, authorities and courts, and at universities and cultural institutions across the region. See Labor and Politics in Philadelphia for how city unions engage in elections.

See also: Organized Labor in Philadelphia, Office of Human Resources, Civil Service Commission.

Fraternal Order of Police Lodge 5

Fraternal Order of Police Lodge 5
TypePublic-sector police union
PresidentRoosevelt L. Poplar (per fop5.org, October 2026)
MembersPhiladelphia police officers and Sheriff's Office deputies
Governing lawPennsylvania Act 111 of 1968 (no strikes; binding interest arbitration)
Latest awardTwo-year interest arbitration award, August 15, 2025
Parent bodyGrand Lodge, Fraternal Order of Police

Fraternal Order of Police Lodge 5 (FOP Lodge 5) is the collective bargaining representative of rank-and-file officers of the Philadelphia Police Department and of deputies in the Sheriff's Office. It is one of the most politically visible unions in the city, with a long record of endorsing candidates and opposing proposals it views as threatening members' due process rights.[1]

1 Leadership

The lodge's website lists Roosevelt L. Poplar as president. John McNesby led the lodge for many years before him. The lodge is a fraternal organization with an elected executive board; its website describes a headquarters in Northeast Philadelphia since 2013 that includes a gym, event spaces and a members-only restaurant and bar, and it posts the contract, the fiscal 2026 pay schedule, grievance information and legal-services information for members.[2]

2 Bargaining under Act 111

Police officers cannot strike in Pennsylvania. Under Act 111 of 1968, unresolved contract issues go to a tripartite interest arbitration panel whose award binds the city and the union; see Public Sector Bargaining in Pennsylvania. As a result, FOP contracts are commonly known as "awards." The city's bargaining team works with the Law Department and the Office of Human Resources, and the cost must fit the five-year plan reviewed by PICA.

3 The 2025 award

On August 15, 2025, Mayor Cherelle Parker and other city officials announced a two-year interest arbitration award for Lodge 5. According to the city's announcement, it provides 3 percent wage increases in Fiscal 2026 and in Fiscal 2027; a one-time $3,000 cash bonus payable within 30 days; and economic adjustments tied to "civilianization," a process of shifting positions that do not involve law-enforcement duties to non-law-enforcement staff, including increases in a longevity pay scale intended to encourage officer retention. The mayor said at the press conference that the award would cost $343 million over the city's current Five-Year Plan.[3]

The announcement does not give a combined percentage for the civilianization adjustments. In July 2026 the Philadelphia Inquirer, comparing the police and firefighter awards, reported that police received about 9 percent over the two years, plus the bonus, with the gap above 3 percent a year attributed to the civilianization-linked raises. Because the city lists 3 percent annual increases and longevity adjustments separately, the two descriptions should be read together rather than as competing figures; the award itself is the controlling document.[3]

4 Discipline, oversight and controversies

The FOP contract and arbitration process govern how officers are disciplined and how firings are appealed. The Philadelphia Inquirer reported in 2019 that between 2011 and 2019 arbitration overturned or reduced discipline in about 70 percent of the cases it examined, and reported in 2024 that arbitrators reinstated 85 percent of fired officers whose terminations the FOP contested between 2022 and early 2024. According to City & State and Inquirer reporting in 2025, the arbitration panel declined the union's proposal to exclude the Citizens Police Oversight Commission from the contract and did not adopt the rollbacks of transparency measures the union had sought; the only discipline-related change reported was making reinstatement contingent on completion of conditions of employment.[4] The details are in The FOP Contract and Police Discipline and Police Accountability Systems. The union has said that arbitration protects officers' due process.

5 Political activity

Lodge 5 takes part in endorsements for city and state offices, including races for mayor and District Attorney. Its role in the broader network of unions is covered in Labor and Politics in Philadelphia.

See also: IAFF Local 22, Organized Labor in Philadelphia, Philadelphia AFL-CIO Council.

IAFF Local 22

IAFF Local 22
TypePublic-sector firefighter and paramedic union
PresidentMichael Bresnan (per the local's website, October 2026)
MembersMore than 4,500 current and retired firefighters, paramedics, EMTs and officers (per the local, October 2026)
Governing lawPennsylvania Act 111 of 1968 (no strikes; binding arbitration)

Parent bodyInternational Association of Fire Fighters (IAFF)

IAFF Local 22 represents the uniformed firefighters, paramedics and emergency medical personnel of the Philadelphia Fire Department. As public safety employees, they are covered by Pennsylvania's Act 111 and settle contract disputes through binding interest arbitration rather than strikes; see Public Sector Bargaining in Pennsylvania.[1]

1 Leadership and membership

The local's website lists Michael Bresnan as president. The local describes itself as having a history of more than 100 years, tracing back to the City Firefighters' Association, and says it represents more than 4,500 current and retired firefighters, paramedics, EMTs and officers of the Philadelphia Fire Department. That figure includes retirees, so it is larger than the number of active bargaining-unit members. Elected officers and building stewards run day-to-day representation; the union's site asks members to volunteer as stewards and to serve on committees.[2]

The local also operates member services that are separate from bargaining, including a health plan (the Local 22 Health Plan) and a banquet hall that it rents to the public. It is affiliated with the national International Association of Fire Fighters.[2]

2 Contracts and Act 111 arbitration

Pennsylvania's Act 111 of 1968 covers police officers and firefighters. It forbids strikes and replaces them with a process in which unresolved bargaining disputes go to a three-member interest arbitration panel: one arbitrator named by the union, one by the employer, and a neutral chairperson. The panel's award is binding on both sides, and courts review it only narrowly. Because of this structure, a firefighters' contract is usually called an "award" when it is decided by a panel rather than agreed at the table.[1]

On the city side, contracts are negotiated by the mayor's administration, working with the Law Department and the Office of Human Resources. The cost of any settlement or award must fit within the five-year financial plan that is reviewed by PICA. The same framework applies to the police union, FOP Lodge 5, whose August 2025 award the city announced in a press release (see that article for its terms). Firefighters' pay is also affected by the department's size and deployment: the Fire Department staffs 63 stations, and its EMS division is among the busiest in the country, according to the city.[4]

3 The July 2026 award

The Philadelphia Inquirer reported on July 9, 2026 that an arbitration panel had issued a two-year award for Local 22 after members had worked without a new contract for more than a year, and that the Parker administration announced it that day. The newspaper compared the firefighters' award with the police award issued the previous summer. The terms of the award are a public record held by the parties; readers who need exact wage figures should consult the city's announcement or the award itself rather than press summaries.[3] The city has said its labor settlements must be balanced against its long-term financial obligations.

4 Politics

Because firefighters cannot strike, their leverage in city politics comes mainly through arbitration, public campaigns over staffing and station closures, and endorsements. See Labor and Politics in Philadelphia for how city unions engage in elections, and Office of Emergency Management for the broader emergency-response system that the Fire Department is part of.

See also: Organized Labor in Philadelphia, Philadelphia AFL-CIO Council.

Policy focusProject labor agreements, prevailing wage, apprenticeship and diversity

The Philadelphia Building and Construction Trades Council (often "the Building Trades") is the coordinating body for the city's construction unions, including electricians, plumbers, steamfitters, laborers, carpenters, ironworkers and others. It speaks for the trades in dealings with developers, the city and the state, and is among the most influential labor organizations in Philadelphia politics.[1]

1 Leadership

For years the council's business manager was John Dougherty, who also led IBEW Local 98; the Justice Department's 2024 sentencing release describes a scheme to help elect Dougherty business manager of the Building Trades. After his federal conviction on November 15, 2021, he resigned his Local 98 post, and Ryan Boyer became the council's head, reported in November 2021 by WHYY and the Inquirer as the first Black leader in the council's history.[2] The Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO's executive board lists Boyer for the Building and Construction Trades Council, together with representatives of many construction unions, among them George Pegram (Plumbers Local 690), Jim Snell (Steamfitters Local 420), Mark Lynch Jr. (IBEW Local 98), Esteban Vera Jr. (Laborers Local 57), Sam Staten Jr. (Laborers Local 332), Jim Reilley (Operating Engineers Local 542), Bryan Bush (Sheet Metal Workers Local 19), Rob Cellucci (Insulators Local 14), and Paul Miraglia and Tim Crowther (IUPAT District Council 21).[3]

2 Role in development and public works

The trades advocate for union labor on public projects and large private developments. Tools include project labor agreements, in which the owner and the unions agree on terms for a specific project, and the prevailing wage rules described in Prevailing Wage and Project Labor Agreements. On city public-works contracts, contractors must meet the Davis-Bacon Act and Chapter 17-107 of the Philadelphia Code, submit weekly payroll information, and accept job-site visits by wage compliance officers from the Department of Labor's Office of Labor Standards. Union labor commitments are also a frequent subject of negotiation with developers; see Developers and the Real Estate Lobby, Tax Abatement and Development Incentives and Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation. The General Building Contractors Association is the employer-side counterpart.[1][4]

3 Training, apprenticeship and diversity

Construction unions run joint apprenticeship programs with their employers. For example, IBEW Local 98 operates an Apprentice Training Academy, and the Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO and the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers have held "Union Experience Fairs" since 2023 to introduce students to union apprenticeship programs. Related city workforce programs are covered in Office of Workforce Development and Office of Economic Opportunity.

4 Politics

The Building Trades Council endorses candidates in city and state races and mobilizes members; Boyer, identified in press coverage as the head of the council, has been a visible participant in local political debates over development proposals. The council's alliances with Philadelphia City Council members and the mayor are discussed in Labor and Politics in Philadelphia.

See also: Philadelphia AFL-CIO Council, Organized Labor in Philadelphia.

IBEW Local 98

IBEW Local 98
TypeConstruction trade union local (electricians)
PresidentJames Foy (per ibew98.org officers page, October 2026)
Business managerMark Lynch Jr. (per ibew98.org, October 2026)
Parent bodyInternational Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW)
Council affiliationPhiladelphia Building and Construction Trades Council
Notable eventsFederal convictions of former business manager John Dougherty (November 2021 and December 2023) and former president Brian Burrows (December 2023); sentenced June-July 2024; Dougherty commutation warrant dated September 3, 2026

IBEW Local 98 is the Philadelphia local of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, representing electricians in the city and surrounding counties. It has long been among the most politically active unions in Pennsylvania, with a history that includes both strong influence on city politics and a federal corruption prosecution of its former leaders.[1]

1 Leadership

The Local 98 website's officers page lists James Foy as president and Mark Lynch Jr. as business manager and financial secretary, along with a vice president, recording secretary, treasurer and executive board; its business-agents page lists an assistant business manager and agents by territory (Center City, Bucks and Montgomery counties, Northeast Philadelphia and Delaware County). The Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO lists Lynch as Local 98's representative on its executive board. For years the local was led by business manager John Dougherty, who also became business manager of the Building and Construction Trades Council, according to the Justice Department's description of the 2021 case. After his 2021 conviction he resigned as business manager of Local 98.[2]

2 The Dougherty prosecutions

In January 2019 a federal grand jury returned a 116-count indictment against Local 98, Dougherty, then-Councilmember Robert (Bobby) Henon and others. The case was tried in two parts. On November 15, 2021, a jury convicted Dougherty of one count of conspiracy to commit honest services fraud and seven counts of honest services wire fraud, and convicted Henon of one count of conspiracy to commit honest services fraud, eight counts of honest services wire fraud and one count of federal program bribery. On December 7, 2023, a second jury convicted Dougherty and former Local 98 president Brian Burrows of conspiracy to embezzle union funds; Dougherty was also convicted of 33 counts of embezzlement, 24 counts of wire fraud, false filings with the Department of Labor and false tax returns, and Burrows of related embezzlement, false-filing and tax counts. The Justice Department described the embezzlement as roughly $600,000 taken from the union between 2010 and 2016.[3]

Judge Jeffrey L. Schmehl sentenced Burrows to 48 months in prison on June 26, 2024 and Dougherty to 72 months on July 11, 2024. The Justice Department's Office of the Pardon Attorney lists a commutation warrant dated September 3, 2026 for John Dougherty (Eastern District of Pennsylvania; 72-month sentence imposed July 11, 2024) among the clemency grants by President Donald J. Trump; the terms are set out in the warrant itself, which the Pardon Attorney's page links. See Political Corruption Cases in Philadelphia for the wider record.[3][4]

3 Political role

Local 98's website describes its political program: it says it supports candidates who support working people and has advocated, for example, statewide licensing of electricians, prevailing wage and project labor agreements. Its political committee spending is a subject examined in Political Action Committees and Big Money and Campaign Finance in Philadelphia. After the convictions, the Board of Ethics and federal oversight remained important in scrutinizing relationships between union money and officials. See also Labor and Politics in Philadelphia.

4 Work and jurisdiction

Local 98 says its mission is to supply its contractor partners in the National Electrical Contractors Association (NECA) and end-users with a trained union workforce, including a Sound & Communication division for telecommunications work. Members work in the electrical, telecommunications and broadcast industries in Philadelphia and surrounding counties, and train through the local's Apprentice Training Academy. Their work on city and authority projects is shaped by prevailing wage and project labor agreements.[5]

See also: Organized Labor in Philadelphia, Conflicts of Interest and Pay-to-Play.

Philadelphia Federation of Teachers

Philadelphia Federation of Teachers
TypePublic-sector education union (AFT Local 3)
PresidentArthur G. Steinberg (per pft.org, October 2026)
PredecessorJerry Jordan (president from 2007; succeeded in 2025, as reported)
MembersMore than 14,200 teachers, paraprofessionals, counselors, nurses, secretaries and other school staff (per pft.org)
EmployerSchool District of Philadelphia
Governing lawPennsylvania Act 195 of 1970
Websitepft.org

The Philadelphia Federation of Teachers (PFT) represents the teachers and many other employees of the School District of Philadelphia. It is an affiliate of the American Federation of Teachers and a member of the Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO. The PFT is an important voice in education politics, including debates over school funding, facilities and charter schools.[1]

1 Leadership and membership

The PFT's website lists Arthur G. Steinberg as president and Wendy G. Coleman as general vice president, with a treasurer, a secretary and vice presidents for different school levels. Steinberg succeeded Jerry Jordan, who had led the union since 2007; the Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO lists Steinberg as the representative of PFT Local 3 on its executive board. The union says it represents more than 14,200 people working in Philadelphia public schools: teachers, librarians, school nurses, counselors, psychologists and social workers, secretaries, paraprofessionals, classroom and non-teaching assistants, supportive services assistants, Head Start and early-learning center staff, Bright Futures teachers and staff, food service managers, and professional and technical employees.[1]

Every school or work location has an elected PFT building representative, backed by regional staff representatives and by information and personnel officers who take calls about emergencies. The union also administers a Health & Welfare Fund (dental, prescription and vision benefits) and a Legal Services Fund. Since 2023 it has worked with the Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO on "Union Experience Fairs" that introduce students to union apprenticeship programs.[2]

2 Bargaining

School employees bargain under Pennsylvania's Public Employe Relations Act, which allows teachers to strike in defined circumstances after mediation and fact-finding; see Public Sector Bargaining in Pennsylvania. The employer is the school district, governed by the mayor-appointed Philadelphia Board of Education, which replaced the School Reform Commission after the state-created commission ended in 2018. The district's funding comes from the city, the state and federal sources, and those streams strongly affect what it can offer; see Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia.

3 The 2025-2028 contract

The collective bargaining agreement posted on pft.org runs from September 1, 2025 through August 31, 2028. Its compensation article provides a 3 percent increase to all salary schedules on each of September 1, 2025, September 1, 2026 and September 1, 2027, and a lump-sum retention and re-engagement bonus of $1,400 for employees on the payroll at ratification, paid in the last payroll of October 2025. It also sets an annual $7,500 bonus for teachers who hold National Board certification, and lump-sum bonuses for eligible teachers who remain in schools designated by the Superintendent: $2,500 in September 2025 and 2026, and up to $5,000 in September 2027 and 2028. The PFT posts the contract, the 2026-2027 salary schedule and a summary of each of the contract's 32 articles on its site.

Other articles cover union security, fair practices, seniority and layoffs, a just-cause standard for discipline, professional development, the Peer Assistance and Review (PAR) program, and a dispute-resolution procedure with a three-step grievance process followed by arbitration. Article XXVIII, "Resolution of Differences by Peaceful Means," says the parties will settle differences peacefully and that the Federation will not engage in strikes or work stoppages during the agreement, and Article XXIX has the District agree to fund and not unilaterally abrogate the contract's economic provisions. Exact language matters in an individual dispute, so members are directed to the posted agreement and to their building representative.[3]

4 Role in education policy

The PFT says it advocates politically on behalf of members and students, and describes its commitments as reducing class sizes, expanding early childhood education, making schools safe and orderly, and providing resources for teachers, staff and students. It is also an affiliate of the American Federation of Teachers and of the Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO; school funding and charter school policy are matters it weighs in on before City Council and in Harrisburg. Its political involvement is part of Labor and Politics in Philadelphia. Also see Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia for state education funding.

See also: Organized Labor in Philadelphia, Teamsters in Philadelphia.

TWU Local 234 and SEPTA Labor

TWU Local 234 and SEPTA Labor
TypeTransit workers' union local
PresidentWill Vera (listed on the Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO board, October 2026)
MembersOperating and maintenance employees of SEPTA
EmployerSEPTA (Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority)
Latest contractTentative two-year agreement reported in December 2025 (SEPTA and the Inquirer)
Parent bodyTransport Workers Union of America

Transport Workers Union Local 234 (TWU 234) is the Philadelphia local of the Transport Workers Union of America. It represents bus, subway, trolley and other operating and maintenance employees of SEPTA, the regional transit authority. Because SEPTA is a state-created authority rather than a city agency, its labor relations are governed by Pennsylvania law and by federal transit labor rules rather than by the city's collective bargaining structure. Disputes involving TWU 234 nonetheless affect city commuters directly and often draw in the governor and the General Assembly.[1]

1 Union and employer

Will Vera is listed as the Local 234 representative on the executive board of the Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO. SEPTA was created by the Pennsylvania General Assembly on August 17, 1963 to coordinate government funding for transit and railroad companies in southeastern Pennsylvania, and began operating on February 18, 1964. It is governed by a 15-member board, most of whose members are appointed by the five counties it serves; two are appointed by the City of Philadelphia, one by the Mayor and one by the City Council President. Labor and fringe benefits made up about 71 percent of SEPTA's roughly $1.53 billion in operating expenses in fiscal 2021, which is why wage settlements are central to the authority's finances.[2]

SEPTA has a long record of stoppages: strikes occurred in 1977, 1981, 1983, 1986, 1995, 1998, 2005, 2009, 2014 and 2016. Not all involved TWU 234; the 1983 and 2014 stoppages, for example, were by Regional Rail unions. The authority's governing structure and its relationship with Philadelphia are described in SEPTA.[2]

2 The 2025 contract

SEPTA announced a tentative contract agreement with TWU 234, which it called its largest transit workers union, in December 2025, and the Philadelphia Inquirer reported on December 8, 2025 that a strike had been averted, and a later Inquirer report on December 18, 2025 covered the deal. Press accounts described a two-year agreement. The individual wage and benefit terms are set out in the agreement itself, which SEPTA and the union can provide; see Public Sector Bargaining in Pennsylvania for the legal framework that applies to public transit employees.[3]

3 Other SEPTA unions and the funding question

SEPTA also bargains with other unions, including those representing rail engineers and supervisors. SEPTA's wage settlements are tied to the authority's operating funding, which depends on state transit funding, local contributions and fare revenue; funding fights in Harrisburg are discussed in Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia. Bus drivers who work for private contractors, such as the school-transportation drivers who joined Teamsters Local 623 in 2024, are outside SEPTA's bargaining units.

4 Politics and public impact

Local 234 is affiliated with the Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO and has been a visible participant in campaigns on transit funding. Transit strikes affect schools, hospitals and businesses; residents can follow service alerts on SEPTA's own channels. See Office of Transportation, Infrastructure and Sustainability for the city's transportation role.

See also: Organized Labor in Philadelphia, Public Sector Bargaining in Pennsylvania.

Teamsters in Philadelphia

Teamsters in Philadelphia
TypePrivate and public-sector union locals
Regional bodyTeamsters Joint Council 53 (Philadelphia area)
Local 623 leaderRichard Hooker Jr., Secretary-Treasurer (per Teamsters releases, 2024-2026)
Locals107, 623, 830, 502 (Commonwealth Association of School Administrators)
Parent bodyInternational Brotherhood of Teamsters

The Teamsters in Philadelphia are the area locals of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters. They represent workers in warehousing, package delivery, bus and paratransit driving, ambulance services and, through one local, school administrators. Teamsters locals in the region are part of the wider network described in Organized Labor in Philadelphia, and several are affiliated with the Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO.[1]

1 Locals and leaders

Teamsters locals are separate unions with their own officers; the Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO's executive board lists James O'Mara for Teamsters Local 107 and Daniel Grace for Teamsters Local 830. Local 623, which describes itself as representing 2,100 warehouse workers, package-car drivers, bus drivers, paratransit drivers and others in the Philadelphia area (April 2026), is led by Secretary-Treasurer Richard Hooker Jr., according to the International Brotherhood of Teamsters' press releases.[2]

Teamsters Local 502 is the Commonwealth Association of School Administrators (CASA), the union of principals and other administrators in the School District of Philadelphia. In a district press release dated November 24, 2025, CASA President Dr. Robin Cooper announced a tentative four-year agreement with the District, which Superintendent Tony Watlington also welcomed. An earlier tentative agreement between the same parties was announced in November 2024.[3]

2 Transport, EMS and school workers

Local 623 has grown through organizing in transportation. On March 1, 2024 the Teamsters announced that 209 bus drivers and attendants at Philadelphia Transportation, a company providing student transportation, had voted by more than 90 percent to affiliate with Local 623; the union said the local had represented the same bus yard (or "barn") years earlier. On March 27, 2025 the Teamsters announced that these workers had ratified their first contract, a three-year agreement that includes a grievance and arbitration procedure and route bidding by seniority. On April 27, 2026 the union announced that 218 paratransit drivers, emergency medical technicians and paramedics at Ambulnz had voted to join Local 623.[4]

Operators of the region's public transit system, SEPTA, are mainly represented by a different union, TWU Local 234, not the Teamsters. The airport and the port, described in Port and Bridge Authorities, also employ freight, logistics and service workers who may be represented by various unions.

3 Legal framework

Private-sector Teamsters locals, such as the units at bus companies and ambulance services described above, are covered by the National Labor Relations Act and the National Labor Relations Board, whose Region 4 office is in Philadelphia; its election and unfair labor practice cases are public records on nlrb.gov.[5] School administrators in Local 502 are public employees and fall under Pennsylvania's laws; see Public Sector Bargaining in Pennsylvania.

4 Politics

Teamsters locals take part in the labor council and in political endorsements; see Labor and Politics in Philadelphia. Endorsements are made by the individual unions and councils, so a local's choices do not necessarily match those of the national union.

See also: Service and Health Care Unions, Philadelphia Building and Construction Trades Council.

Service and Health Care Unions

Service and Health Care Unions
TypePrivate-sector service, health care and hospitality unions
Major unionsDistrict 1199C, SEIU Healthcare Pennsylvania, 32BJ SEIU, UNITE HERE Local 274, UFCW Local 1776, CWA Local 13000
Governing lawNational Labor Relations Act (private sector)
Notable 2026 eventHotel contract dispute in Center City (strike deadline of June 12, 2026 reported in May; picket lines reported by the union as of October 2026)

Service and health care unions represent much of Philadelphia's private-sector workforce outside construction and manufacturing: hospital and nursing home staff, janitors and security officers, hotel and restaurant employees, retail workers and telecommunications workers. They are especially important because "eds and meds" institutions are the city's largest employers; see Eds and Meds Anchor Institutions.[1]

1 Health care unions

District 1199C of the National Union of Hospital and Health Care Employees, an AFSCME affiliate, is the long-standing Philadelphia health care workers' union. Chris Woods took over as president in 2019 from longtime president Henry Nicholas, who became president emeritus; according to the Philadelphia Tribune story republished by the Pennsylvania Capital-Star, Nicholas had built the local to more than 11,000 members. In October 2021 the national union removed the local's leadership and appointed a trustee and a deputy trustee to run it; Woods said the national union cited unpaid per-capita dues and called the move political, while the national union could not be reached for comment in that report.[3] The Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO's executive board lists Dionne Gary as District 1199C's representative (October 2026). SEIU Healthcare Pennsylvania also represents health care and long-term care workers across the region. Both unions press for staffing standards and wages at hospitals and nursing homes, and for state Medicaid funding; see Department of Public Health.

2 Building service and hospitality

32BJ SEIU represents janitors, security officers and other building service workers; its national site says it also includes airport workers, window cleaners, building engineers and school and food-service workers across the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic. The Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO lists Daisy Cruz as the representative of SEIU 32BJ's Mid-Atlantic Region on its executive board.

UNITE HERE's Philadelphia website says the union represents about 7,000 hotel, gaming and food-service workers, including Local 274 (about 4,000 private-sector hotel and food-service workers at stadiums, universities, cafeterias and hotels), Local 634 (about 2,200 public-sector school cafeteria employees and noontime aides in the School District) and Local 54 (about 800 workers at a Chester casino plus Atlantic City gaming workers). Rosslyn Wuchinich is listed as Local 274's representative on the AFL-CIO council's board. In May 2026 the Inquirer reported that Local 274 had set a June 12 strike deadline at five downtown hotels, with the FIFA World Cup and July 4 celebrations approaching. As of October 2026, the union's own "Philly travel alert" page says that union hotel contracts in Center City have expired, that picket lines have gone up at some hotels, and it lists the Hilton Garden Inn Center City and the Four Points by Sheraton Philadelphia Northeast as "at risk" of labor disputes; the page does not describe how the June 12 deadline was resolved at each hotel.[2]

3 Retail, communications and higher education

UFCW Local 1776 represents grocery and retail workers; Wendell Young IV is listed as one of its representatives on the Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO board, and the council's president, Daniel Bauder, is listed as affiliated with UFCW Local 1776. The Communications Workers of America Local 13000 represents communications and public-sector workers; Jim Gardler of CWA Local 13000 is the Council AFL-CIO's secretary-treasurer. Organizing at the University of Pennsylvania has also grown; the Council AFL-CIO says it founded the Coalition of Workers at Penn in 2023 for unionized and not-yet-unionized Penn workers. See Worker Centers and Labor Advocacy for non-union organizing.

4 Role in politics and policy

The Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO, to which many of these unions are affiliated, says it supports city worker-protection legislation, including the National Domestic Workers POWER Act, and the Office of Worker Protections. These unions engage in elections through the AFL-CIO council and through their own committees; see Labor and Politics in Philadelphia.

See also: Organized Labor in Philadelphia, Teamsters in Philadelphia.

Philadelphia AFL-CIO Council

Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO
TypeCentral labor council
PresidentDaniel P. Bauder (UFCW Local 1776)
Other officersJim Gardler, Secretary-Treasurer (CWA Local 13000); Marcial Gonzalez, Recording Secretary (Laborers Local 57); Patrick Eiding, President Emeritus
AffiliatesOver 100 local unions
Workers representedOver 150,000 working people (per the council)
Parent bodyAFL-CIO
Websitephillyaflcio.org

The Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO is the local central labor body that brings together affiliated unions from many sectors for political action, community campaigns and solidarity. It does not itself bargain contracts; individual unions such as DC 33 and the PFT do that. The council is distinct from the Building and Construction Trades Council, which coordinates construction unions.[1]

1 Leadership and structure

The council's website lists Daniel P. Bauder (UFCW Local 1776) as president, Jim Gardler (CWA Local 13000) as secretary-treasurer, Marcial Gonzalez (Laborers Local 57) as recording secretary and Patrick Eiding as president emeritus. Eiding led the council for about two decades, according to the Philadelphia Inquirer, which reported on December 29, 2022 that he was retiring at age 82. The council's delegates, who represent every affiliate, meet monthly; they elect three executive officers and 35 vice presidents from among their ranks, along with trustees and representatives of constituency groups. The executive board includes leaders of unions across the economy, such as AFSCME DC 33 (Greg Boulware), DC 47 (April Gigetts), the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers (Art Steinberg), TWU Local 234 (Will Vera), District 1199C (Dionne Gary), UNITE HERE Local 274 (Rosslyn Wuchinich) and construction unions such as IBEW Local 98 (Mark Lynch Jr.) and the Building and Construction Trades Council (Ryan Boyer).[2]

2 Functions

The council describes its mission as bringing social and economic justice to working people by giving them a voice on the job, in politics and in the community. It runs a year-round political program and a get-out-the-vote effort for union members and their families; works on organizing, with a "Unionize Philly!" intake form for workers who want help forming a union; and has run the Coalition of Workers at Penn, which it founded in 2023 for unionized and not-yet-unionized Penn employees. It also runs Union Experience Fairs with the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers, which have introduced students to union apprenticeship programs since 2023, and "Worker Power 66," a training program for union members who run for committee person or other local offices. It does not itself bargain contracts; individual unions such as DC 33 and the PFT do that.[1]

3 Election activity and policy campaigns

The council prepares union households for elections through voter resources and canvassing; its 2026 voting-resources page says the November 3, 2026 general election is a priority and lists registration and mail-ballot deadlines. See Elections in Philadelphia and Labor and Politics in Philadelphia. Its policy page lists legislation it has supported, including the National Domestic Workers POWER Act, the Philly Black Worker Project's "All Due Respect" campaign and the "ICE Out" legislation sponsored by Councilmembers Kendra Brooks and Rue Landau, along with advocacy for semi-open primaries and for the Office of Worker Protections, for which it says it seeks more funding and staff.[1]

4 Relationship to other labor bodies

Affiliation is voluntary, and the council describes its membership as over 100 local unions. Many unions, such as the Building and Construction Trades Council, also have their own council and political operations. Pennsylvania's state federation and the national AFL-CIO set broader policy, while regional bodies such as the council focus on the Philadelphia area. For other worker organizations see Worker Centers and Labor Advocacy.

See also: Organized Labor in Philadelphia, Political Parties in Philadelphia.

2025 DC 33 Strike

2025 DC 33 Strike
UnionAFSCME District Council 33 (about 9,000 workers)
EmployerCity of Philadelphia (Parker administration)
BeganJuly 1, 2025
Tentative agreementJuly 9, 2025
Ratification1,535 to 838 (vote concluded July 20; announced July 21)
Cost to cityAbout $115 million (as reported)

The 2025 DC 33 strike was a work stoppage by approximately 9,000 blue-collar and related employees of the City of Philadelphia that began on July 1, 2025, and lasted about eight days. It was a major municipal strike that affected trash collection, recreation centers, pools and libraries, while emergency services including 911 continued.[1]

1 Background and demands

The union's previous contract had expired, and it bargained with the administration of Mayor Cherelle Parker. DC 33 initially sought raises of 8 percent per year and later lowered its ask to 5 percent. The union also opposed city proposals concerning control of medical claims payments, a surcharge for smokers and changes to sick leave and work policies. Union leaders emphasized low pay: the Fortune account noted that some sanitation wages were reported as low as $46,000 a year. The city, bound by a five-year plan reviewed by PICA and wary of the cost of precedent for other unions, said it was offering what it could afford.[2]

2 The strike

The union announced the strike early on Tuesday, July 1, 2025. Mayor Parker announced that residential trash collection would be suspended, some city pools would close, recreation center hours would be shortened, and temporary drop-off sites for garbage would be set up, where waste piled up. Libraries closed. Emergency services remained staffed. Many municipal services residents rely on, including those of the Streets Department, Parks and Recreation and Free Library, were affected. Pennsylvania law permits many civilian city employees to strike; see Public Sector Bargaining in Pennsylvania.

3 The agreement

A tentative agreement was reached on July 9, and the strike ended. The three-year deal, for 2025 to 2028, provides 3 percent annual raises, about 9 percent over the term, a $1,500 bonus, a fifth pay step for most members, a third step for school crossing guards, and expanded bereavement leave (four days for the death of a close family member). The city estimated the cost at about $115 million.

4 Ratification and reaction

A seven-day in-person vote at the union's West Philadelphia headquarters ran from July 14 to July 20. Of 2,375 votes counted, 1,535 supported ratification and 838 opposed; the American Arbitration Association certified the result, and union president Greg Boulware said the city should begin issuing bonuses. Roughly three-quarters of members did not vote, according to the Inquirer. Some members expressed dissatisfaction, and union leaders said they would return to the table in three years. DC 47, the city's white-collar union, reached its own tentative agreement on July 15, avoiding a second walkout.[3]

5 Aftermath

The strike became a reference point for subsequent bargaining with police and firefighters, whose Act 111 arbitration awards are covered in FOP Lodge 5 and IAFF Local 22. It also influenced debates about city wages and the city budget, and is an example in Labor and Politics in Philadelphia.

See also: Organized Labor in Philadelphia, Mayor of Philadelphia, Philly311.

References

Labor and Politics in Philadelphia

Labor and Politics in Philadelphia
TypeTopic overview
Key actorsAFL-CIO Council, Building Trades, DC 33, DC 47, FOP Lodge 5, PFT, IBEW Local 98
ChannelsEndorsements, PACs, volunteers, lobbying, bargaining
Related lawCampaign finance, Board of Ethics rules, Acts 111 and 195

Labor and politics in Philadelphia describes how unions influence elections, officeholders and policy in a city where organized workers are numerous and the municipal government is itself a large unionized employer. Unions act in three ways: as bargaining counterparts of the city, as political organizations that endorse and mobilize, and as lobbyists on specific legislation.[1]

1 Unions as bargaining counterparts

The mayor negotiates with unions whose members elected, or could vote against, the mayor. In 2025 the Parker administration settled with DC 47, the DC 33 strike, and the FOP in the same summer; see DC 47 and FOP Lodge 5. City Council sets the budget in which settlements are funded, and PICA reviews the five-year plan.

2 Endorsements and mobilization

Union endorsements in mayoral, Council, District Attorney and statewide races provide money, volunteers and credibility; see Elections in Philadelphia and Political Action Committees and Big Money. The Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO coordinates much of this. In September 2026 FOP Lodge 5 endorsed Gov. Josh Shapiro for a second term, and in August 2026 the Building Trades Council campaigned against Republican gubernatorial candidate Stacy Garrity. In July 2026, after an arbitration award that the union considered inadequate, IAFF Local 22 president Mike Bresnan said the union would approach prospective mayoral candidates, which the Inquirer described as a shift for a traditionally less political union.

3 The building trades and development

The Building Trades have significant influence over development: their support or opposition affects proposals, subsidies and zoning fights, and they press for union labor requirements discussed in Prevailing Wage and Project Labor Agreements. See Developers and the Real Estate Lobby.

4 Corruption cases and oversight

The most prominent labor-related corruption case involved IBEW Local 98. Former business manager John Dougherty was convicted in 2021 of a scheme that included bribery of Councilmember Bobby Henon, and in 2023 of embezzlement from the union. He was sentenced to six years in July 2024; former president Brian Burrows received four years. These cases are summarized in Political Corruption Cases in Philadelphia. City rules on contributions and conflicts are described in Campaign Finance in Philadelphia and Board of Ethics.

5 Recent developments

In 2025 and 2026 labor shaped the agenda on police discipline (The FOP Contract and Police Discipline), municipal wages, worker protection law (Office of Worker Protections) and transit (TWU Local 234). Critics argue that union influence can limit reform or raise costs; supporters argue it secures fair wages and public services. Both are positions attributed to participants in these debates.

See also: Organized Labor in Philadelphia, Democratic City Committee, Progressive and Grassroots Politics.

References

Prevailing Wage and Project Labor Agreements

Prevailing Wage and Project Labor Agreements
TypePublic contracting labor standards
City lawChapter 17-107 of the Philadelphia Code (city public-works contracts)
PLAsSet by project and by mayoral executive order; current order listed on phila.gov
EnforcerOffice of Labor Standards, Department of Labor (laborstandards@phila.gov; 215-683-5492)
RelatedPennsylvania Prevailing Wage Act (state projects); federal Davis-Bacon Act

Prevailing wage laws require contractors on public projects to pay workers at least locally prevailing wage and benefit rates. Project labor agreements (PLAs) are pre-hire collective bargaining agreements between a project owner or contractor and construction unions that set employment terms for a specific project. Both tools are central to the agenda of the Building and Construction Trades Council.[1]

1 Prevailing wage

Three layers apply. Federal projects follow the Davis-Bacon Act; state-funded public works follow the Pennsylvania Prevailing Wage Act of 1961[3]; and the City of Philadelphia applies its own rules to city contracts. The city explains that a contractor with a public-works contract with the City must pay the prevailing wage, a pay package determined by the U.S. Department of Labor or by the City, to anyone performing work on that contract. The wage depends on the type of work (heavy and highway construction, building construction, service or residential) and on whether the contract is federal or City. Employers on City public-works contracts must meet the Davis-Bacon Act and Chapter 17-107 of the Philadelphia Code. Both the City and the federal government update their prevailing wage rates regularly, and the City posts its rates on phila.gov.[1]

The rules are enforced by the Office of Labor Standards in the City's Department of Labor, which also negotiates with City unions and administers the worker-protection laws covered in Office of Worker Protections. The Department of Labor says it makes sure that employers with City contracts pay prevailing wages.[1]

2 Project labor agreements

A project labor agreement is negotiated for a specific project, so its terms can differ from one project to the next: the owner or lead contractor and the building trades agree in advance on wages, hours, hiring and dispute procedures, and typically agree that no strikes or lockouts will occur during construction. Whether the City requires a PLA on a particular public project depends on the City's policy and on mayoral executive orders, which are posted on phila.gov under executive orders; current thresholds and requirements should be confirmed with the Procurement Department or the contracting agency before bidding. The trades' view of PLAs is described in Philadelphia Building and Construction Trades Council, and IBEW Local 98's website lists defending prevailing wage and project labor agreements among its political priorities.[2]

3 Enforcement and how to report problems

The Office of Labor Standards monitors contractors on city public-works contracts, which must submit weekly payroll information through the LCP Tracker system to show they are paying the prevailing wage and must take part in job-site visits by wage compliance officers. A worker who believes there has been a violation can complete the city's prevailing wage violation form, ideally with pay stubs, personal records of hours worked and information about the employer's pay practices, and submit it by email to LaborStandards@phila.gov or by mail; the office can also be reached at 215-683-5492. The process is similar to complaints handled by the Office of Worker Protections. For contract bidding rules, see Understanding City Contracts and Bids.

4 The policy debate

Supporters, including unions, say prevailing wage and PLAs raise standards, support apprenticeships and ensure skilled workers, and that they promote diversity commitments associated with the trades; see Building Trades. Critics, including some open-shop contractors and fiscal conservatives, argue that they raise costs and limit competition. The effect on costs is disputed in academic literature, and the disagreement is not settled. See also Labor and Politics in Philadelphia.

See also: Organized Labor in Philadelphia, IBEW Local 98, Commerce Department.

References

  1. City of Philadelphia, "Report a prevailing wage violation" and "City prevailing wage rates," phila.gov; Philadelphia Code, Chapter 17-107.
  2. City of Philadelphia, Mayor's executive orders, phila.gov/departments/mayor/executive-orders; IBEW Local 98, "Politics," ibew98.org.
  3. Pennsylvania Prevailing Wage Act of 1961 (43 P.S. section 165-1 et seq.); Davis-Bacon Act (40 U.S.C. section 3141 et seq.).

The FOP Contract and Police Discipline

The FOP Contract and Police Discipline
TypePolicy explainer
PartiesCity of Philadelphia and FOP Lodge 5
Legal basisAct 111 of 1968; collective bargaining agreement and interest arbitration awards
Latest awardAugust 15, 2025 (fiscal 2026-2027)
Related bodiesPolice Board of Inquiry, Citizen Police Oversight Commission, labor arbitrators

The FOP contract and police discipline refers to the way the labor agreement between the City of Philadelphia and FOP Lodge 5 governs how officers of the Philadelphia Police Department are investigated, disciplined and, if fired, may appeal. The contract is set by negotiation or by interest arbitration under Pennsylvania's Act 111, not by City Council.[1]

1 How discipline works

Internal Affairs and other units investigate complaints; residents can also file complaints through the Citizens Police Oversight Commission, which refers them to Internal Affairs (see Police Accountability Systems). Where discipline is serious, a Police Board of Inquiry hears the case and recommends a penalty; the police commissioner decides. Officers who are disciplined may grieve the decision, and the union may take a termination to binding labor arbitration before a neutral arbitrator, who decides whether the city had "just cause." Under Act 111, courts review such awards only narrowly.[2]

2 Arbitration outcomes

Newspaper analyses describe a high rate of success for the union. The Philadelphia Inquirer reported in 2019 that, in the cases it examined from 2011 to 2019, arbitration overturned or reduced discipline about 70 percent of the time and that the city paid substantial back pay. A 2024 Inquirer analysis, also reported by Axios Philadelphia, said that between 2022 and early 2024 arbitrators reinstated 85 percent of fired officers whose terminations the FOP contested. The Inquirer also reported in 2025 on disputes over deleted disciplinary records. These are reports of outcomes in individual cases, based on the newspaper's reading of the records, and they do not resolve questions about any particular officer. Arbitration decisions turn on the evidence record, the discipline of other officers in similar situations, and the contract's procedures.[2]

3 The 2025 award and oversight

In the 2025 interest arbitration, the city sought changes to discipline procedures, and the union sought rollbacks of transparency and accountability measures. According to City & State and other reports, the award did not adopt the union's rollbacks, denied the FOP's proposal to exclude the Citizen Police Oversight Commission, and made one discipline-related change: reinstatement is contingent on completing all conditions of employment. Critics, including some reform advocates, said the contract fell short of disciplinary reform, while the union has said that arbitration protects officers' due process. The wage and benefit terms, which the city announced on August 15, 2025 as 3 percent increases in each of fiscal years 2026 and 2027, a $3,000 bonus and longevity-pay adjustments tied to civilianization, are summarized in FOP Lodge 5.[3]

4 Perspectives

City leaders note that Act 111 gives arbitrators wide authority and courts narrow review; see Public Sector Bargaining in Pennsylvania. Reform groups, including those described in Good Government Groups, argue that reinstatement rates undermine accountability. The union responds that its members are entitled to a fair process. Residents with complaints about police conduct can use channels described in Police Accountability Systems and How to File a Complaint. This article is general civic information, not legal advice.

See also: Philadelphia District Attorney's Office, Labor and Politics in Philadelphia.
