  3. City & State Pennsylvania, "New Philly police union contract falls short on disciplinary reform"; Philadelphia Inquirer, "Police arbitration FOP Philadelphia CPOC" (January 29, 2025) and "Philadelphia police arbitration FOP deleted records" (July 10, 2025).

Office of Worker Protections

Office of Worker Protections
TypeCity office (within the Department of Labor)
DirectorCandace Chewning (as reported 2025-2026)
Governing lawPhiladelphia Code, Title 9; POWER Act (Bill No. 250065)
EnforcesPaid sick leave, Fair Workweek, wage theft, domestic worker protections, anti-retaliation
Websitephila.gov (Worker Protections)

The Office of Worker Protections (OWP) is the part of the City of Philadelphia's Department of Labor that investigates complaints and enforces local workplace laws. It is a city office, distinct from state agencies such as the Pennsylvania Department of Labor and Industry and from federal agencies such as the U.S. Department of Labor, whose enforcement of federal wage laws also applies in Philadelphia.[1]

1 Laws enforced

OWP enforces local ordinances in Title 9 of the Philadelphia Code, including paid sick leave, the Fair Workweek law (which requires covered retail, hospitality and food service employers to provide good-faith estimates of schedules and 14 days' advance notice, with predictability pay for changes), wage theft protections and protections for domestic workers. Candace Chewning is listed as the office's director, and has previously served as communications director and outreach coordinator there. Prevailing wage enforcement for city contracts is handled by a separate unit; see Prevailing Wage and Project Labor Agreements.

2 The POWER Act of 2025

City Council unanimously passed the Protect Our Workers, Enforce Rights (POWER) Act, Bill No. 250065, on May 8, 2025. Mayor Cherelle Parker signed it on May 27, 2025. The law updates provisions on paid sick leave, wage theft, domestic worker protections, fair workweek, retaliation and enforcement. It creates a rebuttable presumption of unlawful retaliation if an employer takes adverse action within 90 days after an employee files a complaint, cooperates with OWP, opposes an unlawful practice or tells others about alleged violations, and it strengthens penalties for noncompliant employers. Councilmember Kendra Brooks said Philadelphia was stepping up as federal labor enforcement weakened, and Philadelphia AFL-CIO president Daniel Bauder praised its domestic worker retaliation protections. The Department of Labor and the Commerce Department prepared educational materials for businesses.[2]

3 Making a complaint

Workers can file complaints through phila.gov, for example for a Fair Workweek violation, and the office investigates and may order back pay and penalties. Employers receive notices and an opportunity to respond. Residents who are unsure which agency handles a dispute can start with How to File a Complaint or Philly311. Immigrant workers may also find help from groups listed in Worker Centers and Labor Advocacy and the Office of Immigrant Affairs. This is general information, not legal advice.

4 Results and resources

The city reported that OWP recovered a record $327,976.56 for workers in 2023, an 82 percent increase over 2022. Advocates and Council members have pressed for more staffing and funding in budgets, as reported by WHYY, since enforcement capacity determines how many complaints can be resolved; see Philadelphia City Budget Process. See also Office of Workforce Development.

See also: Organized Labor in Philadelphia, Philadelphia AFL-CIO Council, Philadelphia City Council.

Worker Centers and Labor Advocacy

Worker Centers and Labor Advocacy
TypeCommunity-based nonprofit organizations and coalitions
ExamplesJuntos; Philadelphia Workers Association; domestic worker organizing; Coalition of Labor Union Women chapter
ServesLow-wage, immigrant, domestic and gig workers; workers without union contracts
Related city officeOffice of Worker Protections

Worker centers are community-based organizations that provide education, legal referrals, organizing support and advocacy for workers who generally lack a union contract. Unlike unions, they typically do not bargain collective agreements; they instead pursue wage claims, policy changes and public campaigns. In Philadelphia they operate alongside unions and the Office of Worker Protections.[1]

1 What worker centers do

Typical activities include know-your-rights workshops, assistance filing wage theft and retaliation complaints, English classes, leadership training and organizing campaigns against specific employers. Because many members are immigrants or work informally, centers often coordinate with legal aid providers; see Legal Aid and Public Interest Law. Law school clinics have also supported the model; Temple University's Center for Social Justice has published guidance on creating a worker center in Philadelphia.[2]

2 Organizations in Philadelphia

Juntos is a community-led Latinx immigrant organization in South Philadelphia that combines leadership development with organizing around workers' rights, education and immigration. The Philadelphia Workers Association is another group listed in nonprofit directories. National domestic worker organizations took part in public hearings on the 2025 POWER Act. The Philadelphia chapter of the Coalition of Labor Union Women, led by Koren Parker according to City & State's 2026 list, connects union women and community advocates. Unions such as UNITE HERE Local 274 and 32BJ SEIU also run community organizing programs that overlap with worker centers. The AFL-CIO council frequently partners with them.

3 Policy campaigns

Worker advocates were prominent in supporting the POWER Act and earlier measures such as paid sick leave and Fair Workweek, and in pressing for enforcement resources in the city budget. They also engage with immigration policy; see Office of Immigrant Affairs. Some centers receive foundation support; see Philanthropy in Philadelphia. Their political role is discussed in Labor and Politics in Philadelphia and Progressive and Grassroots Politics.

4 Getting help

Workers with a pay or retaliation problem can contact the city's Office of Worker Protections, the state Department of Labor and Industry or the federal Wage and Hour Division, or a worker center or legal aid group. Tenants who are also workers may find overlapping help in Tenant and Housing Advocacy Groups. This is general information and not legal advice.

See also: Organized Labor in Philadelphia, Civic and Neighborhood Associations.

Finance Department

Office of the Director of Finance
TypeCity-charter executive department (city and county functions)
Led byFinance Director Rob Dubow (as of March 2026)
Appointed byThe Mayor
Budgeted staff147 General Fund positions proposed for FY27 (up from 142 in FY26)
Reports to FinanceRevenue, City Treasurer, Office of Property Assessment, Board of Pensions and Retirement
Seat onEx officio, non-voting member of the PICA board
Websitephila.gov/departments/office-of-the-director-of-finance

The Office of the Director of Finance, usually called the Finance Department, is the City of Philadelphia's central financial office. It writes the Mayor's operating budget and Five Year Plan, keeps the City's books, runs citywide payroll and risk management, and supervises the agencies that collect and hold public money. Because Philadelphia is both a city and a county, the Finance Director's portfolio covers functions that elsewhere are split between municipal and county governments. The post is filled by the Mayor under the Home Rule Charter. As of March 2026 the Director was Rob Dubow, who testified to City Council with First Deputy Finance Director Cat Lamb and Deputy Finance Director Elizabeth Hanley.[1]

1 What Finance does

Finance describes its mission as keeping the City fiscally stable while meeting the Mayor's policy goals. In practice it oversees financial, accounting and budgetary functions, sets fiscal policy guidelines, records and reports all City financial activity, administers payroll and risk management, issues financial reports and monitors expenditures and grants.[1] Its largest internal units include:

  • The Budget Office, which develops the operating and capital budgets and the rolling Five Year Plan and also houses the City's central Grants Office. The Budget Director appointed in November 2024 is Sabrina Maynard, a longtime Finance official.[2]
  • Accounting, which maintains the central accounting system and produces the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report; the department aims for its 46th consecutive Certificate of Achievement for Excellence in Financial Reporting from the Government Finance Officers Association.[1]
  • Central Payroll, which processes weekly payroll for nearly 31,000 active City employees, and the OnePhilly office, which manages the enterprise system for human resources, payroll, pensions and fringe benefits.[1]
  • The Office of Risk Management, which handles insurance, workers' compensation and liability exposure. Beginning in FY27 it also manages a new Vacatur Fund to give early financial and social support to people whose convictions have been vacated.[1]
  • The Administrative Services Center, which provides fiscal and administrative support to several offices, including Procurement, the Treasurer and the Office of Human Resources.

2 Agencies in the Finance cluster

Four agencies report to the Finance Director: the Department of Revenue, the City Treasurer's Office, the Office of Property Assessment and the Board of Pensions and Retirement.[1] Together they set property values, bill and collect taxes, manage cash, debt and investments, and pay retirement benefits. The Finance Director also sits as an ex officio, non-voting member of the board of the Pennsylvania Intergovernmental Cooperation Authority, the state-created body that reviews the City's Five Year Plan.[3]

3 Budget, reserves and credit ratings

The adopted Fiscal Year 2027 General Fund (July 2026 to June 2027) projects revenues of about $6.58 billion and expenditures of about $7.13 billion, with an estimated year-end fund balance of $364.6 million, or 5.5 percent of revenues. The Plan also builds a Budget Stabilization Reserve projected at $290 million in FY27 and re-establishes a $91 million Federal Funding Reserve to cushion possible federal cuts.[4] The FY27-31 Five Year Plan was approved by the PICA board in July 2026.[5] See How to Read the City Budget for a guide to the documents.

Finance and the Treasurer's Office also manage the City's credit. According to the Finance Director's testimony, Fitch upgraded the City from A to A+ in June 2024 and S&P Global did the same in November 2024, citing pension funding and reserve building; in November 2025 Moody's moved its outlook from stable to positive.[1] Higher ratings lower the interest the City pays on borrowing for infrastructure.

4 Systems and oversight projects

With the Office of the Chief Administrative Officer and the Office of Innovation and Technology, Finance is leading Project OPAL (Optimizing Procurement and Accounting Logistics), a replacement of the City's accounting, contracting and procurement systems, with a targeted go-live of July 2027.[1] Finance has also said it will engage an independent outside consultant to evaluate the accuracy, equity and methodology of the Tax Year 2027 property revaluation by the Office of Property Assessment.[1] That review follows questions raised by some Council members about the new assessments, reported in July 2026.[6] Finance also supports the Procurement Department and Treasurer in expanding a purchasing-card pilot.

5 Staffing and size

For FY27 Finance requested 147 budgeted General Fund positions, including two for the new Vacatur Fund. The department reported an average full-time salary of $95,551 and 132 positions filled as of November 2025. Its proposed FY27 General Fund budget for the office itself was about $23.7 million.[1] Much larger sums flow through Finance's appropriation lines, including fringe benefits, indemnities, refunds, the contribution to the School District and the Budget Stabilization Reserve, which the budget ordinance appropriates "to the Director of Finance."[7]

6 How residents encounter Finance

Most residents deal with Finance indirectly: a tax bill from Revenue, a property value from OPA, a pension check from the Board of Pensions. Contract bidders encounter its payment and risk-management rules (see Understanding City Contracts and Bids). Requests for public financial documents, such as Budget in Brief editions and the annual financial report, are published on phila.gov; see also How to Request Public Records. The independent City Controller, an elected official, audits Finance and the rest of City government.

See also: Philadelphia City Budget Process, Philadelphia Taxes, PICA, Revenue Department, City Treasurer.

Revenue Department

Department of Revenue
TypeCity-charter executive department (serves city, county and School District)
Led byRevenue Commissioner Kathleen McColgan (as of March 2026)
Reports toDirector of Finance
Budgeted positions645 across all funds for FY27 (642 in FY26)
FY27 General FundAbout $33 million (adopted $33.1 million)
Other fundsWater Fund about $21.4 million proposed; Grants Fund $22.65 million proposed
Websitephila.gov/departments/department-of-revenue

The Department of Revenue is the agency that collects the money that pays for Philadelphia's government and a large share of its public schools. It bills, collects and enforces the City's taxes, the School District's property tax, water and sewer charges, and a range of fees and fines, and it also administers assistance programs for homeowners and water customers. It is one of four agencies in the cluster led by the Director of Finance. The Revenue Commissioner as of March 2026 was Kathleen McColgan, who testified to City Council with First Deputy Revenue Commissioner Delores Davis and Deputy Commissioner for Policy Rebecca Lopez Kriss.[1]

1 Mission and functions

Revenue's stated mission is the accurate and timely collection of revenue to support City services and the School District of Philadelphia, while enrolling eligible customers in available assistance and relief programs.[1] Its portfolio includes the wage and earnings tax, net profits tax, Business Income and Receipts Tax (BIRT), sales and use taxes, the beverage tax, realty transfer tax, and the real estate tax. The Office of Property Assessment sets the value of each property, and Revenue applies the tax rate, mails the annual bills and collects payment. For Tax Year 2027, for example, Revenue is scheduled to mail real estate tax bills on December 1, 2026, with payment due March 31, 2027.[2]

Revenue also bills and collects water, sewer and stormwater charges on behalf of the Philadelphia Water Department. A share of its budget is paid from the Water Fund rather than the General Fund. The department is working with the Water Department, the Law Department and the Office of Innovation and Technology to replace its legacy water billing system, with vendor selection in FY27 and a planned launch in FY29.[1]

2 Enforcement and collections

Revenue pursues delinquent accounts through liens, payment agreements and legal action in partnership with the Law Department, whose Tax Litigation and Collections work files cases against non-payers. In its FY27 plan the department highlighted data-driven enforcement: automating the linking of delinquencies across tax and debt types, improving audit lead generation and lien management, and bringing consolidated lawsuits against owners of multiple delinquent properties. It also continues Sheriff's Sale and "sequestration" efforts aimed at delinquent commercial, vacant and stormwater-only properties.[1] Sheriff's sales are carried out by the Sheriff's Office. A Tax Benefit Review Unit audits whether homeowners enrolled in tax-relief programs remain eligible.

3 Assistance programs

Revenue administers several programs that reduce what low- and middle-income owners and water customers pay. For real estate taxes, a combined Real Estate Tax Assistance Application launched in the first quarter of FY26 consolidates five programs into one bilingual form.[1] The City's June 2026 assessment announcement lists the Homestead Exemption (a $100,000 reduction in taxable value, saving most homeowners about $1,399), an eleven-month installment plan, a Senior Citizen and Low-Income Tax Freeze, the Longtime Owner Occupants Program (LOOP), and an Owner-Occupied Real Estate Tax Payment Agreement.[2] On water, the Tiered Assistance Program (TAP) and the Senior Citizen Discount reached a record of more than 83,000 customers, and Revenue plans to resume recertification in FY27 and introduce incremental penalty forgiveness for TAP customers who pay their monthly bills in full.[1]

4 Technology and customer service

The Philadelphia Tax Center is the online portal where individuals and businesses file, pay and manage accounts. Revenue's FY27 plans include more self-service tools, increased direct-deposit (ACH) refunds and better internal customer-contact features. The department also participates in the "PHL Open for Business" effort to streamline licensing and tax registration across agencies.[1] The department's FY26 budget included one-time concourse renovation costs for its public service area, which were removed from the FY27 request.

5 Budget and staffing

The FY27 proposed General Fund budget was $33,001,889, an increase of about $1.1 million over FY26 estimated spending, driven by postage, outreach for real estate tax assessments and wage increases. The department budgeted 645 positions across all funds, with 533 filled as of November 2025; its average full-time salary was $63,366 and its General Fund vacancy rate for FY25 was 13.5 percent.[1] Council adopted a General Fund appropriation of $33.1 million in June 2026.[3] Revenue's contracts with outside vendors are subject to the City's goals for minority-, woman- and disabled-owned and small and local business participation, discussed in Office of Economic Opportunity.

6 Disputes and appeals

Different disputes go to different bodies. A property owner who thinks the market value is wrong asks OPA for a First Level Review and then appeals to the Board of Revision of Taxes. Disputes about tax interest, penalties and assessments (rather than property value) go to the separate Tax Review Board. Residents with questions can call the department or use the Tax Center. See How to Get Help From the City and How to File a Complaint.

See also: Finance Department, Philadelphia Taxes, Office of Property Assessment, City Treasurer.

Office of Property Assessment

Office of Property Assessment (OPA)
TypeCity agency within the Finance cluster
Led byChief Assessment Officer James Aros Jr. (as of June 2026)
Properties valuedMore than 580,000
FY27 General Fund$21.97 million (adopted)
Appeals bodyBoard of Revision of Taxes (after OPA First Level Review)
Address601 Walnut St., Suite 300 W., Philadelphia, PA 19106
Websitephila.gov/departments/office-of-property-assessment; property.phila.gov

The Office of Property Assessment (OPA) determines what every piece of property in Philadelphia is worth for tax purposes. Those market values, multiplied by the combined City and School District real estate tax rate, produce the bills that Revenue mails each year, so OPA's work underpins a large part of the budget for both the City and the School District of Philadelphia. The office reports to the Director of Finance. Its Chief Assessment Officer as of June 2026 was James Aros Jr.[1]

1 What OPA does

OPA values more than 580,000 properties using computer-assisted mass appraisal (CAMA) technology, imagery and market data.[1] It maintains the public property database at property.phila.gov, which shows ownership, sales history, valuation and physical characteristics. It also processes applications for the Homestead Exemption, tax abatements (see Tax Abatement and Development Incentives), nonprofit tax exemptions, lot line changes and catastrophic loss adjustments.[2] OPA does not set tax rates; those come from City Council for the City share and from the School District's approved budget and Council action for the schools' share. The combined real estate tax rate has been 1.3998 percent of assessed value, split between the City and the School District, with the split adjusted over time.[3] Since the Actual Value Initiative, which took effect for tax year 2014, assessments are meant to reflect full market value rather than a fraction of it.

2 Relationship to the Board of Revision of Taxes

Historically the independent Board of Revision of Taxes (BRT) both valued property and heard appeals. After disputes in 2010 between the Nutter administration and the BRT over reassessment, valuation was moved to OPA, and the BRT now serves as the appellate body.[4] The City's current description is that OPA sets values and handles First Level Review, and the BRT is the next level of appeal.[5] The separation matters for residents: the office that set the value is not the one that decides whether it was wrong.

3 The Tax Year 2027 reassessment

OPA began mailing Notices of Valuation for Tax Year 2027 on June 29, 2026. The new values take effect January 1, 2027. The City reported that the citywide median valuation change was about 3 percent compared with the 2025 tax year and that the estimated change in the real estate tax bill for the median-valued residential property was approximately $97.[1] The City had skipped a reassessment for Tax Year 2026, and a plan for annual reassessments announced earlier was not carried out in that form, according to news reports.[6] The Philadelphia Inquirer reported large differences between neighborhoods, with median increases of 15.3 percent in Kensington, 15 percent in Mantua and 12 percent in Kingsessing.[7]

4 Appeals and tax relief

Owners who disagree with a value have two steps for Tax Year 2027: ask OPA for a First Level Review by September 1, 2026, then file a formal appeal with the Board of Revision of Taxes by October 5, 2026.[1] A filing may argue that the value is too high, does not match comparable properties, or rests on wrong facts such as square footage or condition. Separately, the City lists relief programs: the Homestead Exemption (a $100,000 reduction in taxable value, enrollment deadline December 1, 2026), an eleven-month installment plan, the Senior Citizen and Low-Income Tax Freeze and the Longtime Owner Occupants Program (both with a September 30, 2027 deadline), and payment agreements.[1] OPA's hours listed at phila.gov are Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., with a hotline at (215) 686-9200.[2] See also How to File a Complaint.

5 Oversight and controversy

The 2027 values drew scrutiny. According to the Inquirer, a letter signed by six Council members and authored by Councilmember Mike Driscoll asked the administration for answers on methodology by August 15; the City Controller was conducting a performance audit; and an outside consultant was engaged to examine the fairness of the reassessment, with a report due at year's end.[7] The Finance Department confirmed in its March 2026 testimony that it would retain an independent consultant to evaluate accuracy, equity and methodology and that it plans a request for proposals for a customer relationship management system for OPA.[8] The City Controller is the elected independent auditor of City agencies.

See also: Board of Revision of Taxes, Philadelphia Taxes, Revenue Department, Tax Abatement and Development Incentives.

Board of Revision of Taxes

Board of Revision of Taxes (BRT)
TypeCity board (appellate body for property assessments)
MembersSeven; chaired by James T. Dintino (as of 2026)
Related panelBoard of View (three members)
FY27 General Fund$1.30 million (adopted)
2027 appeal deadlineOctober 5, 2026
Address601 Walnut St., Suite 325 East, Philadelphia, PA 19106
Contact(215) 686-4343; appealinquiry@phila.gov
Websitephila.gov/brt

The Board of Revision of Taxes (BRT) is the City body that hears appeals from property owners who believe the value assigned to their property by the Office of Property Assessment (OPA) is wrong. Property taxes in Philadelphia are the product of two numbers: the assessed market value and the tax rate. The BRT does not set rates or the tax bill; it reviews the value. For many years the Board also valued property itself, but that function now sits with OPA, leaving the BRT as an independent second look.

1 Role and jurisdiction

The BRT "hears property assessment appeals." Owners can appeal if they believe the assessed value is incorrect, does not match the values of comparable properties, or contains errors about square footage or condition. Beyond market-value cases, the Board also handles denied tax abatement applications, denied nonprofit exemptions, late (nunc pro tunc) petitions, Homestead Exemption matters and eminent domain awards.[1] The City describes the sequence as OPA first, through First Level Review, and the BRT as the next level of appeal.[1] A decision of the Board can in turn be challenged in the Pennsylvania courts, ordinarily the Court of Common Pleas (see Court of Common Pleas and Municipal Court); an owner weighing that step should consult the Board or a lawyer for the current procedure.

2 Structure

The City's website lists seven Board members: James T. Dintino (Chairman), Hon. Eugene E.J. Maier (Vice Chairman), Wayne A. Johns (Secretary), John Paul Simpkins, Janice M. Sulman, Hon. Renee Cardwell-Hughes and Daniel A. Rendine.[2] A separate three-member Board of View, chaired by James J. O'Connell with members Eileen H. Lynn and Ronald C. Panepinto, is listed alongside it.[2] The Board has a small staff and a modest budget: Council's FY27 appropriation was about $1.3 million, of which roughly $1.2 million is personnel.[3] It is distinct from the elected row offices and from the City Controller.

3 How an appeal works

For the Tax Year 2027 reassessment, the City set the following sequence: Notices of Valuation were mailed starting June 29, 2026; the First Level Review request deadline with OPA was September 1, 2026; and the formal appeal deadline for the BRT is October 5, 2026.[4] The Board conducts market-value appeal hearings remotely by Zoom. Appellants log on at their scheduled time and wait in a virtual waiting room until their matter is called.[1] Owners generally strengthen a case with evidence such as recent sales of comparable homes, repair estimates or an appraisal, although the Board's published page does not list a fee schedule or evidence rules, and residents should check current instructions. Assistance programs such as the Homestead Exemption operate separately and can lower the tax bill even when the value stands; see Revenue Department.

4 History and reform

The BRT is one of the older appointed boards in City government. In 2010 a public dispute between Mayor Michael Nutter's administration and the Board over how and by whom properties would be reassessed came to a head when an agreement between them expired in April 2010, and on May 18, 2010 voters were asked whether to amend the Charter to let the City assume assessment duties from the Board, according to WHYY.[5] As the current system shows, valuation now sits with OPA within the Finance cluster, and the "Actual Value Initiative" reassessment took effect with tax year 2014. The Board's City web pages do not state how its members are appointed; see the Charter. Anyone researching the exact legal steps of that reform should consult the Charter and Council records; see Philadelphia Home Rule Charter.

5 Related bodies

The BRT should not be confused with the Tax Review Board, which hears appeals about City tax interest, penalties and other City assessments rather than property values.[1] Disputes over School District taxes, tax-lien sales and delinquency proceedings run through Revenue, the Law Department and the courts. For help finding the right office, see How to Get Help From the City.

See also: Office of Property Assessment, Philadelphia Taxes, Tax Abatement and Development Incentives.

Procurement Department

Procurement Department
TypeCity-charter executive department
Led byProcurement Commissioner Ronald L. Hovey (appointed March 2025)
Part ofOffice of the Chief Administrative Officer cluster
Formal bid thresholdContracts over $34,000 (as listed by the City, 2026)
FY27 General Fund$7.95 million (adopted)
Address1401 John F. Kennedy Blvd., Room 120, Philadelphia, PA 19102
Websitephila.gov/departments/procurement-department; contracts.phila.gov

The Procurement Department is the City of Philadelphia's central purchasing agency. Its stated mission is "managing and acquiring goods and services for the City of Philadelphia using a fair, open, and cost-effective process."[1] It is the office that issues bids and requests for proposals, certifies vendors' compliance with City rules and awards contracts for supplies, equipment, services, concessions and public works, alongside departments that run their own program-specific procurements. It sits within the cluster overseen by the Chief Administrative Officer. Mayor Cherelle Parker named Ronald L. Hovey as Procurement Commissioner in March 2025; his background includes nearly 40 years in public and private sectors, including Amtrak and New Jersey Transit, and negotiation of the contracts for the $1.5 billion Portal North Bridge replacement.[2]

1 How City purchasing works

Contracts valued over $34,000 require formal bidding through the PHLContracts platform. Businesses find opportunities on the Contracts Hub at contracts.phila.gov and submit bids electronically following the instructions in each solicitation.[1] Typical opportunities include supplies, equipment maintenance and repair, concessions on City property and environmentally responsible waste disposal. The department also supports vendors through a "PVCOOP" assistance contact. Smaller purchases may follow simpler quotation procedures. Contracts above certain amounts need approval steps involving the Law Department for form and legality, and the Finance Department for funds and risk management. For a step-by-step guide see Understanding City Contracts and Bids.

2 Public works and professional services

Construction or improvement of public property, streets, bridges, highways and sewers follows a separate public-works bidding process.[1] Professional-services contracts, such as legal, consulting and investment management work, are generally selected through requests for proposals reviewed by committee. Departments report the dollar amounts awarded and the participation of minority-, woman- and disabled-owned firms in annual Council budget testimony; for example, the Finance Department reported $28 million in professional-services contracts for FY26 with 30 percent going to M/W/DSBE firms.[3] Conflict rules for firms that give to campaigns are summarized in Conflicts of Interest and Pay-to-Play.

3 Inclusion and small-business goals

The City sets a goal that 35 percent of contract dollars go to minority, woman and disabled-owned businesses (M/W/DSBEs) each year, monitored by the Office of Economic Opportunity.[4] The administration has also been building a registry of small and local businesses (S/LBEs) and setting participation goals for them; department testimony in 2026 lists goals in the range of 25 to 40 percent depending on the department, with some departments noting that S/LBE data are not yet available for earlier years.[3] In March 2025 Mayor Parker also named Nadir Jones as Director of Business Impact and Supplier Diversity in an Office of Business Impact and Economic Advancement, an office listed in the same announcement as Hovey's appointment.[2]

4 Systems modernization

Procurement is a partner in Project OPAL, the replacement of the City's accounting, contracting and procurement systems led by Finance with the CAO and the Office of Innovation and Technology, targeted to go live in July 2027.[3] The CAO's 2026 testimony said the administration streamlined the professional-services contract conformance process to give vendors fewer hurdles and clearer timelines and templates, and Procurement supported several citywide events in 2026.[5] Procurement's FY27 General Fund appropriation was about $7.9 million.[6] A purchasing-card (P-Card) pilot run with Finance and the City Treasurer aims to speed small purchases.

5 Oversight and ethics

City purchasing is subject to Charter and Philadelphia Code requirements, review by the City Controller, who must audit and can examine contracts and payments, and investigation by the Office of the Inspector General. Procurement officials and bidders are also covered by the rules of the Board of Ethics. Residents may report suspected fraud or waste on a contract to the Office of Economic Opportunity or the Inspector General; see How to Report Corruption or Misconduct.

See also: Understanding City Contracts and Bids, Office of Economic Opportunity, Chief Administrative Officer, Prevailing Wage and Project Labor Agreements.

Office of Human Resources

Office of Human Resources (OHR)
TypeCity-charter executive office
Led byChief Human Resources Officer Candi Blossom Jones (named November 2024)
Part ofOffice of the Chief Administrative Officer cluster
Budgeted positions108 for FY27 (106 in FY26)
FY27 General Fund$23.0 million (adopted)
Works underThe Civil Service Commission
Workforce servedNearly 31,000 active City employees

The Office of Human Resources (OHR) administers Philadelphia's civil service system, the merit-based rules by which most City employees are recruited, tested, classified and promoted. It acts "under the guidance of the Civil Service Commission" and works to attract, select and retain a qualified, diverse and effective workforce.[1] OHR is one of the departments in the cluster led by the Chief Administrative Officer. Mayor Cherelle Parker appointed Candi Jones, formerly Deputy Commissioner for Human Resources and Administration at the Water Department and First Deputy Director of OHR, as Chief Human Resources Officer in November 2024.[2]

1 Civil service functions

OHR's duties include workforce planning, job classification, pay evaluation, exam development and administration, test scoring and review, and drafting new or revised Civil Service Regulations to reflect changes in operations and labor agreements.[1] The Commission, a separate body with its own role in adopting the regulations and deciding appeals, is described in the article on the Civil Service Commission. The merit principle means, in broad terms, that eligible candidates are ranked by examination and hiring managers choose from certified lists, with exempt positions (appointed by officials, including most executives) outside those lists. OHR's staffing figures show that of its own 106 positions in FY26, 10 were exempt.[1]

2 FY27 priorities

In its March 2026 testimony to Council, OHR listed priorities: modernizing Civil Service hiring and identifying barriers, including the time it takes to hire; strengthening HR practice across departments through "HR University" training and circles for department HR managers; streamlining employee records and administration; and improving employee well-being and benefits education.[1] It cited Executive Order 3-24, which promotes alternative pathways to four-year college degrees for suitable jobs. The service-level target for civil service time-to-hire is 90 days or less. OHR also works with the City College for Municipal Employment (CCME), which trains residents for City careers; CCME and OHR are linked to the economic mobility agenda in the FY27 budget.[1][3]

3 Labor relations and unions

Most City workers are represented by unions, notably AFSCME District Council 33 (blue-collar and clerical workers), AFSCME District Council 47 (white-collar and professional workers), the Fraternal Order of Police Lodge 5 and IAFF Local 22. OHR supports the administration's labor-relations function, working with the Law Department and the Mayor's office. Jones's biography credits her with helping negotiate a contract extension for about 8,400 DC 33 members before the July 2025 strike, which is covered in 2025 DC 33 Strike.[2] The FY27-31 Five Year Plan includes a Labor Reserve with deposits totaling more than $605 million from FY26 through FY31 to fund future agreements.[4] The framework governing bargaining is explained in Public Sector Bargaining in Pennsylvania.

4 Size, vacancies and hiring speed

The Finance Department reports that the City has nearly 31,000 active employees paid through Central Payroll.[5] OHR itself had 95 of 106 budgeted positions filled as of November 2025 and requested 108 for FY27, adding two positions transferred from the CAO. The CAO's testimony credits OHR with reducing time to hire and vacancies and creating HR University.[6] Council appropriated about $23.0 million to OHR from the General Fund for FY27.[7]

5 Applying for a City job

Openings, exam announcements and the application portal are listed on the City's jobs website at phila.gov. Applicants for civil service titles typically apply for a specific exam or posting, may be required to take a written or performance test, and are ranked on certified lists. Residency rules (most employees must live in Philadelphia within a set period after hire) are set by ordinance and the Charter. Questions about discrimination or discipline may go to the employee's union, the Civil Service Commission or the Commission on Human Relations. See also How to Get Help From the City.

See also: Civil Service Commission, Chief Administrative Officer, Organized Labor in Philadelphia, Office of Workforce Development.

Law Department

City of Philadelphia Law Department
TypeCity-charter executive department
Led byActing City Solicitor Monique Myatt Galloway (since September 2, 2026, pending Council confirmation)
PredecessorRenee Garcia (City Solicitor from 2024; departure reported July 2026)
Size300+ attorneys, 120+ professional staff, 50+ interns (reported 2025)
FY27 General Fund$38.5 million (adopted)
Address1515 Arch Street, 17th Floor, Philadelphia, PA 19102
Phone(215) 683-5000

The Law Department is the legal counsel for the whole City government. Led by the City Solicitor, it represents the City and its officials and employees in litigation, negotiates and drafts contracts, prepares legislation, advises on regulatory compliance, represents the City in child-welfare and health matters, and collects unpaid taxes, fines and other debts.[1] It is both a municipal and a county law office, because Philadelphia is a consolidated city-county (see City-County Consolidation). The Solicitor is appointed by the Mayor and, as the 2026 transition shows, is subject to confirmation by City Council.

1 Leadership and recent transition

Mayor Cherelle Parker named Renee Garcia, a litigation chair at a private firm, as City Solicitor in December 2023, and she served from the start of the administration.[2] The Philadelphia Inquirer reported her resignation on July 28, 2026.[3] On September 3, 2026 the City announced that Monique Myatt Galloway had begun a transition into the role of Acting City Solicitor on September 2, pending City Council confirmation. Galloway had been an Assistant U.S. Attorney in the Civil Division of the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania since November 2023 and earlier served as regional counsel for the General Services Administration and Federal Transit Administration and as a Navy trial attorney; she also served on the Pennsylvania State Ethics Commission.[4] See US Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania.

2 Structure and practice areas

The department's website organizes its work into four main groups: Compliance and Legislation, Corporate and Tax, Litigation, and Social Services.[1] A 2025 year-in-review booklet describes units including Tax Litigation and Collections, Property Assessment, Boards and Commissions, Commercial Law, Real Estate and Development, Compliance, HIPAA and Privacy, Legislation and Legal Counsel, Right-to-Know, and E-Discovery and Data Strategies, and reports more than 300 attorneys, over 120 professional staff and more than 50 interns.[5] Council appropriated about $38.5 million from the General Fund for FY27, with about $23.7 million for personnel.[6] The Law Department also bills other funds, such as Water, for work done on their behalf.

3 Role in city government

The Law Department is involved in nearly every City function. It reviews contracts for form and legality (see Procurement Department and Understanding City Contracts and Bids), drafts bills for Council members, and issues legal opinions to officials. It defends the City in civil-rights, personal-injury and employment suits, with settlements and judgments paid through the Finance Department's indemnities appropriation. In tax matters, its Tax Litigation and Collections work supports the Revenue Department, including filing cases and pursuing Sheriff's sales. In land-use matters it represents the City before boards and commissions and in the Commonwealth Court. Its Right-to-Know unit advises agencies on requests under state law (see Right-to-Know Law and Public Records). During the federal policy changes of 2025 and 2026, the Budget Office reported working closely with Law to respond to changes in federal funding.[7]

4 Conflicts and limits

The Solicitor's client is the City as an institution, not individual officials or members of the public, and the Department does not give legal advice to residents. Independent elected officials such as the City Controller and the District Attorney are not Law Department clients in the same sense, and disputes among City officials sometimes lead to outside counsel or court rulings. Ethical standards for City lawyers are set by the Pennsylvania Rules of Professional Conduct, and the Board of Ethics enforces the City's ethics code. Tenants and residents seeking representation should look to Legal Aid and Public Interest Law.

5 Dealing with the Law Department

Claims against the City, such as injuries on public property, are subject to notice requirements and statutes under Pennsylvania law and should be pursued with a lawyer. Requests for City records go first to the agency that holds them; see How to Request Public Records. Organizational contacts are available at the department's offices at 1515 Arch Street.

See also: Mayor's Cabinet and Offices, Philadelphia Home Rule Charter, Finance Department, Philadelphia Sheriff's Office.

Office of Innovation and Technology

Office of Innovation and Technology (OIT)
TypeCity executive office (central IT agency)
Led byChief Information Officer Melissa Scott (as of March 2026)
Part ofOffice of the Chief Administrative Officer cluster
FY27 General FundAbout $159.6 million (adopted appropriation to the Mayor, Office of Innovation and Technology)
Senior teamChief Enterprise Officer, Chief Technology Officer, Chief Security Officer, Chief Financial Officer, Chief of Staff
Key projectsProject OPAL, 311 mobile app, citywide AI policy, digital equity

The Office of Innovation and Technology (OIT) is the central technology agency of the City of Philadelphia. It "provides the digital infrastructure, systems, and services that enable secure, efficient, and effective government operations," sets the City's information-technology strategy and oversees major technology projects and cybersecurity for City government.[1] Its head is the Chief Information Officer, Melissa Scott, a longtime OIT employee who joined the City in 2015 and was appointed by Mayor Cherelle Parker.[2] OIT is in the cluster supervised by the Chief Administrative Officer, and its funding is appropriated in the budget ordinance as part of the Mayor's office.[3]

1 Functions

OIT runs the City's networks, data centers and enterprise applications and provides services ranging from geographic information systems (GIS), data analytics and software development to multimedia design and the PHL GovTV channel.[1] It also leads the City's digital equity initiative and supports the 311 contact center's technology (see Philly311) and the City's open-data work (see Open Data and Transparency Tools). Because it serves all departments, from the Police Department to the Free Library, its decisions affect the whole government.

2 Resident-facing projects

In its March 2026 testimony to Council, OIT described several FY27 projects:

  • A new 311 mobile app with mobile-first reporting, photo upload and location services, scheduled to launch in August 2026 and described as the City's first in-house built mobile application.[1]
  • Expansion of PHL GovTV live streaming beyond the studio into neighborhoods and events.
  • A H.O.M.E. mobile application to give residents a single place to find housing resources under the Mayor's Housing Opportunities Made Easy initiative.
  • The 2026 Access Philly app consolidating event schedules and information for the city's 2026 events, including the nation's 250th anniversary celebrations.

3 AI governance and cybersecurity

OIT reported that the City's AI policy was published on March 24, 2026 after review by OIT, security, legal, ethics, integrity and labor stakeholders. Every AI tool must undergo a review process that includes a security evaluation, governance committee approval, risk assessment and operational clearance, with ongoing monitoring involving OIT, IT Security and the Law Department; the stated principles are ethical use, governance frameworks and data security, and employees are told AI should augment, not replace, their work.[1] A Chief Security Officer leads cybersecurity, and OIT is accelerating replacement of older PCs because they cannot support modern protections. The Fiscal Year 2027 budget lists technology as a core-support investment area, with $8.7 million in new core-support operating investments including technology.[4]

4 Digital equity

OIT runs the Power Up Tour, a program to distribute 500 free laptops and hotspots, 50 laptops to pre-registered residents in each of the ten Council districts; 367 had been distributed as of the testimony. Its Power Up Philly Community Tech Expo targeted 1,600 residents with training and laptops through more than 70 community partners, and the Digital Equity team won more than $2 million from the Pennsylvania Broadband Authority to expand capacity at 22 Parks and Recreation centers.[1] The Office for People with Disabilities works alongside OIT on digital accessibility.

5 Budget and internal systems

Alongside the Finance Department, OIT and the CAO are driving Project OPAL, the replacement of the City's accounting, contracting and procurement systems, targeted to go live in July 2027.[5] OIT is also supporting the Board of Pensions and Retirement's pension payroll modernization and Revenue's water-billing system replacement.[6] It runs workforce upskilling: in 2025-26 it held 116 training sessions for 1,014 employees on productivity tools.[1] The adopted FY27 appropriation to the Mayor for OIT was about $159.6 million, which includes personnel costs of about $38.3 million.[3] Large IT contracts follow the process in Procurement Department. The City Controller audits technology contracts and security as it does other City operations.

See also: Philly311, Open Data and Transparency Tools, Chief Administrative Officer, Right-to-Know Law and Public Records.

Chief Administrative Officer

Office of the Chief Administrative Officer (CAO)
TypeMayoral cabinet office (city executive branch)
Led byChief Administrative Officer, appointed by the Mayor Camille Duchaussee, per the City's leadership page
Budgeted positions134 proposed for FY27 (up 28 from FY26)
FY27 General FundAbout $13.6 million proposed; $13.9 million adopted
Address1401 John F. Kennedy Blvd., Suite 630, Philadelphia, PA 19102
Phone(215) 686-5238

The Chief Administrative Officer (CAO) is the senior City official responsible for the internal machinery of government: the offices that hire, buy, record and run technology for everyone else. Its mission is to "create and support conditions for City departments and workforce to deliver efficient, effective, and equitable City services."[1] The office is part of the Mayor's cabinet and works alongside, but separately from, the Managing Director, who oversees most service-delivery departments, and the Director of Finance.

1 The CAO cluster

According to the City's website, the CAO supervises eight entities: the Department of Records, the Office of Administrative Review (OAR), the Office of Innovation and Technology, the Office of Talent and Employee Success, the Office for People with Disabilities, the Procurement Department, the PHL Service Design Studio and Strategic Transformation.[2] In its March 2026 budget testimony the CAO appeared with the Chief Human Resources Officer (see Office of Human Resources), the Chief Information Officer, the Procurement Commissioner, the Records Commissioner, the Executive Director of the City College for Municipal Employment (CCME), and the executive directors of OAR and the Office for People with Disabilities.[1] Mayor Cherelle Parker's announcement of cabinet appointments in early 2024 named Camille Duchaussee as CAO,[3] and the City's department leadership page continued to list her as Chief Administrative Officer in October 2026.[2]

2 Programs run by the office

The CAO's FY27 budget document describes program areas including Administration, Innovation and Transformation, and the Office of Administrative Review, which handles administrative reviews and appeals of certain City actions.[1] The City College for Municipal Employment, a first-in-the-nation partnership to train residents for City jobs, is also in the CAO orbit. The CAO and Finance co-sponsor Project OPAL, the multi-year replacement of the City's accounting, contracting and procurement systems with a targeted July 2027 go-live.[4] The CAO reported in 2026 that its cluster had deployed digital workflow transformation tools for several departments, streamlined the professional-services contract process, expanded upskilling through CCME and the Office of Talent and Employee Success, and launched a national first-of-its-kind deed fraud protection through the Records Department.[1]

3 Budget and growth for FY27

The proposed FY27 General Fund budget for the CAO's own office was $13,599,931, an increase of about $1.5 million over FY26 estimated spending, mostly due to 28 new positions: CCME fellows, an HR manager, digital workflow automation support, a Digital Equity Manager for the Office for People with Disabilities, and staff for an Economic Mobility Cabinet.[1] The adopted appropriation was $13.87 million.[5] Of 106 positions budgeted in FY26 only 81 were filled in November 2025; the average full-time salary was $83,447. The cluster departments have their own separate appropriations, such as about $23 million for OHR and $159.6 million for OIT.

4 Role in the Mayor's agenda

The FY27 budget describes an Economic Mobility Cabinet and an Office of Financial Empowerment ($2.2 million) as part of the economic-opportunity pillar, and $10 million for workforce investments coordinated through CCME.[6] The CAO thus sits at the intersection of the Mayor's priorities and the City's own workforce pipeline: it develops skills inside government and helps open civil-service pathways, in coordination with the Civil Service Commission and municipal unions such as AFSCME District Council 33.

5 Public interaction

Residents rarely deal with the CAO directly. They meet its departments: Records when recording a deed, Procurement when bidding, OIT through apps and 311 technology, and the Office for People with Disabilities for accessibility. The CAO's central office takes inquiries at the number above. Complaints about City services are better routed through Philly311 and How to File a Complaint.

See also: Mayor's Cabinet and Offices, Managing Director's Office, How Philadelphia Government Is Organized, Finance Department.

Department of Records

Department of Records
TypeCity-charter department (also serves the county function of Recorder of Deeds)
Led byCommissioner James P. Leonard, who is also Recorder of Deeds (as of 2026)
DeputyDeputy Commissioner Tracey T. Williams
Part ofOffice of the Chief Administrative Officer cluster
FY27 General Fund$4.89 million (adopted)
AddressCity Hall, Room 156, Philadelphia, PA 19107
Contact(215) 686-2262; records.info@phila.gov

The Department of Records is the City office that keeps Philadelphia's official paper and electronic memory. Its responsibilities include recording real estate documents, managing records for City agencies, providing printing services and operating the City Archives.[1] Its head, the Records Commissioner, also holds the title of Recorder of Deeds for Philadelphia, a county function that in most Pennsylvania counties is performed by a separately elected officer. Philadelphia's consolidation of city and county government (see City-County Consolidation) and the Home Rule Charter placed that function in an appointed department rather than among the elected row offices. As of 2026 the Commissioner was James P. Leonard.[1]

1 Recording of deeds and land records

When a property is sold, mortgaged or otherwise transferred in Philadelphia, the instrument is recorded with the Department of Records, which creates the public chain of title. Recording does not itself prove ownership is valid, but it gives public notice and priority among competing claims. The realty transfer tax due on sales is collected at recording in coordination with the Revenue Department; see Philadelphia Taxes. Property valuations, by contrast, are set by the Office of Property Assessment, and sheriff's sales are run by the Sheriff's Office. The Department also modernized its payment process, according to the Chief Administrative Officer's 2026 testimony.[2]

2 Deed fraud and title programs

The Department reports establishing what the CAO's testimony described as a national first-of-its-kind deed fraud protection, designed to help owners guard against forged or fraudulent deed filings.[2] Its Tangled Title program assists eligible low-income people whose name is not on the deed of the home they live in, a common problem when an owner dies without a will and family members continue occupying the house.[1] Such clean-up of title can affect access to home repair grants, tax relief and the ability to sell. Related help is described in Legal Aid and Public Interest Law and Register of Wills and Clerk of Orphans' Court, since estates are handled by the Register of Wills.

3 City Archives and public access

The Department operates the City Archives, which holds historical City records, and the PhillyHistory.org photograph site, which provides over 30,000 photographs from the archives.[1] Public access to land records is a core function; to reach other City records, use the agency that created them or see How to Request Public Records and Right-to-Know Law and Public Records. The Department maintains records storage for agencies, which supports retention schedules and audit trails. Preserved records also serve historians and journalists; see Local News Media in Philadelphia.

4 Financial disclosures and regulations

Records hosts the public database of financial interest disclosure forms filed by City officials and employees, covering filings since 2015, as well as public safety reports, land records and notices of City regulations.[1] The disclosures are part of the City's ethics system, enforced by the Board of Ethics; see Conflicts of Interest and Pay-to-Play. The department also publishes proposed and adopted City regulations, which must be filed and made available before they take effect.

5 Budget and place in the City

Council appropriated about $4.9 million from the General Fund to the Department for FY27, of which about $4.0 million is personnel.[3] The Department reports to the Chief Administrative Officer, who oversees seven other offices and departments, and James Leonard appeared with the CAO team before City Council in March 2026.[2] Its counter in City Hall is open to the public; residents can call or email for hours and fees.

See also: Chief Administrative Officer, Philadelphia Land Bank, Rental Licensing and Landlord-Tenant Law in Philadelphia.

Department of Public Property

Department of Public Property (DPP)
TypeCity-charter executive department
Led byCommissioner Joseph Brasky (appointed March 2025)
Budgeted positions140 across all funds for FY27, level with FY26
FY27 General FundAbout $107.5 million (adopted main appropriation), plus separate lines for rentals and utilities
DivisionsAdministration, Facilities Management (field operations), Facilities (Quad-Plex), Real Estate and Planning
Websitephila.gov/departments/department-of-public-property

The Department of Public Property (DPP) takes care of the buildings that City government works in. It states its mission as serving "the City's workforce and community responsibly by providing quality facilities and workspaces."[1] That means cleaning, repairing and operating major municipal buildings, managing City-leased space, planning interior workspace and, since 2025-26, deploying vehicle barrier systems at special events. Commissioner Joseph Brasky, appointed by Mayor Cherelle Parker in March 2025, has 18 years with the City, starting as a Fire Department cadet and rising through maintenance and building-services management.[2] The Department should not be confused with the Philadelphia Land Bank or the Philadelphia Redevelopment Authority, which handle vacant and surplus land.

1 Divisions and duties

DPP's FY27 plan lists four areas.[1] Administration handles safety training and staffing. Facilities Management (Field Operations) monitors, updates, repairs and replaces building equipment to extend its life. Facilities (Quad-Plex) improves the experience of visitors in City-run public buildings and uses public spaces to share information about City services. Real Estate and Planning upgrades municipal workspaces through design and standardization of workstations and finishes, and handles leased space for departments. The Department's reach includes City Hall and other major civic buildings; consult phila.gov for the full list. Public access to those buildings and to the City Council chamber depends on DPP operations.

2 Special events and security

A prominent part of the 2026 plan was preparation for the year's mass events: the nation's semi-quincentennial, the FIFA World Cup and the Major League Baseball All-Star Game. DPP's Special Events Unit worked with vendors and other agencies, and the City obtained vehicle barrier systems that DPP is responsible for deploying, in coordination with the Office of Special Events and public safety agencies.[1] The Police Department, Fire Department and Office of Emergency Management lead security planning, while DPP supplies and positions equipment on City property.

3 Energy, sustainability and workforce

DPP works with the Office of Sustainability to replace outdated lighting with LED fixtures and installs energy-efficient materials and equipment in City-owned properties, supporting the Mayor's clean-and-green agenda. The Department also invests in training: it plans to increase high school interns from School District career and technical education programs and from the City College for Municipal Employment, anticipating onboarding three high school students into civil service Public Works Maintenance Trainee positions in FY27.[1] See Civil Service Commission and Office of Human Resources for the civil-service framework. Building trades employees are often represented by municipal unions such as AFSCME District Council 33.

4 Budget

The Department requested 140 budgeted positions across all funds, level with FY26; 116 were filled as of November 2025.[1] The budget ordinance has several Public Property lines for FY27: the main appropriation (about $107.5 million, of which roughly $10.5 million is personnel), a separate city subsidy line, space rentals and utilities for municipal buildings.[3] Because the main appropriation includes occupancy-related costs, it is much larger than the Department's payroll. Capital projects, such as building renovations, are funded through the capital budget; see Philadelphia City Budget Process.

5 Relationship to other agencies

DPP maintains buildings for others but does not make land-use policy. Disposition of City-owned land is guided by Council, the Department of Planning and Development and other land agencies; see Councilmanic Prerogative for the political practice around surplus property. Leases and major real estate contracts are reviewed by the Law Department and follow the rules in Understanding City Contracts and Bids. Fleet vehicles are managed separately by Fleet Services. Residents with a problem in a municipal building can report it through Philly311.

See also: Fleet Services, Department of Records, Managing Director's Office, Philadelphia Land Bank.

Fleet Services

Department of Fleet Services (DFS)
TypeCity-charter executive department
Led byCommissioner Joseph L. Rosati (as of March 2026)
DeputiesDr. K Wilson (Administration); John DeLeo (Operations)
Active fleetAbout 7,000 vehicles, including 700+ pieces of specialized equipment
Budgeted positions403 across all funds for FY27, level with FY26
FY27 General Fund$76.2 million proposed (down $2.8 million from FY26 estimate)
Reports toThe Mayor (City executive-branch department)

The Department of Fleet Services (DFS) keeps Philadelphia government moving. It ensures that "City vehicles and other automotive equipment are available, dependable, and safe to operate so that City departments and agencies can deliver services," and it is responsible for the acquisition, repair, maintenance and disposal of all City-owned vehicles and equipment.[1] That includes police radio patrol cars, fire pumpers and medic units, Streets Department and sanitation trash compactors and riding mowers. DFS also fuels City vehicles, and vehicles of quasi-City agencies such as the School District of Philadelphia, through its department-operated fuel stations.[1] Commissioner Joseph L. Rosati led the Department when it testified to City Council on March 31, 2026.

1 Core operations

DFS maintains an active fleet of approximately 7,000 vehicles, including more than 700 pieces of specialized equipment.[1] Its work-order system tracks vehicle usage and schedules preventive maintenance to reduce unscheduled breakdowns. The Department prioritizes the availability of core-mission vehicles: police radio patrol cars, fire medic units, fire pumpers and tiller ladders, and trash compactors.[1] A vehicle out of service can affect response times for the Police Department and Fire Department and trash collection by the Streets Department, so Fleet's performance is often visible only when it fails. It also handles fuel-tank replacement to comply with Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection mandates.

2 Replacement strategy

DFS pursues what it calls an Optimal Vehicle Replacement Strategy, replacing aged, inefficient vehicles with more fuel-efficient, technologically advanced ones. The focus is on sanitation and safety vehicles for the Police, Fire and sanitation departments.[1] Vehicle purchases are funded through a separate appropriation line, "Fleet Services - Vehicle Purchase," in the operating budget, and larger purchases are supported through the capital program (see Philadelphia City Budget Process). Purchases follow the competitive process described under Procurement Department; the Department told Council that heavy equipment has limited vendors, which affects small and local business participation.[1]

3 Clean fleet and electrification

DFS supports the Philadelphia Municipal Clean Fleet Plan. Its vehicle-procurement policy sets a hierarchy that prioritizes battery electric, then hybrid-electric, hybrid and compressed natural gas vehicles where applicable, and it plans to construct two more electric vehicle fast-charging stations in FY27.[1] This is part of the Mayor's clean-and-green agenda and the work of the Office of Sustainability.

4 Workforce and training

DFS operates a high school automotive internship and training program, planning to enroll 15 students in FY27, in partnership with the City College for Municipal Employment (CCME) for "power skills" training. After the two-year internship, many students are hired as Automotive Apprentices, a permanent civil service position.[1] Mechanics and drivers are among the City employees represented by unions such as AFSCME District Council 33; see Office of Human Resources and Civil Service Commission for hiring rules.

5 Budget and oversight

The proposed FY27 General Fund budget for DFS was $76,159,561, a decrease of $2,781,291 from FY26 estimated obligations, with funds for safety vehicles, fuel, parts and supplies; employee compensation was proposed at about $24.8 million.[1] Council's adopted FY27 appropriation for the main Fleet Services line was $60.8 million, with separate vehicle-purchase funding.[2] Fleet purchases and fuel costs are among the items audited by the City Controller. Residents who see a City vehicle behaving unsafely can report it via Philly311.

See also: Department of Public Property, Managing Director's Office, Streets Department, Office of Sustainability.

City Treasurer

City Treasurer's Office and Sinking Fund Commission
TypeCity office (appointive since 1953)
Led byCity Treasurer Jackie Dunn (as of March 2026)
Appointed byDirector of Finance, with Mayor's approval
DeputiesShakina Clark (Banking); Matt Bowman (Debt Management; Sinking Fund Executive Director)
Budgeted positions23 for FY27
FY27 General Fund$5.4 million (Treasurer); about $431 million proposed for Sinking Fund
GO credit ratingsA1 (Moody's, positive outlook); A+ (S&P, stable); A+ (Fitch, stable)

The City Treasurer's Office is the part of Philadelphia government that holds, moves and borrows money. Its mission is "to safeguard City funds, serve as the disbursement agent for all City-related payments, and invest excess funds to meet daily cash requirements," and it manages new and outstanding debt under the City's debt-management policies to improve and maintain credit ratings.[1] The Treasurer was once an elected official, but the 1951 Home Rule Charter recommended making it appointive, and a Council ordinance of October 16, 1953 provided that the Treasurer is appointed by the Director of Finance with the Mayor's approval.[2] The Treasurer reports within the Finance cluster. As of March 2026 the Treasurer was Jackie Dunn.[1]

1 Cash management and banking

The Treasurer's Office reconciles all 63 centrally managed bank accounts, invests cash to preserve principal and maintain liquidity, and provides departments with banking and treasury tools. It is expanding the purchasing-card (P-Card) program with Finance and the Procurement Department and pursues funds owed to the City that were escheated to the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.[1] The Office works daily with the Finance Director on cash and investments, including state and federal money that flows through City accounts, so delays in payments from Harrisburg or Washington can force changes in cash strategy. Professional-services contracts for investment management, legal counsel and an annual lending study account for most of its non-personnel spending.

2 Debt and credit ratings

According to the Treasurer's testimony, the City's general obligation bonds were rated A1/A+/A+ by Moody's, S&P and Fitch, "the highest combination of City ratings in decades," with Moody's outlook positive and the others stable. Water and wastewater bonds carry the same ratings; Philadelphia Gas Works is rated A3/A/A and the Philadelphia International Airport A1/A+/A+.[1] The upgrades followed pension reforms and reserve building (see Board of Pensions and Retirement). Ratings matter because they set the interest cost of the City's borrowing for streets, facilities and water infrastructure. The Treasurer also monitors the debt portfolio for refunding opportunities that cut debt service.

3 Sinking Fund Commission

The Sinking Fund Commission, whose executive director is the Deputy Treasurer for Debt Management, administers payment of principal and interest on the City's general obligation debt. For FY27 the Treasurer's testimony proposed a Sinking Fund budget of about $430.9 million, of which about $241.2 million was debt service and $189.7 million purchase of services; Council's adopted appropriation was about $421.9 million.[1][3] A portion of the City's General Fund pays this debt service. The Five Year Plan notes that a legacy pension obligation bond balloon payment drives a $64 million spike in debt service in FY29, which pushes the fund balance to a low point.[4]

4 FY27 plans

In the second half of FY26 the Treasurer planned to issue the first $400 million in Housing Opportunities Made Easy (H.O.M.E.) bonds, supporting the Mayor's plan to create or preserve 30,000 housing units, and a fourth $50 million Neighborhood Preservation Initiative transaction. In FY27 the Office planned about $200 million in Philadelphia Municipal Authority bonds and $400 million in Water and Wastewater Revenue bonds.[1] The Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation and the Division of Housing and Community Development are among the agencies that use these funds.

5 Budget and oversight

The Treasurer's General Fund budget for FY27 was proposed at $5,384,350 (23 positions; 21 filled in November 2025; average salary $88,377), mostly for professional services.[1] The Office is not directly affected by changes in state and federal funding. Borrowing requires Council authorization through bond ordinances, and the City Controller and the Pennsylvania Intergovernmental Cooperation Authority review City finances. Residents interested in bond documents can find official statements on the City's investor-relations pages and on EMMA, the municipal securities database.

See also: Finance Department, Philadelphia City Budget Process, PICA, How to Read the City Budget.

Board of Pensions and Retirement

Board of Pensions and Retirement
TypeCity board administering the Municipal Retirement System
Executive DirectorFrancis Bielli (as of March 2026)
Chief Investment OfficerChristopher DiFusco
Funded ratio67.7 percent (preliminary actuarial valuation, FY ending June 30, 2025); 44.8 percent in FY16
Assumed return7.20 percent (reduced March 2026)
Projected full fundingCalendar year 2032 (fiscal year 2033)
Administrative budget$16.5 million (FY27 appropriation, Pension Fund)
Charter dutyFund must always be able to cover current and future payments

The Board of Pensions and Retirement administers the City of Philadelphia's retirement system and pays retirement benefits to eligible members, beneficiaries and survivors. It also manages the assets of the City's Pension Fund, with the goal of "safety of the principal and maximizing returns (net of investment fees) at the lowest level of risk."[1] The Home Rule Charter requires that the fund always be able to cover current and future payments to eligible members who have paid in. The Board sits in the cluster led by the Director of Finance and is advised by an actuary; its trustees act as independent fiduciaries to the Fund and to employees.[1] Under the City's description of the Board, it consists of the Director of Finance (who serves as chairperson), the Managing Director, the City Solicitor, the Personnel Director, the City Controller, and four members elected by Civil Service employees; the City's site lists nine trustees in all. The Board's own website lists its current trustees.

1 The funding record

The preliminary actuarial valuation for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2025 reported an actuarial funding ratio of 67.7 percent. Since the 2016 pension reforms, the ratio has risen from 44.8 percent in FY16, and the Fund's net pension liability has fallen by nearly $3 billion; the Board said the current funding level is the highest in more than two decades.[1] The Fund has had break-even or positive net cash flow, not counting investment earnings, in seven of the last eight years, after only one such year in decades. Based on current assumptions, including City contributions under the Revenue Recognition Policy, the actuary projects 100 percent funding by calendar year 2032 (fiscal year 2033), compared with a projection of 2040 made in 2016.[1] The City Controller has reported that the Fund's assets have grown from about $4.6 billion to more than $10 billion over that period.[2]

2 Investments and fees

In March 2026 the Board voted to reduce the Fund's assumed rate of return for the fifteenth consecutive year, to 7.20 percent.[1] The Fund uses a diversified asset mix, with core public-equity exposure generally through low-cost index funds and active managers retained only where they add value. The investment manager fee ratio at FY25 year-end was 0.24 percent, compared with an average of 0.64 percent during FY11 to FY15, which the Board estimates has saved over $140 million in nine years.[1] Managers who miss objectives can face reduced assets, renegotiated fees or termination. The Board's Chief Investment Officer is Christopher DiFusco.

3 Members and services

The Board serves current and retired employees under several plans, including defined-benefit plans and defined-contribution components for newer hires (Plans 10 and 16). Nationwide is the third-party administrator of the 457 deferred compensation plan and the defined-contribution component of Plans 10 and 16; there were 29,789 participants in the 457 and 401(a) plans as of the first quarter of FY26, up from 24,495 in FY22.[1] About 97 percent of recipients receive benefits by direct deposit, and the Board offers retirement appointments in person, by phone and by mail. It is developing a Request for Information to modernize pension payroll systems, in line with the technology plans of the Office of Innovation and Technology. Questions about individual benefits should go to the Board directly.

4 Link to the City budget and credit ratings

City contributions to the Fund are one of the largest fixed costs in the operating budget. Rating agencies have cited improvement in the pension system; Moody's found in November 2024 that, among the 20 largest cities, only four besides Philadelphia had an adjusted net pension liability lower than 100 percent, and S&P cited the City's long-term commitment to the Fund when it raised the City's bonds to A+.[1] The Five Year Plan also includes a legacy pension obligation bond balloon payment that raises debt service by $64 million in FY29 (see City Treasurer).[3] The Pennsylvania Intergovernmental Cooperation Authority reviews the Five Year Plan, including pension funding.

5 Labor context

Pension benefits are bargained or set by ordinance for most employee groups, so changes affect and are affected by unions such as AFSCME District Council 33, AFSCME District Council 47, the Fraternal Order of Police Lodge 5 and IAFF Local 22. The Board credited a collaboration among trustees, the Mayor, past administrations, City Council, unions, the State Legislature and others in the recovery. See Public Sector Bargaining in Pennsylvania and Office of Human Resources.

See also: Finance Department, City Treasurer, PICA, City Controller.
