Philadelphia City Budget Process

Philadelphia City Budget Process
Fiscal yearJuly 1 to June 30
Prepared byMayor, through the Budget Office in the Finance Department
Adopted byCity Council by ordinance; signed by the Mayor
State reviewPICA must approve the Five Year Plan
FY27 operating budgetAbout $7.1 billion (General Fund expenditures $7.13 billion; revenues $6.58 billion)
FY27 capital budget$6.98 billion (as announced by Council; FY27-32 Capital Program)
Final Council passageJune 11, 2026
Five Year PlanFY27-31, approved by PICA July 28, 2026

The Philadelphia city budget process is the yearly cycle in which the Mayor proposes, City Council amends and adopts, and the state-created Pennsylvania Intergovernmental Cooperation Authority (PICA) reviews how the City will pay for its services. The City runs on a fiscal year that begins July 1, so a budget must be in place by the end of June. Because Philadelphia is a city and a county, its budget covers what other places split among municipal, county and sometimes school governments, although the School District of Philadelphia has its own budget and the City sends it local money.

1 Steps in the cycle

The Finance Department's Budget Office works with departments through the fall and winter to build proposals. The Mayor delivers a budget address to Council in March; Mayor Cherelle Parker gave the FY2027 address on March 12, 2026.[1] Council's Committee of the Whole then holds departmental hearings. In 2026 the Finance Director testified on March 25, the City Treasurer on March 24, and the CAO, Human Resources, Innovation and Technology, Public Property and Fleet Services departments on March 31.[2] Council members negotiate with the administration, changes are made in committee, and Council passes the operating and capital budget bills; the FY27 budgets received final passage on June 11, 2026.[3] The Mayor signed them into law, news reports said, within hours of the vote.[4] Tax bills, including rate changes, are separate ordinances needing votes of at least nine of Council's 17 members; see How a Bill Becomes Law in Philadelphia.

2 Operating, capital and the Five Year Plan

There are three linked documents. The operating budget pays for day-to-day services, salaries, benefits and debt service, mostly from the General Fund, with separate funds for water and sewer, the airport, grants and other purposes. The capital budget and six-year Capital Program finance buildings, streets, parks and water infrastructure, largely through borrowing; City Council's announcement of final passage described a $6.98 billion capital budget for FY27, alongside the FY27-32 Capital Program; capital figures describe borrowing and project authority over a multi-year program and are not comparable to the annual operating budget.[3] The Five Year Plan projects revenues and spending for the current and next four years and must be balanced; under the PICA Act, the City submits it to PICA, whose board votes on it. The PICA board approved the FY27-31 Plan unanimously on July 28, 2026.[6] The Mayor's Budget in Brief summarizes the adopted budget; see How to Read the City Budget.

3 The FY2027 budget

The adopted FY27 General Fund projects revenues of $6.578 billion, of which $4.84 billion (73.7 percent) comes from taxes and $797 million from the PICA portion of the resident wage tax; local non-tax revenue (fees, fines, permits) is projected at $435 million and state aid at $339 million. Expenditures total $7.13 billion, up $335.8 million (about 5 percent) from the FY26 estimate, driven by non-pension benefits, labor awards, a $91 million Federal Funding Reserve and deposits to a Labor Reserve (more than $605 million from FY26 to FY31).[5] New operating investments include $127.2 million for public safety, $51 million for economic opportunity and education, $12.1 million for housing and $9.2 million for clean and green initiatives, and the City's operating investment in SEPTA is $181 million.[5] Council dropped three of the Mayor's proposed revenue measures (a $1-per-trip ride-share tax, a hotel and short-term-rental tax and a retail delivery tax) after they failed to secure nine votes, and instead agreed to $48 million more for the School District and a new cell-tower use-and-occupancy tax change; see Philadelphia Taxes.[4]

4 Reserves and risks

The Plan estimates a fund balance of $364.6 million (5.5 percent of revenues) in FY27, falling to $59.1 million in FY29 as a legacy pension bond balloon payment lifts debt service by $64 million, then rising to $107.4 million at the end of the Plan. Including the Budget Stabilization Reserve (projected at $290 million in FY27) and the Federal Funding Reserve, total reserves are projected at $745.8 million in FY27, $495 million in FY29 and $543.2 million at the end; that meets the City's internal 6-8 percent target but is below the 17 percent recommended by the Government Finance Officers Association.[5] The budget document warns of risks from federal funding cuts (the City received over $2 billion in federal grants in FY25), the exhaustion of $1.4 billion in pandemic-era ARPA funds, and fringe benefits projected to rise 60.3 percent from FY25 to FY31 while total revenues grow 11.5 percent.[5]

5 How residents can take part

Residents can testify at Council's budget hearings and at public hearings on bills; see How to Testify at City Council. Organizations such as good-government groups publish budget analyses, and the independent City Controller reviews revenue estimates and audits spending. Budget documents and testimony are public; see Open Data and Transparency Tools.

See also: How to Read the City Budget, Finance Department, PICA, Philadelphia Taxes, Philadelphia City Council.

Nonresident wage tax3.425 percent from July 1, 2026
Real estate tax1.3998 percent of assessed value (City and School District combined)
Business Income and Receipts Tax5.71 percent net income; 1.410 mills gross receipts (tax year 2025)
Realty transfer tax4.578 percent (3.578 City plus 1 State) since July 1, 2025

Philadelphia taxes are the City's main source of revenue and a frequent subject of political debate. The City levies taxes under the Home Rule Charter and state enabling laws, but its power is limited by Pennsylvania law (see Home Rule Limits and State Preemption). The Revenue Department administers and collects most of them. About three-fourths of General Fund revenue comes from taxes, so changes to tax structure, such as the multi-year wage and business tax cuts adopted in 2025, shape the entire budget.

1 The main taxes and what they raise

The FY2027 adopted budget estimates the following General Fund tax receipts:[1]

  • Wage, earnings and net profits tax (City share): $2,179 million; the separate PICA share of the resident wage tax, remitted to the City after the authority's expenses, adds about $797 million (see PICA).
  • Real estate tax (City share): $1,012 million, up 9.74 percent from the FY26 estimate.
  • Business Income and Receipts Tax (BIRT): $806 million.
  • Real estate transfer tax: $377 million.
  • Sales tax (City share): $342 million. The sales tax is 8 percent in Philadelphia, 6 percent state and 2 percent local, as of 2026.
  • Philadelphia Beverage Tax: $72.5 million.
  • Other taxes (parking, amusement, tobacco and others): $55 million.

The City's budget analysis notes that education, medical institutions and government employment accounted for more than $1 billion in wage tax collections in FY25, about 45 percent, which makes the City's revenue sensitive to federal cuts to research and employment.[2]

2 Wage and business tax cuts

In June 2025 City Council approved, and the Parker administration continued in its FY27-31 Five Year Plan, a gradual reduction of the wage tax and BIRT.[3] The resident wage tax rate fell from 3.79 percent in July 2022 to 3.75 percent in 2023 and 2024, 3.74 percent from July 1, 2025 and 3.735 percent from July 1, 2026; the nonresident rate went from 3.44 percent to 3.43 percent in July 2025 and 3.425 percent in July 2026.[4] The City has said the rates will drop over time to 3.70 percent for residents and 3.39 percent for nonresidents. For BIRT, the net income rate fell from 5.81 to 5.71 percent for tax year 2025, while the gross receipts rate fell from 1.415 to 1.410 mills; the City said the gross receipts rate will decrease each year until it is eliminated in 2038.[3][5] Supporters argue the cuts help attract residents and employers; critics, including some Council members, worry about the loss of revenue at a time of federal uncertainty.

3 Property taxes and relief

The real estate tax rate is applied to the market value set by the Office of Property Assessment; appeals go to the Board of Revision of Taxes. The combined rate is 1.3998 percent, split between the City and the School District, with the split shifting by year (0.6159 percent City and 0.7839 percent School District for tax year 2025).[6] The Tax Year 2027 reassessment, effective January 1, 2027, raised the citywide median value about 3 percent and the estimated bill for the median-valued home by about $97.[7] Relief includes the Homestead Exemption (a $100,000 reduction in taxable value, saving most homeowners about $1,399; enrollment deadline December 1, 2026), an eleven-month installment plan, a senior and low-income tax freeze, the Longtime Owner Occupants Program and payment agreements.[7] Pennsylvania's constitutional uniformity requirement means the City cannot charge different rates to commercial and residential property, a point the Mayor cited when ruling out a property tax increase in 2026.[8] Tax abatements for new construction are covered in Tax Abatement and Development Incentives.

4 Other taxes and the 2026 Council action

The use and occupancy (U&O) tax applies to commercial uses of property at 1.21 percent of assessed value. Effective January 1, 2027 the tax on cell towers will be calculated on the tower's assessed value only, expected to generate about $2.4 million a year for public schools.[9] The realty transfer tax rose to 4.578 percent (3.578 percent City and 1 percent Commonwealth) on July 1, 2025.[3] The Parker administration proposed a $1-per-trip ride-share tax, a hotel and short-term-rental tax and a retail delivery tax for FY27, but all three failed to get the nine votes needed in Council and were dropped in June 2026.[8] A proposed change to require remote sellers to remit the local sales tax, worth about $1.5 million a year, would require action by the state legislature.[10] See Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia.

5 Appeals and where the money goes

Disputes about tax interest, penalties and non-property assessments go to the Tax Review Board; disputes about property value go to the BRT. Revenue also runs assistance programs for water and property tax. Revenue from taxes pays for services in the City budget and helps fund schools, SEPTA and the pension fund. For help understanding a bill see How to Get Help From the City.

See also: Revenue Department, Finance Department, Philadelphia City Budget Process, How to Read the City Budget.

Pennsylvania Intergovernmental Cooperation Authority (PICA)

Pennsylvania Intergovernmental Cooperation Authority (PICA)
TypeState-created authority (Commonwealth of Pennsylvania)
Established1991, under the PICA Act for Cities of the First Class
ChairAlan C. Kessler (as of 2026)
Executive DirectorMarisa G. Waxman, reappointed effective January 29, 2025
BoardFive voting members appointed by state leaders; two non-voting ex officio members
Direct assistance to City$1.138 billion through debt issuance
FY27 PICA City Account$797 million (resident wage tax share after PICA expenses)
Websitepicapa.org

The Pennsylvania Intergovernmental Cooperation Authority (PICA) is a Commonwealth of Pennsylvania authority created by the General Assembly in 1991 in response to a severe fiscal crisis in the City of Philadelphia, which was then running growing deficits with a deteriorating credit rating.[1] It is not a City agency and the Mayor and City Council do not control it. The PICA Act authorized it to provide financial oversight, issue bonds and require the City to develop and adhere to Five Year Financial Plans.[2] More than three decades later, the authority continues its oversight role: each year the City submits a plan, and the PICA board reviews whether it is balanced on reasonable assumptions.

1 Origins

By 1990 and 1991 Philadelphia faced large deficits, and the state stepped in with legislation permitting the City to borrow to eliminate its deficit in exchange for state oversight. The PICA Act clarified that the authority's debt "shall not be a debt or liability of the Commonwealth or a city of the first class." Its stated objectives included enabling access to capital markets for deficit elimination, fostering sound financial planning, and fiscal measures such as better tax collection, asset sales and procurement reform.[2] PICA made available $1.138 billion in direct assistance to the City through debt issuance.[3] Its original bond-issuing powers have expired and it is now limited to refinancing existing PICA debt.[3] The episode is part of the City's political history and the relationship between the City and the state (see Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia).

2 Structure and leadership

The board has five voting members, one each appointed by the Governor, the President pro tempore of the Senate, the Senate minority leader, the Speaker of the House and the House minority leader, and two non-voting ex officio members: the Secretary of the Budget of the Commonwealth and the City's Director of Finance.[4] As of October 2026, PICA's website lists the chair was Alan C. Kessler, with Rosalind W. Sutch as vice chair, Michael A. Karp as secretary/treasurer, Patrick Burns as assistant secretary/treasurer and Kevin Vaughan, who had been chair for ten years, as a member.[4] Marisa G. Waxman, AICP, is Executive Director, with Rob Call as Deputy Executive Director.[5] The staff is small.

3 Powers

The key power is review of the Five Year Plan. Under the Act, the City must produce a plan annually and PICA must find it balanced on reasonable assumptions; the Act (Act 6 of 1991, 53 P.S. § 12720.101 et seq.) provides that the authority approves a plan that meets its criteria by a “qualified majority vote,” defined in section 104 as a majority of the board that includes any four voting members (a four-of-five threshold, per a secondary summary).[3] If the City is out of compliance, PICA may direct the Commonwealth's budget secretary to withhold state financial assistance. PICA also conducts independent audits and financial examinations, and receives reports from the City on its financial results. The authority therefore functions as a check alongside the independent City Controller, the Council, and the credit rating agencies, which have cited PICA oversight in their analysis.

4 The PICA tax

PICA receives a portion of the wage, earnings and net profits tax paid by residents. After debt service and its own operating costs, it remits the balance to the City's General Fund. In the FY27 budget this "PICA City Account" is projected at $796.9 million, about 12 percent of General Fund revenue and the majority of the $1.23 billion the City counts as revenue from other governments.[6] The City's wage tax rate and the PICA share are shown together in Philadelphia Taxes; residents pay one combined rate (3.735 percent from July 2026) and do not see the split on their pay stubs.

5 Recent plan reviews

PICA's board unanimously approved the FY26-30 Five Year Plan in July 2025 after determining it met the requirements of the PICA Act and the Intergovernmental Cooperation Agreement.[7] On July 28, 2026 it unanimously approved the FY27-31 Plan, finding the projections reasonable; its staff recommended continued building of reserves, and the City noted that unrestricted reserves remain below the 17 percent benchmark recommended by the Government Finance Officers Association.[8] The approval came after Council adopted the FY27 budget on June 11 (see Philadelphia City Budget Process). The cycle gives residents and advocates a second venue for budget analysis beyond Council; PICA publishes its board materials and annual reports.

See also: Philadelphia City Budget Process, Finance Department, City Treasurer, Philadelphia Taxes, Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia.

Philly311

Philly311
TypeCity non-emergency contact center
Led byExecutive Director Jocelyn Jones (as of 2026)
Phone311 within Philadelphia; (215) 686-8686 from outside the city
Hours8 a.m. to 8 p.m., Monday through Friday (phone contact center)
LanguagesPhone interpreters in over 200 languages
ChannelsPhone, website, iOS and Android apps
New appIn-house built 311 mobile app scheduled for August 2026
Websitephila.gov/311

Philly311 is "the City of Philadelphia's contact center for non-emergency City services and information."[1] Residents use it to report problems such as potholes, trash and graffiti, request services, or look up how a City program works. It is not for emergencies; those go to 911 (see Office of Emergency Management). NBC Philadelphia has reported on the call center reaching its six millionth call, and the City lists Jocelyn Jones as Executive Director.[1][2] The service is the main entry point for neighborhood-level complaints and is the way many residents first interact with City government.

1 How to use it

Residents can call 311, use the web portal or the mobile apps, or ask for information about City services and programs. The phone center is staffed 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Monday through Friday.[1] The online portal and apps let residents follow the progress of a request. The City has recently restricted anonymous submissions after inappropriate content was submitted, encouraging residents to create accounts so they can receive status updates.[3] A typical request names a type (such as illegal dumping, a street light, an abandoned vehicle or a property maintenance complaint), an address and details, and may include a photo.

2 What happens to a request

Philly311 does not itself fix problems. Agents log the request and route it to the responsible department, for example the Streets Department for potholes and trash, Licenses and Inspections for building and property complaints, Water Department for hydrants and sewer issues, or Parks and Recreation for park conditions. Each department has a service-level target. When a request is closed, the status is updated in the system. Housing complaints such as landlord repair problems may be routed to inspectors; see Rental Licensing and Landlord-Tenant Law in Philadelphia and Safe and Healthy Homes Act. Council members' district offices often intervene when 311 requests stall; see Councilmanic Prerogative.

3 Technology and the new app

The Office of Innovation and Technology told Council in March 2026 that it is delivering a new 311 mobile app, with a mobile-first interface, photo upload, location services and clearly defined service categories, scheduled to launch in August 2026 and described as the City's first in-house built mobile application.[4] Service-request data are a prominent part of the City's open-data offerings (see Open Data and Transparency Tools), allowing journalists and neighborhood groups to analyze response times by area.

4 Language access and accessibility

Philly311 "can provide an interpreter over the phone in over 200 languages."[3] The City is also working to improve digital accessibility through the Office for People with Disabilities, and the Office of Immigrant Affairs coordinates language-access policy; see Office of Immigrant Affairs. Residents without internet access should use the phone line.

5 Limits and accountability

A 311 ticket is not a legal complaint, and it does not create enforcement rights for the individual who files it. For disputes with a landlord, discrimination or police misconduct there are other channels; see How to File a Complaint and How to Get Help From the City. The City Controller has reviewed City service delivery and complaint response in the past; residents who want data on performance can use public dashboards. Questions about how to use the system can be directed to 311 itself.

See also: How to Get Help From the City, Office of Innovation and Technology, Managing Director's Office, Open Data and Transparency Tools.

Open Data and Transparency Tools

Open Data and Transparency Tools
TypePublic data portals and disclosure systems
Community catalogOpenDataPhilly (opendataphilly.org): 300+ datasets, applications and APIs
Property dataproperty.phila.gov (Office of Property Assessment)
Contractscontracts.phila.gov (Procurement Department)
Officials' financesFinancial disclosure database (Department of Records, filings since 2015)
Legal basisPennsylvania Right-to-Know Law; City open data policy

Open data and transparency tools are the web portals, databases and public documents that let residents see what the City of Philadelphia spends, owns, approves and does. Data are not a substitute for a records request, but they often answer the question faster. The main tools are run by different agencies, so knowing which one holds what saves time. The Office of Innovation and Technology builds and hosts much of the City's technology, including GIS and analytics, while individual departments publish their own datasets.

1 OpenDataPhilly

OpenDataPhilly describes itself as "a data catalog and portal that provides access to more than 300 data sets, applications, and APIs related to the Philadelphia region." It launched in 2010 with pro bono support from the geospatial software company Azavea, which maintained it through 2023; it received funding from the William Penn Foundation (2011) and the Knight Foundation (2015), moved to the JKAN platform in spring 2023 and has been volunteer-run as a standalone organization since December 2023.[1] The City of Philadelphia publishes many of its own datasets through its Office of Innovation and Technology, and OpenDataPhilly links to them alongside regional, state and community data. OpenDataPhilly's own page notes a partnership with the City's Office of Innovation and Technology.

2 Property, permits and service requests

The property search at property.phila.gov shows ownership, sales history, valuation and physical characteristics for each parcel, maintained by the Office of Property Assessment.[2] Licenses, permits, violations and inspections are published by the Department of Licenses and Inspections, which is vital for tenants checking a landlord's rental license (see Rental Licensing and Landlord-Tenant Law in Philadelphia). Requests submitted to Philly311 are also available as data, which lets residents compare response times across neighborhoods. Land records, deeds and mortgages are kept by the Department of Records.

3 Money: budgets, contracts and disclosures

Budget documents, including the Mayor's Budget in Brief, the Five Year Plan and each department's budget testimony to City Council, are public (see How to Read the City Budget and Philadelphia City Budget Process). The Contracts Hub at contracts.phila.gov lists solicitations and awards from the Procurement Department. The Office of Economic Opportunity registry of certified minority-, woman- and disabled-owned businesses is published as an open dataset on the federal data.gov catalog.[3] The Department of Records hosts a database of financial interest disclosures by City officials and employees covering filings since 2015.[4] Campaign finance filings are public; see Campaign Finance in Philadelphia and City Commissioners for where they are filed. The City Controller publishes audits and reports, and the Board of Ethics posts guidance and enforcement actions.

4 Meetings and legislation

City Council posts bills, resolutions, hearing schedules and videos on its legislative site, and the Sunshine Act requires public notice of meetings of boards and commissions; see Sunshine Act and Open Meetings. The OIT-run PHL GovTV broadcasts government proceedings and is expanding live remote coverage.[5] To follow a bill, see How a Bill Becomes Law in Philadelphia and How to Testify at City Council.

5 When data are not enough

Not everything is published. The state Right-to-Know Law lets anyone request records from City agencies, and the process is described in How to Request Public Records. Data quality varies; datasets may lag, contain errors or omit fields, and residents should read the documentation. Journalists and watchdogs use these tools together (see Local News Media in Philadelphia and Good Government Groups). Concerns about misuse of public money can be reported through How to Report Corruption or Misconduct.

See also: Right-to-Know Law and Public Records, Office of Innovation and Technology, Sunshine Act and Open Meetings, Philly311.

Office of Economic Opportunity

Office of Economic Opportunity (OEO)
TypeCity office (listed by the City as a division of the Office of Business Impact and Economic Advancement)
Led byDeputy Director Lynn T. Newsome listed (as of 2026; no executive director named on the City page)
Other staffMichelle A. Gumbs, Senior Director for Capacity Building; Jennifer Ricciardi-Wise, Registry Manager
Participation goal35 percent of City contract dollars to M/W/DSBEs each year
Address30 S. 15th St., 17th Floor, Philadelphia, PA 19107
Contact(215) 683-2057; oeo.phila@phila.gov
Registryphila.sbecompliance.com

The Office of Economic Opportunity (OEO) works "to support fair and open access to City contracting opportunities." It promotes transparency in procurement, monitors compliance with City contract requirements and helps businesses navigate participation through workshops and resources.[1] The City's current web page lists OEO as a division of the Office of Business Impact and Economic Advancement, an economic-development office that works alongside the Department of Commerce, and OEO ensures that the City is working with diverse businesses to fulfill its needs for goods and services. In practice it is the office that registers minority-owned, woman-owned and disabled-owned business enterprises (M/W/DSBEs), reviews and monitors City contracts for compliance with participation commitments, and supports businesses that want to become prime contractors.[2]

1 The registry and certification

To join the OEO Registry, a business must first be certified by an approved outside agency. The City accepts certifications from the National Minority Supplier Development Council (NMSDC), the Women's Business Enterprise Council (WBEC), the Women's Business Enterprise National Council (WBENC), the Pennsylvania Unified Certification Program and federal or regional transit authorities.[1] To qualify, a business must be at least 51 percent owned by a minority, a woman or a person with a disability.[2] Businesses use an online system to apply for registration, renew and see outreach opportunities. A public list of registered firms is available as an open dataset (see Open Data and Transparency Tools).

2 Participation goals and how they work

Each year the City aims for 35 percent participation by M/W/DSBEs on its contracts.[2] Bid solicitations from the Procurement Department and other agencies may set ranges of participation for minority-, woman- and disabled-owned firms, and bidders must show a good-faith plan, often by naming subcontractors. OEO reviews those plans and monitors the contract. Department testimony to City Council reports results: the Finance Department reported M/W/DSBE participation of 31 percent on $26.4 million of professional-services contracts in FY25, and the Revenue Department 34 percent on $20.1 million.[3] Because contract data differ by department, aggregate results require OEO annual reports. The City is also building a registry of small and local businesses (S/LBEs) with department-level goals, in the range of 25 to 40 percent in 2026 testimony.[3] The rules apply to City contracts and not to state or federal contracts, which have their own programs. See Understanding City Contracts and Bids.

3 Programs and workshops

OEO runs "Doing Business with the City" and "Business Development Series" workshops that teach firms how to find bids, price work and meet insurance and compliance requirements. Its capacity-building staff help small firms scale to become prime contractors. It also receives complaints about fraud and waste on contracts (the OEO page directs the public to a fraud and waste reporting channel).[1] OEO's nine listed staff include business enterprise specialists and coordinators. Its work overlaps with the Commerce Department's small-business services (see Commerce Department) and with the Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation lending programs, and with trade-labor requirements on public projects (see Prevailing Wage and Project Labor Agreements).

4 Related initiatives and reorganization

In March 2025 Mayor Cherelle Parker named Nadir Jones as Director of Business Impact and Supplier Diversity within an Office of Business Impact and Economic Advancement.[4] The City's OEO web page now places OEO within that Office of Business Impact and Economic Advancement and lists a deputy director as its leader; the page does not describe the reorganization, so residents with questions about who handles a particular registry or compliance matter should call the OEO number above. The Mayor's FY27 budget also added an Economic Mobility Cabinet and an Office of Financial Empowerment, which aim to widen access to economic opportunity.[5] The earlier history of M/W/DSBE contracting in Philadelphia, including Council legislation, is outside the scope of the sources consulted.

5 Reporting problems

Businesses and workers who believe a contractor is violating participation commitments can contact OEO at the number above. Suspected fraud can also be reported to the Office of the Inspector General and the City Controller; see How to Report Corruption or Misconduct. Contract-related ethics rules are enforced by the Board of Ethics. Community groups that support local business include community development corporations and the Chamber of Commerce for Greater Philadelphia.

See also: Commerce Department, Procurement Department, Understanding City Contracts and Bids, Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation.

Commerce Department

Department of Commerce
TypeCity-charter executive department
Led byActing Commerce Director Karen Fegely (since May 1, 2025; still listed as acting on the City's staff directory in October 2026)
PredecessorAlba Martinez (Director, 2024 to April 2025)
FY27 General Fund$16.8 million, plus $15.0 million Convention Center subsidy and $80.0 million economic stimulus line (adopted)
IncludesEconomic-opportunity functions (see Office of Economic Opportunity)
Address1515 Arch St., 12th Floor, Philadelphia, PA 19102
Contact(215) 683-2100; business@phila.gov

The Department of Commerce is the City of Philadelphia's economic development agency. Its motto is "making Philadelphia a business-friendly city where companies choose to start, stay, and grow."[1] The department attracts companies to the region, supports small-business access to funding, revitalizes commercial districts, builds workforce talent pipelines and expands economic opportunities for underserved entrepreneurs. Its Director is appointed by the Mayor. Alba Martinez, a former Vanguard executive and the first Latina and LGBTQ+ person to lead the department, left effective May 1, 2025 to produce a musical, and Mayor Cherelle Parker named Karen Fegely, a Commerce employee for almost 18 years who had been deputy director for policy and strategic initiatives, as Acting Director.[2][3] News coverage in May 2026 noted that a permanent director had not yet been named.[3]

1 Services for businesses

Commerce staff manage business services by geographic area, provide financial support and lending programs, offer location-based incentives, support key industries and promote international business development.[1] The Martinez tenure oversaw the Small Business Catalyst Fund, the Philly Biz Hub, an expansion of "PHL Taking Care of Business" cleaning corridors and a new Business Navigator team to help entrepreneurs through permitting and licensing, according to the City's announcement of her departure.[2] The department released an inaugural annual report for 2025 in May 2026.[4] Navigators coordinate with the Department of Licenses and Inspections and the Revenue Department through the PHL Open for Business effort.

2 Programs

Programs listed by the City include the Catalyst Fund, Storefront Improvement Program, Business Security Camera Program, Quality Jobs Program and PHL PRIME, which supports high-impact economic development projects.[1] Commerce also works closely with the quasi-public Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation (PIDC), which provides loans and land, and with the Convention Center, which the City subsidizes ($15 million in the FY27 appropriation). The Tax Abatement and Development Incentives article describes the tax side of these policies, and the wage and business tax cuts that are a core part of the Parker administration's competitiveness strategy are described in Philadelphia Taxes.

3 Office of Economic Opportunity and equity

The Office of Economic Opportunity is listed on the City's website as part of the Office of Business Impact and Economic Advancement, which works alongside Commerce, and registers minority-, woman- and disabled-owned businesses, monitors their participation in City contracts and supports capacity building. The City's goal is 35 percent participation each year.[5] Procurement itself is handled by the Procurement Department, while Commerce and OEO focus on opening doors for businesses; see Understanding City Contracts and Bids. Related initiatives on workforce are in the Office of Workforce Development.

4 Budget and partners

Council's FY27 appropriation to the Director of Commerce was about $16.8 million, with $15 million for the Convention Center subsidy and about $80 million under an "Economic Stimulus" line.[6] The department partners with business groups such as the Chamber of Commerce for Greater Philadelphia and business improvement districts (see Center City District and Business Improvement Districts) and with community development corporations on commercial corridors. The Department of Planning and Development handles land use and housing development.

5 Criticism and debates

Economic development policy is contested. Supporters of tax cuts and incentives, including the Parker administration, argue they keep the city competitive; whether benefits reach small businesses and neighborhoods as much as large projects is a recurring question in Council debates (see Developers and the Real Estate Lobby). Leadership has been in acting status for over a year, which news reports noted. Small-business owners can start with the Commerce phone or email above and the Business Navigator service; for complaints see How to Get Help From the City.

See also: Office of Economic Opportunity, Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation, Mayor's Cabinet and Offices, Philadelphia International Airport.

Department of Licenses and Inspections

Department of Licenses and Inspections (L&I)
TypeCity department (Philadelphia Home Rule Charter)
Led byCommissioner(s); the department was split into two commissioner-led divisions in 2024; the City's leadership page lists Ralph DiPietro (Inspections, Safety & Compliance) and Bridget Collins-Greenwald (Quality of Life)
Core functionsPermits, inspections, licensing, code enforcement, demolitions
Governing lawPhiladelphia Code Titles 4, 9, 14 and 16 (Building, Property Maintenance, Fire and Zoning codes)
Address1401 John F. Kennedy Blvd., 11th Floor
Websitephila.gov/li (311 or 215-686-8686)

The Department of Licenses and Inspections (L&I) is the City of Philadelphia agency that issues construction, zoning and trade permits, inspects buildings, licenses businesses and rental properties, and enforces the property, building and fire codes. Its stated mission is "building a safer city by enforcing building-related codes through inspections, licensing, permitting, and demolitions."[1] It is a city department answerable to the mayor, not a state or county body.

1 Structure and leadership

In February 2024 Mayor Cherelle Parker announced that L&I would be divided into two distinct divisions with separate commissioners: Basil Merenda, previously the city's Director of Labor, to lead Inspections, Safety and Compliance (construction, building operation and demolition), and Bridget Collins-Greenwald, previously Commissioner of Public Property, to lead Quality of Life (nuisance and business-code enforcement).[2] Following a July 2026 cabinet reshuffle,[3] the City's leadership page in October 2026 lists Ralph DiPietro as Commissioner of the Inspections, Safety & Compliance division and Bridget Collins-Greenwald as Commissioner of the Quality of Life division; Basil Merenda, named in 2024, is no longer listed.

The department reports through the Managing Director's Office and is funded in the annual city budget. Its inspectors are represented by municipal unions such as District Council 33.

2 How permitting works

Most applications are filed online through the department's eCLIPSE system. The usual path for building work is:

  1. Zoning review. The application is checked against the Zoning Code. If the project complies, a zoning permit is issued. If it does not, L&I issues a "refusal" (or a "referral" for a special exception), which the applicant may take to the Zoning Board of Adjustment.
  2. Building plan review. Larger projects are reviewed against the Building Code; simple work may be permitted over the counter.
  3. Other approvals. Properties on the historic register need sign-off from the Historical Commission; work in the right of way may involve the Streets Department; connections involve the Water Department.
  4. Permit issuance and inspections at specified stages (footings, framing, electrical, plumbing, final).
  5. Certificate of occupancy or final approval at completion.

As of July 1, 2026, new permit applications must comply with updated building codes.[1]

3 Inspections and violations

Inspections are triggered by permit milestones, license applications, and complaints. Anyone may report a suspected violation, such as missing heat, structural hazards, work without a permit or an unsafe vacant building, through Philly311 or the department's online request portal. An inspector visits, and if a violation is found the department issues a notice or Code Violation Notice with a deadline to correct it. Unsafe or imminently dangerous buildings can be ordered vacated, secured or demolished, and the City may bill owners for emergency work. Failure to comply can lead to fines and prosecution in Municipal Court; see Court of Common Pleas and Municipal Court. Rental properties must hold a rental license and a certificate of rental suitability, which ties L&I to landlord-tenant law and the Safe and Healthy Homes Act.

4 Licenses

L&I administers commercial activity licenses (for example food-establishment and general business licenses), rental licenses, and trade licenses for contractors. A business generally needs a license for each activity, and some licenses require inspection or other agency approvals first.

5 Appeals

Anyone who receives a permit, violation or notice can appeal it, and all appeals must be filed with the relevant board within 30 days of the initial notice. The board depends on the subject:[4]

  • Board of License and Inspection Review: general permits, violations and notices from L&I.
  • Zoning Board of Adjustment: zoning permit refusals, referrals and zoning decisions.
  • Board of Safety and Fire Prevention: Fire Code violations.
  • Board of Building Standards: unsafe or imminently dangerous building designations.
  • Plumbing Advisory Board: plumbing code matters.

Appeals of Code Violation Notices go to the Office of Administrative Review. Board decisions can generally be taken further to the Court of Common Pleas.

6 Criticism and reform

L&I has long been criticized by residents, developers and watchdogs for slow permit turnaround and inconsistent enforcement. The June 2013 collapse of a building at 22nd and Market Streets onto a Salvation Army thrift store, which killed six people, prompted a major review of demolition oversight, and the department has since been the subject of Controller audits and Council hearings. The 2024 division of the department was described by the Parker administration as a response to longstanding calls for reform.[2]

See also: Department of Planning and Development, Zoning Board of Adjustment, Philadelphia Zoning Code, How to File a Complaint.

  3. WHYY, "Philadelphia Managing Director Adam Thiel steps down as Parker's administration undergoes staffing shuffle," July 28, 2026.

Department of Planning and Development

Department of Planning and Development (DPD)
TypeCity department / umbrella of boards and agencies
Led byJessie Lawrence, Director of Planning and Development (as of 2026)
ComponentsCity Planning Commission, Zoning Board of Adjustment, Historical Commission, Art Commission, Division of Housing and Community Development, Land Bank and others
Related authoritiesRedevelopment Authority, Housing Development Corporation
Address1515 Arch Street
Websitephila.gov/departments/department-of-planning-and-development

The Department of Planning and Development (DPD) is a Philadelphia city department created in 2010 to coordinate land-use planning, preservation, zoning appeals and housing and community-development programs under one director. It is a city body; it is distinct from the state-created Redevelopment Authority and the Philadelphia Housing Authority, although it works closely with both.

1 Structure

DPD is best understood as a cluster. Its component bodies include the City Planning Commission (comprehensive planning, Civic Design Review, capital program), the Zoning Board of Adjustment (zoning appeals), the Historical Commission (preservation), the Art Commission (design review of public projects), and the Division of Housing and Community Development. Allied entities such as the Philadelphia Land Bank, the Redevelopment Authority and the Housing Development Corporation share leadership coordination with it.[1] The Planning Commission and ZBA remain legally distinct bodies with their own members and rules even though they are housed in the department.

2 Leadership and the housing plan

As of 2026, the department is led by Jessie Lawrence, Director of Planning and Development, who previously served as an associate deputy mayor and as real estate director of the Housing Development Corporation. He leads work on Mayor Cherelle Parker's plan for 30,000 units of new, restored and repaired housing, described by the administration as a $1 billion housing plan.[2] The director also chairs the Planning Commission in an ex officio capacity.[3] The department is funded through the annual city budget and federal housing and community-development grants.

3 How a development moves through DPD bodies

A typical project touches several DPD bodies in sequence:

  1. The applicant applies to L&I, which checks the plan against the Zoning Code.
  2. If the plan needs a variance or special exception, the applicant files with the ZBA, notifies nearby residents and the relevant Registered Community Organization, and attends a public hearing.
  3. Large or prominent projects first undergo Civic Design Review by the Planning Commission, a non-binding design critique open to the public.
  4. Properties on the historic register are reviewed by the Historical Commission before permits issue.
  5. Projects on public land, or using public financing, may also involve the Redevelopment Authority or Land Bank.

4 Working with residents

Residents can attend ZBA hearings, Historical Commission and Planning Commission meetings, and RCO meetings; written comments are generally accepted. Planning staff also run district and neighborhood planning processes that feed the comprehensive plan and zoning remapping. For housing programs, the Division of Housing and Community Development funds home repair, counseling and affordable development. Complaints about code enforcement should go to 311, not to DPD.

5 History and debates

DPD was formed in the Nutter administration to merge planning, development, and housing functions. Its leaders have often been at the center of disputes over density, affordability, and neighborhood input. A 2023 resignation of the prior director, Anne Fadullon, was covered by the Philadelphia Inquirer in the context of housing policy tensions with City Council.[4] Developers and housing advocates frequently disagree with civic associations over how much weight neighborhood opposition should carry, and Council members' informal influence over zoning (see councilmanic prerogative) is a recurring subject of debate.

See also: Commerce Department, Tax Abatement and Development Incentives, Developers and the Real Estate Lobby.

Philadelphia City Planning Commission

Philadelphia City Planning Commission (PCPC)
TypeCity commission under the Home Rule Charter
Members7 mayoral appointees plus 4 ex officio members (11 total)
ChairJessie Lawrence, Director of Planning and Development (ex officio); appointed Vice-Chair Ximena Valle, AIA (as of 2026)
Parent bodyDepartment of Planning and Development
Governing lawPhiladelphia Home Rule Charter; Philadelphia Code Title 14
Websitephila.gov/departments/philadelphia-city-planning-commission

The Philadelphia City Planning Commission (PCPC) is the city body responsible for long-range planning of Philadelphia's physical development. Established in 1929, according to the City, and continued under the Home Rule Charter, it prepares the comprehensive plan, the capital program and budget, reviews zoning legislation and the design of major projects, and oversees the registration of Registered Community Organizations.[1]

1 Membership and staff

The Commission has seven members appointed by the mayor plus four ex officio members, for 11 in all. The director of the Department of Planning and Development chairs it ex officio, and the appointed members elect a vice-chair.[2] A professional staff led by an executive director carries out planning work. Eleanor Sharpe served as executive director from 2018 to 2024 and then became Chief of Planning in the Office of the Council President.[3] The City's staff directory lists Octavia Howell as Executive Director and also lists Martine Decamp, AICP, as an interim executive director; residents seeking a contact should use the Commission's main line, (215) 683-4615.

The City's commissioner listing shows how the 11 seats are filled. The seven appointed members include a traffic engineer, an urban planner, two land-use attorneys, an architect and two community representatives, and the vice-chair is Ximena Valle, AIA. The four ex officio seats are held by the Managing Director, the Director of Finance, the Commerce Director and the Director of Planning and Development, who chairs; each may send a designee.[2] Staff directors listed by the City oversee development, transportation, legislation and the Citizens Planning Institute, a public education program on planning.

2 Core functions

  • Comprehensive plan. The Charter requires a comprehensive plan guiding physical development; the most recent citywide plan is Philadelphia2035, implemented through district plans.
  • Capital program and budget. The Commission prepares a six-year capital program and annual capital budget for municipal buildings, streets and facilities, which the mayor submits to City Council. See Philadelphia City Budget Process.
  • Review of legislation. Zoning and land-use bills, street vacations and some land transfers are referred to the Commission for a recommendation before Council acts.
  • Civic Design Review and RCO administration (below).

3 Civic Design Review

Under the Zoning Code, certain larger projects must go through Civic Design Review (CDR) before a building permit issues. The Civic Design Review Committee, which includes design professionals, holds a public meeting at which the applicant presents and the committee offers advice on site design, access and neighborhood fit. The committee's recommendations are advisory rather than binding, but the process must be completed for the permit to move forward.[1]

4 Zoning, remapping and Council

Zoning map changes are made by ordinance of City Council. The Commission reviews proposed remappings and text amendments and issues recommendations, and it has carried out citywide remapping efforts through its district planning program. Because Council members also exercise informal influence over projects in their districts (see Councilmanic Prerogative), the Commission's advisory voice is one of several in the land-use system.

5 Participating as a resident

The Commission holds regular public meetings, publishes agendas and plans on its website, and invites comment on district plans. The Commission also maintains the RCO registry: groups register annually with a geographic boundary, and applicants for zoning hearings and Civic Design Review must notify them. Residents can find which RCO covers their address on the Commission's website. Appeals of zoning permit decisions are not heard by the Commission but by the Zoning Board of Adjustment.

See also: Department of Licenses and Inspections, Philadelphia Neighborhoods Guide, Civic and Neighborhood Associations.

  3. WHYY, "Planning Commission hires Eleanor Sharpe to help implement Philadelphia2035"; Philadelphia Inquirer, March 29, 2024 (Sharpe's move to Council).

Zoning Board of Adjustment

Zoning Board of Adjustment (ZBA)
TypeQuasi-judicial city board
Members7 (Chair William Bergman as of 2026)
Parent bodyDepartment of Planning and Development
Governing lawPhiladelphia Code Title 14; Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code; ZBA regulations (revised effective July 10, 2026)
Address1515 Arch Street, 18th Floor; (215) 686-2429
Websitephila.gov/zba

The Zoning Board of Adjustment (ZBA) is the quasi-judicial board that hears appeals from decisions of the Department of Licenses and Inspections on zoning permits and violations. When a proposed use or building does not comply with the Zoning Code, the ZBA can grant a variance or special exception, or uphold the refusal.[1]

1 Composition

The ZBA has seven members. As listed on phila.gov in 2026, William Bergman chairs, Tonnetta Graham is vice chair, and Cheryl L. Gaston is secretary; other members are Layla Bibi, Michael Johns, Ryan McAdams and Tya Winn, with Hilary Emerson as board counsel.[1] Members are appointed by the mayor under the Home Rule Charter. Staff are housed within the Department of Planning and Development at 1515 Arch Street. Revised ZBA regulations were adopted on June 10, 2026 and took effect July 10, 2026.[2]

2 Variances and special exceptions

A variance is permission to depart from the Code, such as building taller or using land in a way the district does not allow. Under Pennsylvania law the applicant must generally show an unnecessary hardship arising from the property's unique conditions, not self-created, and that the variance is the minimum needed and will not harm the public interest. A special exception is a use the Code allows in a district if specified criteria are met. The ZBA also decides appeals by people who argue that L&I wrongly issued a permit or violation.

3 The appeal process step by step

  1. Refusal or referral. L&I refuses a zoning permit application or refers it for a special exception.
  2. File within 30 days. The applicant has 30 days to file an appeal application with the ZBA.[3]
  3. Notice. For variances and special exceptions, the applicant must notify neighbors and the relevant Registered Community Organization, attend a community meeting, and post a notice on the property.
  4. Hearing. The ZBA schedules a public hearing. The applicant presents, and anyone wishing to testify, including neighbors and the RCO, may be heard.
  5. Decision. The Board votes to grant (sometimes with conditions called provisos), deny, or continue the case.

4 Fees and representation

Effective August 1, 2026, the posted filing fee is $125 for one- and two-family homes and affordable housing projects and $811 for other properties, with an administrative-review fee of $265, a reposting fee of $177, and an accelerated-hearing option at $995 per property.[3] Individuals may appear on their own behalf; corporations and LLCs must be represented by a Pennsylvania-licensed attorney.

5 Appealing the ZBA's decision

A party aggrieved by a ZBA decision, including an applicant who is denied or a neighbor who objects to a grant (if they have standing), has 30 days to appeal to the Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas.[3] See Court of Common Pleas and Municipal Court. Further appeals go to the Commonwealth Court of Pennsylvania, whose opinions on Philadelphia variances regularly refine the standards.

6 Debates

Neighborhood groups and developers disagree about how much weight RCO opposition should carry before the ZBA, and some critics argue the number of variance requests shows the Code is out of step with the city's housing needs. The Board's decisions are legal rulings on the record, not votes on popularity, and testimony on hardship and Code criteria is what matters in court review.

See also: Philadelphia City Planning Commission, Philadelphia Historical Commission, How to File a Complaint.

References

  2. Zoning Board of Adjustment, Final Regulations, adopted June 10, 2026, effective July 10, 2026, phila.gov.
  3. City of Philadelphia, "Appeal a zoning decision to the Zoning Board of Adjustment (ZBA)," phila.gov/services (accessed October 2026; fee schedule effective August 1, 2026).

Philadelphia Zoning Code

Philadelphia Zoning Code
TypeMunicipal ordinance (Title 14, Philadelphia Code)
AdoptedRewrite effective August 2012, after the Zoning Code Commission (created by 2007 voter-approved Charter amendment)
Administered byL&I; appeals to ZBA
Amended byCity Council ordinance
Enabling lawPennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code; Home Rule Charter

The Philadelphia Zoning Code is Title 14 of the Philadelphia Code and regulates what may be built where in the city: permitted uses, building height and bulk, parking, signs and community-notice rules. Zoning is a function of city government under the Home Rule Charter and Pennsylvania's Municipalities Planning Code. Because Philadelphia is a consolidated city and county, there is a single citywide code rather than separate municipal codes.

1 History of the 2012 rewrite

Philadelphia's earlier code dated to 1962 and had been amended so often that it was widely seen as unwieldy. Voters approved a 2007 Charter amendment creating the Zoning Code Commission, which drafted a new code. Council enacted it in 2011 and it took effect in August 2012, simplifying district names, adding "by-right" categories and formalizing community notice.[1] The Code has been amended many times since.

2 Districts and overlays

The Code groups land into base districts: residential (such as RSA and RM series for single-family and multifamily), commercial and commercial mixed-use (CMX), industrial (I series), special-purpose districts, and others. Overlays add extra rules in particular areas, for example height or design controls near the Delaware waterfront, along corridors, or in historic and neighborhood conservation areas. Each district lists permitted, special-exception and prohibited uses, plus dimensional standards.

3 Approval paths

  • By right. A project that complies with the Code receives a zoning permit from L&I without a hearing.
  • Variance or special exception. A refusal or referral can be taken to the ZBA within 30 days; see that article for the steps and fees.
  • Civic Design Review. Large projects undergo design review by the City Planning Commission.
  • Legislative change. An owner may ask Council to rezone land or amend the Code by ordinance, which goes through Planning Commission review and Council committee and floor votes.

4 Community involvement

Section 14-303 sets rules for community involvement and notice. Neighborhood groups register with the Planning Commission as Registered Community Organizations. For projects needing a ZBA hearing or Civic Design Review, applicants must notify affected RCOs and nearby residents and hold a community meeting, and the ZBA considers the record of that process.[2]

5 Amendments and remapping

Only Council can amend the Code or the zoning map. Bills are introduced by members, referred to committee, and reviewed by the Planning Commission before hearings; see How a Bill Becomes Law in Philadelphia. District Council members' practical say over projects in their districts is discussed in Councilmanic Prerogative. Citywide efforts to increase housing supply, for example by revisiting restrictive districts, are common subjects of Council debate and are tied to affordability goals in the Department of Planning and Development's housing plan.

See also: Philadelphia Historical Commission, Rental Licensing and Landlord-Tenant Law in Philadelphia, Developers and the Real Estate Lobby.

  3. City of Philadelphia, Zoning Board of Adjustment and City Planning Commission pages, phila.gov (accessed October 2026).

Philadelphia Historical Commission

Philadelphia Historical Commission
TypeCity commission (Home Rule Charter and Philadelphia Code Title 14)
Executive DirectorJon Farnham (per the City's staff directory, October 2026)
Parent bodyDepartment of Planning and Development
Key productPhiladelphia Register of Historic Places
Address1515 Arch Street, 13th Floor; (215) 686-7660
Websitephila.gov/departments/philadelphia-historical-commission

The Philadelphia Historical Commission protects the city's historic resources by designating landmarks and districts, maintaining the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places, and reviewing building permit applications for work on listed properties.[1] It is a city commission, separate from the state Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission and the federal National Register of Historic Places, although a property can be on more than one list. Only the local register carries legal review of exterior changes and demolition.

1 Structure and committees

The Commission consists of nine members appointed by the Mayor, including a real estate developer who serves as chair, an architect, a historian, an architectural historian and representatives of community organizations and development corporations, plus five ex officio members: the City Council President, the City Planning Commission chair, and directors or commissioners from Commerce, Planning and Development, Licenses and Inspections, and Public Property (one appointed seat was vacant on the City's page in October 2026). It is staffed by preservation planners within the Department of Planning and Development and is led by an executive director.[1] It meets monthly, in person and by Zoom, and does much of its detailed work through advisory committees: the Committee on Historic Designation reviews nominations, and the Architectural Committee reviews permit proposals. Agendas, applications and minutes are posted publicly.

2 Designation process

  1. Nomination. Anyone, including residents, civic groups, owners or the Commission itself, can nominate a building, object, site or district, using a nomination form that documents its significance against criteria in the Code.
  2. Notice. The owner and the relevant City Council office are notified before review.
  3. Committee on Historic Designation holds a public meeting and makes a recommendation.
  4. Commission vote. The full Commission votes at its monthly meeting. Listing places the property on the Register.

Designations can be rescinded; for example, the Committee on Historic Designation agenda of July 22, 2026 included a rescission matter for a property on West Montgomery Avenue.[2]

3 Permit review

When an owner of a listed property applies to L&I for a permit affecting the exterior (or the interior of designated public spaces), the application is routed to the Commission. According to the city, staff approve over 90 percent of building permit applications without referral to a committee.[1] The rest go to the Architectural Committee and then, if needed, to the Commission. Standards follow the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Rehabilitation as adopted in Commission rules.

4 Demolition, hardship and appeals

Demolition of a listed building requires Commission approval. An owner may seek relief by showing that the building cannot be used for a reasonable purpose or that demolition is necessary in the public interest, commonly called a financial-hardship or public-interest claim; such applications are decided by the Commission after a hearing. The Commission's decisions can be appealed, and the city identifies the Board of License and Inspection Review as one body that hears some appeals involving the Commission.[3] Because the correct forum and deadlines depend on the type of decision, applicants should confirm on phila.gov and may wish to consult a lawyer. This article is general information, not legal advice.

5 Controversy and public participation

Preservation sits in tension with housing production and property rights. Preservation groups argue designation protects neighborhood character and heritage; some owners and developers argue it limits use of their property and raises costs. The Commission's approach, including how aggressively to designate, has been the subject of City Council and press debate over many years. Residents may nominate properties, attend meetings and submit written comment before votes. Related design review for public projects is done by the Art Commission, also within the planning cluster, and zoning relief for the same sites goes separately to the Zoning Board of Adjustment.

See also: Philadelphia Zoning Code, Philadelphia City Planning Commission, Civic and Neighborhood Associations.

Registered Community Organizations

Registered Community Organizations (RCOs)
TypeNeighborhood groups recognized under the Zoning Code
Registered withPhiladelphia City Planning Commission, annually
Governing lawPhiladelphia Code, section 14-303 and related amendments
RoleReceive notice, hold meetings, and give input to ZBA and Civic Design Review
Websitephila.gov/rconotification

Registered Community Organizations (RCOs) are community groups, such as civic associations, community development corporations and neighborhood nonprofits, that register with the City Planning Commission to receive formal notice of development proposals in a defined geographic area. The system was created by the 2012 Zoning Code and replaced a looser practice of informal neighborhood notice.[1]

1 Registration

A group becomes an RCO by registering with the Planning Commission and renewing each year. Registration includes basic information on the group and the boundaries of the area it covers; boundaries may overlap, so more than one RCO can be entitled to notice for the same property.[1] The Commission posts a map and a list so applicants and neighbors can find the RCOs for any address. Registration does not make a group a government body; RCOs are private associations.

2 Applicant duties

For any project requiring a Zoning Board of Adjustment hearing, or going through Civic Design Review, the Code requires the applicant to send detailed written notice to every affected RCO, generally within a short window after filing, and to hold or offer a community meeting. The Commission publishes notification templates. The applicant also notifies nearby property owners and posts notice on the site.[2] After the meeting, the RCO can submit a position (support, non-opposition or opposition, sometimes with conditions) that the ZBA receives.

3 What RCOs can and cannot do

  • Can: receive notice, host a public meeting, submit a position and testify at the ZBA.
  • Cannot: approve or veto a project. The ZBA decides on legal criteria, and an RCO's opposition is evidence the Board weighs, not a binding decision.

An RCO that wants to challenge a ZBA decision in court needs legal standing, as any party does; see Court of Common Pleas and Municipal Court.

4 Criticism and reform

Supporters say RCOs give residents an early voice. Critics, including some housing advocates, argue that RCOs can be unrepresentative of renters and newer residents, that overlapping boundaries confuse applicants, and that opposition can slow housing. Council has amended the RCO provisions several times; changes take the form of ordinances amending Title 14 of the Philadelphia Code. See also Councilmanic Prerogative on the separate informal power of district Council members.

5 How residents can use the system

Find the RCO for your address on the Commission's website, ask to be added to its notification list, and attend its meetings. Tenants and other residents can also testify directly at ZBA hearings without being members of an RCO. To start a new group, see How to Organize a Block or Neighborhood Group and Civic and Neighborhood Associations.

See also: Department of Planning and Development, Community Development Corporations.

References

  2. Philadelphia City Planning Commission, RCO Applicant Notification Templates and RCO training materials, phila.gov.

Streets Department

Streets Department
TypeCity department (Home Rule Charter)
Led byStreets Commissioner Kristin Del Rossi (per the City's department leadership page, October 2026), appointed by the mayor; reports within the Managing Director's cabinet
DivisionsSanitation (trash, recycling, litter) and Transportation (paving, signals, street lights, traffic engineering)
Related officesOTIS; Philly311
WorkforceLargely represented by AFSCME District Council 33
Websitephila.gov/departments/streets-department; StreetSmartPHL

The Streets Department is the Philadelphia city department that maintains the public right of way and collects household waste. It runs weekly trash and recycling collection, sweeps and cleans streets, plows snow, paves and repairs roads, and operates and maintains traffic signals, street lights and signs. It is a city department, but many of the roads it maintains also connect to state and federal highways managed by PennDOT; see Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia.

1 Organization

The department is organized around a Sanitation Division and a Transportation Division, under the Commissioner. Carlton Williams, who previously held senior posts in Streets, Parks and Recreation, and Licenses and Inspections and most recently directed the mayor's Clean and Green initiatives, was named Managing Director effective August 17, 2026.[1] The City's Department of Streets leadership page lists Kristin Del Rossi, a longtime department employee, as Commissioner. The department's policy direction is coordinated with OTIS.

2 Sanitation and recycling

Trash and recycling are collected from residences and small businesses on assigned days; collection routes and schedules are published on the department site and in the StreetSmartPHL tool, which also shows street sweeping, paving, closures and snow operations.[2] The department reported that on-time trash collection (completed by 3 p.m.) reached about 97 percent in a 2025-26 period, a level officials called better than in the prior decade or more, even as residents continued to report piled-up trash in some neighborhoods.[3] The city has also expanded twice-weekly collection in some areas. Illegal dumping and litter enforcement involve the Streets Department, the L&I Quality of Life division and the city's Clean and Green initiatives.

3 Paving, potholes and permits

The Transportation Division paves city streets on a multi-year schedule and fills potholes after reports. Anyone planning work in the right of way, such as a dumpster, scaffolding, sidewalk closure, street opening or utility cut, needs a permit; street closures for block parties also go through the department. Property owners are generally responsible for sidewalk upkeep adjacent to their property. Construction projects frequently also need approval from Water for connections and from L&I for building permits. Traffic-calming and Vision Zero street-design projects are coordinated with the Parking Authority (parking enforcement) and OTIS.

4 Labor and service disruptions

Because sanitation workers are mostly members of District Council 33, the July 2025 strike halted regular trash collection; see 2025 DC 33 Strike. The disruption illustrated how heavily residents depend on this one department and how labor negotiations affect basic services.

5 How to request service or complain

Most requests, including missed collection, potholes, dumping, street light outages and damaged signs, are submitted through Philly311 by phone (311), app or web. Requests receive a tracking number and can be followed online. Persistent problems can be raised with the district Council member; see How to Get Help From the City and How to File a Complaint.

See also: Fleet Services, SEPTA, Managing Director's Office.

References

  1. WHYY, "Philadelphia Managing Director Adam Thiel steps down as Parker's administration undergoes staffing shuffle," July 28, 2026; City of Philadelphia biography of Carlton Williams.
  2. City of Philadelphia, Streets Department, phila.gov/departments/streets-department (accessed October 2026).
  3. CBS News Philadelphia and WHYY coverage of Streets Department trash-collection performance and City Council budget hearings, 2025-2026.

Philadelphia Water Department

Philadelphia Water Department (PWD)
TypeCity-owned utility department
Led byCommissioner Benjamin Jewell (appointed October 2025)
ServicesDrinking water, sewer/wastewater, stormwater management
Rate settingIndependent Water, Sewer and Storm Water Rate Board
AssistanceTiered Assistance Program (TAP), about 70,000 customers (July 2026)
Websitewater.phila.gov

The Philadelphia Water Department (PWD) is the city-owned utility that treats and delivers drinking water, collects and treats wastewater, and manages stormwater runoff for Philadelphia. Its commissioner is appointed by the mayor and, along with the Streets Department, the department is coordinated through the Managing Director's cabinet and OTIS. As of 2026 Benjamin Jewell, appointed Water Commissioner in October 2025 according to the City's department page, is commissioner.[1]

1 Operations

PWD operates drinking water plants drawing from the Delaware and Schuylkill rivers, three wastewater treatment plants, and thousands of miles of pipes. It also issues water and sewer connection approvals, which developers and contractors coordinate with L&I permits. It is funded almost entirely by customer rates and bond financing rather than the general tax base, although its budget and bond issuance pass through the Finance Department and City Council.

2 Rates and the Rate Board

Under the Charter, water, sewer and stormwater rates are not set by the department or by Council but by an independent Rate Board after a public proceeding in which PWD proposes rates, advocates and the public submit testimony, and a hearing officer reviews evidence. New rates took effect September 1, 2026: for a typical residential customer using 3,220 gallons per month, the bill rose by $6.74, or 7.5 percent, to $96.16.[2] The Rate Board filed its decision on the 2026 TAP-R (assistance cost recovery) proceeding on July 1, 2026, and that adjustment is added to the increase approved for fiscal year 2027 in the 2025 general rate proceeding.[3] PWD says rising labor, materials, laboratory, regulatory and capital costs drive the increases.

3 Assistance and billing disputes

The Tiered Assistance Program (TAP) lowers bills for income-eligible customers based on household income, and nearly 70,000 customers received a TAP discount as of July 31, 2026.[3] Customers can also request payment agreements, report leaks, and dispute bills with the Water Revenue Bureau, which is part of the Revenue Department. The Water Department's customer pages describe how to dispute a bill and request further review if the dispute is not resolved; confirm the current steps and deadlines on water.phila.gov. Unpaid water and sewer charges can become liens on property.

4 Stormwater and Green City, Clean Waters

Because older parts of the system combine sewage and rainwater, heavy storms can cause overflows into rivers. PWD's long-term plan, Green City, Clean Waters, uses green infrastructure such as rain gardens, porous pavement and tree trenches to reduce overflow, in partnership with Parks and Recreation and the Office of Sustainability. Non-residential properties pay stormwater charges based on impervious area, with credits available for on-site management.

5 Controversies

Rate increases and the affordability of bills have drawn recurring criticism from consumer and housing advocates. In March 2023 a chemical release from a Bucks County plant into the Delaware River led PWD to take precautions at its intake and to advise residents about water supply. PWD has also faced scrutiny over lead service lines, which the department is replacing under federal rules. Commissioner and Council oversight occurs through budget hearings and Controller audits; see City Controller.

See also: Philadelphia Gas Works, Philadelphia Taxes, How to Get Help From the City.

References

  1. Philadelphia Water Department, water.phila.gov (accessed October 2026).
  2. Philadelphia Water Department, "Philadelphia Water Department Requests Necessary Rate Increase," water.phila.gov; CBS News Philadelphia coverage of rate increase.
  3. City of Philadelphia, Water Rate Board, 2026 TAP-R proceeding documents and PWD notices, phila.gov (decision filed July 1, 2026).

Parks and Recreation

Philadelphia Parks & Recreation (PPR)
TypeCity department
Led byCommissioner Susan Slawson (appointed 2024)
Formed2010 merger of the Fairmount Park Commission and the Department of Recreation
AssetsMore than 10,200 acres of public land and waterways (per the City), recreation centers, playgrounds, pools, trails, athletic fields, urban forest
PartnersPhiladelphia Parks & Recreation Conservancy, friends-of groups, Rebuild
Websitephila.gov/departments/philadelphia-parks-recreation

Philadelphia Parks & Recreation (PPR) is the city department that operates and maintains the city's park system, recreation centers, playgrounds, pools, golf and trail facilities, and street and park trees, and that runs recreation, aquatics, and sports programs. It is led by a commissioner appointed by the mayor; Susan Slawson was appointed to the position in 2024 under Mayor Cherelle Parker.[1]

1 History and structure

Fairmount Park, one of the nation's largest urban park systems, was long governed by an independent Fairmount Park Commission. After a Charter change, the commission and the former Recreation Department were merged into a single department; Parks & Recreation became their successor in 2010 under the mayor's cabinet.[2] The department's work is coordinated within the Managing Director's cabinet (see Managing Director's Office) and sits alongside the Mayor's Clean and Green initiatives. Its employees are largely represented by District Council 33 and, for certain trades, other unions.

2 Facilities and programs

PPR operates a citywide network of recreation centers, playgrounds and playing fields, outdoor and indoor pools, ice rinks and cultural sites. Programs include after-school and summer camps, aquatics, senior fitness, athletics and arts. It also includes Philadelphia's urban forestry work and the planting of street trees, working with the Office of Sustainability on climate resilience and with the Water Department on green stormwater infrastructure.

The City describes the department as managing more than 10,200 acres of public land and waterways.[4] For information, residents can call (215) 683-3600 or write to parksandrecreation@phila.gov. Philadelphia City Council's announcement of the FY27 budget in June 2026 listed workforce, violence-prevention and library investments, and advocates have argued over how parks and recreation centers fare in the same cycle.

3 Permits and public use

Residents can apply to PPR for permits to use fields, pavilions and other park spaces and to hold events, and can register for programs at recreation centers. Large events on parkland, such as festivals and races, require permits and coordination with other city agencies. Concerns about maintenance, safety or hazards can be reported through Philly311, or by contacting the local recreation center or the district Council member.

4 Funding, Rebuild and partners

PPR is funded through the city budget, grants and private philanthropy. The city's beverage tax, enacted in 2016, has funded Rebuild, a capital program to renovate parks, recreation centers and libraries, alongside universal pre-K; see Philadelphia Taxes. Nonprofit partners include "friends of" groups and the Philadelphia Parks & Recreation Conservancy, on whose board the commissioner holds an ex officio seat.[1] Council members and advocates have urged larger budgets for parks and libraries in recent budget cycles.[3]

5 Debates

Recurring issues include deferred maintenance, equity in investment across neighborhoods, staffing for recreation centers and pools, and the balance between public funding and philanthropy. Reports and hearings in Council examine these questions annually, and the department's relationship with the Free Library in sharing Rebuild capital funds is a frequent topic.

See also: Mural Arts Philadelphia, Office of Sustainability, Philadelphia Neighborhoods Guide.
