Free Library of Philadelphia

Free Library of Philadelphia
TypeCity library system (independent city agency with a board of trustees); supported by the nonprofit Free Library Foundation
Led byKelly Richards, President and Director (since 2022)
Established1891
LocationsMore than 50 locations, including Parkway Central Library, regional libraries and neighborhood branches
BudgetMayor's proposed FY2027 allocation about $78 million
Websitefreelibrary.org

The Free Library of Philadelphia is the city's public library system. It operates the Parkway Central Library on the Benjamin Franklin Parkway, regional libraries and neighborhood branches, offering lending, internet access, programs, literacy and workforce services, and community space. Kelly Richards has been President and Director since 2022.[1]

1 Governance and legal basis

The Free Library was chartered in 1891 as “a general library which shall be free to all,” and is established under the Home Rule Charter, which gives it a board of trustees and a director. Although it is a city institution funded in the city budget, it functions with considerable independence from mayoral departments. The Free Library Foundation raises private funds to support programs and collections. Most city library staff are covered by municipal union contracts (see District Council 33 and District Council 47).

The Parkway Central Library opened on June 2, 1927, at 1901 Vine Street on Logan Square, in a Beaux-Arts building designed by Julian Abele and modeled on Parisian landmarks on the Place de la Concorde; construction had been planned since 1911 and was delayed by World War I.[4] The system holds about 4.24 million items and includes the Rosenbach Museum and Library among its locations, according to a summary on Wikipedia. Philadelphia City Council's June 2026 announcement of the FY27 budget listed $33 million for library HVAC improvements among its investments.[5]

2 Services

Services include book, media and digital lending, free computer and Wi-Fi access, children's and teen programming, English-language and adult literacy classes, job and small-business help, and rooms for community meetings. Library cards are free to anyone who lives, works, attends school or owns property in Pennsylvania. The library's Rare Book Department and special collections are citywide cultural assets, as are the Parkway Central Library's historic reading rooms. Libraries have also been used as cooling or warming locations during extreme weather, in coordination with the Office of Emergency Management.

3 Funding and hours

Most of the system's funding is the city appropriation, supplemented by state aid and private donations. The mayor's proposed budget for fiscal year 2027 allotted about $78 million to the Free Library, and Richards testified that up to nine libraries, including Parkway Central, the three regional libraries (Northeast, Lucien E. Blackwell West Philadelphia, and Joseph E. Coleman Northwest) and up to five neighborhood libraries, could add Sunday hours if the proposal were approved.[2] Under Richards, expanding hours has been a priority: all operating libraries are now open on Saturdays, hours that were cut during the pandemic.[2] Budget requests are decided by City Council in the spring.

4 Capital improvements and partners

Branch renovations have drawn on the Rebuild program funded by the city's beverage tax (see Philadelphia Taxes), as well as city capital funds and philanthropy. The library works with the School District of Philadelphia and community organizations on student access and literacy, and with Parks and Recreation on shared neighborhood facilities.

5 Access and accountability

Hours, building condition and staffing are the most frequent subjects of public comment. Residents can contact the library or branch managers, testify at Council budget hearings (see How to Testify at City Council), or submit service issues through Philly311. Advocates have repeatedly asked the mayor and Council for increased funding for libraries and parks.[3]

See also: Community College of Philadelphia, Office of Arts, Culture and the Creative Economy.

Office of Sustainability

Office of Sustainability (OOS)
TypeMayoral office within the executive branch
Led byDirector Elizabeth H. Lankenau, AICP (per the City's leadership page)
Established2008 (first Greenworks plan 2009)
Key documentsGreenworks Philadelphia (2009); Climate Action Playbook (2021)
Headline goalCarbon neutrality by 2050
Websitephila.gov/departments/office-of-sustainability

The Office of Sustainability (OOS) is the Philadelphia city office that sets and coordinates environmental, energy and climate policy across city departments. It does not issue permits or run utilities; it develops plans, convenes agencies, applies for grants and tracks progress. Its work links closely to the Office of Transportation, Infrastructure and Sustainability, the Water Department, Parks and Recreation and Philadelphia Gas Works.

1 Origins and plans

Mayor Michael Nutter established the office in 2008 and released the Greenworks Philadelphia plan in 2009, setting targets for energy, environment, equity, economy and engagement. The original Climate Action Plan was introduced in 2009 as the foundation for later strategies. Later directors included Christine Knapp, who departed in 2022; the City's leadership page lists Elizabeth Lankenau, AICP, as Director of Sustainability.[1] The office's reporting line has shifted between administrations.

2 Climate Action Playbook

In January 2021 the city committed to carbon neutrality by 2050 and released the Climate Action Playbook, a framework to guide equitable climate action, while also hiring its first chief resilience officer.[2] The Playbook covers cutting emissions from buildings, which are the city's largest source, transportation and waste, and preparing for heat, flooding and storms. The office publishes periodic updates on progress; one issued in June 2025 reported on implementation.[3]

3 Programs and building rules

OOS runs or supports programs for municipal building energy efficiency, the Municipal Energy Office, building energy benchmarking and performance rules for large commercial buildings, solar and electrification incentives, and urban tree canopy goals. Implementation of building-related rules runs through L&I, which enforces the Energy Code during permitting. Changes to local law require action by City Council, and energy-sector policy is shaped by state regulators such as the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission, which oversees PGW.

4 Resilience and equity

The office works with departments on heat-health response, flood mitigation and green stormwater infrastructure with the Water Department, and with Office of Emergency Management and the Department of Public Health on extreme-heat planning. Equity commitments direct investment toward neighborhoods with fewer trees, higher heat and older housing stock. See also Safe and Healthy Homes Act for housing-quality legislation that overlaps with energy and health goals.

5 Residents and criticism

Residents can find rebate and efficiency programs through the office, comment on plans in public meetings, and report conditions through Philly311. Environmental advocates have pressed for faster emission cuts and for ending reliance on gas; utility consumer advocates emphasize bill affordability. These tensions appear in the debate over PGW's future, in which coalitions have opposed rate increases while the utility says natural gas remains affordable. Progress against the 2050 target is reported by the city rather than independently audited.

See also: Streets Department, Managing Director's Office.

References

  2. City of Philadelphia, "City commits to carbon neutrality by 2050, releases Climate Action Playbook and hires first Chief Resilience Officer," January 15, 2021.
  3. City of Philadelphia Office of Sustainability, Philadelphia Climate Action Update 2025 (June 2025), phila.gov.

Office of Transportation, Infrastructure and Sustainability (OTIS)

Office of Transportation, Infrastructure and Sustainability (OTIS)
TypeCoordinating office within the Managing Director's cabinet
PredecessorOffice of Transportation and Infrastructure Systems (oTIS), created under Mayor Jim Kenney
CoordinatesStreets Department, Water Department, Office of Complete Streets, sustainability policy
Reports toManaging Director
Websitephila.gov/departments/office-of-transportation-and-infrastructure-systems

The Office of Transportation, Infrastructure and Sustainability (OTIS) is the cabinet-level coordinating office through which the Philadelphia mayor's administration sets policy for the city's roads, transportation, water and related infrastructure. It operates within the office of the Managing Director. Its name and leadership have changed across administrations: city webpages still describe the earlier Office of Transportation and Infrastructure Systems (oTIS), and this article describes both. The City's web page for the office lists Michael Carroll, P.E., as Deputy Managing Director.

1 Origins

Under Mayor Jim Kenney, the city created the Office of Transportation and Infrastructure Systems and named Michael A. Carroll, P.E., a former acting Streets Commissioner, as Deputy Managing Director for oTIS.[1] The City's current page for the office describes its programs, including Vision Zero Philadelphia, Complete Streets and Indego bike share, and this article uses the name Office of Transportation, Infrastructure and Sustainability to reflect the overlap of its work with the Office of Sustainability. On July 28, 2026, Mayor Cherelle Parker announced that Carlton Williams would become Managing Director, with whom OTIS's leadership works, effective August 17, 2026.[2]

2 What it coordinates

According to the city's description of oTIS, the office coordinates and sets policy direction for the Streets Department (including both Transportation and Sanitation), the Philadelphia Water Department, and the Office of Complete Streets, which advances safe, multimodal street design.[1] It does not replace those departments' commissioners, who run operations, but it aligns their capital plans and priorities and represents the city with outside partners.

3 Planning documents and projects

The office is associated with the city's strategic transportation plan, Connect, updated in 2021, and with Vision Zero, the goal of eliminating traffic deaths, as well as with federal infrastructure grant strategy. A director of federal infrastructure strategy was added in 2022 to pursue funds from the federal infrastructure law.[3] Projects it coordinates include street redesigns, bike and bus lanes, bridge and road capital work, and facilities such as the interim intercity bus facility at 1001 Filbert Street, for which Mayor Parker signed funding legislation in January 2026.

4 Relationship to authorities and the state

Transportation in Philadelphia is split among many governments. SEPTA is a state-created regional authority; the Parking Authority is a separate authority; state highways belong to PennDOT; the airport is a city asset (see Philadelphia International Airport); and the bridges and ports involve interstate bodies (see Port and Bridge Authorities). OTIS acts as the city's coordinating voice, but capital budgets must be approved by City Council, and state and federal funding shapes what can be built. See Home Rule Limits and State Preemption.

5 Resident access

Residents typically interact with OTIS-coordinated services through Philly311, community meetings on street projects, and Council budget hearings. Street-safety requests, neighborhood traffic-calming petitions and comments on projects are generally handled by the Streets Department's Transportation Division or the Office of Complete Streets. For other help, see How to Get Help From the City.

See also: Mayor's Cabinet and Offices, Fleet Services.

Philadelphia International Airport

Philadelphia International Airport (PHL)
TypeCity-owned airport operated by the Division of Aviation (within the Commerce Department)
PassengersMore than 30 million in each of 2024 and 2025
2026 outlookAbout 9.4 million summer passengers expected, up 6.3 percent over summer 2025
Hub carrierAmerican Airlines
RegulatorsFederal Aviation Administration; Transportation Security Administration
Websitephl.org

Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) is the region's main commercial airport, owned by the City of Philadelphia and operated by the Division of Aviation, part of the city's Commerce Department. Located in Southwest Philadelphia and Tinicum Township, Delaware County, it is a hub for American Airlines. It is a city enterprise funded mainly by airline rents and fees, passenger facility charges, parking and concessions, not by city taxes.[1]

1 Governance and finance

The airport is run by a chief executive of the Division of Aviation who reports through the Commerce Department to the mayor. The airport's management-team page at phl.org lists Tracy Borda as CFO and Interim CEO; any later appointment of a permanent chief executive would appear at phl.org. The airport operates under federal rules from the Federal Aviation Administration; security screening is by the Transportation Security Administration. Airport bonds are issued by the city and repaid from airport revenues. Airline agreements and major contracts are subject to City Council approval; see Procurement Department. PHL also operates Northeast Philadelphia Airport, a general-aviation facility.

2 Traffic and the 2026 surge

PHL surpassed 30 million passengers in both 2024 and 2025.[2] Airport officials said in 2026 that they expected 9.4 million passengers over the summer, a 6.3 percent increase over 2025, driven by events including the FIFA World Cup, the Major League Baseball All-Star Game and America's 250th anniversary celebrations; July was projected to be the busiest month at 3.2 million passengers.[3] The airport issued a statement marking an unofficial end to the 2026 summer travel season around Labor Day.

3 Capital projects

The airport has carried out a program of terminal, concourse, baggage and roadway upgrades. In March 2026 the Philadelphia Inquirer and PhillyVoice reported on a package of roughly 250 upgrades timed to the 2026 events.[4] Major construction requires FAA approval, and funding comes from federal grants, bonds and passenger facility charges. Transit access is provided by SEPTA's Airport Line regional rail.

4 Jobs, labor and community

The airport supports thousands of jobs for airlines, concessions and contractors, and many service workers are represented by unions such as the service unions described in Service and Health Care Unions. Airport concession and minority-participation programs are a recurring issue in Council hearings, as are noise and air-quality concerns for neighbors in Southwest Philadelphia and Delaware County and the impact of expansion plans on nearby communities and the Eastwick area.

5 Complaints and customer issues

Passengers file complaints about flights with the airline and the U.S. Department of Transportation; complaints about airport facilities can go to the airport or Philly311. The airport has drawn criticism in national passenger-satisfaction rankings: the Inquirer reported in September 2024 that a J.D. Power survey ranked it poorly.[5] Officials have said terminal improvements aim to address those concerns.

See also: Port and Bridge Authorities, Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation, OTIS.

Philadelphia Gas Works

Philadelphia Gas Works (PGW)
TypeCity-owned natural gas utility, operated by a non-profit management entity under contract with the city
President and CEOSeth Shapiro (per PGW's leadership page)
RegulatorPennsylvania Public Utility Commission (PUC), replacing the Philadelphia Gas Commission
Latest base rate casePUC-approved settlement, about $62 million (approx. 9.3 percent) annual increase, effective October 9, 2025
AssistanceCustomer Responsibility Program, Hardship Fund, LIHEAP
Websitepgworks.com

Philadelphia Gas Works (PGW) is the municipally owned natural gas utility serving Philadelphia and is the largest city-owned gas utility in the United States. The City owns it, but it is run by the Philadelphia Facilities Management Corporation, a nonprofit under contract with the city, and it has no shareholders.[1] Its president and CEO is Seth Shapiro.[2]

1 Ownership and governance

PGW traces its origins to 1836, when Philadelphia began gas service, and it is now owned by the city. Because the city owns the system, its debt and finances interact with the city's budget and bond rating, and its dividends or payments to the city have been a subject of mayoral and Council attention. PGW's board of directors is appointed through city processes, and the mayor and City Council have historically influenced it. PGW is not a state-created authority like SEPTA; it is a city asset managed through a nonprofit contractor.

2 Regulation: from Gas Commission to the PUC

For decades PGW was the only major Pennsylvania gas utility not regulated by the state utility commission; rates were instead reviewed by the Philadelphia Gas Commission, a body of Council appointees. State law moved PGW under the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission, ending the Gas Commission's role as sole regulator. The PUC now sets rates, investigates complaints and reviews safety and customer service.[3] The change was supported by consumer advocates who sought professional, independent review, and it brought PGW into the same process as other Pennsylvania utilities. See Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia.

3 How a rate case works

  1. PGW files a request with the PUC to increase base rates; in 2025 the request was $105 million (about 15.7 percent).
  2. The PUC suspends the increase and investigates; parties such as the Office of Consumer Advocate, the Office of Small Business Advocate, the PUC's Bureau of Investigation and Enforcement, and advocacy coalitions intervene.
  3. Testimony is filed and public input hearings are held.
  4. Parties may settle. In October 2025 the PUC approved a settlement of about $62 million (about 9.3 percent), $43 million less than requested, and directed PGW to continue evaluating methane detection, decarbonization and customer assistance.[3]

PGW says a typical heating customer's annual bill has fallen $259 (18.5 percent) over ten years despite the increase.[4] Opponents, including environmental and consumer coalitions, argued the proposed increase would raise residential bills substantially and opposed a revenue-guarantee mechanism.[5] Rate complaints from the Office of Consumer Advocate and the Office of Small Business Advocate were also docketed in early 2026 (dockets C-2026-3060261 and C-2026-3060961).

4 Assistance and complaints

Customers struggling with bills can use the Customer Responsibility Program (income-based payment), PGW's Hardship Fund and the federal LIHEAP heating grants.[4] Billing or service complaints are filed with PGW first; if unresolved, customers can contact the PUC's consumer services bureau. Gas leaks and smells of gas should be reported immediately to PGW's emergency line and 911.

5 Climate and sale debates

PGW is central to debates over decarbonization. The Office of Sustainability goal of carbon neutrality by 2050 implies reducing natural gas use, while PGW argues gas remains the most affordable heating option. In the past the city explored selling PGW (a proposed sale of PGW to UGI Corporation was negotiated by the Nutter administration but was not approved by Council and lapsed in 2014), and workers and consumer advocates have opposed privatization. Utility bills also feature in tenant disputes; see Tenant and Housing Advocacy Groups.

See also: Philadelphia Water Department, Philadelphia Taxes, Organized Labor in Philadelphia.

Division of Housing and Community Development

Division of Housing and Community Development
TypeCity-charter agency (division of the Department of Planning and Development)
Also known asDHCD (formerly the Office of Housing and Community Development, OHCD)
Parent bodyDepartment of Planning and Development
Main fundingFederal HUD block grants, the city Housing Trust Fund, and city bond and general funds
Address1234 Market Street, 17th Floor, Philadelphia, PA 19107
Websitephila.gov/departments/division-of-housing-and-community-development

The Division of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) is the part of Philadelphia city government that plans and funds housing and neighborhood programs. It sits inside the Department of Planning and Development and is the city's main channel for federal housing and community development money from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), along with local dollars such as the Housing Trust Fund. It is a city agency, distinct from the state-chartered Philadelphia Housing Authority and from the nonprofit Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation that carries out many of its programs.[1]

1 Role and structure

DHCD describes its mission as helping Philadelphia offer homes for people at all income levels, commercial corridors with thriving businesses, and healthy neighborhoods.[1] It was formerly a freestanding Office of Housing and Community Development reporting directly to the mayor's administration; it was later reorganized under the Department of Planning and Development, which also houses the City Planning Commission staff and development services. The division does not usually build or manage housing itself. Instead it sets priorities, writes federally required plans, awards funding to nonprofit and for-profit developers, counseling agencies and community groups, and monitors compliance.

At the top of the housing portfolio, Mayor Cherelle Parker created in 2025 a new position of Chief Housing and Urban Development Officer, filled by Angela D. Brooks, to oversee the administration's housing plan.[2] That office coordinates DHCD with other bodies, including the Land Bank, the Redevelopment Authority and the Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation.

2 Funding sources

Much of DHCD's money comes from federal formula programs administered by HUD, commonly the Community Development Block Grant (CDBG), the HOME Investment Partnerships program and the Emergency Solutions Grant. Because these funds carry federal rules, the city must publish a multi-year Consolidated Plan and an Annual Action Plan, take public comment and report results; the Annual Action Plan for 2025-2026 was published as a proposed document in mid-2025.[3] Local sources include the city Housing Trust Fund, which is supported by a dedicated recording-fee revenue stream, and bond proceeds authorized through the capital and operating budget process. DHCD's total spending varies year to year with federal appropriations and city bond issuances, so readers seeking a current dollar figure should consult the latest budget documents.

3 Programs

DHCD's programs fall into several groups.

  • Home repair and preservation. Programs help low- and moderate-income owners repair or stabilize the homes they live in, including the long-running Basic Systems Repair Program for emergencies such as heating, plumbing, electrical and roof failures, delivered with partner agencies.[4]
  • Homeownership and housing counseling. Funding supports HUD-certified counseling agencies that help residents buy first homes, avoid foreclosure and manage tax and mortgage problems.
  • Affordable rental and homeownership development. The division finances new construction and rehabilitation by awarding gap funding, often alongside Low-Income Housing Tax Credits allocated by the state Pennsylvania Housing Finance Agency.
  • Neighborhood and commercial corridor investment. This includes the Neighborhood Preservation Initiative and funding for community development corporations (see Community Development Corporations).
  • Homelessness and special-needs housing. DHCD coordinates with the Office of Homeless Services on supportive housing funded through HUD programs.

4 The H.O.M.E. initiative

In 2025 Mayor Parker signed an executive order creating Housing Opportunities Made Easy (H.O.M.E.), and in March 2025 announced a plan with about $2 billion in public-sector resources to create and preserve 30,000 homes, of which 13,500 would be newly constructed and 16,500 preserved. The funding described at the time included about $800 million in bonds, with the first $400 million issued in fiscal year 2026, plus other local, state and federal sources and the use of publicly owned land.[2] DHCD is one of the delivery arms for the repair, preservation and development strands of this plan, while land-disposition goals depend heavily on the Land Bank and councilmanic prerogative.

5 Working with the public

Residents typically encounter DHCD through home-repair applications, housing counseling referrals and public hearings on funding plans. Information is available at phila.gov, by email at info.dhcd@phila.gov or by phone at (215) 686-9749.[1] The division also supports a Housing Advisory Board and holds public comment periods on its HUD-required plans. Tenants with problems such as missing repairs or an unlicensed landlord are normally directed instead to Licenses and Inspections or the Fair Housing Commission.

6 Relationships and debates

Housing advocates and developers have long debated how DHCD funds should be divided among preservation, new construction, rental and ownership, and how quickly vacant land reaches projects (see Tenant and Housing Advocacy Groups and Developers and the Real Estate Lobby). City Council appropriates the local funds and approves many land transactions, while HUD sets conditions on federal dollars. Statements about outcomes of the 30,000-home goal should be checked against the administration's progress reports.

See also: Department of Planning and Development, Philadelphia Land Bank, Philadelphia Housing Authority, Federal Government and Philadelphia.

  3. DHCD, Proposed Annual Action Plan, Year 2025-2026 (City of Philadelphia, June 2025).

Philadelphia Land Bank

Philadelphia Land Bank
TypeCity land bank authority created under the Pennsylvania Land Bank Act and city ordinance
EstablishedAuthorized by Council legislation in 2013 under the Pennsylvania Land Bank Act
Governing bodyBoard of directors (11 members listed on its website as of October 2026), appointed by the Mayor and the Council President
StaffingDay-to-day work carried out by PHDC staff
Related bodiesPhiladelphia Redevelopment Authority, Vacant Property Review Committee
Websitephdcphila.org (Land Bank pages)

The Philadelphia Land Bank is a public entity that holds, manages and disposes of vacant and tax-delinquent land and buildings, with the stated aim of returning them to productive use for housing, gardens, businesses and community facilities. Philadelphia has tens of thousands of vacant lots and buildings, spread among private owners, the city, the Redevelopment Authority and other agencies. The Land Bank was designed to replace a fragmented process, in which a buyer might need approvals from several bodies, with a more predictable one.[1]

1 Origins and legal basis

Land banks are authorized in Pennsylvania by the state Land Bank Act, which allows municipalities to create entities with special powers to acquire tax-delinquent property. Philadelphia's version was proposed by advocates and debated in City Council in 2013, with disputes over how much control Council members should retain over land in their districts. The resulting legislation made the Land Bank a distinct public body while preserving a Council role: the Land Bank's strategic plan and policies are reviewed and approved annually by Council, and individual dispositions generally require a Council resolution.[2] That compromise reflects councilmanic prerogative, the informal tradition by which district Council members control land decisions in their districts.

2 How land is disposed of

A buyer seeking a Land Bank property typically submits an application describing the intended use, the development plan and financing. The Land Bank's board must approve the sale, and a Council resolution is needed for conveyance. Before the Land Bank, the Vacant Property Review Committee played an important approving role, and a 2019 bill proposed to eliminate that committee and transfer its authority to the Land Bank to further centralize decisions.[3] Sale prices may be discounted when a project serves a public purpose such as affordable housing, and side lots are sometimes sold to adjacent homeowners. A related program, Turn the Key, sells inexpensive city land to developers who build for-sale homes under price caps, with city assistance for low-income buyers.[4]

3 Relationship to PHDC and the PRA

The Land Bank has its own board but few of its own employees. Following a 2019 reorganization, the Land Bank and the Redevelopment Authority combined their staffs and day-to-day operations under the Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation (PHDC), with each public body's board remaining intact. Officials described the arrangement as a "one-stop shop" for acquiring, disposing of and developing public land.[3] Strategic direction of the broader housing agenda comes from the mayor's office, which in 2025 set a goal of creating and preserving 30,000 homes; the Land Bank is a key source of the publicly owned land that plan relies on (see Division of Housing and Community Development).

4 Board and 2025 changes

As reported by the Philadelphia Inquirer in October 2025, Mayor Cherelle Parker asked longtime board chair Herb Wetzel and board member Majeedah Rashid, who leads the Nicetown Community Development Corporation, to step down. Alexander Balloon, executive director of the Passyunk Avenue Revitalization Corporation and a former board member, replaced Rashid, and Angela D. Brooks, the city's chief housing officer, joined the board.[5] The mayor's office stated that a strong and effective Land Bank is essential to reaching the housing goal. The Land Bank's website lists an 11-member board, appointed by the Mayor and the Council President, chaired by Angela D. Brooks, the city's chief housing officer; other listed members include the PHA's president and CEO Kelvin Jeremiah, a Revenue Department deputy commissioner and a representative of Council's housing staff.[7]

5 Criticisms and challenges

The Inquirer described the board as split between members who favored earmarking land for nonprofits, community uses and deeply affordable housing and those who prioritized speed and private development to reduce vacancy. It reported that several Turn the Key proposals had been delayed, that projects can stall because of the need for Council approval even with mayoral backing, and that Council members questioned staff capacity during budget hearings, with an outside assessment by the consulting firm Guidehouse pending at that time.[5] Observers have also argued that the Land Bank's effectiveness is limited by multiple political checkpoints. Supporters respond that Council's role guards against displacement and gives neighborhoods a voice. Annual fiscal reports on land transfers have at times shown fewer transfers than the stated goals.[6]

6 Interacting with the Land Bank

Residents can look up whether a lot is publicly owned through the city's property tools (see Open Data and Transparency Tools), contact PHDC's land management staff, and attend Land Bank board meetings, which are subject to the Sunshine Act. Community groups can weigh in through their Registered Community Organization and district Council office. This article is general information, not advice about any specific property.

See also: Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation, Philadelphia Redevelopment Authority, Councilmanic Prerogative.

References

  4. CBS Philadelphia and City Council reporting on the Turn the Key initiative.
  5. Philadelphia Inquirer, "Philadelphia Land Bank, Parker and 30,000 houses," October 20, 2025; City of Philadelphia press release, October 20, 2025, on Land Bank board appointments.

Philadelphia Housing Authority

Philadelphia Housing Authority
TypePublic housing authority created under Pennsylvania law (not a city department)
Led byKelvin A. Jeremiah, President and CEO (since March 2013, as of 2026)
Size (agency-reported)About 13,000 affordable units owned and managed; 22,000+ Housing Choice Vouchers; 800+ employees; about $650 million annual operating and capital budget
Main funderU.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)
Governing lawPennsylvania Housing Authorities Law; federal Housing Act of 1937 programs
Websitepha.phila.gov

The Philadelphia Housing Authority (PHA) is the city's public housing agency and one of the largest in the United States. It owns and operates public housing developments and scattered-site homes, administers the Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) program that subsidizes rent in private apartments, and acts as a developer of mixed-income housing. Although its name and board are tied to the city, PHA is an independent public authority created under state law and funded mainly by the federal government; it is not part of the mayor's cabinet and is distinct from the city's Division of Housing and Community Development.[1]

1 Structure and leadership

PHA operates under a nine-member Board of Commissioners and is led day to day by a president and chief executive officer. According to the agency's website, most commissioners are appointed by the mayor and confirmed by City Council, and two are resident commissioners elected by PHA residents under the Pennsylvania Housing Authorities Law; Lynette M. Brown-Sow has chaired the board since 2013.[5] Kelvin A. Jeremiah has held that post since March 2013, according to the agency's own biography, after earlier leadership turnover at the authority.[2] The agency reports responsibility for about 13,000 affordable units, a voucher program of more than 22,000 households, over 800 employees and an annual operating and capital budget of roughly $650 million (the agency's website gives about $700 million elsewhere).[2] Because it is a state-created authority, its employees are not under the city's civil service system, and its procurement follows federal HUD rules and state authority law rather than the city's Procurement Department.

2 Programs

  • Public housing. Developments and scattered-site homes owned by PHA, where tenants typically pay a share of income as rent.
  • Housing Choice Vouchers. Households find a private landlord who agrees to participate; PHA pays part of the rent and inspects the unit for HUD housing quality standards. Voucher holders are also protected by the city's source-of-income anti-discrimination rules, enforced by the Commission on Human Relations.
  • Resident services and self-sufficiency programs, and homeownership assistance.
  • Development. PHA partners with private and nonprofit developers on replacing obsolete public housing with mixed-income communities.

In April 2025 PHA detailed an "Opening Doors" plan to preserve, build or acquire about 20,000 affordable units over eight years, at an estimated cost of $6.3 billion, as reported by WHYY.[6]

3 Funding and federal oversight

Most of PHA's money comes from HUD through annual appropriations, subject to federal budget decisions. HUD can audit the agency, designate it as troubled, or take over operations in extreme cases; in earlier decades the federal government intervened in PHA's management and reviews and audits have repeatedly examined its finances and maintenance. The authority also publishes an Annual Plan each year that must be available for public comment: in March 2026 PHA held a public hearing on a proposed amendment to its fiscal year 2027 Annual Plan, including a significant amendment related to HUD's Rental Assistance Demonstration (RAD) program.[3]

4 Waiting lists and applying

Demand for subsidized housing in Philadelphia far exceeds supply, and waiting lists open only occasionally. In January 2023 PHA reopened the Housing Choice Voucher list for the first time in more than a decade, accepting applications from January 23 to February 5, 2023, and selecting 10,000 applicants by random lottery (2,000 to receive vouchers immediately and 8,000 to be placed on a waiting list), as the Inquirer reported; applicants needed household income at or below 50 percent of area median income.[7] PHA announces any future openings through its website and the media, so applicants should rely only on PHA's own announcements for opening dates and should be wary of third parties charging fees. Residents and applicants can reach PHA through its website or at 215-684-4000.

5 Redevelopment and conversion

Like many authorities, PHA has used federal programs to demolish and replace aging public housing and, more recently, to convert units to project-based subsidies through RAD, which lets the authority borrow private capital for repairs. Tenant advocates and some residents have raised concerns about relocation, long-term affordability and resident rights during such conversions, while PHA argues that the conversions preserve units that federal appropriations alone cannot maintain. These debates connect to the wider discussion in Tenant and Housing Advocacy Groups.

6 Complaints and relationships

Residents of PHA housing have grievance procedures set by federal rules, and unresolved matters can go to HUD or to the courts, including Municipal Court landlord-tenant proceedings, where PHA tenants have specific federal notice protections. PHA works with the Redevelopment Authority, the Land Bank and the City on land and development, and with the Office of Homeless Services on vouchers for people exiting homelessness. For general help finding a city service, see How to Get Help From the City.

See also: Division of Housing and Community Development, Office of Homeless Services, Federal Government and Philadelphia.

Philadelphia Redevelopment Authority

Philadelphia Redevelopment Authority
TypePublic authority created under the Pennsylvania Urban Redevelopment Law
Established1945
Key powersEminent domain (condemnation), redevelopment area planning, land acquisition, sale and lease
StaffingOperations carried out by PHDC staff since a 2019 reorganization
Related bodiesPhiladelphia Land Bank, City Planning Commission
Websitephdcphila.org

The Philadelphia Redevelopment Authority (PRA) is a public authority created under Pennsylvania's Urban Redevelopment Law to eliminate blight and carry out redevelopment. It is a state-law entity whose board is appointed by city officials; it is not a city department and is separate from the Philadelphia Housing Authority. The PRA played a major role in mid-twentieth-century urban renewal, including the redevelopment of Society Hill and Center City areas in the 1950s and 1960s, and its legacy of clearing neighborhoods remains a subject of historical debate.[1]

1 Legal basis and powers

Pennsylvania's Urban Redevelopment Law of 1945 allows cities to create redevelopment authorities. Their central tool is the ability to designate a redevelopment area through a plan reviewed by the City Planning Commission and approved by City Council, and then to acquire land, including by eminent domain, in order to assemble sites for development. The PRA can also sell or lease land to developers, enter agreements for cleanup, and hold property on behalf of public purposes. Because eminent domain affects private owners, such acquisitions involve notice, compensation under state eminent domain law, and the opportunity to contest the taking in court.

2 History

From the late 1940s, the PRA, working with the planning commission under planners such as Edmund Bacon, used federal urban renewal funds to clear and rebuild areas near Center City. Later decades involved the Neighborhood Transformation Initiative of the early 2000s, a large-scale effort to demolish blighted buildings and assemble land, in which the PRA acquired property. Critics have argued that urban renewal displaced residents, particularly in Black neighborhoods, while supporters point to revitalized core districts and new housing. Gregory Heller, named executive director in 2016, led the agency before its staff consolidation.[2]

3 Consolidation with PHDC and the Land Bank

The creation of the Philadelphia Land Bank in the 2010s meant that both bodies controlled public land. Bisnow Philadelphia reported that in a reorganization announced in 2019 the PRA and the Land Bank combined their duties and staffs under the Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation (PHDC), led by President and CEO David Thomas. The two public boards remained intact, and staff and operations moved to PHDC through memoranda of understanding. Heller became PHDC senior vice president of community investment, and Angel Rodriguez, who had led the Land Bank, became senior vice president of land management. Officials called the change a "one-stop shop" intended to make land transactions predictable, transparent and consistent, and said no jobs were lost.[3]

4 What the PRA does today

Today the PRA is best understood as a legal vehicle with a board and statutory powers, run through PHDC. It holds title to a portfolio of properties acquired over decades and handles transactions that need its special powers, including condemnation, conveyances of redevelopment-area land and agreements with developers. It also works with community development corporations and with the Division of Housing and Community Development on projects that combine land, subsidy and financing (see Division of Housing and Community Development). The agency can partner with the Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation and other economic development bodies on commercial sites, but each has distinct legal powers.

5 Oversight and public input

As a public authority the PRA must hold open meetings under the Sunshine Act and is subject to the Right-to-Know Law. City Council's role is chiefly in approving redevelopment area plans and certain land conveyances, which links the PRA to councilmanic prerogative. The City Controller may audit the entity as a city-related body. Residents who want to comment on a plan can attend planning commission or Council hearings and work through their Registered Community Organization.

See also: Philadelphia Land Bank, Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation, Department of Planning and Development.

References

  3. Bisnow Philadelphia, "Philadelphia Housing Development Corp. Absorbs Redevelopment Authority, Land Bank in Department Merger."

Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation

Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation
TypeNonprofit corporation closely tied to the City; implementing agency for housing programs
Also known asPHDC
Led byDavid Thomas, President and CEO (as reported in 2019 and later)
StaffsPhiladelphia Land Bank and Philadelphia Redevelopment Authority (since 2019 reorganization)
Main fundersCity and federal housing funds passed through DHCD, state funds, loan repayments
Websitephdcphila.org

The Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation (PHDC) is a nonprofit that carries out many of Philadelphia's housing programs, including home repair and land transactions. It is neither a city department nor a state authority: it is a private nonprofit corporation that works under agreements with the City and with the two public land bodies it staffs. Understanding PHDC is useful because residents who apply for home repair help or ask about a vacant lot are often dealing with PHDC staff even when the legal decision-maker is another body.[1]

1 Role

PHDC acts as an implementing partner for the City's housing policy. The policy and funding come from the mayor's office, City Council and the Division of Housing and Community Development; PHDC administers programs, processes applications, manages construction and repair work through contractors, and handles property transactions. Using a nonprofit gives the City flexibility to hire specialized staff, take on loans and move faster than some municipal processes allow, but it also means that the corporation is not directly covered by every rule that applies to city departments, such as the civil service system.

2 The 2019 consolidation

Bisnow Philadelphia reported that the Land Bank and the Redevelopment Authority combined their duties and staffs into PHDC in a reorganization announced in 2019. The two public boards remained intact, and the staff transferred through memoranda of understanding with support from Council. PHDC's President and CEO David Thomas kept his position; Angel Rodriguez, formerly head of the Land Bank, became senior vice president of land management; and Gregory Heller, former executive director of the Redevelopment Authority, became senior vice president of community investment. Thomas said no jobs were lost and no office space was added or vacated.[2] The purpose, officials said, was a "one-stop shop" for how Philadelphians engage with the City's acquisition, disposition and development of public land. A bill was then pending to transfer the functions of the Vacant Property Review Committee to the Land Bank.

3 Programs

  • Home repair. PHDC administers programs for low- and moderate-income homeowners, including the Basic Systems Repair Program for emergency system failures and loan programs for larger repairs, funded mainly through DHCD.[1]
  • Land management. Staff handle applications for vacant lots and buildings held by the Land Bank and the Redevelopment Authority, including side-yard sales and Turn the Key developer sales.
  • Community investment. PHDC coordinates funding and technical help for community development corporations and commercial corridors (see Community Development Corporations).
  • Real estate development. The corporation can partner with developers on affordable housing projects and manage city-owned property.

Under the mayor's 2025 H.O.M.E. plan to create and preserve 30,000 homes, PHDC's land and repair functions are central to delivery.[3] Specific figures on current PHDC budget and staffing should be taken from its annual reports and the City's budget documents.

4 Accountability

Because PHDC spends public funds, it is subject to audits by funders and the City Controller, and the public bodies it staffs are subject to the Sunshine Act and Right-to-Know Law. Critics and reporters have at times examined the pace of vacant land transfers and the size of home-repair waiting lists; Bisnow reported, for example, that fiscal-year transfers in 2022 picked up but fell short of goals.[4] Supporters note that demand for repairs and land consistently exceeds available funding.

5 Contacting PHDC

Residents seeking repair help usually begin with DHCD or PHDC application pages and may be referred to partner agencies. For questions about whether a lot is publicly owned, see the Land Bank article and the City's open data tools. Complaints about a contractor or service can be raised with PHDC directly, then with DHCD, and as a last step through the City's complaint channels.

See also: Philadelphia Land Bank, Philadelphia Redevelopment Authority, Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation.

Rental Licensing and Landlord-Tenant Law in Philadelphia

Rental Licensing and Landlord-Tenant Law in Philadelphia
TypeOverview of city and state law (general information, not legal advice)
State lawPennsylvania Landlord and Tenant Act of 1951; Rent Withholding Act; common-law warranty of habitability
City lawPhiladelphia Code, including the rental license provisions and the Fair Housing Ordinance (Chapter 9-800)
EnforcementLicenses and Inspections, Fair Housing Commission, Municipal Court
Recent changeSafe and Healthy Homes Act (passed 2026; expected effective November 2026)

Rental licensing and landlord-tenant law in Philadelphia is a layered system. Pennsylvania state law sets the basic rules of the landlord-tenant relationship, while the City of Philadelphia adds licensing, inspection and fair housing requirements through its Code. This article describes the general framework for residents, tenants, owners and students; it does not give legal advice and does not address any individual dispute. Anyone with a specific problem should consult a lawyer or one of the organizations described in Legal Aid and Public Interest Law.

1 Rental licenses

A property owner who rents out housing in Philadelphia needs a rental license from the City. The City's guidance states that one license can cover all units at a single address, and that failing to obtain and maintain a current license carries heavy penalties, including daily fines and in some circumstances the inability to collect rent or to evict.[1] Licenses are applied for online through the City's eCLIPSE system and are administered by the Department of Licenses and Inspections (L&I). Licensing links to other requirements such as paying taxes owed to the City (see Revenue Department) and, for older housing, lead-safe or lead-free certification for units where young children may live.

2 Certificate of Rental Suitability

Separately, landlords must give new tenants a Certificate of Rental Suitability when a lease is signed. The certificate states that the owner has the necessary licenses, that there are no unabated code violations that make the unit unsafe or unfit, and that the unit meets basic fire and safety requirements such as working smoke detectors. It is free to obtain, and landlords who do not provide one may face penalties and difficulty enforcing the lease.[1] Related materials are published by the Fair Housing Commission, which also maintains tenant information. Landlords are also required to give tenants a copy of the City's "Partners for Good Housing" handbook with a lease.

3 State law basics

Pennsylvania law governs many core questions. The Landlord and Tenant Act of 1951 sets limits on security deposits (generally two months' rent in the first year of a lease and one month's rent afterward), requires that deposits be held in specified accounts, and sets notice-to-quit periods for ending a tenancy: generally 10 days for nonpayment of rent and, for other causes, 15 days for leases of one year or less and 30 days for longer leases, unless the lease says otherwise. Pennsylvania courts recognize an implied warranty of habitability, established in Pugh v. Holmes (Pa. 1979), meaning a landlord must keep the premises fit to live in. The Rent Withholding Act allows rent to be paid into escrow when a dwelling has been certified unfit by the local authority. Landlords may not use "self-help" such as changing locks or removing belongings to evict a tenant; they must use the court process.

4 City protections and the Fair Housing Ordinance

Philadelphia's Fair Housing Ordinance, in Chapter 9-800 of the Code, prohibits specified unfair rental practices, including ending or changing a lease while there are open code violations reported on the unit, retaliating against a tenant for exercising legal rights, terminating a lease because of status as a victim of domestic violence or sexual assault, terminating a lease of less than one year without good cause, and self-help evictions.[2] Discrimination in housing based on protected characteristics is addressed by the Commission on Human Relations and by federal and state fair housing laws. The ordinance is enforced through the Fair Housing Commission, a five-member body appointed by the mayor.

5 Repairs, inspections and complaints

Tenants who need repairs typically start by notifying the landlord in writing, then calling 311 to request an L&I inspection. L&I can issue violations to owners, who may be fined, and unsafe units may be declared unfit. Housing code violations, rental license status and some complaint information can be searched through the City's online property tools (see Open Data and Transparency Tools). Community and legal organizations help tenants understand the options (see Tenant and Housing Advocacy Groups), and landlord groups provide education to owners (see Landlord and Property Owner Associations).

6 Evictions and courts

Landlord-tenant cases in Philadelphia are heard in the Landlord-Tenant division of the Municipal Court, part of the First Judicial District. Before filing for nonpayment, a landlord must participate in the City's pre-filing Eviction Diversion Program, and eligible low-income tenants may have access to free counsel under the Right to Counsel program. Details, including appeals and enforcement by the Sheriff's Office, are in Eviction Diversion and Landlord-Tenant Court.

7 Recent changes

In 2026 Philadelphia enacted the Safe and Healthy Homes Act, a package of two bills expanding rental license requirements, repair obligations, anti-retaliation protections and good-cause rules, with an expected effective date of November 2026. See Safe and Healthy Homes Act. Because rules change, readers should check phila.gov for current requirements.

See also: Fair Housing Commission, Safe and Healthy Homes Act, Eviction Diversion and Landlord-Tenant Court, Court of Common Pleas and Municipal Court.

References

  1. City of Philadelphia, "Rent your property" and "Get a Certificate of Rental Suitability," phila.gov/services (accessed October 2026).
  2. City of Philadelphia, "File a complaint about unfair rental practices," phila.gov (Fair Housing Commission).
  3. Pennsylvania Landlord and Tenant Act of 1951, 68 P.S. section 250.101 et seq.; Rent Withholding Act, 35 P.S. section 1700-1 et seq.; Pugh v. Holmes, 405 A.2d 897 (Pa. 1979).

Fair Housing Commission

Fair Housing Commission
TypeCity board with staff (city-charter body)
MembersFive, appointed by the Mayor
Governing lawPhiladelphia Fair Housing Ordinance, Philadelphia Code Chapter 9-800 (including section 9-804)
Address601 Walnut Street, Suite 300 South, Philadelphia, PA 19106
Phone / email(215) 686-4670; FairHousingComm@phila.gov
Walk-in hoursMonday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. (as published)
Websitephila.gov/FairHousingCommission

The Fair Housing Commission (FHC) is the City of Philadelphia body that enforces the city's Fair Housing Ordinance and helps tenants and landlords understand their rights and responsibilities. Despite its name, it is not the main agency for discrimination claims, which are handled by the Commission on Human Relations; rather, the FHC focuses on landlord-tenant practices, such as retaliation, improper lease terminations and licensing compliance. The FHC is a city body, not a court, and its powers are those given by the ordinance.[1]

1 Structure

The FHC consists of five commissioners appointed by the Mayor, supported by a small staff that handles intake, scheduling and information. Commissioners hold hearings and issue decisions. Like other city boards, its public hearings are subject to open-meetings rules (see Sunshine Act and Open Meetings). The commission sits in the municipal services area of Center City and offers walk-in assistance on weekdays.

2 What the Commission does

According to the City, the FHC works to ensure that renters have safe housing and that landlords comply with housing laws. Its functions include enforcing the Fair Housing Ordinance, conducting hearings on unsafe or poorly maintained properties, verifying that landlords have the required rental licenses and certificates, educating tenants and landlords about rights and responsibilities, and connecting both sides to other resources.[1] It complements Licenses and Inspections, which issues licenses and code violations, and the courts, which decide eviction and money claims.

3 Types of complaints

The FHC accepts two broad kinds of complaint: unfair rental practices by landlords, and housing or property discrimination. Examples of unfair rental practices listed by the City include terminating a lease or changing its terms while there are open code violations reported on the unit, terminating a lease because the tenant is a victim of domestic violence or sexual assault, terminating a lease with a term of under one year without good cause, retaliating against a tenant for exercising legal rights, and self-help eviction (for example, lockouts without a court order).[2] Complaints about lead paint, heat or structural defects are normally directed first to L&I through 311.

4 The complaint and hearing process

To file a complaint, the City says a person must be a Philadelphia resident currently living in the rental unit. Complaints can be made using the FHC intake form or in person. When a complaint is accepted, the tenant and landlord receive a copy of the signed complaint, instructions, and a notice of the hearing date and time.[2] At the hearing both sides can present evidence. The ordinance gives the Commission authority to hold hearings and conduct investigations; the possible outcomes and remedies, and any appeal rights to the Court of Common Pleas, are set out in the ordinance and the FHC's notices and should be confirmed there rather than assumed. The FHC is not a substitute for legal advice, and parties may wish to consult counsel (see Legal Aid and Public Interest Law).

5 Rental suitability and education

The FHC publishes information on the Certificate of Rental Suitability that landlords must give to new tenants, which confirms licensing and the absence of serious code problems. It also distributes guidance for owners and renters, drawing on the "Partners for Good Housing" materials that landlords must provide with leases. Landlord and tenant organizations frequently refer people to the FHC (see Tenant and Housing Advocacy Groups and Landlord and Property Owner Associations). For an overview of the legal framework, see Rental Licensing and Landlord-Tenant Law in Philadelphia.

6 Relationship to other bodies and recent law

The FHC is separate from Municipal Court landlord-tenant proceedings, though a tenant may raise the same underlying facts in more than one forum. The Safe and Healthy Homes Act, passed in 2026 and expected to take effect in November 2026, expands anti-retaliation, good-cause and licensing rules, and may affect how the FHC's work is structured; readers should check phila.gov for updated procedures. For general complaint routing, see How to File a Complaint.

See also: Commission on Human Relations, Department of Licenses and Inspections, Safe and Healthy Homes Act.

References

  1. City of Philadelphia, "Fair Housing Commission," phila.gov/FairHousingCommission (accessed October 2026).
  2. City of Philadelphia, "File a complaint about unfair rental practices," phila.gov/services.
  3. Philadelphia Code, Chapter 9-800, Fair Housing Ordinance.

Eviction Diversion and Landlord-Tenant Court

Eviction Diversion and Landlord-Tenant Court
TypeCity program plus state court process (general information, not legal advice)
CourtMunicipal Court of Philadelphia (Landlord-Tenant), First Judicial District
Diversion programMandatory pre-filing mediation and rental assistance step for landlords, required by city ordinance since January 1, 2022 (Ord. 210920)
Right to CounselFree lawyers for eligible lower-income tenants in ten designated zip codes (income threshold: confirm with the Philly Tenant hotline)
EnforcementSheriff's Office carries out court-ordered removals

Eviction diversion and landlord-tenant court describe the two-part system through which Philadelphia handles most disputes over unpaid rent or ending a tenancy: a city-created diversion step before a landlord files, and the Landlord-Tenant division of the Municipal Court, a state-created court in the First Judicial District. This article is general information; it does not assess any particular case.

1 Origins of diversion

The Eviction Diversion Program began in summer 2020 under emergency housing-relief legislation passed by City Council during the COVID-19 pandemic. It was run by the Good Shepherd Mediation Program, using volunteer mediators and housing counselors who prepared tenants.[1] Council later extended it, and a city ordinance (No. 210920) made participation mandatory from January 1, 2022.[2] The city's Municipal Court supported the approach. As of 2026, landlords are reported to be required to apply to the program before they can file most eviction cases in Philadelphia, with the program continuing to be administered with partner organizations and funded through the City; readers should confirm current rules at phila.gov.

2 How the Eviction Diversion Program works

Before filing most nonpayment cases, a landlord must send the tenant a Notice of Diversion Rights and apply to participate through the City's online portal; the program materials describe a waiting period before filing, and the exact number of days should be confirmed with the City, because it has changed since the program began.[2] A housing counselor contacts the tenant to explain the process and help gather documents, and the parties meet with a mediator to try to reach a payment plan, assistance agreement or other resolution. Outcomes may include payment of arrears from city or state rental assistance, a repayment plan, or an agreed move-out. If no agreement is reached, the landlord may then file in court. Reported participation figures have been high: early evaluations found most mediated cases ended in an agreement or ongoing negotiation, with one summary citing about 93% of participants reaching an agreement or continuing to negotiate.[2]

3 Right to Counsel

In November 2019, City Council passed legislation creating a right to legal representation in eviction and housing-risk matters for eligible tenants. The Right to Counsel (RTC) program began in a small number of zip codes and has been expanded over time; the City's Philly Tenant website currently lists ten covered zip codes: 19121, 19124, 19131, 19132, 19134, 19139, 19141, 19144, 19153 and 19154.[3] It provides a lawyer at no cost to eligible lower-income tenants in those zip codes, who can apply through the Philly Tenant hotline at (267) 443-2500; it sits alongside other legal and supportive services delivered by legal aid and nonprofit partners (see Legal Aid and Public Interest Law).

4 The Municipal Court process

The Municipal Court is a state court that handles landlord-tenant matters in Philadelphia (see Court of Common Pleas and Municipal Court). In general, a landlord must first give a written notice to quit under the Pennsylvania Landlord and Tenant Act, then file a complaint; the court schedules a hearing, serves the tenant, and a judge decides. Possible results include judgment for possession, a money judgment, a continuance, an agreement between the parties, or dismissal. A losing party may generally appeal to the Court of Common Pleas within a short deadline, and a tenant who wishes to remain during an appeal usually has to meet conditions such as paying rent into court. Only the Sheriff's Office, after a court order and a notice period, may physically remove a tenant; "self-help" evictions by landlords are not allowed. Philadelphia's Safe and Healthy Homes Act, which takes effect on November 1, 2026, adds rules on good cause for lease nonrenewal, retaliation and rental-license compliance that may bear on some cases (see Safe and Healthy Homes Act). The landlord's rental license and Certificate of Rental Suitability are relevant to the case (see Rental Licensing and Landlord-Tenant Law in Philadelphia).

5 Results and debates

Council materials in December 2021 put annual eviction filings at about 19,000 before the pandemic, and the same materials reported that more than 93 percent of mediated cases reached a successful resolution; many observers credit the diversion requirement with helping keep filings below pre-pandemic levels.[3] Tenant advocates generally support mediation and counsel as ways to prevent displacement, while some landlord groups have argued that mandatory pre-filing steps delay recovery of unpaid rent and depend on adequate rental-assistance funding (see Landlord and Property Owner Associations and Tenant and Housing Advocacy Groups). Funding for rental assistance and counsel is set in the city budget.

6 Getting help

A tenant or landlord who receives a notice or court paperwork should read deadlines carefully and seek help promptly. Resources include the City's housing counseling and Eviction Diversion Program contacts, legal aid organizations, and the Municipal Court's self-help materials. See also How to Get Help From the City.

See also: Rental Licensing and Landlord-Tenant Law in Philadelphia, Safe and Healthy Homes Act, Fair Housing Commission, Office of Homeless Services.

References

  2. PhillyVoice, CBS Philadelphia and Axios Philadelphia reporting on extension of the program through 2022 and Ordinance 210920 (Bill No. 210920, introduced by Councilmember Helen Gym; Philadelphia City Council press release, December 8, 2021); City of Philadelphia, Eviction Diversion Evaluation (2023).
  3. City of Philadelphia, Philly Tenant (phillytenant.org), Right to Counsel and Eviction Diversion pages, accessed October 2026; WHYY reporting on the Right to Counsel expansion; Eviction Lab summaries.

Safe and Healthy Homes Act

Safe and Healthy Homes Act
TypePackage of two City Council bills amending the Philadelphia Code
BillsBill No. 250329 ("Right to Repairs"); Bill No. 250330 ("Right to Safety")
IntroducedSpring 2025
Final Council voteApril 23, 2026 (passed 16-1, after a court settlement sent the bills back to committee)
MayorCherelle Parker; signing reported May 7, 2026
Effective dateNovember 1, 2026
EnforcementLicenses and Inspections, Fair Housing Commission, courts

The Safe and Healthy Homes Act is the name used for two Philadelphia City Council bills, 250329 and 250330, that change the rules for rental housing in the city. Supporters, including tenant advocates, framed them as strengthening repair, safety and anti-retaliation protections; some landlords challenged the process and argued the measures did not target bad actors. This article summarizes publicly reported provisions and is not legal advice. Readers should confirm current requirements and forms with the City.

1 Background and legislative history

The bills were introduced in City Council in spring 2025 and moved through the Housing Committee over the following year. They build on existing law: Philadelphia already requires rental licenses and Certificates of Rental Suitability and bars certain unfair rental practices (see Rental Licensing and Landlord-Tenant Law in Philadelphia). Advocates argued that enforcement gaps allowed owners with serious unresolved violations to avoid accountability and that tenants who complained risked retaliation. A Council housing committee action in 2026 also backed a budget request for implementation, reflecting that inspections and enforcement would require resources (see Philadelphia City Budget Process).[1]

2 Bill 250329: Right to Repairs

Bill 250329 updates the rental license and Certificate of Rental Suitability provisions so that landlords with serious, unaddressed code violations cannot evade detection and accountability.[1] According to summaries by a public-interest law group and a law-firm client alert, key provisions include: landlords must correct any unsafe, unfit or imminently dangerous violations within 30 days of notice unless a timely appeal is filed, and failure to do so makes the landlord noncompliant; landlords may not collect rent while out of compliance or during license suspension; tenants are entitled to rent abatement or a refund for periods in which rent was collected without a valid rental license; evictions are barred where the landlord has outstanding violations; and licensing and violation information must be posted and made transparent. The law also authorizes the City to create a proactive rental inspection program, rather than inspecting only after complaints.[2]

3 Bill 250330: Right to Safety

Bill 250330 strengthens anti-retaliation protections by broadening what counts as retaliation, adds protections for tenants who organize, and establishes new protections related to habitability and harassment. It also expands good-cause protections so they apply to all tenants regardless of lease type, and requires landlords to provide written notices to renters regarding lease terminations.[1] Tenants may seek remedies in court, including damages reported as $1,000 per violation or actual compensatory damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees.[2]

4 Lawsuit and passage

In March 2026, two landlords sued, alleging that Council violated Pennsylvania's Sunshine Act because public comment was opened only after the bills passed through the Housing Committee. The suit delayed a scheduled Council vote (see Sunshine Act and Open Meetings).[3] The Inquirer and WHYY reported that the case was settled on March 18, 2026, the day before the scheduled vote, with the bills returning to the Housing Committee for a new hearing; the committee voted again on March 30.[4] The plaintiffs, reported as property owners Erica Hadley and Seth Floyd, then sought to hold the city in contempt and added constitutional claims; a second challenge was reported in federal court, where a judge was reported to have denied most of the requests, and Council gave final approval on April 23, 2026, by a 16-1 vote.[5] The Inquirer reported on May 7, 2026, that Mayor Cherelle Parker had signed the bills and that a contempt hearing was scheduled for June 2026; the outcome of that hearing and the later status of the litigation should be checked in court records and current news reports.[5]

5 Effective date and implementation

The legislation takes effect on November 1, 2026, according to the Inquirer, Bisnow and a Legal Intelligencer analysis.[5][6] Implementation depends on L&I and other agencies issuing forms, notices and procedures, funding for any proactive inspection program, and training for the Fair Housing Commission and courts. Landlords are advised by counsel and trade groups to review licensing, certificates, violation histories and lease notice practices ahead of the effective date (see Landlord and Property Owner Associations). Tenants can find guidance from advocacy groups and legal aid (see Tenant and Housing Advocacy Groups).

6 Positions and open questions

Supporters say the package fills gaps that let unsafe conditions persist and discourages retaliation. Landlord organizations and some owners have said the measures add compliance risk and liability, and the plaintiffs in the 2026 suit said the legislation did not hold bad actors accountable.[4] Open questions include the pace of inspections, how the new good-cause rules interact with state law governing evictions (see Home Rule Limits and State Preemption), and how courts will treat the new private right of action. See Eviction Diversion and Landlord-Tenant Court for the court process.

See also: Rental Licensing and Landlord-Tenant Law in Philadelphia, Department of Licenses and Inspections, Fair Housing Commission.

Tax Abatement and Development Incentives

Tax Abatement and Development Incentives
TypeCity real estate tax incentives authorized by state law and city ordinance
Main program10-year abatement on improvements (value added by construction or rehabilitation)
ReformCouncil voted on December 12, 2019 to phase down the new-residential-construction abatement by 10 percentage points a year; permit cutoff December 31, 2020
Other incentivesLERTA (commercial and industrial), Keystone Opportunity Zones, financing and grant programs
Pending (Oct 2026)Mayoral proposal for a 20-year abatement for building conversions; no Council bill yet introduced as of late September 2026
Administered byOffice of Property Assessment and Revenue Department

A tax abatement in Philadelphia is a temporary exemption from real estate tax on the added value of a property, intended to encourage building and renovation. The best-known is the ten-year abatement for improvements, which the city has offered for decades and which became one of its most debated policies. The abatement applies to the increase in assessed value from construction, not to the land value, so owners still pay taxes on the land. This article is a general overview.[1]

1 How abatements work

Property owners pay city real estate taxes based on assessments set by the Office of Property Assessment and collected by the Revenue Department (see Philadelphia Taxes). Under an abatement, the added value from new construction or rehabilitation is exempted from tax for a set period. The abatement is attached to the property, so it transfers to later owners until it expires. Property tax revenue is shared between the city and the School District of Philadelphia, so a large share of the revenue foregone is revenue that would otherwise support schools, which is central to the debate.

2 The 2019 reform

On December 12, 2019, City Council passed legislation reducing the new-residential-construction abatement. As Hidden City Philadelphia reported, the first year remains fully abated and the exemption then shrinks by 10 percentage points a year (90 percent in year two, and so on) until the full tax is owed in year 11; the full ten-year exemption for improvements to existing residential properties was preserved. The reported effective-date cutoff for building permits was December 31, 2020, a compromise between the mayor's preferred date of July 1, 2021 and an earlier date favored by Council leadership, which is why projects permitted in 2020 and projects permitted from 2021 are treated differently.[2] Commercial and industrial abatements were not part of the change. Industry groups warned of reduced construction while supporters of the change said the old subsidy was too generous (see Developers and the Real Estate Lobby). Owners should confirm which abatement applies to a given permit with the Department of Revenue.

3 Other incentives

Besides the residential abatement, Philadelphia uses the Local Economic Revitalization Tax Assistance (LERTA) program for commercial and industrial improvements, state Keystone Opportunity Zones, and financing programs run through the Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation and the Commerce Department. Tax increment financing is also available through redevelopment tools in particular projects, and the Division of Housing and Community Development offers subsidy for affordable housing. Wage-related conditions may attach to some subsidized projects (see Prevailing Wage and Project Labor Agreements).

4 The 20-year conversion proposal

In November 2025 Mayor Cherelle Parker announced an initiative to offer a 20-year abatement to encourage converting deteriorated buildings, such as vacant Center City office towers and empty school buildings, into apartments, after working with state legislators on changes to Pennsylvania law. As of the Philadelphia Inquirer's September 24, 2026 report, the administration had not sent a bill to Council; Chief of Staff Tiffany W. Thurman said the administration was ensuring the legislation would be legally sound. Council President Kenyatta Johnson said Council had not seen any legislation and that the administration should "send the bill over." Several Council members were reported to be hesitant given the school district's funding difficulties and the 2027 municipal elections.[3] The proposal's status may change.

5 Why it is contested

Supporters argue abatements spur construction and eventually enlarge the tax base. Critics, including some neighborhood advocates, argue that abatements starve the city and schools of revenue and mostly benefit higher-income housing in already-growing areas. Research and analysis from the City Controller, think tanks and academic studies has produced differing conclusions about how much building would occur without the subsidy; readers should consult the original studies rather than rely on summaries. Debates also involve councilmanic politics and school funding.

6 Legal constraints and oversight

Pennsylvania's constitution requires uniformity in taxation, which limits how the city can target relief (for example, by income or by deed restriction), and state enabling laws set what kinds of abatements are allowed. Changes thus require Council action and sometimes state legislation (see Home Rule Limits and State Preemption). Abatement costs appear in the city's tax expenditure reporting (see How to Read the City Budget).

See also: Philadelphia Taxes, Office of Property Assessment, Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation.

References

  1. City of Philadelphia, Office of Property Assessment and Revenue Department guidance on abatements, phila.gov.
  2. Hidden City Philadelphia, "10-year Tax Abatement Bill Approved, But a New Battle is Brewing," December 13, 2019; WHYY, "Equitable or not enough? Philly Council just changed the 10-year tax abatement," December 12, 2019; City of Philadelphia, "Get a property tax abatement," phila.gov.
  3. Philadelphia Inquirer, report on the 20-year abatement proposal, September 24, 2026.
