Adult Probation and Parole Department

Adult Probation and Parole Department (APPD)
TypeUnit of the First Judicial District (Criminal Section, Trial Division, Court of Common Pleas), not a city department
Parent bodyFirst Judicial District of Pennsylvania
ChiefAnthony Aner, Chief Probation/Parole Officer (per courts.phila.gov, October 2026)
SupervisesAdults on county probation and county parole: approximately 36,000 offenders and 55,900 cases (figure on the court's website)
Address714 Market Street, Philadelphia
Websitecourts.phila.gov/appd

The Adult Probation and Parole Department (APPD) supervises adults in Philadelphia whom judges have sentenced to probation, or who have been released on county parole after serving part of a short jail sentence. It is part of the First Judicial District, which makes it an arm of the state-created courts rather than a mayoral department. Probation officers are court employees who report to the judges and its work is carried out under the court's orders. [1]

1 Probation, county parole and state parole

Three terms are often confused. Probation is a sentence served in the community instead of, or after, incarceration, and is imposed by a judge. County parole applies to people sentenced to county jail terms with a maximum under two years, and release is decided by the sentencing judge. State parole applies to people serving state sentences with a maximum of two years or more; it is decided and supervised by the Pennsylvania Parole Board and its agents, not by the APPD. The APPD handles the first two categories for Philadelphia, using the sentencing orders of the Court of Common Pleas and Municipal Court. People released from the city's jails after serving their sentences may be moved to supervision by APPD.

2 How supervision works

A sentencing judge sets the length and conditions of supervision, which can include reporting to an officer, paying fines and costs, drug testing, treatment, employment or school requirements, no-contact orders and travel limits. Officers meet with clients, verify compliance and report to the court. Specialized units supervise people with mental-health needs, sex-offense convictions, and gun or domestic-violence cases; the court also runs problem-solving courts with their own supervision. Supervision fees and the level of reporting vary with risk assessments and policy, and the department publishes forms and office hours on its page. [1]

3 Violations and detainers

If an officer believes a client has violated conditions, the matter goes to a judge. Violations can be technical (missed appointments, positive drug tests, unpaid costs) or new criminal arrests. A judge may issue a detainer, which holds a person in jail pending a hearing, and can continue, modify or revoke supervision, including re-sentencing to incarceration. Because many people have lawyers appointed only for the original case, advocates have pointed to representation at violation hearings as an issue, and the Defender Association frequently appears at those hearings.

4 Reform debates

The department's own figure of roughly 36,000 people under supervision has made probation length and conditions a recurring subject of study and reform proposals. A 2010 Pew Charitable Trusts report on the city's jails examined the interaction of probation and detention. The case of rapper Meek Mill brought national attention: in 2017 a Philadelphia judge sentenced him to two to four years for probation violations from a 2008 case, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court ordered his release on bail in April 2018, and his original conviction was vacated and charges dropped in 2019. [2] District Attorney Larry Krasner's office announced policies in 2018-2019 to reduce reliance on lengthy probation and parole terms, such as seeking shorter terms and ending supervision for people who are compliant, which the courts and defenders have discussed. [3] The District Attorney sets prosecutors' recommendations, but judges decide the sentence. State legislation has also addressed probation length and early termination; check current law at legis.state.pa.us.

5 Getting information or help

Clients should contact their assigned officer or the main office at 215-683-1000. Questions about the legal merits of a violation should go to a lawyer; see Legal Aid and Public Interest Law. Expungement and record-sealing, including Pennsylvania's Clean Slate law, are handled through the courts and not by the APPD. Complaints about an officer can be raised with the department's leadership or the court administration; see How to File a Complaint.

See also: First Judicial District, Philadelphia Department of Prisons, Defender Association of Philadelphia, Philadelphia Sheriff's Office.

References

  1. First Judicial District of Pennsylvania, Adult Probation and Parole Department, courts.phila.gov/appd.
  2. Pennsylvania Supreme Court and Philadelphia Inquirer coverage of the Commonwealth v. Williams (Meek Mill) release (April 2018) and the 2019 dismissal.
  3. Philadelphia District Attorney's Office, probation and parole policy announcements (2018-2019), phillyda.org; Pew Charitable Trusts, Philadelphia's Crowded, Costly Jails (2010).

Medical Examiner's Office

Philadelphia Medical Examiner's Office (MEO)
TypeCity office within the Department of Public Health; performs the county coroner function
Chief Medical ExaminerDr. Lindsay Simon (reported as chief by CBS News Philadelphia; the city's department page does not list a chief)
CaseloadAbout 1,600 autopsies per year; 1,721 in 2021 (reported)
ParentDepartment of Public Health
Related laborStaff represented in part by AFSCME District Council 33
Websitephila.gov/departments/medical-examiners-office

The Medical Examiner's Office determines the cause and manner of death in Philadelphia when a death is sudden, violent, unattended, or otherwise suspicious. In most Pennsylvania counties this duty belongs to an elected coroner; Philadelphia, as a consolidated city-county, instead has an appointed, physician-led medical examiner's office within city government. [1] Its findings feed into criminal investigations by the Police Department and the District Attorney, public-health surveillance (notably overdose deaths) and family matters such as death certificates.

1 Legal role

Under the City's Home Rule Charter and Pennsylvania law the medical examiner investigates deaths that occur by violence, suddenly while in apparent health, unattended by a physician, in custody, or under suspicious or unusual circumstances. The office takes custody of the body, performs examinations including autopsies and toxicology, and issues the cause and manner of death (natural, accident, suicide, homicide or undetermined). A "homicide" ruling in this context is a medical classification that a death resulted from another person's actions; it is not a finding of criminal guilt. Decisions to charge belong to prosecutors.

2 Structure and leadership

The office is part of the Department of Public Health and is led by a Chief Medical Examiner who is a licensed forensic pathologist. Deputy and associate medical examiners perform autopsies, supported by forensic investigators, toxicologists and histology staff, and administrative workers. Press reports describe several changes in the chief's position in recent years, including the reported December 2023 resignation of Dr. Constance DiAngelo, who had been named chief in 2022; CBS News Philadelphia reported that Dr. Lindsay Simon, a forensic pathologist, then took over the role. [2] The city's department page lists the office at 400 N. Broad Street, with a 24-hour line for reporting a death and a separate line for general inquiries; it describes seven investigation units that contribute information to individual cases.

3 Workload and standards

Reported figures indicate the office performs roughly 1,600 autopsies a year; the Philadelphia Inquirer reported 1,721 autopsies in 2021, above the 250-per-pathologist annual limit recommended by the National Association of Medical Examiners for accreditation, and that the office was not accredited. [3] The city has since moved to modernize facilities and staffing; readers should consult the Public Health Department's current announcements. Overdose, firearm and traffic deaths account for a large share of cases, and the office's data are used by the Health Department in its surveillance reports.

4 Controversies on the public record

The office was at the center of public controversy in 2021 over the remains of children killed in the 1985 MOVE bombing. The bones of two of the children had been kept at the University of Pennsylvania Museum and were later transferred to Princeton University researchers, a fact first reported by Billy Penn in 2021. Separately, on May 13, 2021, Mayor Jim Kenney requested the resignation of Health Commissioner Thomas Farley after it became public that Farley had ordered in 2017 that victims' remains be cremated and disposed of without notifying the families; the next day, staff at the Medical Examiner's Office found a box labeled "MOVE" containing un-cremated remains. The Inquirer also reported on the office's leadership turnover. [3][4] In July 2025, during the municipal strike by AFSCME District Council 33, courts issued injunctions requiring some striking city employees, such as 911 dispatchers, to return to work (NBC10), and 6abc reported that this included striking medical examiner's office employees; see 2025 DC 33 Strike. [5]

5 What families should know

When a death comes under the office's jurisdiction, the body is taken to the morgue and the next of kin are contacted by investigators; release of the body to a funeral home usually follows after the examination. Families can request autopsy reports and death certificates through the procedures posted by the city, and a request to a medical examiner for records of a death is separate from the Right-to-Know Law. Concerns about the handling of remains can be raised with the Health Department or the City Controller. See also How to File a Complaint.

See also: Department of Public Health, Philadelphia Police Department, Philadelphia District Attorney's Office, AFSCME District Council 33.

U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania

U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania (USAO-EDPA)
TypeFederal agency (U.S. Department of Justice); not part of city or state government
U.S. AttorneyDavid Metcalf (interim from March 12, 2025; court-appointed June 30, 2025; Senate-confirmed October 7, 2025 and sworn in October 15, 2025 for a four-year term)
TerritoryPhiladelphia, Bucks, Chester, Delaware, Montgomery, Berks, Lehigh, Northampton and Lancaster counties
CourthouseU.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania
ParentU.S. Department of Justice
Websitejustice.gov/usao-edpa

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania prosecutes federal crimes and represents the United States in civil cases in Philadelphia and eight surrounding counties. It is a federal office led by a U.S. Attorney, a presidential nominee who is confirmed by the U.S. Senate. It is distinct from the local District Attorney's Office, which prosecutes violations of Pennsylvania law in state court, and from the Pennsylvania Attorney General. [1]

1 Jurisdiction and role

Federal prosecutors bring cases under federal statutes, including fraud, public corruption, drug trafficking, firearms offenses, child exploitation, civil-rights violations and cybercrime. Cases are investigated by federal agencies such as the FBI, the Drug Enforcement Administration and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, and are tried in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, with appeals to the Third Circuit. The office also handles civil litigation involving the federal government, civil rights enforcement, and affirmative civil cases such as health-care fraud and fair-housing matters. The federal-local relationship is described in Federal Government and Philadelphia.

2 Leadership and how the post is filled

U.S. Attorneys are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate. Attorney General Pamela Bondi appointed David Metcalf, previously corporate counsel at Amazon and a former assistant U.S. attorney, as interim U.S. Attorney on March 12, 2025. After the 120-day interim period the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania appointed him, and Chief Judge Mitchell Goldberg swore him in on June 30, 2025. The Senate confirmed his nomination on October 7, 2025, and he was sworn in on October 15, 2025 to serve the full four-year term. [2] His predecessor was Jacqueline Romero, who served from 2021 until early 2025. In May 2026 the Justice Department announced that Metcalf had been appointed to the Attorney General's Advisory Committee of U.S. Attorneys. [3]

3 Priorities

Each U.S. Attorney sets priorities within Department of Justice policy. The office has long prioritized violent crime and gun cases in Philadelphia, often through partnerships with the Police Department and the state, and public-corruption cases. For example, in February 2026 the office announced a 188-month sentence for a man who committed an armed robbery and shot at Philadelphia police officers, and in July 2025 it announced a 75-year sentence for a member of a Frankford-based drug gang convicted in the killing of a Philadelphia police officer. Priorities can change with new administrations, so the office's current press releases at justice.gov/usao-edpa are the best source. [3]

4 Public corruption and civil rights cases

The office has brought many of the best-known prosecutions of Philadelphia officials, and its record is documented in Justice Department press releases. Examples on the public record, with the most recent first:

  • John Dougherty and Bobby Henon. The office announced a 116-count indictment on January 30, 2019 against IBEW Local 98 leader John Dougherty, then-Councilmember Robert Henon and others. On November 15, 2021, a jury convicted Dougherty and Henon of honest services fraud charges (Henon also of federal program bribery). On December 7, 2023, a second jury convicted Dougherty and former Local 98 president Brian Burrows of embezzlement-related charges; Burrows was sentenced to 48 months on June 26, 2024 and Dougherty to 72 months on July 11, 2024. Henon was later reported sentenced to about 3.5 years in prison. The Justice Department's Office of the Pardon Attorney lists a commutation warrant dated September 3, 2026 for John Dougherty (E.D. Pa.). See IBEW Local 98.
  • District Attorney Seth Williams. Williams was indicted in March 2017 and pleaded guilty on June 29, 2017 to a federal bribery charge; he was sentenced on October 24, 2017 to 60 months in prison. That case was prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of New Jersey, not the Eastern District of Pennsylvania.
  • Chaka Fattah. Former Congressman Chaka Fattah Sr. was indicted in July 2015, sentenced to 120 months in prison on December 12, 2016 for participating in a racketeering conspiracy, and resentenced to 10 years on July 12, 2019. His son, Chaka Fattah Jr., was convicted in November 2015 of fraud and tax charges and sentenced in February 2016 to 60 months.
  • Traffic Court. A January 31, 2013 indictment charged former Philadelphia Traffic Court judges in a ticket-fixing scheme. After several guilty pleas, a federal jury on July 23, 2014 convicted three former judges (Michael Lowry, Robert Mulgrew and Thomasine Tynes) of perjury before the grand jury and a fourth (Willie Singletary) of lying to the FBI, and acquitted three other defendants. The state abolished Traffic Court in 2013; see First Judicial District.
  • State Senator Vincent Fumo. Fumo was convicted on 137 counts on March 16, 2009 and was reported sentenced to 55 months in prison in July 2009 (his term was increased by six months on judicial review in November 2011, according to reference summaries); he was released in August 2013.
  • City Treasurer Corey Kemp. Kemp was convicted in 2005 and sentenced to 10 years in a pay-to-play case that followed the 2003 discovery of an FBI listening device in Mayor John Street's office (Street was not charged).

Each case produced sentences and, in some instances, appeals; the court record is controlling.[4] See Political Corruption Cases in Philadelphia and Conflicts of Interest and Pay-to-Play. The office can also prosecute officers who violate federal civil-rights law; see Police Accountability Systems.

5 Reporting a federal crime

Tips can be reported to the FBI's Philadelphia field office or to the U.S. Attorney's Office, which also operates victim-witness services. Concerns about local officials' ethics may belong with the Inspector General or Board of Ethics instead; see How to Report Corruption or Misconduct. Federal prosecutors do not give legal advice to the public; individuals who need legal help should consult a lawyer.

See also: Philadelphia District Attorney's Office, Federal Government and Philadelphia, Political Corruption Cases in Philadelphia, Conflicts of Interest and Pay-to-Play.

References

  3. U.S. Department of Justice press releases, including "U.S. Attorney David Metcalf Appointed To Attorney General's Advisory Committee" (May 22, 2026) and USAO-EDPA sentencing announcements of July 23, 2025 and February 12, 2026, justice.gov.

Department of Public Health

Philadelphia Department of Public Health
TypeCity department (also serves as the county health department)
Led byHealth Commissioner Dr. Palak Raval-Nelson (as of May 2026)
General Fund budget$158.5 million proposed for FY2027; FY2026 estimated obligations about $165.3 million
Staffing1,084 budgeted positions across all funds requested for FY2027
Legal basisPhiladelphia Home Rule Charter; Philadelphia Health Code; Pennsylvania local health administration law
Websitephila.gov/departments/department-of-public-health

The Philadelphia Department of Public Health (PDPH) is the city government agency responsible for protecting and promoting the health of Philadelphia residents and providing a safety net for the most vulnerable. Because Philadelphia is a consolidated city and county, PDPH also performs the functions that in most of Pennsylvania are split between a county or municipal health department and the state Department of Health. It is a city department under the Home Rule Charter, not an independent authority or nonprofit. Its mission statement, quoted in its May 2026 budget testimony, is to protect and promote the health of all Philadelphians and to provide a safety net for the most vulnerable.[1]

1 Structure and leadership

The department is headed by the Health Commissioner, who is appointed by the Mayor and sits in the Mayor's Cabinet. As of May 2026 the commissioner is Dr. Palak Raval-Nelson, who presented the department's Fiscal Year 2027 budget testimony to City Council on May 4, 2026, accompanied by a chief financial officer, a chief of staff, two deputy commissioners and division directors.[1] The Board of Health, a body with regulatory authority over the Philadelphia Health Code, works alongside the department; its members are appointed under the Charter.

Work is organized into divisions. Those named in recent budget testimony include Ambulatory Health Services (the city-run health centers), Disease Control, Environmental Health Services, Air Management Services, Chronic Disease and Injury Prevention, HIV Health, Reproductive, Adolescent and Child Health, Health Analysis, Information and Strategy, and the Public Health Laboratory.[1] The Medical Examiner's Office is also housed within the department's budget.

2 Programs and divisions

Health centers. PDPH operates a network of primary care and dental health centers aimed at residents who are uninsured or underinsured. The FY2027 testimony lists development of two new health centers in Northeast Philadelphia as a top priority, and describes expanding care for patients with substance use disorder and mental health conditions, including medications for opioid use disorder.[1]

Disease control and immunization. The Division of Disease Control tracks reportable infectious diseases, runs immunization programs, and screens for sexually transmitted infections. The department planned in FY2027 to work with the Pennsylvania Department of Health on a state program supplementing the federal Vaccines for Children Program.[1]

Environmental health and air quality. Environmental Health Services inspects food establishments and other regulated facilities and handles lead and vector-control matters. Air Management Services regulates air pollution sources and, per the testimony, planned a public dashboard drawing on 76 newly installed sensors measuring fine particulate matter and nitrogen oxides.[1]

Medical examiner and laboratory. The Medical Examiner investigates sudden, suspicious and unexplained deaths; the Public Health Laboratory supports disease testing and emergency response.

3 Budget and staffing

The proposed FY2027 General Fund budget is $158,498,176, a decrease of $6,816,066 from FY2026 estimated obligations. The department attributed the decrease mainly to one-time capital transfers in FY2026 for the two new health centers.[1] The department also receives substantial federal and state grant money, much of it passed through from agencies such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; its FY2025 federal and state grants revenue budget was reported at $136.6 million.[1] The department requested 1,084 budgeted positions across all funds for FY2027, eight fewer than FY2026, reflecting the planned end of certain grants.[1] Annual budgets run through the city budget process.

4 Relationship to other bodies

PDPH coordinates with the state Department of Health on disease reporting and licensing, with federal agencies that fund its programs, and with the Department of Behavioral Health and Intellectual disAbility Services on overdose and mental health response. It works with the School District of Philadelphia on school health and with the Department of Licenses and Inspections on housing-related health hazards. The Safe and Healthy Homes Act debate reflects overlapping concerns between housing and health departments.

5 Residents: using the department

Residents can use city health centers, request immunizations, report food-safety or environmental problems through Philly311, and request birth and death records through the department's Vital Records program. See How to File a Complaint for general guidance. Specific services and hours change, so confirm on the department's website.

See also: DBHIDS, Medical Examiner's Office, Mayor's Cabinet and Offices, Office of Violence Prevention.

Department of Behavioral Health and Intellectual disAbility Services

Department of Behavioral Health and Intellectual disAbility Services (DBHIDS)
TypeCity department; also the county mental health/intellectual disability program
Led byCommissioner Kehinde "Kenny" Solanke (since September 2, 2024)
DivisionsSix, including Behavioral Health, Intellectual disAbility Services, and Community Behavioral Health
Crisis line988 (call or text); Mental Health Delegate Hotline 215-685-6440
Websitedbhids.org

The Department of Behavioral Health and Intellectual disAbility Services (DBHIDS) is the Philadelphia city department that provides and funds behavioral health care, intellectual disability supports and early intervention services. Its own description is "one comprehensive integrated system."[1] The unusual capitalization of "disAbility" is the department's official styling. DBHIDS is a city department, but much of its service delivery is carried out by contracted nonprofit and private provider agencies.

1 Mission and structure

The department's stated mission is to educate, strengthen and serve individuals and communities so that all Philadelphians can thrive.[1] According to its website it operates through six divisions: Behavioral Health; Intellectual disAbility Services; Community Behavioral Health; Planning and Innovation; Administration, Finance and Quality; and Behavioral Health and Justice.[1] The department partners with community provider agencies, the School District of Philadelphia, the child welfare system and the courts.

In Pennsylvania, counties are responsible for administering mental health and intellectual disability programs under state law and with state funding. Because Philadelphia is a consolidated city-county, DBHIDS fills the role that a county mental health/intellectual disability office fills elsewhere in the state.

2 Community Behavioral Health

DBHIDS is the principal funder of, and provides oversight to, Community Behavioral Health (CBH), a not-for-profit 501(c)(3) corporation contracted by the City to manage mental health and substance use services for Philadelphia County Medicaid recipients through the state's HealthChoices program.[2] The CBH division is led by its own chief executive officer. Residents with Medicaid who need treatment typically reach providers through CBH's network; its non-emergency member line is 1-888-545-2600.[1]

3 Leadership and history

Mayor Cherelle Parker announced Kehinde Solanke as commissioner on July 30, 2024, and she took office September 2, 2024. Solanke holds a master's degree in social work from Temple University and previously served as senior director of operations for crisis services at DBHIDS, where she helped implement the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline locally.[3] The commissioner is appointed by the Mayor and is a member of the Mayor's Cabinet. The department has historically been one of the largest in the city's health and human services cluster, with a budget dominated by Medicaid-funded services flowing through CBH rather than city tax dollars; consult the annual budget documents for current figures, which this article does not state.

4 Crisis and everyday access

The department promotes 988 as the 24-hour suicide and crisis line, and runs a Mental Health Delegate Hotline (215-685-6440) used in involuntary commitment situations. Intellectual disAbility Services can be reached at 215-685-5900 on weekdays.[1] DBHIDS also funds treatment and recovery services in the context of the opioid epidemic and works with the criminal legal system through its Behavioral Health and Justice division, including work connected to the Department of Prisons and the courts.

5 Connections to other bodies

DBHIDS works closely with the Department of Public Health on overdose and harm reduction, the Department of Human Services on children's behavioral health, and the Office of Homeless Services on residents with behavioral health needs who are unhoused. State oversight comes from the Pennsylvania Department of Human Services, which administers Medicaid and sets HealthChoices rules. See Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia.

See also: Department of Public Health, Office of Homeless Services, Office for People with Disabilities, Office of Violence Prevention.

Department of Human Services

Philadelphia Department of Human Services
TypeCity department; county children and youth agency
Led byCommissioner Kimberly Ali (as of April 2026)
BudgetFY2027 proposed all-funds appropriation about $926.7 million in the General/Grants summary
Staffing1,830 budgeted positions requested for FY2027
Parent officeOffice of Children and Families
Websitephila.gov/departments/department-of-human-services

The Department of Human Services (DHS) is the Philadelphia city department responsible for child welfare, juvenile justice services and related prevention programs. In Pennsylvania, county governments run children and youth agencies under state law; because Philadelphia is a consolidated city-county, DHS serves as the county agency, subject to oversight by the Pennsylvania Department of Human Services. Its stated mission is to serve the city's children, youth, families and communities by building on their strengths and advancing safe and supportive environments.[1]

1 Structure and leadership

DHS is headed by a commissioner, Kimberly Ali, who presented the department's FY2027 budget testimony to City Council on April 1, 2026.[1] The department sits within the Office of Children and Families, which supervises DHS along with out-of-school time, Career Connected Learning, PHLpreK and other programs.[2] Divisions include child welfare operations, Juvenile Justice Services and administrative functions.

2 Child welfare and Community Umbrella Agencies

When a report of suspected child abuse or neglect is made, the state's ChildLine system and DHS screen and investigate. Ongoing case management for many families is delivered by Community Umbrella Agencies (CUAs), nonprofit contractors that each serve designated regions of the city. Six organizations operate CUAs across ten regions, and DHS publishes annual CUA scorecards on performance.[3] The CUA model is part of the city's Improving Outcomes for Children reform effort.

DHS reported in its FY2027 testimony that the number of children and youth in out-of-home placement fell 52 percent, from 4,690 in December 2020 to 2,269, and that 43 percent of those in placement in December 2025 were in kinship care. It also reported that 7 percent of youth in placement were in residential settings, below the 9 percent national average it cited.[1]

3 Juvenile justice and prevention

Juvenile Justice Services runs the Philadelphia Juvenile Justice Services Center and works with Family Court, Juvenile Probation, the District Attorney's Office and the Defender Association. DHS testified that the center has been at or below its licensed capacity of 184 youth since June 2024. It operates six Community Evening Resource Centers for youth and, since January 2025, a citywide police diversion program; as of December 31, 2025, 1,537 youth were arrested and 769 diverted, according to the testimony.[1] Community-based prevention services served 2,337 families across FY2025 and the first quarter of FY2026.[1]

4 Budget and staffing

The FY2027 proposed General/Grants summary totals $926,657,093, up about $9.7 million from FY2026 estimated obligations, with most spending on purchased services (about $703 million) such as CUAs, placement providers and prevention contractors. The department requested 1,830 budgeted positions, 25 fewer than FY2026.[1] Because large shares of funding come from state and federal sources, the city budget shows only part of the picture.

5 Oversight and controversy

DHS has been the subject of recurring public scrutiny, including a critical report on the city's child welfare system that drew a City Council hearing, as covered by WHYY.[4] Critics and officials disagree about caseloads, placement stability and agency capacity; this article reports only that such scrutiny has occurred and refers readers to the cited coverage. Family Court judges in the First Judicial District decide dependency cases. Residents with concerns can contact DHS directly or use complaint routes; this is general information, not legal advice.

See also: Office of Children and Families, Office of Homeless Services, DBHIDS, Court of Common Pleas and Municipal Court.

Office of Homeless Services

Office of Homeless Services (OHS)
TypeCity office; lead agency of the local HUD Continuum of Care
Led byExecutive Director Cheryl Hill (as of 2026)
2026 point-in-time count5,163 people (February 25, 2026), down 7 percent from 5,516 in 2025
FundingCity, state and federal (including HUD) sources
Websitephila.gov/departments/office-of-homeless-services

The Office of Homeless Services (OHS) is the City of Philadelphia agency that plans, funds and coordinates services for people experiencing or at risk of homelessness. It works largely through contracts with nonprofit providers that operate shelters, outreach, rapid rehousing and permanent supportive housing. OHS is a city office, not an authority; it should not be confused with the Philadelphia Housing Authority, which is a separate public housing agency.

1 Role and structure

OHS is led by Executive Director Cheryl Hill, who appears in 2026 city announcements on homelessness data and grants.[1] The office serves as the collaborative applicant and lead agency for Philadelphia's Continuum of Care, the local planning body through which the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) distributes homelessness funding. It also maintains the local homeless data system and oversees the annual point-in-time count, a one-night census of sheltered and unsheltered people required by HUD.

2 Services

Core functions include emergency housing (shelter), street outreach, homelessness prevention and diversion, rapid rehousing, and permanent supportive housing. OHS works with its contracted providers and with other city agencies such as the Department of Behavioral Health and Intellectual disAbility Services and the Division of Housing and Community Development. During extreme weather the city declares "Code Blue" or "Code Red" to expand access to shelter; in January 2025 the Parker administration announced warming centers in recreation centers and libraries during Code Blue periods.[1]

3 The 2026 count and recent initiatives

The city's July 2026 report on the February 25, 2026 count found 5,163 people experiencing homelessness, a 7 percent decline from 5,516 in 2025. Unsheltered homelessness fell 39 percent, from 1,178 to 711, the first decline in two years, while the sheltered count rose 2 percent to 4,452.[1] The report credited initiatives under Mayor Cherelle Parker, including the December 2025 "One Philly Response" executive order, which calls for 1,000 additional shelter beds, the HOPE 220 Solution Center (70-plus beds with wraparound services, opened March 2026), the "One Philly Ambassadors of Hope" outreach program and expanded encampment resolution teams.[1] These are the city's own characterizations; advocates and journalists have debated how encampment enforcement and shelter capacity affect residents, and readers should consult local reporting for those views. In July 2026 the city also announced OHS had been awarded a $5 million grant for homelessness prevention.[2]

4 Connections and getting help

Homelessness intersects with eviction and housing law: see Eviction Diversion and Landlord-Tenant Court, Tenant and Housing Advocacy Groups and Rental Licensing and Landlord-Tenant Law. Residents who are homeless or at imminent risk can use the city's housing assistance and outreach lines listed on the OHS website, or report an unsheltered person in need through Philly311. Services and phone numbers change; confirm on phila.gov. This article is general information, not legal advice.

See also: Philadelphia Housing Authority, Department of Human Services, Office of Community Empowerment and Opportunity, Safe and Healthy Homes Act.

Office of Children and Families

Office of Children and Families (OCF)
TypeCity office within the Managing Director's cluster of the executive branch
Core areasSafe children; strong families; supported schools and communities
OverseesDepartment of Human Services, Out-of-School Time, Career Connected Learning PHL, PHLpreK, adult education, community schools
Address1515 Arch St., 8th Floor
Websitephila.gov/departments/office-of-children-and-families

The Office of Children and Families (OCF) is a Philadelphia city office that, in the city's words, "aligns the City's policies, resources, and services for children and families."[1] It is not a direct-service department in the way the Department of Human Services is; it is a coordinating layer within the executive branch that supervises several programs and one large department. Like many offices, it has changed form and leadership as mayors reorganize the executive branch.

1 Purpose and structure

OCF focuses on three areas: safe children, strong families, and supported schools and communities.[1] Its portfolio includes the Department of Human Services, Out-of-School Time (OST), Career Connected Learning PHL, PHLpreK, adult education and community schools initiatives.[1] The office is part of the mayor's executive hierarchy described in How Philadelphia Government Is Organized and the Managing Director's Office, and is led by a senior appointee who answers to the Mayor.

2 Programs

PHLpreK provides publicly funded pre-kindergarten seats for three- and four-year-olds; the FY2027 Five Year Plan, as described in DHS testimony, proposed 100 new slots. Career Connected Learning places youth in paid, hands-on experiences; DHS testimony states a plan to add 1,000 opportunities, bringing summer slots to 9,000.[2] Out-of-School Time funds after-school and summer programming through community providers. Community schools programs connect public schools with services; these operate alongside the School District of Philadelphia, which is a separate legal entity.

3 Leadership and history

Vanessa Garrett Harley served as Chief Deputy Managing Director for Children and Families, then moved in October 2024 to become Chief Deputy Mayor for Social Impact and Strategic Initiatives, according to city personnel announcements.[3] City pages also identify Latonia Irving-Dasent as Chief of Children and Family Support Services. The office's public page lists its portfolio but does not name a top official; the office can be reached at (215) 683-6012 or OCFCommunications@phila.gov.

4 How it fits the system

Because DHS manages roughly 1,800 budgeted positions and a budget near $927 million in the FY2027 proposal, the office's oversight role is significant even though OCF itself is small.[2] It coordinates with the Department of Public Health, DBHIDS, the Free Library and Parks and Recreation on youth programming. For policy changes to its role, see Mayor's Cabinet and Offices.

See also: Department of Human Services, Board of Education, Office of Workforce Development.

Office of Community Empowerment and Opportunity

Office of Community Empowerment and Opportunity (CEO)
TypeCity office; designated Community Action Agency
Led byExecutive Director Orlando Rendón (named March 2024, per City announcement; the office page does not list a director)
EstablishedCommunity Action Agency role since 1964
Address1617 JFK Blvd., Suite 1800, Philadelphia, PA 19103

The Office of Community Empowerment and Opportunity (CEO) is the City of Philadelphia office that advocates for and invests in programs to reduce poverty. Its stated aim is "promoting a more equitable Philadelphia where all residents can share in the city's prosperous future."[1] It is the city's Community Action Agency, a federally recognized designation created by the Economic Opportunity Act of 1964 under which local agencies receive Community Services Block Grant money to fight poverty. CEO is a city office, not a nonprofit.

1 Mission and focus areas

CEO describes four areas of work: benefits access, financial empowerment, housing security and workforce development.[1] Because it is a Community Action Agency, it is expected to use needs assessments to shape priorities; the office published a 2024 community needs assessment on phila.gov.[2]

2 Key programs

BenePhilly offers free help applying for public benefits such as food assistance and utility help. Financial Empowerment Centers provide free one-on-one financial counseling and help opening affordable bank accounts. In housing security the office partners on initiatives including the West Philadelphia Promise Zone. In workforce development it runs programs such as the Civic Engagement Academy.[1] Historically CEO also housed other anti-poverty functions; the city's workforce functions were reorganized in 2018 and again around 2020, as described in Office of Workforce Development.

The City's page also lists the West Philadelphia Promise Zone, a partnership addressing housing, economic opportunity, education, health and safety, and the Philadelphia Consumer Financial Protection Task Force, which coordinates enforcement and outreach on consumer finance.[1] The Civic Engagement Academy trains community leaders. As a Community Action Agency, the office has served in that role since 1964 and awards grant funding to community organizations working on benefits access, financial empowerment, housing security and workforce development. Residents are most likely to meet the office through BenePhilly counselors, who help people apply for benefits, or through the free one-on-one sessions at Financial Empowerment Centers.

3 Leadership

Mayor Cherelle Parker named Orlando Rendón, the former Parks and Recreation commissioner, as executive director in March 2024, citing his experience in the Managing Director's Office and at Aspira.[3] The executive director is appointed by the Mayor. The office also supports a tripartite advisory board required of Community Action Agencies, with representatives of government, the private sector and low-income communities; confirm current membership with the office.

4 Relationships with other bodies

CEO works with the Division of Housing and Community Development, the Office of Homeless Services, the Department of Human Services and nonprofit partners such as community development corporations and legal aid groups (see Legal Aid and Public Interest Law). Funding comes from the city, federal block grants and philanthropic partners; see Philanthropy in Philadelphia.

5 Using CEO services

Residents can contact the office at (215) 685-3600 or ceoinfo@phila.gov to find benefits help or a financial counseling center.[1] Eligibility rules vary by program. This is general information, not legal or financial advice.

See also: Office of Children and Families, Mayor's Cabinet and Offices, How to Get Help From the City.

  2. Office of Community Empowerment and Opportunity, Community Needs Assessment 2024 (phila.gov).

Office of Immigrant Affairs

Office of Immigrant Affairs (OIA)
TypeCity office within the Mayor's administration
Led byDirector Charlie Elison; Deputy Director Alain Joinville (per city website, 2026)
Legal basisHome Rule Charter section 8-600 (Language Access Plans)
AddressCity Hall, Room 162
Phone / email(215) 686-0876; OIA@phila.gov
Websitephila.gov/departments/office-of-immigrant-affairs

The Office of Immigrant Affairs (OIA) is a City of Philadelphia office that, in its own words, promotes immigrant well-being by "recommending and developing policies and programs, which in turn provide opportunity and access to services."[1] It facilitates immigrant integration into civic, economic and cultural life. OIA is a city office; it does not enforce immigration law, which is a federal responsibility (see Federal Government and Philadelphia).

1 Role and legal basis

The Home Rule Charter, as amended, directs city agencies to develop Language Access Plans so residents with limited English proficiency can reach services; the office's website cites Charter section 8-600 as guiding its operations.[1] The office advises the Mayor, coordinates with departments on language access, and acts as liaison with immigrant communities. See Philadelphia Home Rule Charter.

2 Commissions and programs

OIA supports two mayoral commissions: one on Asian Pacific American affairs and one on African and Caribbean immigrant affairs.[1] Its work includes policy recommendations, community events, referrals to legal and social services, and training city staff on language access. Direct legal representation is provided by nonprofits; see Legal Aid and Public Interest Law.

The office lists Language Access Philly, which works to make City services available in multiple languages, and the Welcoming Network initiative among its programs. Its website identifies ten languages it supports: English, Spanish, Chinese, Arabic, Haitian Creole, French, Kiswahili, Portuguese, Russian and Vietnamese.[1] Language access matters in practice because residents with limited English proficiency otherwise face barriers when they call 311, apply for permits, seek benefits or deal with courts and police. The office does not provide legal representation or decide immigration cases; residents who need legal help are referred to nonprofit providers and accredited representatives. The Mayor's two immigrant-focused commissions advise the administration and give community members a formal channel for raising concerns, and City departments looking to translate materials or arrange interpretation are the office's main internal clients.

3 Leadership changes

Executive Director Amy Eusebio announced her resignation on January 23, 2025, with her last day on January 24, 2025, according to CBS Philadelphia.[2] The Parker administration began interviewing candidates in April 2025, as the Inquirer reported.[3] The City's website now lists Charlie Elison as director.

4 Federal-local tension

Philadelphia's stance on cooperating with federal immigration enforcement, including its "sanctuary city" policies, has been a recurring subject of litigation and political debate involving the federal government, City Council, the Police Department and the Department of Prisons. Supporters say limited cooperation builds trust in public safety; critics argue it hinders enforcement. This article does not attempt to resolve that dispute; see local news coverage and Local News Media in Philadelphia.

5 Contact

Residents can call (215) 686-0876 or email OIA@phila.gov. Information is general civic education, not legal advice; those with immigration cases should consult a licensed attorney or accredited representative.

See also: Commission on Human Relations, Office of LGBT Affairs, Mayor's Cabinet and Offices.

References

  2. CBS News Philadelphia, "Philadelphia's Office of Immigrant Affairs executive director resigns," January 2025.
  3. The Philadelphia Inquirer, report on Office of Immigrant Affairs candidate interviews, April 9, 2025.

Commission on Human Relations

Philadelphia Commission on Human Relations (PCHR)
TypeCity agency under the Home Rule Charter; nine-member mayoral commission plus staff
Led byExecutive Director Renee Chenault-Fattah (per the City's leadership page)
Laws enforcedFair Practices Ordinance; Fair Criminal Records Screening Standards (Fair Chance Hiring) law
Address601 Walnut St., Suite 300 South, Philadelphia, PA 19106
Phone(215) 686-4670
Websitephila.gov/departments/philadelphia-commission-on-human-relations

The Philadelphia Commission on Human Relations (PCHR) is the city's official civil rights agency. It enforces local anti-discrimination law, investigates complaints, and works on community relations and tension reduction. It is a city body created under the Home Rule Charter, distinct from the Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission (a state agency) and the federal Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and Department of Housing and Urban Development.[1]

1 Structure

The agency is led by a nine-member commission appointed by the Mayor. The commission decides disputed complaints and conducts public hearings, and meets in both executive and public sessions.[1] A professional staff headed by an executive director handles intake, investigation, mediation and outreach. The FY2025 annual report lists Renee Chenault Fattah as executive director.[2]

2 Laws and jurisdiction

PCHR accepts complaints about discrimination in employment, housing or property, and public accommodations, and about criminal record discrimination in employment.[1] The core law is the Fair Practices Ordinance, found in the Philadelphia Code, which bars discrimination on listed protected classes beyond those in state and federal law. Amendments to the Fair Chance Hiring law took effect in January 2026.[1] Coverage by the Fair Practices Ordinance overlaps with state and federal statutes, so a complainant may have choices about where to file, with different deadlines and remedies. Filing deadlines differ by law and by agency, so a complainant should ask PCHR at (215) 686-4670 about the time limit that applies before waiting to file.

3 Complaint process

Residents call (215) 686-4670 to schedule an in-person appointment; the agency lists Monday through Thursday, 9 a.m. to 3 p.m.[1] After a complaint is filed, staff notify the respondent, investigate, and may attempt mediation or settlement. Unresolved cases can go to a finding of probable cause and a public hearing before the commission, which can order remedies under the ordinance. Parties can generally seek review in court. For the broader range of complaint avenues, see How to File a Complaint. This is general information, not legal advice.

4 Community relations

Beyond enforcement, PCHR runs education and community-relations work, including responding to bias incidents and conflicts among groups. It collaborates with Office of Immigrant Affairs, Office of LGBT Affairs and Office for People with Disabilities.

5 Relationship to other bodies

Housing discrimination complaints can also involve the Fair Housing Commission, which handles landlord-tenant rent and repair disputes rather than discrimination, and landlord-tenant courts (see Eviction Diversion and Landlord-Tenant Court). Employment complaints may also go to the Office of Worker Protections for wage and leave issues. City Council amends the ordinances PCHR enforces.

See also: Fair Housing Commission, Office of Worker Protections, Philadelphia City Council.

References

  1. City of Philadelphia, Philadelphia Commission on Human Relations, department page, phila.gov.
  2. Philadelphia Commission on Human Relations, FY25 Annual Report (phila.gov, December 2025).
  3. Philadelphia Code, Chapter 9-1100 (Fair Practices Ordinance), via American Legal Publishing.

Office for People with Disabilities

Office for People with Disabilities (OPD)
TypeCity office created by Charter amendment (approved November 2023)
Led byExecutive Director Adrienne Moore (since May 13, 2024)
ParentOffice of the Chief Administrative Officer
AddressMunicipal Services Building, 1401 John F. Kennedy Blvd., 1st Floor
Contact(215) 686-2798; ada.request@phila.gov
Websitephila.gov/departments/office-for-people-with-disabilities

The Office for People with Disabilities (OPD) is a Philadelphia city office working to ensure that the City is "inclusive to people of all abilities through advocacy and education."[1] It was formalized after Philadelphia voters approved a Home Rule Charter amendment in November 2023, and it succeeded the earlier Mayor's Commission on People with Disabilities structure, which continues within the office.[2]

1 Creation and leadership

The 2023 ballot question was one of several charter changes put before voters. Mayor Cherelle Parker appointed Adrienne Moore as executive director effective May 13, 2024. Moore previously served as the office's director of ADA compliance from June 2020, and the city describes her as having more than 25 years of experience in accessible architectural design and ADA policy.[2] The office sits within the Chief Administrative Officer's portfolio, intended to embed disability considerations in citywide administration.[2] City staff listed on the website include an ADA coordinator and a constituent services administrator.[1]

2 Functions

The office combines two main components. The Mayor's Commission on People with Disabilities advocates for policy and systemic changes, provides resources and referrals, and educates the community about disability rights laws. The Office of ADA Compliance develops policies for equal access to city programs, trains city employees, oversees the transition plan and building accessibility, and handles grievances.[1] The office also helps residents navigate employment, housing, education, healthcare, recreation and government services.

The City's page describes the office as working toward “employment opportunities,” “accessible and affordable housing,” and access to education, healthcare, recreation and government services for people with disabilities.[1] The office is listed by the City among the entities supervised by the Chief Administrative Officer, alongside the Department of Records, the Office of Innovation and Technology and the Procurement Department. That placement matters because accessibility depends on how the City buys, builds and publishes: digital services, contracts for buildings and equipment, and public documents all pass through those offices. In its FY27 budget testimony the Chief Administrative Officer's cluster described funding for a Digital Equity Manager for the office. Residents can reach the office at (215) 686-2798 or ada.request@phila.gov, and visit it at the Municipal Services Building, 1401 John F. Kennedy Blvd., first floor.

3 ADA compliance and grievances

Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act requires state and local governments to provide equal access to programs and services, and many city grievances concern buildings, sidewalks, transit or communications. Residents who believe a city program or facility is inaccessible can contact the office; other avenues include the Commission on Human Relations for discrimination in housing, employment and public accommodations, and federal agencies. Deadlines and remedies differ; this is general information, not legal advice. See also How to File a Complaint.

4 Connections

OPD interacts with the Streets Department on curb ramps and sidewalks, SEPTA (a state-created authority with its own ADA obligations), the Philadelphia Housing Authority, and service agencies such as the Philadelphia Corporation for Aging and the intellectual disability division of DBHIDS.

See also: Chief Administrative Officer, Office of Immigrant Affairs, Mayor's Cabinet and Offices.

References

  2. City of Philadelphia, "Mayor Cherelle L. Parker appoints leadership, announces the formalization of the Office for People with Disabilities," May 17, 2024 (phila.gov).
  3. Americans with Disabilities Act, Title II, 42 U.S.C. sections 12131-12165.

Office of LGBT Affairs

Office of LGBT Affairs (now Office of LGBTQ+ Affairs)
TypeCity office within the Mayor's administration
Established2008 by executive order; made permanent in the Home Rule Charter in 2015
Led byExecutive Director Tyrell Brown (appointment reported March 2025; the City's office page does not list a director)
AddressCity Hall, Room 110, Philadelphia, PA 19107
Contact(215) 686-0330; LGBTinfo@phila.gov
Websitephila.gov/departments/office-of-lgbtq-affairs

The Office of LGBT Affairs, which the city now styles the Office of LGBTQ+ Affairs, is a Philadelphia city office that aims "to foster equitable working and living conditions" for lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex, asexual and other community members.[1] This article uses the long-standing name; the city's current web page uses the LGBTQ+ name, an example of how city offices are renamed over time.

1 History and legal status

The office was established in 2008 through a mayoral executive order and gained permanent status in the Home Rule Charter in 2015.[1] A Charter office cannot be eliminated by a mayor alone; changes require a Charter amendment approved by voters. Philadelphia's local anti-discrimination protections for sexual orientation and gender identity, enforced by the Commission on Human Relations, predate and operate separately from the office.

2 Functions

The office develops civil rights policy affecting LGBTQ+ residents, implements diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives, coordinates services across city departments, supports community growth and serves as a liaison, and educates the public about community needs.[1] It also provides guidance on supporting transitioning city employees and maintains a resource list covering food, health, employment and other services.[1] The office is associated with the city's recognition of Pride events and community organizations.

3 Leadership

Celena Morrison, appointed under Mayor Jim Kenney, was the first Black transgender woman to head the office, per Pennsylvania Capital-Star coverage; she was later succeeded after leaving in November 2024.[2] Mayor Cherelle Parker appointed Tyrell Brown, previously of GALAEI and Philly Pride 365, as executive director in March 2025.[3] The City's current office page does not name a director, so the March 2025 appointment is the most recent public announcement.

4 Connections and complaints

The office is not an enforcement agency. A resident who believes they faced discrimination in employment, housing or public accommodations can contact the Commission on Human Relations; see How to File a Complaint. The office collaborates with the Department of Public Health on HIV and health issues, the Police Department on community relations, and the Office of Immigrant Affairs on intersectional work. The politics of LGBTQ+ policy at the state and federal level shape its work; see Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia. This is general information, not legal advice.

See also: Commission on Human Relations, Office for People with Disabilities, Mayor's Cabinet and Offices.

Office of Arts, Culture and the Creative Economy

Office of Arts, Culture and the Creative Economy (now Creative Philadelphia)
TypeCity department (cabinet-level) in the Parker administration
Current nameCreative Philadelphia (OACCE formerly)
Led byValerie V. Gay, Chief Cultural Officer and executive director
General Fund budget$5,395,601 proposed for FY2026 (down from $13.4 million FY2025 estimated)
AddressCity Hall, Room 116
Contact(215) 686-8446; creativephl@phila.gov

The Office of Arts, Culture and the Creative Economy (OACCE) was a city office supporting arts and culture; it is now known as Creative Philadelphia. Under Mayor Cherelle Parker the office became a department in the Mayor's Cabinet, and its executive director, Valerie V. Gay, holds the title Chief Cultural Officer. The FY2026 budget testimony describes Creative Philadelphia as "formerly the Office of Arts, Culture and the Creative Economy."[1]

1 Name, status and leadership

The budget testimony notes that Creative Philadelphia was a newly formed department starting in FY2025; before that its budget was reflected in the Managing Director's Office.[1] Gay is described as the first executive director of the office to serve in the Mayor's Cabinet.[2] The department's mission is to provide creative and economic opportunities for all Philadelphians to thrive through the arts, advance public access to arts and culture, and collaborate with local creative communities.[1] See Mayor's Cabinet and Offices.

2 Programs

Public art. The office oversees the city's Percent for Art program, which requires that one percent of the budget of certain city-funded construction projects be set aside for site-specific public art; the ordinance dates to 1959 and was shaped with the Redevelopment Authority. It also manages conservation of the city's collection. Projects named in FY2026 testimony include a Harriet Tubman statue at City Hall and a Sadie T.M. Alexander statue scheduled for fall 2026.[1]

Cultural Plan. The department planned to deliver the city's first Cultural Plan in spring 2026 as part of the 2035 Comprehensive Plan, with planning sessions in all ten council districts.[1] Art in City Hall expands exhibition space. Funding. The office distributes grants to artists and arts organizations, including Illuminate the Arts funding, and supports the nighttime economy and events around the 2026 Semiquincentennial.[1]

3 Budget

The FY2026 General Fund proposal was $5,395,601, a decrease of $8,030,000 from FY2025 estimated obligations, driven mostly by a drop in Class 500 contributions from $12.58 million to $4.3 million.[1] Its contracts are with nonprofit vendors. The fall in funding reflects one-time FY2025 contributions; see Philadelphia City Budget Process. Later fiscal years are set in each year's budget; see the Creative Philadelphia testimony and the adopted Appropriation Ordinance for the current figure.

4 Relationships

The office works with Mural Arts Philadelphia, the Free Library, Parks and Recreation, the Commerce Department on the creative economy, the Historical Commission and philanthropy. The Art Commission, an independent body, reviews design of public art and municipal structures. Artists can find calls for proposals on creativephl.org.

See also: Mural Arts Philadelphia, Free Library of Philadelphia, Philanthropy in Philadelphia.

  3. Philadelphia Code, Percent for Art provisions; WHYY, reporting on public art in Philadelphia.

Mural Arts Philadelphia

Mural Arts Philadelphia
TypeNonprofit (501(c)(3), Philadelphia Mural Arts Advocates) in partnership with city government; not a city department
Origins1984 Anti-Graffiti Network; nonprofit established 1996
Led byExecutive Director Emily Mello (from September 1, 2026, as reported by PhillyVoice); founder Jane Golden advising through year-end
GovernanceVolunteer Board of Directors (chair Hope Comisky per its website)
Address1727-29 Mt. Vernon Street, Philadelphia, PA 19130

Mural Arts Philadelphia describes itself as the nation's largest public art program. It evolved from the Anti-Graffiti Network launched in 1984 into the Mural Arts Program, and the nonprofit Philadelphia Mural Arts Advocates was established in 1996 as a 501(c)(3) organization.[1] It is a nonprofit working with the City, not a standard city department. The program has historically had a close relationship with city government, and its board includes ex-officio city officials.[1]

1 Mission and programs

Its stated purpose is to "provide transformative experiences, progressive discourse, and economic stimulus to the City of Philadelphia through participatory public art."[1] The organization reports 50 to 100 public art projects annually, more than 150 public and private partners yearly, and about 15,000 residents and visitors on tours, injecting roughly $2.7 million into the creative economy each year, according to its website.[1] Programs include a restorative justice program with classes at SCI Phoenix and apprenticeships for people returning from incarceration, and Porch Light, which links art and behavioral health.[2]

2 Leadership transition

Founder Jane Golden led the program since 1984 and announced in August 2025 that she would step down in 2026 after a search that began in fall 2025.[3] The organization named Emily Mello, a museum curator and educator formerly at the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago, as executive director effective September 1, 2026; Golden stays in an advisory role through year-end.[2]

Mural Arts reports about 150 public and private partners each year and says its outdoor art collection draws roughly 15,000 residents and visitors on tours annually.[1] Its board chair, Hope Comisky, a principal at Comisky Law, LLC, joined the board in 2015, according to the organization's website. The organization says it has operated for more than 40 years, which places its beginnings in the City's Anti-Graffiti Network of the 1980s.

3 Relationship to the City

Funding includes city, state, philanthropic and earned revenue; its annual budget is not summarized here; the organization reports roughly $2.7 million injected into the creative economy each year. It collaborates with Creative Philadelphia, Parks and Recreation, the Department of Prisons and DBHIDS. Because it is a nonprofit, it is governed by its board rather than the Mayor; see Philanthropy in Philadelphia.

4 Community involvement

Mural projects typically involve community meetings and neighborhood input, which may connect with Registered Community Organizations and neighborhood associations. Property owners must consent to murals on their walls. Residents can propose projects or join tours through the organization's website.

See also: Office of Arts, Culture and the Creative Economy, Civic and Neighborhood Associations, Philanthropy in Philadelphia.

Office of Workforce Development

Office of Workforce Development
TypeFormer stand-alone city office; functions now in the Department of Commerce
CreatedMarch 2018 under Mayor Kenney
Current successorOffice of Business Development and Workforce Solutions (Department of Commerce)
Related nonprofitPhiladelphia Works, Inc. (workforce development board), CEO Patrick Clancy
Contacttalent.development@phila.gov

The Office of Workforce Development (OWD) was launched in March 2018 to consolidate staff engaged in workforce efforts from several city agencies, including the Managing Director's Office, the Department of Commerce and the Office of Community Empowerment and Opportunity, as well as the Office of Adult Education.[1] Sheila Ireland was announced as its first executive director.[2] The office has since been reorganized: the city's 2020-2021 revised budget proposed eliminating it, with some resources and functions moving to the Commerce Department, and the city's website for the office now describes the Office of Business Development and Workforce Solutions.[3]

1 Origins and reorganization

The office was created to coordinate a fragmented set of programs for job seekers and employers. During the budget pressures of 2020, the city moved to eliminate it as a stand-alone office, as reported by Technical.ly; Commerce absorbed workforce functions.[3] This article therefore treats the Office of Workforce Development as a historical name and describes the current arrangement. The exact date and extent of the transfer of functions into Commerce are described here as Technical.ly reported them.

2 Current structure and programs

The Office of Business Development and Workforce Solutions, a division of Commerce, attracts and retains businesses and convenes workforce partners, preparing residents for jobs across sectors.[4] It runs the Workforce Professional Alliance, a partnership of 24 workforce organizations, and the Fair Chance Hiring Initiative, which reimburses employers who hire people returning from incarceration. It has also awarded Workforce Solutions Grants to nonprofit training organizations.[4] Gianna Grossmann is listed as senior director of workforce development.

3 Philadelphia Works

Philadelphia Works, Inc. is the region's federally designated workforce development board under the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act. It is a nonprofit, not a city department, and funds employment and training services; the city's Chief Administrative Officer, Camille Duchaussee, was appointed to its board in March 2026.[5] The mayor appoints the board's members under federal rules, and Patrick Clancy serves as president and CEO. Residents seeking job services typically use the PA CareerLink centers it oversees.

4 Connections

The office connects to Office of Community Empowerment and Opportunity, Community College of Philadelphia, building trades apprenticeship programs, prevailing wage and project labor agreements, organized labor and PIDC.

See also: Commerce Department, Chief Administrative Officer, Worker Centers and Labor Advocacy.

Philadelphia Corporation for Aging

Philadelphia Corporation for Aging (PCA)
TypePrivate nonprofit; Area Agency on Aging for Philadelphia County (not a city department)
Established1973
Led byPresident and CEO Najja R. Orr, DBA
Population served322,258 adults 60 and over in Philadelphia (20.4 percent of the population, 2024 ACS estimate)
Helpline215-765-9040
Websitepcacares.org

The Philadelphia Corporation for Aging (PCA) is a private, nonprofit organization established in 1973 that serves as the Area Agency on Aging for Philadelphia County.[1] Area Agencies on Aging are created by the federal Older Americans Act and designated by states; in Pennsylvania the Department of Aging oversees them. PCA is not a city department, though the City contributes funding and PCA testifies at City Council budget hearings. Its mission is to improve the quality of life for older Philadelphians and people with disabilities and help them achieve maximum health, independence and productivity.[1]

1 Status and governance

Najja R. Orr, who assumed the role in 2020 according to PCA's website, is president and CEO.[2] As a nonprofit, PCA has a board of directors rather than a mayor-appointed head, but it works under contract with the Pennsylvania Department of Aging and the City. Its June 2026 presentation reported 322,258 residents aged 60 and older, about 21.2 percent of whom live below the federal poverty level, and 58.7 percent of whom are members of a minority group.[1]

2 Services

PCA groups services as community and connection (the Helpline, senior community centers, congregate meals, employment services, transportation, health and wellness); help in the home (eligibility assessment, care management through the OPTIONS program, adult day services, home-delivered meals, home modifications, the Domiciliary Care Program); protection and advocacy (Older Adult Protective Services, the Ombuds Program, insurance and benefits counseling, legal services); and caregiver support.[1] Reports of suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation of older adults are taken by protective services.

3 Recent initiatives

FY2026 initiatives listed include a benefits enrollment partnership screening for programs such as PACE, SNAP, the Property Tax/Rent Rebate and Low-Income Subsidy; a Caregiver Navigation Program; a Victims of Crime Act program for older victims; a Cooling Project that installed 150 air conditioners in FY2023, 190 in FY2024 and 400 in FY2025 in heat-island zip codes with city funding, in partnership with the Department of Public Health; and a home modification program funded by the federal housing department.[1]

4 Funding and accountability

PCA's presentation noted that Governor's FY2027 state budget proposals included increases for the PENNCARE line and PA Link modernization, and a 2027 proposed federal budget for related agencies.[1] PCA's presentation did not break out its revenue by source in the portions summarized here. Public budget review occurs at hearings with City Council and annual public hearings; see Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia and Federal Government and Philadelphia.

5 Getting help

Call the PCA Helpline at 215-765-9040 or email AskHelpline@PCACares.org for benefits screening and referrals.[1] PCA collaborates with the Department of Human Services on family issues, Office for People with Disabilities, legal aid organizations, and the Philadelphia Housing Authority. This is general information, not legal advice.

See also: Department of Public Health, Office for People with Disabilities, Philadelphia Taxes.

  2. Philadelphia Corporation for Aging, leadership and press kit, pcacares.org.

School District of Philadelphia

School District of Philadelphia
TypeHome-rule school district (a state-law "first class" district coterminous with the city, separate from city departments)
Led bySuperintendent Tony B. Watlington Sr. (since 2022; contract extended through 2030)
Governing bodyBoard of Education (nine members appointed by the mayor and confirmed by City Council)
Operating budgetApproximately $4.6 billion adopted for 2026-27
Enrollment198,405 public-school students citywide in October 2025, including 64,469 in charter schools
Websitephilasd.org

The School District of Philadelphia is the public school system for the city of Philadelphia and the largest school district in Pennsylvania. It is a legally distinct local government from the City of Philadelphia: it has its own budget, its own board and its own employees, although it depends on the city for a large share of its local revenue and on the state for most of the rest. [1]

1 Structure and governance

Policy is set by the nine-member Board of Education, which the mayor appoints from candidates recommended by an Educational Nominating Panel, with confirmation by City Council. The Board hires the superintendent, adopts the budget and approves major contracts, facilities decisions and charter-school actions. Tony Watlington has been superintendent since 2022; in September 2025 the Board voted to extend his contract through 2030, with annual raises of 3 percent on a salary then reported at about $367,700. [2]

The administration is organized into central-office divisions (academics, operations, finance, human resources, facilities) and neighborhood-based "learning networks" that supervise principals. Teachers are represented by the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers, and school-based support staff and building engineers are represented by other unions. The District is subject to the Pennsylvania Public School Code, the Sunshine Act and the Right-to-Know Law. Before 2018 the District was governed by the state-dominated School Reform Commission, created in 2001; the SRC voted to dissolve in November 2017 and the appointed Board replaced it in July 2018. [1]

2 Students and schools

According to the District's research office, 198,405 students were enrolled in Philadelphia public schools as of October 1, 2025, a net increase of 106 over the previous year. Of that total, 64,469 attended charter schools, which are publicly funded but independently operated. The District has reported a 12 percent enrollment decline between 2014-15 and 2024-25, driven in part by the growth of charters and by population changes. [3]

District-run schools include neighborhood schools, citywide-admission and special-admission high schools, and alternative programs. Students living within a school's catchment have a right to attend; many high schools admit by application.

3 Money and the budget

The Board approved a roughly $4.6 billion operating budget for 2026-27. The District has described a structural deficit of about $300 million and, in the plan advanced by Superintendent Watlington, ordered about $225 million in reductions: about $56 million in school-level changes (including the elimination of roughly 340 teaching, counseling and climate positions) and about $169 million from the central office and lower-return programs, as reported by local education press. [4]

Revenue comes from the state (basic education funding and the adequacy supplement that followed the 2023 Commonwealth Court school-funding ruling), local sources (chiefly the school share of the city property tax, plus other local taxes), and federal programs. City Council approves the school property-tax rate but cannot direct how the Board spends funds. The budget process interacts with the City budget process and with tax policy described in Philadelphia Taxes.

4 Facilities plan and school closures

The District operates some of the oldest school buildings in the country. The Board has approved a ten-year facilities plan estimated at about $3 billion that calls for closing 17 schools beginning with the 2027-28 school year (the Board approved the plan on April 30, 2026), modernizing about 169 campuses and co-locating six others. Closure proposals were contested by some families, teachers and elected officials, and the plan's roll-out has generated ongoing public debate over enrollment projections, building conditions and neighborhood impact. [5]

5 Who holds influence

Formal authority sits with the Board, the superintendent and the mayor (who appoints the Board and sets city-side funding priorities). The state legislature and the Governor control basic-education appropriations and the Charter School Law. The teachers' union is the District's largest organized constituency. Major philanthropies, higher-education partners and business groups such as the Chamber of Commerce for Greater Philadelphia participate through advisory roles and grants (see Philanthropy in Philadelphia). Parents and neighborhood groups influence decisions through public testimony, school advisory councils and, increasingly, organized opposition to closures.

6 Working with the District

Residents can speak at Board meetings by signing up in advance, request records through the Right-to-Know process, and raise school-level concerns with the principal, then the learning network, then the Office of Family and Community Engagement. See also How to File a Complaint.

See also: Philadelphia Board of Education, Charter Schools in Philadelphia, Philadelphia Federation of Teachers, Community College of Philadelphia.
