Philadelphia Board of Education

Philadelphia Board of Education
TypeLocal school board (appointed)
MembersNine, appointed by the mayor and confirmed by City Council
Led byPresident Reginald Streater (as listed on the District website, 2026)
Established2018, succeeding the School Reform Commission (2001-2018)
Governing lawPennsylvania Public School Code; Philadelphia Home Rule Charter provisions on the Board and the Educational Nominating Panel
Websitephilasd.org/schoolboard

The Philadelphia Board of Education is the governing body of the School District of Philadelphia. Its nine members are appointed by the mayor, and it hires and evaluates the superintendent, adopts the District's budget and policies, approves contracts and oversees charter schools authorized by the District. [1]

1 From the SRC to an appointed board

From 2001 to 2018 the District was run by the School Reform Commission (SRC), a five-member body created during the state takeover, with three members appointed by the Governor and two by the mayor. After years of criticism from parents, Council members and the teachers' union, the SRC voted in November 2017 to dissolve itself, and local control returned in July 2018 with a board appointed by the mayor. During the SRC era the District saw rapid charter-school growth, school closures and recurring budget crises, which critics cited in calling for a return to local control. [2]

2 Appointment and composition

Under the Home Rule Charter, an Educational Nominating Panel made up of community, parent, student and civic representatives reviews applicants and submits names to the mayor, who appoints nine members, subject to confirmation by City Council. According to the District, members serve four-year terms that align with the mayor's term.[1] Mayor Cherelle Parker has appointed members to the board during her term, according to Inquirer and Chalkbeat reporting. [3] Members serve without pay. Because the mayor selects the members, the Board is closely tied to the Mayor's education priorities, and there is no direct election of members by voters.

3 Powers and duties

The Board has the powers of a Pennsylvania school board: it adopts the annual operating and capital budgets, sets the District's share of local tax requests, approves collective bargaining agreements, votes on school openings, closings and boundary changes, and acts as the charter authorizer for the District's charter schools under the state Charter School Law (including renewal, revocation and charter amendments). It holds regular public Action Meetings and committee meetings, subject to the Sunshine Act. [1]

4 Current leadership and recent decisions

Reginald Streater serves as Board president, according to the District's website and Philadelphia Tribune reporting on his return to the post.[4] On April 30, 2026 the Board approved a facilities master plan under which 17 schools are set to close beginning with the 2027-28 school year, a decision that followed weeks of public testimony and pushback from City Council members, parents and others, according to WHYY and Chalkbeat. The Board's spring 2026 decisions also took place during a District budget shortfall. [5]

5 The elected-board debate

Whether the Board should be elected remains an ongoing civic question: after the closure vote, City Council voted unanimously in May 2026 to hold hearings on changes to how board members are selected, according to the Philadelphia Tribune and the Inquirer. Supporters of appointment argue that it fixes responsibility on one elected official and avoids low-turnout board elections; supporters of election argue that it gives residents direct control. A change would require amending the Home Rule Charter through a ballot question (see Ballot Questions and Charter Changes) and possibly state action.

6 Participating in Board meetings

Members of the public can sign up in advance to testify at Action Meetings, submit written comments, and watch meetings by livestream. Records, including budgets and resolutions, are available on the Board's website and through the Right-to-Know Law. See also How to Testify at City Council for comparable practices.

See also: School District of Philadelphia, Charter Schools in Philadelphia, Mayor of Philadelphia, Philadelphia Home Rule Charter.

Charter Schools in Philadelphia

Charter Schools in Philadelphia
TypePublicly funded schools run by independent nonprofit boards
Enrollment64,469 students in October 2025 (about 32.5 percent of 198,405 public-school students)
AuthorizerPhiladelphia Board of Education (brick-and-mortar charters); Pennsylvania Department of Education (cyber charters)
Governing lawPennsylvania Charter School Law (Act 22 of 1997, as amended)
AppealsState Charter Appeal Board; Commonwealth Court

Charter schools in Philadelphia are public schools that operate under a charter granted by a public authorizer but are managed by independent nonprofit boards rather than by the School District of Philadelphia. Philadelphia has one of the highest charter shares of any large American city: the District reported 64,469 charter students on October 1, 2025, about one third of all public-school students in the city. [1]

1 Legal framework

Charters in Pennsylvania are governed by the 1997 Charter School Law, a state statute. A local school board (here, the Board of Education) can grant, renew, amend or revoke a brick-and-mortar charter, typically for five-year terms. Applicants and charter operators can appeal adverse decisions to the State Charter Appeal Board and then to the courts. Cyber charter schools are chartered by the state Department of Education, not by the District, even though the District pays tuition for Philadelphia students who enroll in them. Charter schools are subject to the Right-to-Know Law and the Sunshine Act, though disputes about their transparency have arisen. [2]

2 History in Philadelphia

Charter growth accelerated during the era of the School Reform Commission (2001-2018), when the state-influenced body authorized new charters and invited private managers to run some District schools. Enrollment in charters then plateaued: the District's data show a 1.6 percent rise, or 1,028 students, in charter enrollment between 2015-16 and 2025-26, while District-run enrollment fell. The mix includes small neighborhood charters, large networks and a number of schools converted from District management. [1]

3 Funding and the fiscal debate

Charter schools do not charge tuition. The District pays each charter a per-pupil amount set by a state formula based on the District's own spending, with separate rates for special education. The District and its supporters argue that stranded fixed costs remain when students leave for charters, contributing to budget pressure; charter operators and parents counter that the schools educate public-school children at lower per-pupil cost and that families choose them. Both arguments appeared during the District's 2026 deficit debate over a budget of about $4.6 billion. Reform proposals at the state level, including changes to the funding formula and to cyber-charter tuition, have been debated in Harrisburg for years. [3]

4 Oversight, renewal and closure

The District's Charter Schools Office evaluates schools on academic performance, financial health and organizational compliance and makes recommendations to the Board. The Board has declined to renew or has moved to revoke charters at schools with weak academic or financial results, and those schools have appealed. Staff, families and neighbors typically testify at public hearings, and decisions can end in settlements or negotiated charter amendments, including enrollment caps. [2]

5 Who holds influence

The Board and Charter Schools Office hold authorizing power; the state legislature controls the law and funding formulas; and the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers has long sought stronger limits on charter growth, though some charter staff are also union-represented. Charter networks and trade associations lobby for stable funding. Philanthropies have funded both District and charter initiatives (see Philanthropy in Philadelphia), and the mayor's appointments to the Board shape authorizing priorities.

6 Information for families

Charter admission is by application and lottery rather than by address. Families can find school profiles and performance data on the District's website and the state's Future Ready PA Index. Complaints about a charter go first to the school's board, then to the District's Charter Schools Office, and, for cyber charters, to the state Department of Education. See How to File a Complaint.

See also: School District of Philadelphia, Philadelphia Board of Education, Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia.

  2. Pennsylvania Charter School Law, 24 P.S. 17-1701-A et seq.; Pennsylvania Department of Education charter-school pages.
  3. Chalkbeat Philadelphia and Philadelphia Inquirer coverage of District budget and charter funding debates (2025-2026).

Community College of Philadelphia

Community College of Philadelphia
TypePublic, open-admission community college (CCP)
Led byPresident Alycia Marshall (named October 2025; seventh president)
SponsorCity of Philadelphia, with Commonwealth of Pennsylvania funding
Governing bodyBoard of Trustees (appointed through the City as sponsor)
Governing lawPennsylvania Community College Act of 1963
Websiteccp.edu

Community College of Philadelphia (CCP) is the city's public two-year college. It admits any student with a high-school diploma or equivalent, offers associate degrees, certificates and non-credit workforce programs, and is the largest public provider of higher education in the city by headcount of local residents. It is one of Pennsylvania's community colleges, with the City of Philadelphia acting as its local sponsor. [1]

1 Governance and sponsorship

Under Pennsylvania's Community College Act, a community college is created by a sponsoring local government. CCP was established in 1964 with the City of Philadelphia as its sponsor, and its first classes began in September 1965 in a former downtown department-store building under founding president Allen T. Bonnell. Today a Board of Trustees, appointed through the City as the college's sponsor (see the mayor's role in local appointments), governs the college, sets tuition, approves budgets and hires the president. The college is a separate legal entity from both the City and the School District of Philadelphia, and its employees are represented by unions including a faculty and staff federation. [1]

2 Funding

Pennsylvania community colleges are funded in roughly three parts: student tuition and fees, state operating appropriations, and sponsor (local) support. In CCP's case the City contributes an annual appropriation through the City budget, and the college has also relied on state capital programs and federal Pell Grant revenue. Amounts change annually and are published in the City budget and the college's own financial statements. Because many students are low-income, adult or part-time, enrollment and revenue respond to labor-market conditions and to financial-aid policy. [2]

3 Leadership change 2025

In April 2025 the Board of Trustees voted unanimously not to renew the contract of Donald "Guy" Generals, who had been president since 2014; the board cited performance discrepancies and a growing misalignment with board expectations, and local press noted the absence of detailed public explanation. Alycia Marshall, the provost, became interim president. In May 2025 WHYY reported that a judge had denied an effort to reinstate Generals. After a national search with four finalists, the Board announced her appointment as the college's seventh president on October 21, 2025, and the Inquirer reported in December 2025 that the board approved a contract for her. [3]

4 Role in workforce and city policy

CCP is a major partner in city workforce efforts, offering job-training programs and pipelines into health care, trades, public safety and information technology. It coordinates with the Office of Workforce Development, employers and unions, and it is a common landing point for city-supported scholarship and last-dollar aid initiatives. It also provides adult-education and English-language programs and works with the District on dual-enrollment for high-school students.

5 Who holds influence

The City, as sponsor, appoints the trustees, and City Council shapes the appropriation, so City Hall holds substantial leverage. The state legislature sets operating support, and employers and philanthropies influence program priorities through grants (see Philanthropy in Philadelphia). Faculty and staff unions have a voice in bargaining and public testimony, and student groups participate in trustee meetings, which are open under the Sunshine Act.

See also: School District of Philadelphia, Office of Workforce Development, Eds and Meds Anchor Institutions.

Chamber of Commerce for Greater Philadelphia

Chamber of Commerce for Greater Philadelphia
TypePrivate nonprofit business association (regional chamber)
Led byPresident and CEO Chellie Cameron (since mid-2022)
PredecessorRob Wonderling (CEO 2009-2022)
TerritoryPhiladelphia and surrounding Pennsylvania suburban counties
FundingMember dues, events, programs and sponsorships
Websitechamberphl.com

The Chamber of Commerce for Greater Philadelphia is the region's principal business membership organization. It is a private nonprofit, not a government body, and has no regulatory authority; its influence comes from its membership of major employers, its advocacy before City Council, the mayor and the state legislature, and its convening role in regional economic development. [1]

1 Structure and leadership

A board of directors drawn from member companies and institutions governs the Chamber, and a paid president and CEO runs day-to-day operations. Rob Wonderling, a former Pennsylvania state senator, led the Chamber from 2009 until he stepped down in mid-2022. He was succeeded by Chellie Cameron, who was named the Chamber's new president on May 19, 2022, after about eleven years as head of the City's aviation department and CEO of Philadelphia International Airport, according to the Inquirer and the Business Journals (see Philadelphia International Airport). The Inquirer reported on September 22, 2026, that the chief executive of Jefferson would chair the Chamber's board, a reminder that the board is drawn from the region's largest employers and institutions. As of 2026 Cameron remains president and CEO, and the Chamber publishes annual progress reports and messages to its members. [2]

2 Policy positions

The Chamber's public agenda has centered on business-tax competitiveness, workforce development, public safety, transportation and infrastructure, and regional economic growth. It has supported reductions in city wage and business taxes and has commented on proposals such as changes to the Business Income and Receipts Tax and the real-estate transfer tax (see Philadelphia Taxes). As with any advocacy group, its positions are those of its membership and can be disputed: labor unions, tenant groups and progressive organizations have at times opposed Chamber positions on wages, taxes and development incentives (see Tax Abatement and Development Incentives). [1]

3 Programs and affiliates

The Chamber runs networking and leadership programs, a regional leadership-exchange trip, small-business services and a political-engagement arm that endorses and hosts candidate forums in election years. In 2026 it worked with member institutions on visitor-welcome efforts tied to the nation's 250th anniversary; Temple University announced in July 2026 that it had joined the Chamber in welcoming visitors during the milestone year. It collaborates with the Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation, the Commerce Department, and downtown organizations such as the Center City District. Its political-spending activity is subject to the rules described in Campaign Finance in Philadelphia. [2]

4 Place among business groups

The Chamber is one of several organized business voices. Others include the Building Industry Association and realtor groups (see Developers and the Real Estate Lobby), neighborhood commercial corridors, minority-business chambers, the Central Philadelphia Development Corporation, and sector associations in health care, hospitality and life sciences. Large anchor institutions also lobby on their own (see Eds and Meds Anchor Institutions).

5 How residents and small businesses interact with it

Membership is open to firms of any size for dues. Residents encounter the Chamber mainly through public testimony on tax bills, candidate forums and policy reports. Its filings and lobbying registrations are public; Pennsylvania lobbying disclosure and the City's lobbying rules are described in Conflicts of Interest and Pay-to-Play.

See also: Commerce Department, Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation, Organized Labor in Philadelphia.

Center City District and Business Improvement Districts

Center City District and Business Improvement Districts
TypeProperty-owner-funded special assessment districts (nonprofit management authorities)
Led byCenter City District: President and CEO Prema Katari Gupta (since January 2024; succeeded founder Paul Levy)
Number in city15 BIDs reported, with annual budgets from about $20,000 to nearly $29 million
Governing lawPennsylvania Neighborhood Improvement District Act; City ordinances
Websitecentercityphila.org

A business improvement district (BID), called a neighborhood improvement district in Pennsylvania law, is a defined area in which commercial property owners agree to pay an additional assessment collected by the city, which funds supplemental services run by a nonprofit. The largest and oldest in Philadelphia is the Center City District (CCD), which supplements city services in the downtown core. [1]

1 How BIDs work

Under state law and a City ordinance, property owners in a proposed district petition and vote, and the City then levies the approved assessment and passes it to the district's nonprofit. Services are meant to supplement, not replace, municipal ones: typical BID work includes sidewalk cleaning and trash removal, community-service ("ambassador") patrols, marketing, lighting, streetscape capital projects and data-driven planning. Districts must renew periodically by a process that gives owners a chance to object. Because the assessment is a charge on property rather than a tax on residents, residential-only blocks generally are not part of a BID. [1]

2 Center City District

CCD was created in the early 1990s by Center City property owners, with City approval, as an answer to downtown decline, and it has been renewed on multi-year plans. Paul Levy led it from its founding in 1991; Prema Katari Gupta became president and CEO on January 1, 2024, under a two-year leadership transition. CCD publishes plan-and-budget documents and an annual report that break down sources and uses of funds. Its work includes the downtown cleaning and safety teams, capital projects such as the Dilworth Park redevelopment and lighting and streetscape improvements, and research reports on downtown economics, office occupancy and retail. It has also published positions on business-tax reform. Its sister organization, the Central Philadelphia Development Corporation, handles planning and advocacy. [2]

3 Other BIDs

As of reporting, Philadelphia had about 15 BIDs. Examples include the University City District in West Philadelphia and the East Passyunk Avenue BID in South Philadelphia, and others serve Old City and commercial corridors elsewhere. The smallest have budgets of tens of thousands of dollars while the largest, CCD, operates at nearly $29 million. Smaller commercial corridors often rely instead on community development corporations and the City's corridor-management programs run through the Commerce Department. [3]

4 Influence and criticism

Supporters point to measurable improvements in cleanliness, foot traffic and downtown investment, and CCD is frequently cited in studies of BIDs nationally. Critics argue that BIDs concentrate public-space management in organizations governed by property owners rather than residents, that their patrols raise questions about oversight and treatment of people experiencing homelessness, and that wealthier districts can fund services unavailable in poorer neighborhoods. CCD and other BIDs respond that they supplement a baseline of City services and operate transparently under public plans. These disagreements often appear in debates over open streets, street cleaning and homeless outreach (see Office of Homeless Services).

5 Relationship to the City

BIDs have no police power; they depend on the Streets Department, the Philadelphia Police Department and other agencies for enforcement. Their leaders sit on commissions, testify before City Council and take part in zoning and design reviews (see Registered Community Organizations). Residents can contact a BID for cleaning requests in its district and use Philly311 for all other city services.

See also: Chamber of Commerce for Greater Philadelphia, Commerce Department, Developers and the Real Estate Lobby.

Eds and Meds Anchor Institutions

Eds and Meds Anchor Institutions
TypeNonprofit universities and health systems (private and state-related)
Key institutionsUniversity of Pennsylvania and Penn Medicine; Children's Hospital of Philadelphia; Thomas Jefferson University and Jefferson Health; Temple University and Temple University Health System; Drexel University; Saint Joseph's University; La Salle University
Largest private employerUniversity of Pennsylvania (more than 40,000 local employees reported)
Tax statusProperty-tax exempt as purely public charities in most respects

"Eds and meds" is the common shorthand for the universities ("eds") and hospital systems ("meds") that anchor Philadelphia's economy. Together they are the city's largest private-sector employers, among its largest landowners and, because most are tax-exempt charities, a recurring subject of debate about their fiscal contribution to the city. [1]

1 Economic weight

Lists of the region's largest private employers consistently place the University of Pennsylvania first, followed by the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, Thomas Jefferson University Hospitals, Temple University and Temple University Hospital. Penn alone reports more than 40,000 local employees. The sector's payrolls generate city wage-tax revenue and its research generates federal and philanthropic funding, which makes it central to economic-development strategy and to initiatives run by the Commerce Department and the Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation. [1]

2 Tax exemption and PILOTs

Under Pennsylvania's Institutions of Purely Public Charity Act (Act 55 of 1997), organizations that meet statutory criteria are exempt from property tax. A WHYY analysis found that universities and hospitals that could pay voluntary payments in lieu of taxes (PILOTs) held at least $3.6 billion in property, about 6.4 percent of the city's total market value, which at prevailing rates would equate to at least about $106 million in tax. The same reporting said the city then collected less than $700,000 a year in PILOTs, down from a goal near $10 million a year in the mid-1990s, and that several major universities had no agreement with the City. Institutions respond that they provide charity care, scholarships, community programs and employment, and that they contribute through wage and other taxes paid by employees and by their own payroll-related taxes. Individual institutions have periodically announced voluntary commitments, such as the University of Pennsylvania's $100 million commitment reported by WHYY in December 2020, while WHYY noted at the time that the region's other large universities had not announced comparable pledges. The Inquirer reported in March 2025 that Mayor Cherelle Parker was asking the city's "eds and meds" to help fill holes in the city budget, citing sources. The PILOT figures above date from the time of that reporting and change, so readers should consult current City Controller and budget reports. [2]

3 Land use and neighborhoods

Campus and hospital expansion has repeatedly shaped West Philadelphia, North Philadelphia and Center City, and it is reviewed through the zoning process (see Philadelphia Zoning Code and Registered Community Organizations). Community groups have negotiated benefits and raised concerns about displacement and rising housing costs near campuses, while institutions point to jobs, safety and commercial revitalization. The University City District, a business improvement district, was founded with Penn and other institutional backing (see Center City District and Business Improvement Districts).

4 Civic and political roles

Institution presidents and senior executives sit on civic boards, philanthropic boards and the Chamber; they work with the mayor on education, workforce and public safety programs. Unions representing health-care workers and graduate students have organized at several institutions (see Service and Health Care Unions). The institutions also lobby at the state level on funding for Temple (a state-related university), Penn's veterinary school, medical assistance reimbursement and research.

5 Public-sector connections

The Community College of Philadelphia, Temple and the School District run partnerships with these institutions. Temple University Hospital, Jefferson and Penn also serve as major trauma and emergency care providers, which links them to the city's public health system.

See also: Philanthropy in Philadelphia, Tax Abatement and Development Incentives, Philadelphia Taxes.

Philanthropy in Philadelphia

Philanthropy in Philadelphia
TypePrivate and community foundations, donor-advised funds, corporate giving
Largest local funderWilliam Penn Foundation (reported assets about $3.4 billion; about $148.8 million in giving in 2024)
Community foundationThe Philadelphia Foundation (reported assets about $900 million)
Other major namesThe Pew Charitable Trusts; Lenfest Institute for Journalism; Knight Foundation; corporate foundations

Philanthropy in Philadelphia is the network of private foundations and donors whose grants support schools, arts institutions, parks, housing, health and civic organizations. Because the city government and the School District operate under tight budgets, foundation money often shapes which pilot programs, studies and nonprofits get started. Foundations are private actors, not government bodies; their influence comes from funding decisions rather than legal authority. [1]

1 Major funders

The William Penn Foundation, established in 1945, is described by the Inquirer as the biggest foundation focused solely on Greater Philadelphia and, after other funders such as the Annenberg Foundation moved their focus elsewhere, has assumed primacy among local funders. Its annual giving grew from about $110 million in 2020 to about $149 million in 2024, according to a grant-database summary of its filings. The Pew Charitable Trusts, based in Philadelphia, has billions in assets but directs most grants nationally and internationally. The Philadelphia Foundation, the regional community foundation, manages donor-advised and designated funds and awards tens of millions of dollars annually. The Lenfest Foundation, created by the late Gerry Lenfest, gave away more than $1.3 billion but was designed as a spend-down vehicle rather than a perpetual one. [2]

2 Funding priorities

In 2024 the William Penn Foundation announced changes to what it funds, and its May 2026 docket reported 128 grants totaling about $57.2 million, with 41 percent in children and families. Local philanthropy typically concentrates in education, early childhood, arts and culture, parks and public spaces (for example through the Fairmount Park Conservancy), neighborhood development and, increasingly, housing and racial-equity work. [3]

3 Funding the public sector and media

Foundation grants have supported Mural Arts Philadelphia, the Free Library and Parks and Recreation through friends groups and conservancies. Philanthropy also underwrites local journalism: the Lenfest Institute owns the Philadelphia Inquirer and has invested more than $117 million in news initiatives, as it reports (see Local News Media in Philadelphia). Foundation-supported groups such as community development corporations, legal-aid organizations and good-government groups rely on grants and, in some cases, on City contracts.

4 Debates about foundation power

Observers of philanthropy raise recurring questions. Supporters say foundations can take risks government cannot, fund long-term projects and convene stakeholders. Critics argue that a small number of funders set priorities with limited public input, that grantee organizations may avoid criticizing their funders, and that grant-driven programs may not last. Foundations typically respond with community advisory structures and published grant lists. Grassroots groups have sometimes called for more unrestricted, community-led funding. These debates arise in education reform, charter-school funding and neighborhood redevelopment (see Charter Schools in Philadelphia).

5 Transparency and access

Private foundations file annual Form 990-PF returns with the IRS, which are public through services such as ProPublica's Nonprofit Explorer. Most local foundations publish grant lists and application guidelines on their websites, and many fund only invited or pre-qualified applicants. Residents seeking funding for neighborhood projects can start with the Philadelphia Foundation and neighborhood-focused funds.

See also: Eds and Meds Anchor Institutions, Civic and Neighborhood Associations, Office of Arts, Culture and the Creative Economy.

  2. Philadelphia Inquirer, "William Penn Foundation, Philly's biggest focused solely on Philly, is changing what it funds" (June 27, 2024); Granted AI and Kindora foundation profiles for the William Penn Foundation and the Philadelphia Foundation (summaries of IRS filings).
  3. William Penn Foundation grant dockets (williampennfoundation.org); Lenfest Institute for Journalism 10-year report (May 2026).

Developers and the Real Estate Lobby

Developers and the Real Estate Lobby
TypePrivate trade associations, firms and lobbyists
Key groupsBuilding Industry Association of Philadelphia (BIA); Greater Philadelphia Association of Realtors; Development Workshop; commercial brokers and law firms
Main arenasCity Council, Zoning Board, Planning Commission, Department of Licenses and Inspections, state legislature
DisclosureCity lobbying registration; campaign-finance reports

The real estate lobby in Philadelphia is a loose term for the developers, builders, brokers, realtors, property managers and attorneys who organize to influence policy that affects construction and property values. It is not one organization. Different groups sometimes disagree with each other, and with tenant, neighborhood and labor groups. [1]

1 Who is involved

The Building Industry Association of Philadelphia represents builders, developers and contractors; its president, Jim Maransky, has been its public face on tax and zoning debates. The Greater Philadelphia Association of Realtors represents real estate agents and brokers. Development Workshop, a group led by David Feldman, has spoken for builders on abatement proposals. Individual developers also engage directly through zoning attorneys, lobbyists and community meetings. Building trades unions often ally with developers on projects that create union jobs but may disagree on wage standards (see Philadelphia Building and Construction Trades Council and Prevailing Wage and Project Labor Agreements). [2]

2 Tax abatement fights

The clearest example of organized real estate lobbying is the 10-year property-tax abatement on new construction (see Tax Abatement and Development Incentives). When Council President Darrell Clarke proposed in 2019 to phase the abatement down, which the city estimated would raise about $270 million over a decade, the BIA opposed the bill and circulated alternatives, the Realtors offered an amendment keeping the full benefit for several years, and developers warned that projects in the pipeline would stall. Council ultimately voted to shrink the abatement, and industry representatives forecast negative effects. Subsequent reporting has addressed how the revised abatement and later amendments played out. Supporters argue the abatement drives construction and tax-base growth; critics, including housing advocates and some Council members, argue it benefits high-end projects and reduces school revenue. [2]

3 Zoning and permitting

Developers interact with the zoning code, the Zoning Board of Adjustment, the Planning Commission and the Department of Licenses and Inspections. In practice a district Council member's support is often decisive for zoning changes and land sales, a practice discussed in Councilmanic Prerogative. Developers must also meet with Registered Community Organizations before certain approvals. Trade groups lobby for faster permits and against requirements such as inclusionary housing mandates, while advocates seek affordability set-asides.

4 Campaign money and disclosure

Real estate and construction interests are among the larger sources of political contributions in city races. Contributions are limited under the City's campaign-finance law and reported to the City Board of Ethics and the City Commissioners; the rules and independent-expenditure channels are described in Campaign Finance in Philadelphia and Political Action Committees and Big Money. Lobbyists must register with the City. Contributions and lobbying are lawful; the ethics system focuses on disclosure, limits and conflicts (see Conflicts of Interest and Pay-to-Play).

5 Counterweights

Organized counterweights include neighborhood associations, tenant groups, labor unions, community development corporations and the mayor's housing initiatives, including the housing plan of about $2 billion in the fiscal 2026 budget. The real estate sector is also not uniform: affordable-housing developers, for example, often favor public subsidy and may differ from market-rate developers on abatement and zoning policy.

See also: Landlord and Property Owner Associations, Division of Housing and Community Development, Philadelphia Redevelopment Authority.

References

  1. Philadelphia Board of Ethics, lobbying registration and campaign-finance guidance; Philadelphia Code, Chapter 20-1000 (campaign finance) and lobbying provisions.
  2. Pennsylvania Capital-Star, "Philly's real estate industry mobilizes to lobby City Council on 10-year tax abatement proposal"; WHYY, "Philly Council votes to shrink 10-year abatement, stoking real estate industry doomsday fears"; Philadelphia Inquirer, "Philadelphia tax abatement developers amendment" (December 2, 2019).
  3. City of Philadelphia, press release on the FY26 budget (June 2025).

Community Development Corporations

Community Development Corporations
TypeNeighborhood-based nonprofit organizations (CDCs)
Citywide associationPhiladelphia Association of Community Development Corporations (PACDC): over 150 members, including over 60 CDCs
Main fundersCity housing and commerce programs, state and federal grants, foundations, developer fees
Typical workAffordable housing, corridor revitalization, home repair, financial counseling, organizing
Websitepacdc.org

A community development corporation (CDC) is a nonprofit organization rooted in a particular neighborhood, usually governed by a board that includes residents, whose purpose is to improve the area's housing, businesses and services. CDCs are private nonprofits, not government agencies, though they rely heavily on public funds and often work as partners to city departments and authorities. [1]

1 What CDCs do

Philadelphia's CDCs emerged from the civil-rights and anti-poverty movements of the 1960s and expanded through federal housing and community-development programs. Contemporary activities include developing and managing affordable rental and homeownership housing, preserving existing homes through repair programs, providing housing counseling and foreclosure prevention, managing neighborhood commercial corridors, running workforce and youth programs, and organizing residents. Many hold property through the Philadelphia Land Bank or the Redevelopment Authority, developing vacant lots into housing or open space.

2 PACDC and the CDC network

The Philadelphia Association of Community Development Corporations is the trade and advocacy association for the sector. Its website reports more than 150 members, of which more than 60 are CDCs, and the rest are other stakeholders such as lenders, developers, architects and service providers. PACDC provides training, publishes economic-impact research and advocates before City Council, the state legislature and Congress for housing and neighborhood-investment funding. It also holds an annual gala and award ceremony. According to its website, PACDC runs a Community Development Leadership Institute that trains future neighborhood leaders in real estate finance, community engagement, communications and fundraising, and its policy work has covered investor ownership of homes, quick-strike property acquisition, commercial corridor development and a set of 22 equitable-development recommendations. Its office is at 1315 Walnut Street, Suite 920, and its phone number is (215) 732-5829. [2]

3 Funding and city partnerships

CDCs are funded through a mix of city programs (administered by the Division of Housing and Community Development, the Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation and the Commerce Department), federal block grants and tax credits, state housing finance, and foundation and bank grants (see Philanthropy in Philadelphia). Developer fees from completed housing projects often pay for operating expenses. Because many depend on a limited set of public programs, changes in federal and city budgets directly affect their capacity.

4 Influence, tensions and criticism

CDC leaders also serve on public bodies: the Philadelphia Land Bank's board, for example, includes the executive directors or presidents of the Passyunk Avenue Revitalization Corporation and the HACE Community Development Corporation (see Philadelphia Land Bank). In April 2025 Councilmember Jamie Gauthier introduced a bill intended to help CDCs build affordable housing and resist displacement, according to a City Council press release. CDCs shape local land-use decisions through zoning review (many are also Registered Community Organizations), through site control of vacant parcels and through their relationships with District Council members. Supporters credit them with delivering affordable housing and stabilizing neighborhoods. Critics and some residents have argued that some CDCs lack broad resident accountability, that their funding dependency can limit advocacy, or that their projects can themselves contribute to gentrification pressures. CDCs differ widely in size, from small volunteer-led organizations to multi-million-dollar developers.

5 Working with a CDC

Residents can find their local CDC through PACDC's member directory or the City's housing counseling list. CDCs commonly host community meetings, offer home-repair and tax-assistance programs, and take part in the block and neighborhood organizing that feeds into city decision-making. Boards are open to resident membership in many cases.

See also: Civic and Neighborhood Associations, Tenant and Housing Advocacy Groups, Philadelphia Housing Authority.

  3. PACDC, home page and contact information (pacdc.org, accessed October 2026); Philadelphia City Council, press release on Councilmember Gauthier's April 10, 2025 bill; Philadelphia Land Bank, Board of Directors page (phillylandbank.org).

Civic and Neighborhood Associations

Civic and Neighborhood Associations
TypeVolunteer nonprofits and informal groups organized by block, neighborhood or corridor
Formal statusRegistered Community Organizations (RCOs) under the zoning code; 268 active as of a 2020 city announcement
Main arenasZoning variance hearings, Civic Design Review, District Council offices, 311 and police district meetings
Governing lawPhiladelphia Zoning Code (2012) RCO provisions

Civic and neighborhood associations are the volunteer-run groups through which many Philadelphians engage with local government. They range from block captains and "friends of" park groups to long-established civic associations covering many blocks. Unlike elected bodies they have no legal authority of their own, but the City gives those that register formal roles in development review, which makes them among the most influential community actors on land-use questions. [1]

1 Types of groups

Common forms include block and town-watch groups, civic associations with dues-paying members and monthly meetings, neighborhood improvement and park-friends groups, business associations on commercial corridors, tenant and homeowner associations, and ad hoc coalitions that form around a specific issue. Some are incorporated nonprofits; others are informal. Larger neighborhoods often have several overlapping groups, which can lead to disagreements about who speaks for a community. [2]

2 The RCO system

When the City adopted its new zoning code in 2012, it codified the role of Registered Community Organizations. An organization applies to the Planning Commission to represent a defined geographic area; once registered, it receives notice of zoning variance or special-exception requests before the Zoning Board of Adjustment and of projects requiring Civic Design Review, and it must be offered a community meeting by the applicant. Registrations are renewed periodically, and the Commission publishes a map and list. Details are in Registered Community Organizations. The City announced 268 active RCOs in 2020; the number changes with each registration cycle. [1]

3 Influence with Council and city agencies

RCO positions are advisory: the Zoning Board and the Commission weigh them, but are not bound by them. In practice, a recommendation from the RCO and the district Council member often carries weight, linking associations to the informal system of councilmanic prerogative. Associations also work with police district advisory councils, the Streets Department, Philly311 and Parks and Recreation on neighborhood quality-of-life issues, and they often host candidate forums at election time. Ward committee people also sit in many of these rooms (see Ward Leaders and Committeepersons).

4 Criticisms and reform debates

Supporters say RCOs give residents an early and meaningful voice in development. Critics, including some developers, housing advocates and planners, argue that participation skews toward homeowners and longtime residents, that boundaries can overlap, and that the process can delay housing. Planning Commission staff and advocates have debated bills that would change RCO notice, boundary and accountability rules, and the Commission has at times opposed proposed changes. Some civic associations have sought tighter regulation of the RCO map. [3] Neighbors who are not part of an RCO can still testify at hearings.

5 Getting involved

To find your registered organization, use the Planning Commission's RCO map. Meeting notices, bylaws and elections are set by each group. For guidance on starting one, see How to Organize a Block or Neighborhood Group.

See also: Community Development Corporations, Developers and the Real Estate Lobby, Philadelphia Neighborhoods Guide.

References

  2. Next City, "Philly's Community Organizations Have a Critical Role in Development."

Faith Communities and Black Clergy

Faith Communities and Black Clergy
TypeReligious congregations and clergy associations (private, tax-exempt)
Key organizationBlack Clergy of Philadelphia and Vicinity (Bishop J. Louis Felton reported as president in January 2024; Rev. Robert Collier was president from 2020)
Political roleCandidate forums, endorsements by clergy bodies, public-safety summits, voter engagement
Legal limitChurches as 501(c)(3) organizations may not endorse candidates as organizations

Faith communities are among the oldest and most extensive civic networks in Philadelphia, from the Quaker founders to Black churches that have served as centers of community life since the 18th century. The Free African Society and Mother Bethel African Methodist Episcopal Church were founded in Philadelphia in the 1790s. Today congregations of many faiths provide social services, host community meetings and polling places, and take part in political and policy debates. The best-known political formation is the network of Black clergy. [1]

1 Historic role

Black churches in Philadelphia were centers of mutual aid, education, abolitionist organizing and, later, civil-rights and labor organizing. Their pastors often served as community spokespeople when formal political access was limited. This history is the background to the continuing practice of candidates seeking pulpit and clergy-breakfast appearances. See also Philadelphia Political History.

2 Black Clergy of Philadelphia and Vicinity

The Black Clergy of Philadelphia and Vicinity is a long-standing association of pastors from Black congregations. Pennsylvania Capital-Star has described its members as influential in the city's mayoral politics, and local press has reported leadership changes: the Rev. Robert Collier served as president from 2020, and the Philadelphia Tribune reported in January 2024 that Bishop J. Louis Felton was the group's new president. Later leadership changes, if any, should be checked with the organization. The group holds breakfast meetings with candidates, issues statements and hosts summits, including a public-safety summit at Mt. Zion Baptist Church in North Philadelphia that Cherelle Parker, then the Democratic mayoral nominee, was invited to attend. [2]

3 Elections and politics

In the 2023 mayoral race the Black Clergy of Philadelphia endorsed Cherelle Parker, as the Tribune reported. As described in Political Parties in Philadelphia and Ward Leaders and Committeepersons, ward organizations, unions and clergy overlap in Black-majority wards, where church congregations serve as networks for voter mobilization and turnout. Candidates for mayor, Council and judge routinely appear at church forums. Influence varies: an endorsement from a clergy body is one signal among many, and its effect on turnout is debated. [3]

4 Social services and public safety

Congregations run food pantries, youth programs, senior services and housing ministries, and some partner with the City on programs such as the Office of Violence Prevention, the Office of Homeless Services and health outreach by the Department of Public Health. Clergy have taken public positions on gun violence, policing and school policy, and some have joined police-district community advisory councils. Clergy have not been of one mind: on issues such as police oversight, school closures and housing policy, individual pastors have taken different sides.

5 Other faith networks

Philadelphia also has large Catholic, Jewish, Muslim, Hindu and evangelical communities, multi-faith coalitions that advocate on poverty and housing, and faith-based organizing networks such as POWER Interfaith, which in March 2026 was reported by the Inquirer to be calling on City Hall to address the city's affordability crisis. Archdiocesan and Jewish federation institutions run hospitals, schools and social agencies, and many congregations are also landlords of significant property, which links them to zoning and land-use debates. Religious institutions are generally exempt from property tax.

6 Legal boundaries and debate

Under federal tax law, congregations that hold 501(c)(3) status may not endorse or oppose candidates as organizations, though individual clergy may speak personally. Supporters of clergy engagement argue that faith leaders speak for residents who are otherwise underrepresented; critics argue that elected officials can rely too heavily on a small number of leaders as proxies for broad communities. See also Progressive and Grassroots Politics.

See also: Civic and Neighborhood Associations, Political Parties in Philadelphia, Elections in Philadelphia.

Good Government Groups

Good Government Groups
TypeNonpartisan nonprofit watchdog, research and advocacy groups
FlagshipCommittee of Seventy (founded 1904), President and CEO Lauren Cristella
Other groupsLeague of Women Voters of Philadelphia; Common Cause Pennsylvania; The Philadelphia Citizen (nonprofit news and civic organization); Fairmount Park Conservancy (parks)
FundingFoundation grants, individual donors, corporate sponsors

Good government groups, often called "good-government" or "goo-goo" organizations, are nonpartisan civic nonprofits that work to improve the transparency, fairness and efficiency of public institutions. In Philadelphia the tradition runs from reform movements of the early twentieth century that challenged machine politics. They have no governmental powers; their influence comes from research, public information, litigation threats, endorsements of reforms and the credibility of their reports. [1]

1 Committee of Seventy

The Committee of Seventy was established in 1904 to combat corruption in Philadelphia and describes itself as nonpartisan. Lauren Cristella, its president and CEO since 2023, is the first woman to lead the organization; she was previously its chief program officer, and has overseen a statewide expansion, according to the organization. Previous leaders included David Thornburgh, Zack Stalberg and Al Schmidt, who resigned as a City Commissioner to head the group. Seventy runs voter-education programs and an election-protection effort; according to its website, its WeVote initiative has reached more than one million Pennsylvanians, WeVote Next has involved 48,000 students, and its Election Academy has prepared 8,500 poll workers, with a related Election Academy for voters launched in 2026. It also supports Philadelphia Documenters, a program that trains community members to document government meetings, and it can be reached at 215-557-3600 (123 S. Broad Street, Suite 2830). Seventy publishes research on election administration and campaign finance, and advocates for changes such as open primaries, ranked-choice voting, redistricting reform and judicial-selection reform. [2]

2 Other organizations

The League of Women Voters of Philadelphia hosts candidate forums and publishes voter guides. Common Cause Pennsylvania works on redistricting, ethics and voting access. The Philadelphia Citizen is a nonprofit news and civic-action outlet. Spotlight PA, a statewide nonprofit newsroom, covers Harrisburg. Organizations such as the Fairmount Park Conservancy, Philadelphia Parks Alliance and neighborhood watchdogs play a related accountability role for specific services. Civil-liberties and civil-rights organizations such as the ACLU of Pennsylvania engage in oversight of policing and elections. For labor, tenants and other advocacy groups, see Progressive and Grassroots Politics.

3 What these groups do

Typical functions include monitoring polling places on Election Day and explaining voter registration and mail voting; analyzing campaign finance data; reviewing City budgets and testifying at City Council hearings; recommending charter amendments (see Ballot Questions and Charter Changes); and supporting the work of the Board of Ethics and Inspector General. They also train residents to use public-records and open-meetings laws.

4 Influence and limits

Good-government groups are generally listened to on process issues, and several Philadelphia reforms trace to their campaigns, including changes to the City's campaign-finance law and election administration. Limits: they depend on foundation and donor support (see Philanthropy in Philadelphia), their boards often include business and professional leaders, and critics from the left and from neighborhoods have argued that their agenda tends to emphasize process over distributional issues such as housing and wages. Proponents reply that fair rules benefit all residents. Party organizations sometimes disagree with their proposals (see Democratic City Committee).

5 Using their resources

Most publish nonpartisan voter guides, how-to pages and election-day hotlines; see How to Report Corruption or Misconduct for official channels, which these groups do not replace.

See also: Political Corruption Cases in Philadelphia, Conflicts of Interest and Pay-to-Play, City Commissioners.

  3. Committee of Seventy, home page (seventy.org, accessed October 2026); Philadelphia Magazine, "Lauren Cristella Becomes First Woman to Lead Committee of Seventy," June 6, 2023.

Legal Aid and Public Interest Law

Legal Aid and Public Interest Law
TypeNonprofit legal service organizations and pro bono programs
Key providersCommunity Legal Services (CLS); SeniorLAW Center; Legal Clinic for the Disabled; Philadelphia VIP (Volunteers for the Indigent Program); Tenant Union Representative Network (TURN); Public Interest Law Center
Criminal defenseHandled separately by the Defender Association of Philadelphia
Eviction right to counselPassed by Council November 2019; city-funded program expanded in phases

Legal aid in Philadelphia refers to free civil legal services for low-income residents, covering housing, public benefits, family law, consumer debt, employment and immigration. Public interest law refers to organizations that also bring systemic cases (class actions, policy advocacy) on behalf of groups of people. Civil legal aid is distinct from criminal defense, where the Constitution guarantees counsel. [1]

1 Major organizations

Community Legal Services, founded in the 1960s, is the city's largest civil legal aid provider and a common first stop for eligibility screening; it operates from Center City and neighborhood offices. SeniorLAW Center serves older adults. The Legal Clinic for the Disabled represents people with disabilities. Philadelphia VIP coordinates volunteer private attorneys. The Tenant Union Representative Network (TURN) combines legal help with tenant education and organizing. Law school clinics and bar association programs add capacity. [2]

2 Right to counsel in eviction

City Council passed a right-to-counsel law in November 2019, guaranteeing free legal representation to eligible low-income tenants facing eviction; the program began in selected ZIP codes and has expanded in phases. The City's description of the program lists coverage for eviction cases, lease terminations and terminations of Philadelphia Housing Authority subsidy, in both court proceedings and administrative proceedings such as those of the Fair Housing Commission. Eligibility depends on household income (the City's program description has used 200 percent of the federal poverty level) and ZIP code, and the City's Philly Tenant website currently lists ten covered ZIP codes: 19121, 19124, 19131, 19132, 19134, 19139, 19141, 19144, 19153 and 19154. The list has changed over time, so check it before relying on it. Participating providers include CLS, SeniorLAW Center, the Legal Clinic for the Disabled, Philly VIP and TURN. The Philly Tenant Hotline is (267) 443-2500. See Eviction Diversion and Landlord-Tenant Court. [3]

3 Impact litigation and policy work

The Public Interest Law Center, a nonprofit law firm, brings systemic cases. For example, it has represented tenants in a class action against a large landlord over alleged unsafe conditions and unlawful rent collection, and it has litigated education-funding and civil-rights cases. Legal aid organizations also participate in rule-making and testify on bills, such as the Safe and Healthy Homes Act, and help shape landlord-tenant law. Allegations in pending litigation remain allegations until decided.

4 Funding and capacity

Legal aid funding comes from the federal Legal Services Corporation (with restrictions), state Interest on Lawyers Trust Accounts, City contracts, foundations (see Philanthropy in Philadelphia), bar associations and individual donations. Advocates routinely report that demand exceeds capacity, and providers triage by case type and merit. Because many offices rely on federal funds, changes in federal policy and budgets affect services.

5 Finding help

Start with a screening call or walk-in at a legal aid office, the Philadelphia Bar Association's lawyer referral service, or the City's tenant resources. See How to Get Help From the City. This page is general information, not legal advice.

See also: Tenant and Housing Advocacy Groups, First Judicial District, Court of Common Pleas and Municipal Court.

Tenant and Housing Advocacy Groups

Tenant and Housing Advocacy Groups
TypeTenant unions, nonprofits, coalitions and legal-aid-linked networks
ExamplesPhiladelphia Tenants Union (founded 2015); Tenant Union Representative Network (TURN); building-based tenant unions; PACDC; legal-aid and public-interest law organizations
GrowthFrom about five known tenant associations before 2020 to more than 20, per WHYY
Recent policy winSafe and Healthy Homes Act bills passed by City Council in April 2026

Tenant and housing advocacy groups in Philadelphia organize renters, provide education and referral, and lobby on housing law. Roughly half of city residents are renters, many with modest incomes, which makes tenant organizing a significant part of local politics. These groups are private organizations without governmental power. [1]

1 Types of organizations

The field includes (a) tenant unions, which are membership groups of renters in a building, landlord portfolio or neighborhood; (b) citywide organizations such as the Philadelphia Tenants Union, established in 2015, and the Tenant Union Representative Network; (c) legal-aid and public-interest law offices (see Legal Aid and Public Interest Law); (d) housing-counseling agencies and community development corporations; and (e) coalitions that bring these together for legislative campaigns. Historic groups include the North Philadelphia Tenants Union and the Northwest Tenants Organization of earlier decades, which Council has honored by resolution. [2]

2 Growth of tenant unions

WHYY reported that the number of tenant unions in Philadelphia roughly quadrupled since the pandemic, from about five known associations to more than 20, and that they pressed for habitability standards, limits on retaliation and, in one West Philadelphia building, a first collectively bargained lease. Some formed autonomously in a single building; others emerged from partnerships with tenant-rights organizations. [1]

3 Policy campaigns

Advocates supported the right to counsel in eviction cases and the City's eviction-diversion program (see Eviction Diversion and Landlord-Tenant Court). A recent campaign centered on the Safe and Healthy Homes Act, bills by Councilmember Nicolas O'Rourke. The legislation provides rent abatement when a landlord lacks an active rental license or fails to repair code violations in a timely way, protects tenants against retaliation for complaints, requires "good cause" for lease non-renewal and increases penalties for repeated violations. A lawsuit by two landlords in March 2026 alleging violations of the state Sunshine Act delayed a Council vote; after a settlement the bills returned to committee, and Council passed the final bills in April 2026. See Rental Licensing and Landlord-Tenant Law in Philadelphia. [3]

4 Allies, opponents and criticism

Tenant groups frequently work with progressive Council members and organizations (see Progressive and Grassroots Politics) and labor unions. Their principal opponents on housing law are landlord and property-owner associations (see Landlord and Property Owner Associations) and parts of the real estate sector. Opponents argue that added regulation raises costs and may reduce rental supply; advocates argue that it protects safety and stability. Both sides appeal to data from Licenses and Inspections and the courts.

5 Getting help or joining

Tenants can call the Philly Tenant Hotline, reported as (267) 443-2500, or the Fair Housing Commission for rent-related disputes (see Fair Housing Commission). Organizing basics appear in How to Organize a Block or Neighborhood Group. This is general information, not legal advice.

See also: Philadelphia Housing Authority, Office of Homeless Services, Division of Housing and Community Development.

Landlord and Property Owner Associations

Landlord and Property Owner Associations
TypePrivate trade and advocacy associations
Key groupsHAPCO Philadelphia (reported about 1,000 members; largest advocacy group for independent landlords); Pennsylvania Apartment Association; Greater Philadelphia Association of Realtors; Building Industry Association
Primary arenasCity Council, Licenses and Inspections, Municipal Court, state legislature
Related lawPhiladelphia rental-licensing and Safe and Healthy Homes provisions; Pennsylvania Landlord and Tenant Act

Landlord and property owner associations represent people and firms that own rental housing in Philadelphia, from small owners with a single rental property to large multifamily operators. They provide members with education, forms and legal updates, and they lobby on laws and regulations affecting rental housing. They are private organizations. [1]

1 Main organizations

HAPCO Philadelphia, historically the Home and Property Owners Association, describes itself as a membership group for independent landlords; WHYY reported it as the city's largest advocacy group for such owners, with about 1,000 members. The Pennsylvania Apartment Association represents multifamily owners and managers statewide. The Greater Philadelphia Association of Realtors and the Building Industry Association also engage on housing policy (see Developers and the Real Estate Lobby). Larger management companies sometimes lobby directly. [2]

2 What they do

Associations offer members training on leases, screening, rental licensing and eviction procedure, discounts on services and legislative alerts. They testify at City Council hearings and meet with elected officials and agencies such as the Department of Licenses and Inspections. They typically support streamlined court procedures and oppose measures they view as raising costs or limiting owners' discretion, while many also state support for safe housing and for cooperation with code enforcement. They can also collect political contributions subject to the rules described in Campaign Finance in Philadelphia.

3 The Safe and Healthy Homes dispute

The Safe and Healthy Homes Act bills, sponsored by Councilmember Nicolas O'Rourke, would entitle tenants to rent abatement if a landlord lacks an active rental license or fails to repair code violations in a timely manner, add protections from retaliation, require good cause for non-renewal and increase penalties for repeated violations. HAPCO opposed the legislation. In March 2026 two landlords, both HAPCO members but not HAPCO itself as an organization, sued, alleging that Council violated the Sunshine Act by opening public comment only after the Housing Committee had passed the bills. The suit temporarily blocked the Council vote; after a settlement, the bills returned to committee for a new hearing and the final bills passed in April 2026. Reporting also described escalating confrontation between the landlord group and supporters of the legislation. [3]

4 Perspectives and counter-arguments

Owner groups argue that small landlords face thin margins, that new mandates may lead some to sell or leave the market and that enforcement should target negligent operators rather than all owners. Tenant advocates and legal-aid organizations (see Tenant and Housing Advocacy Groups) argue that habitability and anti-retaliation protections are necessary because many tenants cannot move. Council and the mayor weigh these positions; in this case Council passed the legislation. Landlord interests are not uniform: nonprofit and affordable-housing owners may take different positions from market-rate owners.

5 Practical information for owners

Owners must hold a rental license and meet code requirements; see Rental Licensing and Landlord-Tenant Law in Philadelphia, Eviction Diversion and Landlord-Tenant Court and the Fair Housing Commission. This is general information, not legal advice.

See also: Tax Abatement and Development Incentives, Office of Property Assessment, Sunshine Act and Open Meetings.

Local News Media in Philadelphia

Local News Media in Philadelphia
Largest newsroomThe Philadelphia Inquirer (owned by the nonprofit Lenfest Institute for Journalism through a public benefit corporation)
Other outletsPhiladelphia Tribune; WHYY and Billy Penn; The Philadelphia Citizen; Spotlight PA (statewide); Axios Philadelphia; neighborhood and ethnic-community papers; broadcast TV and radio
Ownership modelMix of nonprofit, public-media, family-owned and commercial
Legal toolsPennsylvania Right-to-Know Law; Sunshine Act

Local news media in Philadelphia are the newspapers, public and commercial broadcasters and digital outlets that report on city government, schools, courts and neighborhoods. Their coverage is a primary way residents learn about the work of the City Council, the Police Department and other bodies, and their investigative reporting has driven several of the reform episodes in Political Corruption Cases in Philadelphia. [1]

1 The Inquirer and the Lenfest Institute

The Philadelphia Inquirer is a public benefit corporation owned by the nonprofit Lenfest Institute for Journalism. Businessman H.F. "Gerry" Lenfest bought Philadelphia Media Network, the Inquirer's parent company, in June 2014 and in 2016 donated it to The Philadelphia Foundation so that the papers would remain in Philadelphia; the Lenfest Institute for Journalism, a nonprofit, holds the newsroom, a structure widely described as the first of its kind in which a nonprofit owns a for-profit newsroom. The Philadelphia Daily News, a tabloid founded in 1925, became an edition of the Inquirer in 2019. The Institute reports having invested more than $117 million in over 600 news organizations and initiatives. The Inquirer reported its first revenue growth since 2004 in 2025, along with an operating profit of several million dollars, according to coverage of its finances. Nonprofit ownership means that the paper is insulated from a single owner's commercial or political interests but still depends on subscribers, advertisers and philanthropy (see Philanthropy in Philadelphia). [2]

2 The Philadelphia Tribune

The Philadelphia Tribune, founded in 1884, is regarded as the nation's oldest continuously published Black newspaper. It covers political developments of particular interest to Black Philadelphians, including clergy, ward and school-board politics (see Faith Communities and Black Clergy), and is regularly cited in reporting on local candidates. Other community papers serve the Northeast, South Philadelphia, Spanish-speaking, Asian American and other communities.

3 Public media and digital outlets

WHYY, the region's public broadcaster, operates radio, television and its news site; Billy Penn, a local digital outlet, joined WHYY. WHYY has had staff reductions in past years. The Philadelphia Citizen is a nonprofit news and civic-engagement outlet. Spotlight PA is a statewide nonprofit newsroom covering Harrisburg, which matters for a city whose finances and powers depend on state law (see Home Rule Limits and State Preemption). Chalkbeat Philadelphia covers education, and national newsletters such as Axios have local editions. Television and radio stations provide breaking and election coverage. [3]

4 Economics and consolidation

Like local news elsewhere, Philadelphia outlets have faced declining print advertising, layoffs and mergers over two decades. Examples include the merger of the Inquirer, Daily News and Philly.com newsrooms with tens of layoffs, the end of City Paper's print run and WHYY layoffs of about 8 percent of staff in a prior restructuring. New nonprofit and digital outlets have partly offset the loss, but coverage of some neighborhoods and of routine government meetings has thinned, a pattern researchers call a news gap.

5 Media as a political actor

Editorial endorsements, investigative series and agenda-setting coverage influence campaigns and policy debates, and politicians use media and social media to speak around reporters. Debates include whether coverage focuses on conflict over policy substance, how outlets disclose ties to funders, and whether the City provides records and press access promptly. Journalists and civic groups have pressed for stronger open-records enforcement; see Right-to-Know Law and Public Records.

6 Using records laws

Journalists and residents use the Right-to-Know Law and the Sunshine Act. For a how-to, see How to Request Public Records.

See also: Good Government Groups, Open Data and Transparency Tools, Philadelphia Political History.

References

  1. Lenfest Institute for Journalism, "The Philadelphia Inquirer" and 10-year report (May 2026).
  2. Press Gazette, "Philadelphia Inquirer: philanthropy and profit"; Columbia Journalism Review, "Philadelphia journalism nonprofit"; Nieman Lab coverage of the Lenfest Institute.
  3. WHYY announcements on Billy Penn; Philadelphia Tribune, "About the Tribune"; Poynter and local trade reporting on Philadelphia newsroom layoffs.

Sports Teams and Public Subsidy

Sports Teams and Public Subsidy
TeamsPhiladelphia Phillies (MLB), Philadelphia Eagles (NFL), Philadelphia 76ers (NBA), Philadelphia Flyers (NHL)
LocationSouth Philadelphia Sports Complex
Arena projectNew Sixers-Flyers arena on the former Spectrum site, targeted to open in 2030, described by the teams as fully privately funded
OwnersHarris Blitzer Sports and Entertainment (Sixers); Comcast Spectacor (Flyers)
Public bodies involvedCity Council, Planning Commission, Zoning Board, PIDC, state legislature

Sports teams and public subsidy refers to the debate over how much public money, land and regulatory support professional teams should receive. Philadelphia is unusual in having all four major league franchises clustered at one South Philadelphia site, so decisions about leases, stadium financing and event-day services recur at City Hall and in Harrisburg. [1]

1 The Sports Complex

The Phillies (Citizens Bank Park), the Eagles (Lincoln Financial Field), and the Sixers and Flyers (the arena currently on site) play on land that the City owns or controls, much of which is leased to the teams. Lincoln Financial Field (2003) and Citizens Bank Park (2004) opened with a mix of public and private funds from city and state sources. Sports-related public services include event-day policing and traffic management by the Philadelphia Police Department, Streets Department and SEPTA. Teams are large taxpayers through wage, amusement and other taxes (see Philadelphia Taxes).

2 The failed Market East arena plan

In 2022 the 76ers, through a development company called 76 Devcorp, unveiled plans for a roughly $1.3 billion arena on the Fashion District site in Center City, targeted for the 2031-32 season. The plan met strong opposition from Chinatown residents and organizations concerned about displacement and traffic, and in January 2025 the team abandoned it. [2]

3 The South Philadelphia arena

In January 2025 Harris Blitzer Sports and Entertainment and Comcast Spectacor announced that they would jointly build a new arena in the South Philadelphia complex to house both the Sixers and the Flyers, targeted for 2031 or sooner. By September 2026 the teams released first renderings and said the arena, designed by Populous and Moody Nolan, would open in 2030 ahead of a WNBA expansion team's first season. They describe it as the largest privately funded project in city history, with no public contribution to construction, and project nearly 15,000 jobs and almost $6 billion in economic activity over ten years, including tax revenue for the city and the School District; those projections are the teams' own. The partnership also pledged to invest in the Market East area. Some regulatory approvals, lease and land arrangements, and public-service commitments remain to be reviewed by public bodies. [3]

4 Debates over subsidies

Supporters of public support argue that teams generate jobs, tourism and civic identity. Economists who study stadium finance have often found limited net economic benefit relative to public cost, and critics, including journalists who track stadium deals, argue that infrastructure support, tax breaks or leases at low rent can function as indirect subsidies even when construction is private. Questions often asked about the South Philadelphia project include whether it benefits from tax abatement and development incentives, who pays for infrastructure and event services, and how the project affects nearby residents. The teams say the project will not rely on public construction funds.

5 Who holds influence

Team owners and Comcast hold large business and political relationships; City Council, the mayor and district Council members hold land-use and legislative leverage; the state legislature controls state-level incentives. Building trades unions typically support construction projects (see Philadelphia Building and Construction Trades Council), while neighborhood and Chinatown groups were pivotal in the Market East outcome (see Civic and Neighborhood Associations).

See also: Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation, Developers and the Real Estate Lobby, Philadelphia Zoning Code.

References

  1. City of Philadelphia and Controller budget documents; Field of Schemes, "Sixers abandon Chinatown arena plan, pivot to sharing South Philly venue with Flyers" (January 13, 2025).
  2. CBS Sports, "76ers unveil plans to build new $1.3 billion arena in Center City"; Billy Penn (July 21, 2022) on the 76 Place proposal.
  3. 6abc, "Arena for 76ers, Flyers to open in 2030, marks 'new era'"; Axios Philadelphia (September 8, 2026); Bisnow Philadelphia on arena renderings; TicketNews (September 2026).

Philadelphia Neighborhoods Guide

Philadelphia Neighborhoods Guide
City populationAbout 1.6 million (2020 Census: 1,603,797)
Planning districts18, used by the City Planning Commission
Council districts10 districts plus 7 at-large seats
Official neighborhood bordersNone; common names do not match police, planning or political boundaries

Philadelphia neighborhoods are the named communities, such as Fishtown, Germantown and Point Breeze, that residents use to describe where they live. Unlike wards, Council districts and police districts, neighborhoods have no official legal boundaries, so the names and borders people use often differ by source. This guide summarizes the main regions and the government units that overlay them. [1]

1 Neighborhoods versus government boundaries

Several overlapping maps govern a Philadelphia address. There are 66 political wards (see Council Districts and Wards), ten Council districts, police divisions and districts, school catchments, ZIP codes, and the Planning Commission's planning districts. A person can live in one neighborhood, one ward and a different Council district than neighbors a few blocks away. The Planning Commission and others note that common usage does not respect the official borders, and residents do not always agree where one neighborhood ends. [1]

2 The regions

Common groupings, which are customary rather than legal, include:

Center City, the downtown and Rittenhouse, Washington Square West, Old City, Logan Square and Fairmount areas, with the city's densest employment (see Center City District). South Philadelphia, including Passyunk, Bella Vista, Queen Village, Pennsport, Point Breeze and Grays Ferry, plus the Sports Complex (see Sports Teams and Public Subsidy). Southwest Philadelphia, including Eastwick and the airport area (see Philadelphia International Airport). West Philadelphia, including University City, Cedar Park, Spruce Hill and Cobbs Creek, near large campuses (see Eds and Meds Anchor Institutions). Northwest Philadelphia, including Germantown, Mount Airy, Chestnut Hill and Roxborough-Manayunk. North Philadelphia, including Brewerytown, Strawberry Mansion, Cecil B. Moore, Sharswood, Norris Square and Kensington areas. The River Wards, along the Delaware, including Fishtown, Port Richmond and Bridesburg. Northeast and Far Northeast Philadelphia, including Fox Chase, Rhawnhurst, Mayfair, Tacony and Somerton, which are largely rowhouse and single-family areas with their own civic traditions. [2]

3 Planning districts

The Planning Commission divides the city into 18 planning districts and prepares district plans that translate the citywide comprehensive plan to clusters of similar neighborhoods. The districts are Upper Far Northeast, Lower Far Northeast, Central Northeast, Lower Northeast, North Delaware River Wards, Upper North, Lower North, North, Central, Lower Northwest, Upper Northwest, West Park, West, Lower South, South, Lower Southwest, University Southwest and River Wards. A community planner is assigned to each district. District plans guide future zoning remapping and investment. [2]

4 Who speaks for a neighborhood

Several kinds of organizations claim to represent neighborhoods: civic and neighborhood associations and zoning-designated Registered Community Organizations (see Civic and Neighborhood Associations), community development corporations, business associations, congregations (see Faith Communities and Black Clergy), and ward committee people (see Ward Leaders and Committeepersons). Their views can differ, and none has exclusive authority. Neighborhood wealth, housing costs, school quality and public-safety conditions vary widely across regions, which makes issues like displacement, tax abatement and school closures play out differently by place.

5 Finding your representatives and services

To find your Council district, ward and elected officials, see How to Find Your Elected Officials. For service requests, use Philly311. To get started on local organizing, see How to Organize a Block or Neighborhood Group.

See also: Philadelphia Overview, Council Districts and Wards, Philadelphia Political History.

References

  1. City of Philadelphia Planning Commission, "Community planners by district" (phila.gov); Delaware Valley Regional Planning Commission, "Philadelphia Planning Districts" map.
  2. Philadelphia GeoHistory Network, "Philadelphia regions"; U.S. Census Bureau, 2020 Census.
