How to Get Help From the City

How to Get Help From the City
TypeCitizen guide
First stopPhilly311 (dial 311; 215-686-8686 from outside the city)
Onlinephila.gov/311; Philly311 mobile app
In personPhilly311 walk-in center, Room 167, City Hall
EscalationDistrict Council office, department, Managing Director's Office, Controller
EmergenciesCall 911, not 311

Getting help from the city in Philadelphia usually means choosing the right door. Philadelphia is both a city and a county, so a single resident problem can belong to a city department, an elected row office, a state-created authority, a state court, or a federal agency. This guide explains how to route a request, what to expect, and how to escalate when nothing happens. It is general civic information, not legal advice.[1]

1 Step 1: Decide if it is an emergency

Immediate threats to life, active crimes, fires and medical emergencies go to 911, which dispatches the Police Department and Fire Department. Philly311 is the city's non-emergency line. Longer-term emergency planning and disaster information is handled by the Office of Emergency Management.

2 Step 2: Use Philly311

Philly311 is the city's central contact center for non-emergency services and information. As of 2026, requests can be made by:

  • Phone: dial 311 (the contact center is staffed 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays, per the city); from outside Philadelphia call 215-686-8686.
  • Online or mobile app: through phila.gov/311 or the Philly311 app, which lets you attach a photo and location.
  • Email: philly311@phila.gov.
  • In person: the walk-in center in Room 167, City Hall, during business hours.

Typical 311 matters include missed trash collection, potholes and street defects handled by the Streets Department, abandoned vehicles, graffiti, vacant lots, and complaints routed to the Department of Licenses and Inspections, such as unsafe buildings or unlicensed contractors. Every request receives a service request number. Write it down: it is the key to tracking the case online, asking a department for an update, and showing a Councilmember's office that you already tried the normal channel.[2]

3 Step 3: Go to the right department

Some matters are better taken directly to the responsible body. Examples:

  • Water bills, leaks and sewer problems: Philadelphia Water Department.
  • Property tax bills, business taxes and payment plans: Revenue Department; disputes over a property's assessed value: Office of Property Assessment.
  • Rental problems: Fair Housing Commission and the Rental Licensing rules summarized in Rental Licensing and Landlord-Tenant Law.
  • Shelter and homelessness: Office of Homeless Services.
  • Child welfare and family services: Department of Human Services.
  • Health clinics and public health concerns: Department of Public Health.
  • Voting and registration: City Commissioners.
  • Parks, recreation centers and trees: Parks and Recreation.

Not everything is a city matter. SEPTA service, the Parking Authority, PHA public housing and the courts are separate bodies; see SEPTA, Philadelphia Parking Authority, Philadelphia Housing Authority and First Judicial District. The guide How Philadelphia Government Is Organized explains the map.

4 Step 4: Involve your Councilmember

Each of the ten council districts has a district Councilmember, and seven members are elected at large; all can help constituents. District offices commonly handle constituent services, such as following up on stalled 311 cases, connecting residents to departments, and attending community meetings. Find your district with the steps in How to Find Your Elected Officials. Because of councilmanic prerogative, the district member also has unusual influence over land-use matters in the district, so for zoning or vacant-land issues the district office is often an essential contact.

5 Step 5: Escalate

  1. Ask the department for a supervisor and quote the 311 number.
  2. Contact the Managing Director's Office (see Managing Director's Office), which oversees most operating departments.
  3. Contact the Mayor's office (Mayor of Philadelphia) for broader service failures.
  4. Report misconduct or waste to the City Controller or the Office of the Inspector General; see How to Report Corruption or Misconduct.
  5. Formal complaints against police, landlords, workers or contractors follow different routes: How to File a Complaint.
  6. Speak publicly at City Council: How to Testify at City Council.

6 Tips for a stronger request

  • Give a precise address or cross streets, the date it started, and photographs.
  • Keep a written log: dates, names, case numbers and what you were told.
  • Ask for a written response by email when possible.
  • If a record is needed, see How to Request Public Records.
  • Neighbors strengthen a request; see How to Organize a Block or Neighborhood Group.
  • For legal problems such as eviction, free civil legal help is described in Legal Aid and Public Interest Law.

See also: Philly311, Open Data and Transparency Tools, Philadelphia Neighborhoods Guide, Glossary

References

  1. City of Philadelphia, "Philly311," phila.gov/311 and phila.gov/departments/philly311 (accessed October 2026).
  2. City of Philadelphia, Philly311 "Our process" page, phila.gov/departments/philly311/our-process/ (accessed October 2026).
  3. City of Philadelphia, "Report an unlicensed contractor or unpermitted work," phila.gov/services (accessed October 2026).

How a Bill Becomes Law in Philadelphia

How a Bill Becomes Law in Philadelphia
TypeCitizen guide / legislative process
Legislative bodyCity Council (17 members: 10 district, 7 at-large)
Governing lawPhiladelphia Home Rule Charter; Rules of Council
Passage thresholdMajority of all members (9 of 17)
Veto overrideTwo-thirds of Council (12 of 17)
Tracking toolCouncil's Legislative Information Center (phila.legistar.com)

A bill in Philadelphia is a proposed ordinance introduced in City Council. Because Philadelphia is a home rule city, Council can legislate on local matters under the Home Rule Charter, within the limits discussed in Home Rule Limits and State Preemption. This guide follows a bill step by step and shows where residents can intervene.[1]

1 Step 1: Drafting and introduction

Only a member of Council can introduce a bill, but ideas come from many sources: residents, advocacy groups, unions, business associations, and the administration, which often asks a member to introduce its proposals. Council's legislative drafting staff and the Law Department help turn an idea into legal text. A recent example is the Safe and Healthy Homes Act: Bills 250329 and 250330 were introduced in 2025, passed 16-1 on April 23, 2026 after a court settlement sent them back to committee for a new hearing, and were reported signed by Mayor Cherelle Parker on May 7, 2026 (see Safe and Healthy Homes Act). Bills are introduced at a stated meeting of Council, which meets regularly on Thursday mornings while in session and takes a summer recess; check the Legislative Information Center for the calendar. Each bill receives a number and is posted online.

Some matters are not bills but resolutions, which express Council's position, authorize hearings, or honor people, and do not have the force of law. Ordinances amending the Zoning Code, authorizing tax incentives or changing tax rates are all bills.

2 Step 2: Referral to committee

After introduction the President of Council assigns the bill to a standing committee, such as Finance, Law and Government, or Rules; see Council Committees and the Legislative Process. The committee chair controls scheduling, so a bill may be heard promptly, held for months, or never heard. The Council President, currently Kenyatta Johnson (as of 2026), holds substantial control over referral and the floor schedule.

3 Step 3: Hearing and committee vote

Under the Charter, a bill must be considered at a public hearing and a committee meeting before Council can enact it. At the hearing, the sponsor presents the bill, the administration and affected agencies testify, and members of the public may offer testimony. Amendments are often negotiated here. The committee can report the bill out favorably, with amendments, or not at all. Reported bills are printed in their amended form and made available to members and the public before the floor vote. Advance notice requirements apply to certain categories, including zoning bills, which also require review by the City Planning Commission.

4 Step 4: Final passage

Bills reported from committee are placed on the Council calendar for second reading and final passage. Passage requires the affirmative vote of a majority of all members, not merely of those present, which means nine of seventeen votes. Roll-call votes are recorded and posted. Bills that are not enacted generally do not carry over into the next four-year Council term, which produces the "end of term" rush of legislation familiar to local reporters; the Rules of Council govern exactly how pending bills are handled.[2]

5 Step 5: Mayor signs or vetoes

Passed bills go to the Mayor. Under the Charter a bill becomes law when the Mayor signs it, or when the Mayor lets it become law without a signature after the Charter's review period, which is reported as ten days after a bill is presented to the Mayor (the Charter text controls). If the Mayor vetoes it, Council may override by a two-thirds vote, which is twelve of seventeen members. Signed bills are assigned an ordinance number and published in the Philadelphia Code. Some measures, such as amendments to the Charter itself, must go to voters; see Ballot Questions and Charter Changes.

6 Where residents can act

  • Track a bill by number in the Legislative Information Center and read the text, amendments, fiscal notes, and hearing agendas.
  • Testify at the committee hearing or comment at a stated meeting: How to Testify at City Council.
  • Contact your district member and the at-large members: How to Find Your Elected Officials.
  • Submit written comment and organize neighbors: How to Organize a Block or Neighborhood Group.
  • Watch for the Mayor's decision after passage; veto messages are public.

Council meetings fall under the Sunshine Act. State law can override city ordinances in some fields, so a local law may be limited or reversed by Harrisburg; see Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia. Budget bills follow a particular cycle: Philadelphia City Budget Process.

See also: Councilmanic Prerogative, Council Districts and Wards, How Philadelphia Government Is Organized

References

  1. Philadelphia Home Rule Charter, Article II (Legislative Branch), as published by American Legal Publishing (library.amlegal.com).
  2. Philadelphia City Council, Legislative Information Center and Rules of Council, phlcouncil.com and phila.legistar.com (accessed October 2026).
  3. City of Philadelphia, "City Council," phila.gov (accessed October 2026).

— end of section — back to contents

How to Testify at City Council

How to Testify at City Council
TypeCitizen guide
VenueCouncil Chamber / Room 400, City Hall (Broad and Market)
Phone sign-upChief Clerk's Office, 215-686-3406
Advance deadline3 p.m. the day before the meeting
Speaking timeUp to three minutes (stated meetings)
ScopeItems on the printed agenda

Testifying at City Council means addressing the legislature of Philadelphia, either in public comment at a full stated meeting or in testimony at a committee hearing. Both are open to the public under the Sunshine Act. The rules below reflect Council's published procedures as of 2026; always confirm on phlcouncil.com or with the Chief Clerk before going.[1]

1 Step 1: Pick the bill and the venue

Identify the bill or resolution number you care about using the Legislative Information Center (see How a Bill Becomes Law in Philadelphia). Where a bill is in the process decides your best venue. If it has not yet had a hearing, committee testimony is where amendments are shaped; if it is on the full Council's agenda, public comment at a stated meeting is available. Public comment at stated meetings applies only to items printed on that meeting's agenda.[2]

2 Step 2: Sign up

For a stated meeting, Council's procedures allow three routes:

  1. Call the Chief Clerk's Office at 215-686-3406.
  2. Email your registration or written comment to the address published on Council's public-comment page, by 3 p.m. the day before the meeting. Written comments are best sent as a PDF; they are recorded but not read aloud.
  3. In person on the day: check in at the desk in Room 400, City Hall.

Provide your full name (with the pronunciation if needed), the bill or resolution number, whether you support or oppose it, and your contact phone number and street address. If you need an interpreter or other accommodation, tell the Chief Clerk's Office when you register. Language-access information is also posted on Council's site.

3 Step 3: Prepare your remarks

  • Be short. Speakers receive up to three minutes at stated meetings; the Council President may shorten the time or limit repetitive comment. About 350 to 400 words fits in three minutes.
  • Open with your name, neighborhood, and the bill number, and say whether you support or oppose it.
  • Make one to three points, each with a specific fact, number, or personal example.
  • Ask for something concrete: pass, amend, or reject, and name the amendment if you have one.
  • Bring written copies for the record and for staff.
  • Group testimony: coordinate so speakers do not repeat each other; see How to Organize a Block or Neighborhood Group.

4 Step 4: On the day

Stated meetings of City Council are generally held on Thursday mornings during session. Arrive early, pass building security, and check in. Public comment is typically taken near the start of the meeting's business. Address the presiding officer, speak into the microphone, and stop when time is called. Council members generally do not debate public speakers; members may ask brief questions. Meetings are also broadcast and archived online, so you can share your testimony afterward.

5 Committee hearings

Committee hearings are where most substantive testimony happens. Hearings are noticed on Council's calendar, normally with the bill list for the day. Rules for registering vary by committee and may differ from stated meetings, so call the Chief Clerk's Office or the committee chair's office to confirm how to be added to the witness list and how much time you receive. Experts, agencies, and advocacy groups often testify first; residents commonly follow. Written testimony may be submitted in addition to or in place of speaking. Committees and their jurisdictions are described in Council Committees and the Legislative Process. Budget hearings in spring are a major opportunity; see Philadelphia City Budget Process and How to Read the City Budget.

6 After you testify

  • Email your district member and the committee chair a short thank-you with your key request. Find them via How to Find Your Elected Officials.
  • Watch for amendments and the committee vote.
  • If the bill passes, the Mayor can sign or veto; see Mayor of Philadelphia.
  • Other bodies hold their own meetings, such as the City Planning Commission, Zoning Board of Adjustment and Board of Education, each with its own public-comment rules.

See also: Councilmanic Prerogative, Right-to-Know Law and Public Records, Council Districts and Wards

References

  1. Philadelphia City Council, "Offering Public Comment at Council Sessions," phlcouncil.com/offering-public-comment-at-council-sessions/ (accessed October 2026).
  2. The Philadelphia Citizen / Resolve Philly, "Demystifying public comment: your step-by-step guide for Philly meetings."
  3. Pennsylvania Sunshine Act, 65 Pa.C.S. 701 et seq.

— end of section — back to contents

How to File a Complaint

How to File a Complaint
TypeCitizen guide / routing table
PoliceCitizens Police Oversight Commission (215-685-0891) or Police Internal Affairs
LandlordsFair Housing Commission (215-686-4670); L&I via 311
City workersInspector General (215-686-1770); Controller hotline (215-686-3804)
ContractorsL&I via 311 (licensing); PA Attorney General (fraud)
DiscriminationCommission on Human Relations

A complaint in Philadelphia reaches the right body only if it is filed with the right body. Because the city has separate bodies for police oversight, housing, ethics and licensing, plus state and federal agencies, this guide routes common complaints. It is civic information, not legal advice, and some matters have strict legal deadlines that only a lawyer can assess; see Legal Aid and Public Interest Law.

1 Before you file

  • Write down dates, times, places, names, badge or license numbers, and witnesses.
  • Keep copies of texts, photos, receipts, notices and letters.
  • For a service failure rather than a wrongdoing, start with How to Get Help From the City and Philly311.
  • Ask each agency what its own time limits are. Deadlines for lawsuits, discrimination charges and appeals can be short and are set by different laws.

2 Police complaints

Complaints about Philadelphia police officers can be made to the department's Internal Affairs Division or through the Citizens Police Oversight Commission (CPOC), an independent city body. As of 2026 CPOC lists an office at 2401 Walnut Street, 6th Floor, phone 215-685-0891 and email CPOC@phila.gov. CPOC staff review a complaint, speak with the complainant about the process, and refer it to Internal Affairs, then monitor and report on outcomes. Complaints can also be filed with the department directly. Discipline then follows the department's process and union contract rules, described in Police Accountability Systems and The FOP Contract and Police Discipline. For possible crimes by officers, the District Attorney's Office and the federal U.S. Attorney's Office have separate roles. Ask CPOC about any filing time limit that applies to your situation.[1]

3 Landlord and housing complaints

  • Unsafe or unlicensed conditions: report to 311; the Department of Licenses and Inspections inspects and can cite owners. Rental license rules are in Rental Licensing and Landlord-Tenant Law.
  • Unfair rental practices: the Fair Housing Commission, 601 Walnut Street, Suite 300 South, 215-686-4670, fairhousingcomm@phila.gov, handles tenant and landlord complaints under city rental law.
  • Discrimination: see the Commission on Human Relations below.
  • Eviction cases are in court, not an agency; see Eviction Diversion and Landlord-Tenant Court.
  • Public housing: start with the Philadelphia Housing Authority.
  • Legal help: the Philly Tenant Hotline at (267) 443-2500, Community Legal Services (see its website for current intake numbers) and groups in Tenant and Housing Advocacy Groups.

New tenant protections are summarized in Safe and Healthy Homes Act.

4 City worker complaints

For fraud, waste, abuse or misconduct by city employees, the Office of the Inspector General (215-686-1770, online form, anonymous or confidential reports accepted) investigates; the City Controller runs a fraud hotline (215-686-3804). Ethics-law concerns, such as conflicts of interest or gifts, go to the Board of Ethics. Rude or slow service by an employee is best raised first with the department's supervisor and 311. Employees with workplace grievances use human resources and Civil Service channels. Detail is in How to Report Corruption or Misconduct.

5 Contractor complaints

Report an unlicensed contractor or unpermitted work to 311, then send the case number and address to the L&I address listed on phila.gov. L&I does not resolve contractor fraud, breach of contract or warranty disputes; for those the city points residents to the District Attorney, the Pennsylvania Attorney General's Bureau of Consumer Protection, or a private attorney. Home improvement contractors must register with the Attorney General (1-888-520-6680). Complaints about contractors on city projects, such as wage or diversity violations, can go to the Office of Economic Opportunity hotline; see Understanding City Contracts and Bids.[2]

6 Other complaint routes

  • Discrimination in housing, jobs or public accommodations: Commission on Human Relations.
  • Wage theft, sick leave, and similar workplace laws: Office of Worker Protections.
  • Elections: City Commissioners and the District Attorney.
  • Open records denials: How to Request Public Records.
  • Court-related problems: First Judicial District.
  • Parking tickets: Philadelphia Parking Authority.

See also: Board of Ethics, Police Accountability Systems, Glossary

References

  1. City of Philadelphia, "File a complaint against a Philadelphia police officer," and CPOC complaint explainer, phila.gov/cpoc (accessed October 2026).
  2. City of Philadelphia, "Report an unlicensed contractor or unpermitted work," phila.gov (accessed October 2026).
  3. City of Philadelphia, "File a complaint about unfair rental practices," and "Report wrongdoing in city government," phila.gov (accessed October 2026).
  4. Philadelphia City Controller, "Fraud Reporting," controller.phila.gov/fraud-reporting.

How to Request Public Records

How to Request Public Records
TypeCitizen guide
Governing lawPennsylvania Right-to-Know Law (RTKL), 65 P.S. 67.101 et seq.
FormWritten request; statewide standard RTKL form accepted
City contactRightToKnowLaw@phila.gov (Law Department); 215-683-5227
Agency response5 business days (one extension up to 30 days)
Appeal deadline15 business days from denial
Appeal bodyPennsylvania Office of Open Records (most records)

A public records request in Philadelphia is a written request under the state's Right-to-Know Law (RTKL) for records held by a city agency. The RTKL presumes that records of a government agency are public unless an exemption applies. Background on the law is in Right-to-Know Law and Public Records. This guide explains how to file and follow up as of 2026; check phila.gov/open-records-policy for updates.[1]

1 Step 1: Check whether it is already online

Many records need no request. Property data, permits, violations, crime incidents, contracts and budget documents are published through the city's open data portals; see Open Data and Transparency Tools. Deeds, mortgages and other recorded documents come from the Department of Records. Court case files are held by the courts (First Judicial District), not under the RTKL's agency process. Council legislation is on the Legislative Information Center; see How a Bill Becomes Law in Philadelphia.

2 Step 2: Find the right Open Records Officer

Each city department, board or commission has an Open Records Officer listed on phila.gov/open-records-policy. If none is listed for the body you want, send the request to the Law Department (the Office of the City Solicitor), at RightToKnowLaw@phila.gov, and name the department. The city asks for one request per email. Separate offices follow their own policies: the Police Department and the District Attorney's Office publish their own open-records pages, and elected row offices (see Philadelphia Row Offices) and authorities such as the Philadelphia Housing Authority and School District have their own officers.

3 Step 3: Write the request

  1. Put it in writing (email, mail, or hand delivery). Oral and anonymous RTKL requests are not accepted by the city; the Pennsylvania standard RTKL request form is accepted.
  2. Include your name, a way to reach you, and how you want to receive records (email is usually cheapest).
  3. Be specific: the agency, a date range, the type of record, and the subject. "All emails between X and Y about Z from January to March 2026" is better than "everything about Z."
  4. Ask for existing records only; agencies do not have to create records or answer questions.
  5. Keep a copy and note the date sent. The clock starts when the Open Records Officer receives it.
  6. Do not include personal reasons; you do not need to explain why you want them.

4 Step 4: Deadlines and responses

The agency must respond within five business days. It may invoke one extension of up to 30 calendar days for specified reasons and must tell you in writing. Possible responses are: grant, partial grant with redactions, denial citing an exemption, or an extension. If the agency fails to respond in time, the request is "deemed denied," which you may appeal. Exemptions cover items such as personal security information, certain investigative records, some drafts and internal deliberations, and attorney-client privileged material. Meetings, as opposed to records, are governed by the Sunshine Act.[2]

5 Step 5: Fees

Agencies may charge reasonable duplication fees set by the state Office of Open Records and, for certified copies or enhanced access, additional fees. Police body-worn and audio recordings under Act 22 are subject to higher fees, reported as $125 per recording plus labor in the city's policy. Ask for an estimate before authorizing costs, and request electronic copies.

6 Step 6: Appeal a denial

You have 15 business days from the denial (or deemed denial) to appeal in writing. For most records the appeal goes to the Pennsylvania Office of Open Records in Harrisburg (333 Market Street, 16th Floor). For criminal investigative records held by the city's agencies the appeal goes to the District Attorney's Office. The appeals officer generally must decide within 30 days, after which parties may seek court review. The appeal should attach your request and the agency's response and explain why the records are public. Legal aid groups and press organizations can help; see Legal Aid and Public Interest Law and Local News Media in Philadelphia.

Records requests are a complement to complaints (How to File a Complaint) and oversight (How to Report Corruption or Misconduct); a request is also the main way to see contracts in detail (Understanding City Contracts and Bids).

See also: Open Data and Transparency Tools, Sunshine Act and Open Meetings, Glossary

References

  1. City of Philadelphia, "Open Records Policy," phila.gov/open-records-policy (accessed October 2026).
  2. Pennsylvania Office of Open Records, Right-to-Know Law guidance and standard request form, openrecords.pa.gov.
  3. Pennsylvania Right-to-Know Law, Act 3 of 2008, 65 P.S. 67.101 et seq.

How to Find Your Elected Officials

How to Find Your Elected Officials
TypeCitizen guide
City-wideMayor; Controller; District Attorney; Sheriff; City Commissioners; Register of Wills; at-large Council (7)
By addressCity Council district (10), state House and Senate, U.S. House, ward and division
Council PresidentKenyatta Johnson (as of 2026)
MayorCherelle Parker (since January 2024)
Voter lookupvote.pa.gov (PA Department of State)

Finding your elected officials in Philadelphia requires looking at several overlapping maps. Where you live determines your City Council district, your state House and Senate districts, your U.S. House district, and your ward and voting division. Others, such as the Mayor and District Attorney, represent the whole city. This guide shows how to look each one up as of October 2026. Office-holders change at elections, so confirm names on official sites.[1]

1 Step 1: Get your address and voter record

Use the Pennsylvania Department of State's voter services site (vote.pa.gov) to confirm your registration, polling place, and districts; see Voter Registration and Mail Voting. The City Commissioners maintain Philadelphia's voter rolls and divisions, and Philadelphia's open data and mapping tools (see Open Data and Transparency Tools) can show district boundaries for an address. Council district lines were redrawn after the 2020 Census; see Council Districts and Wards.

2 Step 2: City officials

  • Mayor: Cherelle Parker took office in January 2024; see Mayor of Philadelphia.
  • District Councilmember: one of ten, elected by district, handles constituent services and land-use influence (Councilmanic Prerogative).
  • Councilmembers at large: seven, elected city-wide; any of the seventeen may be contacted. Council is led by its President, Kenyatta Johnson as of 2026. See Philadelphia City Council.
  • City Controller: the city's elected auditor; see City Controller.

3 Step 3: Row officers and judges

Philadelphia is a city and county, so county-type offices are elected as well. They are described in Philadelphia Row Offices: the District Attorney, Sheriff, City Commissioners and Register of Wills. Judges of the Court of Common Pleas, Municipal Court, and statewide appellate courts appear on ballots too; see Court of Common Pleas and Municipal Court. Because several of these offices were on the 2025 ballot and terms differ, check each official site for the current holder.

4 Step 4: State and federal

State representatives and senators are found by address at legis.state.pa.us and palegis.us, which list district offices. Members of the U.S. House serving Philadelphia are found at house.gov through a ZIP code lookup; the two U.S. Senators represent all of Pennsylvania (senate.gov). The city's overall delegation is covered in Philadelphia Congressional and State Delegation. State and federal levels matter to city residents: see Pennsylvania State Government and Philadelphia and Federal Government and Philadelphia.

5 Step 5: Party officials

Each voting division elects Democratic or Republican committee people, who sit on ward committees; ward leaders are chosen by committee people. These are party positions rather than government offices but are influential in endorsements and Election Day operations. See Ward Leaders and Committeepersons, Democratic City Committee and Republican City Committee. Your division's committee people are listed with the City Commissioners.

6 Contacting them effectively

  • Use the district office for service problems and the Harrisburg or Washington office for legislation.
  • Be brief, include your address (offices serve constituents), and state one clear request.
  • Attend town halls and Council meetings: How to Testify at City Council.
  • For ordinary service problems start with How to Get Help From the City.
  • To run yourself, see Running for Office in Philadelphia.
  • For campaign money behind the officials, see Campaign Finance in Philadelphia.

See also: Elections in Philadelphia, Political Parties in Philadelphia, Mayors of Philadelphia Timeline

References

  1. Pennsylvania Department of State, voter services, vote.pa.gov (accessed October 2026).
  2. Philadelphia City Council, member directory, phlcouncil.com (accessed October 2026).
  3. Pennsylvania General Assembly, "Find your legislator," legis.state.pa.us (accessed October 2026).

How to Report Corruption or Misconduct

How to Report Corruption or Misconduct
TypeCitizen guide
City Inspector General215-686-1770; online form; anonymous or confidential reports
City Controller fraud hotline215-686-3804; online form
Board of Ethics215-686-9450
Contract complianceOEO Compliance Hotline, 215-683-1798
CriminalDistrict Attorney; U.S. Attorney (federal); FBI
Whistleblower protectionCity Executive Order 9-17 (employees and contractors)

Reporting corruption or misconduct in Philadelphia means choosing among several bodies with different powers. Some investigate and recommend discipline, some enforce the ethics code, some audit, and some prosecute. A report to the right body is more likely to lead to action. This guide describes the channels as of 2026; it does not assess any individual's guilt, and a report is an allegation to be investigated, not a finding. See also Political Corruption Cases in Philadelphia for history.[1]

1 Step 1: Identify the kind of problem

  • Fraud, waste, abuse, mismanagement of city funds, employee misconduct: inspector general or controller.
  • Conflicts of interest, gifts, campaign-finance and political-activity violations: ethics board.
  • Bribery, extortion, theft or other crimes: law enforcement.
  • Police conduct: Citizens Police Oversight Commission; see How to File a Complaint.
  • Contract wage or diversity noncompliance: Office of Economic Opportunity.

2 Step 2: Choose the body

  • Office of the Inspector General (mayoral appointee): receives reports of wrongdoing by city employees, officials, contractors and vendors by phone (215-686-1770) or online form. It can refer matters to prosecutors. The School District has a separate inspector general.
  • City Controller (elected): audits, and runs a Fraud Hotline (215-686-3804) and online form for suspected misuse of city resources by an employee, contractor or vendor.
  • Board of Ethics: administers and enforces the city's ethics, campaign-finance and lobbying laws; it also gives confidential advice to officials and employees (215-686-9450). See Conflicts of Interest and Pay-to-Play and Campaign Finance in Philadelphia.
  • District Attorney: state criminal law prosecutions, including public corruption, within Philadelphia.
  • U.S. Attorney's Office and the FBI: federal crimes, such as bribery involving federal funds, which have produced many Philadelphia cases.
  • Office of Economic Opportunity Compliance Hotline (215-683-1798, 24 hours, free and anonymous): contract compliance; see Understanding City Contracts and Bids.
  • Housing authority and other authorities have their own oversight; see Philadelphia Housing Authority.

If unsure, report to the Inspector General, which routes matters it does not handle.

3 Step 3: Prepare your report

  • Say who, what, when, where, and how you know. Distinguish what you saw from what you heard.
  • Name the department, contract or program and any amounts or dates.
  • Note documents, emails, or witnesses, and where they are. Do not take records you are not authorized to have; ask the agency how to submit evidence.
  • Use public records to corroborate: How to Request Public Records.
  • Stick to facts and avoid conclusions about motive.

4 Step 4: Anonymity and retaliation

The city lets reporters choose: anonymous (no name, so the office cannot contact you) or confidential (name known only inside the Inspector General's office). Giving a name usually helps investigators ask follow-up questions. City employees and contractors who report wrongdoing in good faith are protected under Executive Order 9-17; tell the Inspector General at the time of reporting if you fear retaliation, and file a separate whistleblower retaliation complaint if it occurs. City workers may also have rights through union contracts and the Civil Service Commission. For legal advice on retaliation, consult an attorney; see Legal Aid and Public Interest Law.[2]

5 Step 5: After you report

Investigations can take months or years, and agencies often cannot discuss them. Outcomes may include no action, administrative discipline, referral for prosecution, contract termination, or published audit and enforcement results. Board of Ethics settlements and Controller reports are public. Journalists sometimes pursue tips independently; see Local News Media in Philadelphia, and good-government groups in Good Government Groups.

6 Other settings

Misconduct in other systems goes elsewhere: courts and judges to the Pennsylvania Judicial Conduct Board; lawyers to the Disciplinary Board of the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania; state officials to the state Attorney General or State Ethics Commission; unions to the U.S. Department of Labor (see Organized Labor in Philadelphia). Voting problems go to the City Commissioners and the District Attorney.

See also: Police Accountability Systems, Sunshine Act and Open Meetings, Good Government Groups

References

  1. City of Philadelphia, "Report wrongdoing in city government," phila.gov/services/ethics-transparency (accessed October 2026).
  2. Philadelphia Office of the Inspector General, Integrity Works and Executive Order 9-17, phila.gov (accessed October 2026).
  3. Philadelphia City Controller, "Fraud Reporting," controller.phila.gov/fraud-reporting.
  4. City of Philadelphia, "Report possible fraud, waste, or other issues on contracts," phila.gov (accessed October 2026).

How to Read the City Budget

How to Read the City Budget
TypeCitizen guide
Fiscal yearJuly 1 to June 30 (FY2027 began July 1, 2026)
FY2027 operating budgetRoughly $7 billion; the Mayor proposed $6.97 billion on March 12, 2026 and Council approved the budget on June 11, 2026
Key documentsBudget in Brief; budget detail; Five Year Plan; capital program
Decision makersMayor proposes; City Council amends and adopts
Fiscal oversightPICA; City Controller

Reading the city budget starts with knowing which documents exist and what each answers. Philadelphia's budget covers city and county functions in one plan. In 2026, the Mayor presented a $6.97 billion fiscal year 2027 budget and five-year plan to Council on March 12, and Council approved the FY2027 operating and capital budgets on June 11, a total the Northeast Times reported as about $7 billion; the city's own adopted "Budget in Brief" is the authoritative source for exact totals. The process is explained in Philadelphia City Budget Process; this guide is the practical companion.[1]

1 Step 1: Learn the calendar

The fiscal year runs July 1 to June 30. The Mayor submits a proposed budget and five-year plan to Council in March (the FY2027 proposal was presented on March 12, 2026). Council's committees hold department-by-department hearings in spring, where department heads testify. Council can amend the budget and must adopt it by June so the new year can start July 1. Council cannot generally add spending beyond projected revenues. Tax changes in the budget require separate Council bills; the FY2027 debate included proposals by the Mayor that Council did not adopt, per press reports. See Philadelphia City Council and Philadelphia Taxes.

2 Step 2: Know the documents

  • Budget in Brief: a short summary of revenues, spending by department, and priorities; start here.
  • Budget detail: department-level pages of spending by class (personal services, contracts, materials) and positions; Council also posts department detail from each hearing on phlcouncil.com.
  • Five Year Plan: multi-year projections the state-created PICA reviews.
  • Capital budget and program: the six-year plan for buildings, streets, and equipment financed largely by bonds.
  • Controller reports: the City Controller issues budget reviews and the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report.
  • Open data: spending and contract datasets; see Open Data and Transparency Tools.

Most are published by the Finance Department and its Budget Office on phila.gov.[2]

3 Step 3: Follow revenue

The General Fund is the main operating fund. Its largest sources are tax revenues, especially the wage and earnings tax, real estate tax, business taxes and the sales tax; other sources are state and federal aid, and fees. Property tax revenue depends on assessed values set by the Office of Property Assessment and collected by the Revenue Department. Tax breaks, such as those in Tax Abatement and Development Incentives, reduce revenue and are described in tax-expenditure reports. Ask: is a revenue line one-time or recurring? Is it dependent on state or federal decisions?

4 Step 4: Follow spending

Spending is grouped by department and by object class. Look at three things: the size of the department, the share going to personnel (salaries and benefits, tied to union contracts), and how much goes to pensions and debt service, which are fixed costs; see Board of Pensions and Retirement. Public safety departments, such as the Police Department, Fire Department and Department of Prisons, together account for a very large share of General Fund personnel costs. Compare the proposed budget with the prior year's adopted budget and with year-end actuals, because departments often differ from their budgets. Labor settlements, such as the 2025 DC 33 strike outcome, shape later years.

5 Step 5: Capital budget and Five Year Plan

The capital budget funds long-lived projects, with items listed by department and funding source (city bonds, state, federal, private). The Five Year Plan shows whether projected balances turn negative in later years; PICA and rating agencies watch these. A small fund balance means less cushion against recessions or cuts in federal aid. The Finance Department manages bond issuance, and the City Treasurer handles cash.

6 Step 6: Get involved

  • Read the Council hearing schedule and sign up to speak: How to Testify at City Council.
  • Ask your district member which amendments are being considered: How to Find Your Elected Officials.
  • Request budget details not published: How to Request Public Records.
  • Follow contracts: Understanding City Contracts and Bids.
  • Join budget-watch groups: Good Government Groups.

See also: Finance Department, Philadelphia City Budget Process, Glossary

References

  1. City of Philadelphia, "FY2027 Budget in Brief" (as adopted by Council, June 2026), phila.gov.
  2. City of Philadelphia, "FY27-31 Five Year Plan per Council Approved Budget," phila.gov (July 2026).
  3. Philadelphia City Council, "Council approved the Fiscal Year 2027 operating and capital budgets on Thursday, June 11," phlcouncil.com.
  4. Northeast Times, "City Council approves $7 billion budget while rejecting mayor's tax proposals," June 12, 2026.

How to Organize a Block or Neighborhood Group

How to Organize a Block or Neighborhood Group
TypeCitizen guide
Smallest unitBlock group / block captain
Larger unitCivic association; Registered Community Organization (RCO)
City contact311; district Council office; Philly311 for service requests
Land-use roleRCOs get notice and meet with zoning applicants
RelatedCommunity development corporations, ward committees

Organizing a block or neighborhood group in Philadelphia means bringing neighbors together to solve shared problems and to speak to government with one voice. Groups range from informal block captain networks to incorporated civic associations. They matter because city agencies, Council offices and developers respond to organized, documented, repeated requests. This guide is general and not legal advice.[1]

1 Step 1: Start with a specific issue

People join for concrete problems: a vacant lot, trash and dumping, speeding, a proposed development, a landlord's building, or a missing streetlight. Pick one or two winnable goals. Document them with photos, dates and 311 numbers (Philly311), as in How to Get Help From the City. Many groups also run cleanups, street parties and tool-sharing, which keep members engaged between crises.

2 Step 2: Map and recruit neighbors

  • Define the area, such as one block, a few blocks, or a neighborhood within a council district and ward.
  • Knock on doors, leave flyers, and collect names, addresses and preferred contacts (with permission).
  • Include renters, older residents and those who speak other languages; see Office of Immigrant Affairs for language resources.
  • Recruit a few leaders so the work is shared.
  • Set up a simple list, group chat or newsletter.

3 Step 3: Hold the first meeting

Meet somewhere accessible: a library branch (Free Library of Philadelphia), recreation center (Parks and Recreation), place of worship (see Faith Communities and Black Clergy) or a porch. Publicize the date a week ahead. Use an agenda: introductions, the problem, options, next steps, and who does what. Take notes and share them. Agree how decisions are made and keep meetings short and regular. Hostile or private disputes between neighbors are not group business.

4 Step 4: Connect to the city

  • Council office: invite your district member's staff; see How to Find Your Elected Officials.
  • Police and public safety: districts hold community meetings; see Philadelphia Police Department and Office of Violence Prevention.
  • Streets and cleaning: Streets Department; vacant land via the Land Bank.
  • Housing problems: Licenses and Inspections and Fair Housing Commission.
  • Planning and development: Department of Planning and Development.
  • Public meetings: testify together; How to Testify at City Council.

Track every contact in a shared log. If requests stall, escalate as in How to File a Complaint, or ask for documents using How to Request Public Records.

5 Step 5: Formalize if needed

Many groups stay informal. Formalizing helps when you want a bank account, grants, insurance, or RCO status. Options include incorporating as a Pennsylvania nonprofit and applying for IRS tax-exempt status, or using a fiscal sponsor (an established nonprofit that receives funds on your behalf). Adopt simple bylaws covering membership, officers, elections, finances, and conflicts of interest. Look for support from Civic and Neighborhood Associations, Community Development Corporations and philanthropy. For tenant organizing, see Tenant and Housing Advocacy Groups.

6 Land use and zoning

The city's zoning process gives special roles to Registered Community Organizations (RCOs): applicants for certain zoning approvals must notify and meet with the RCO whose boundaries cover the property, and RCOs may appear before the Zoning Board of Adjustment. To become an RCO a group must apply to the city and meet the requirements in the Zoning Code, including open meetings and a defined boundary; check the City Planning Commission's current rules. RCOs are sometimes criticized when meetings are unrepresentative, so open outreach and transparent votes matter; see also Councilmanic Prerogative and Developers and the Real Estate Lobby.

See also: Philadelphia Neighborhoods Guide, Progressive and Grassroots Politics, Ward Leaders and Committeepersons

References

  1. City of Philadelphia, Philly311 and Department of Planning and Development neighborhood resources, phila.gov (accessed October 2026).
  2. Philadelphia City Planning Commission, Registered Community Organization information, phila.gov/departments/philadelphia-city-planning-commission (accessed October 2026).
  3. Philadelphia Zoning Code, Title 14, Philadelphia Code, library.amlegal.com.

Understanding City Contracts and Bids

Understanding City Contracts and Bids
TypeCitizen guide
Lead agencyProcurement Department
Bid portalPHLContracts (phila.gov Contracts Hub)
Formal bidsSealed competitive bids at about $34,000 or more (per city)
Informal buysOver $500 and under $34,000 (small order purchases)
Diversity goal35% of for-profit contract dollars to M/W/DSBEs (city goal)
Compliance hotlineOEO, 215-683-1798

City contracts are how Philadelphia converts budget dollars into goods, services and construction, from road paving and software to legal services and food for shelters. The rules aim at competition, price, quality, fairness and local economic opportunity. This guide explains the system as of 2026 for residents, vendors and watchdogs. Thresholds and goals can change; confirm on phila.gov.[1]

1 Who does what

The Procurement Department runs bidding and contracting for supplies, equipment and services. Public works (construction) contracts are managed with the Department of Public Property and agencies such as the Streets Department and Water Department; see Department of Public Property. The Law Department reviews contracts as to form. The Office of Economic Opportunity sets and monitors participation goals for minority-, woman- and disabled-owned businesses. The Finance Department and City Controller handle payment authorization and audits. Authorities such as PHA, SEPTA, the School District and PIDC have their own procurement.

2 Types of contracts

  • Public works: construction and repair, usually requiring prevailing wages, bonds and insurance; see Prevailing Wage and Project Labor Agreements.
  • Supplies, equipment and non-professional services: competitively bid.
  • Professional services: legal, engineering, consulting; typically selected by qualifications through a request for proposals (RFP) rather than lowest price, with a selection committee.
  • Small purchases: informal quotes below the formal threshold.
  • Sole-source or emergency contracts: allowed in limited circumstances with justification; these draw the most scrutiny.
  • Grants and leases are different instruments but also public money; see Department of Public Property.

3 How a competitive bid works

  1. The department defines needs and the Procurement Department posts an invitation for bids on PHLContracts.
  2. Vendors register an account, complete the required disclosures and consent agreements, and submit sealed bids by the closing date. Requirements include insurance, bonds or bid security where applicable, wage and labor compliance, and city contract terms.
  3. Bids are opened, and for formal bids the contract goes to the lowest responsive and responsible bidder (not simply the cheapest if the bidder is unqualified or the bid is non-compliant).
  4. For RFPs, evaluators score technical and cost proposals, interview finalists and recommend an award.
  5. The contract is executed after legal review and, where required, ordinance authority or board approval. Formal contracts at or above $34,000 are the competitive sealed bid category per city guidance.
  6. Payments follow vouchers and performance, with oversight from the Controller.

4 Diversity, local preference, and wages

The city has a stated goal of directing at least 35 percent of for-profit contract dollars to minority-, woman- and disabled-owned business enterprises (M/W/DSBEs), which register with the Office of Economic Opportunity. Bidders must submit participation plans, and the city may give consideration to Local Business Entities under local bidding preference regulations. Compliance is monitored; the OEO Compliance Hotline (215-683-1798, free and anonymous, 24 hours) takes reports of non-compliance. Critics and audits have at times questioned how well goals are met, and the Controller and press have reported on them; evaluate such claims from the primary reports. Workers on city projects may be covered by prevailing wage and the city's labor standards. See Office of Worker Protections and Philadelphia Building and Construction Trades Council.[2]

5 Approvals and money

Contracts come from budgeted funds; see How to Read the City Budget. Large or long-term arrangements, land sales and some development deals require ordinances passed by City Council (see How a Bill Becomes Law in Philadelphia). Pay-to-play restrictions limit contributions by contractors; see Conflicts of Interest and Pay-to-Play and Campaign Finance in Philadelphia. Employees and officials are subject to the ethics code enforced by the Board of Ethics.

6 How residents can follow and report

  • Search open bids and awards on PHLContracts and the city's open data portal: Open Data and Transparency Tools.
  • Read Council ordinance texts and hearing records for large contracts.
  • Request contract documents, scoring sheets and invoices: How to Request Public Records.
  • Report suspected fraud or waste to the Inspector General or Controller: How to Report Corruption or Misconduct.
  • Small businesses seeking work should contact the Procurement Department, OEO and the Commerce Department.

See also: Procurement Department, Commerce Department, Glossary

References

  1. City of Philadelphia, "Bid on a supplies, equipment and non-professional services contract" and "Bid on a public works contract," phila.gov/services/business-self-employment (accessed October 2026).
  2. City of Philadelphia, Procurement Department, "Types of contracts," and Office of Economic Opportunity compliance hotline, phila.gov (accessed October 2026).
  3. Philadelphia Home Rule Charter, provisions on the Procurement Department and on competitive bidding for city contracts, as published at library.amlegal.com; City of Philadelphia, "Bid on a supplies, equipment and non-professional services contract" (formal bids at $34,000 or more; informal purchases over $500 and under $34,000), phila.gov.
